Ill 1 BILL MINES.! I A News Man Spends a Few Hours Sight Seeing. Going Down the Shaft. The Tunnel. ???? FOREMAN HUNTER AS GUIDE. Who lias not hoard of the wonderful; Trcadwell mines? The greatest, mine? the largest stamp mill in the world. Ono pf the first things the News man j thought of after locating at Douglas j City was a trip to Treadwell, not to go and look at the buildings and see the ! stamps pound the ore so fine that it j looks like buckwheat flour, but to go down into the bowols of old mother j earth and follow the ore until it passes through the various stages and becomes; a thing of real value. Our wishes were made known to Foreman Hunter and in part our desire was realized 011 last Saturduy; leaving ; a portion of our sight seeing for some future time. Wo met Mr. Qonter at. the shaft about ten oclock in the fore- | . ii 1 _r ii.? 1

i noon ana me engineer ui rue uui?ui j engines stopped one of the skips and : wo climbed on. We stood on the edge ! of the box and were let down so easily I ! and gently that it remiudcd us of a I ; beautiful dream. Wo made our land ! ing on the first level, which is down i 110 feet below the surface. We were j ; each provided with a candle, for the' electric light is not in all parts of the j many tunnels through which we | passed. At tho place where we landed are tiu- j 1 merous iron tracks on which the ore is conveyed on cars to a bin some fifty j feet in depth and. which holds 200 tons ! of ore. We started out toward tho l end of the tunnel, which has a high! ceiling and is wide enough for a team and wagon to travel on. Along either 1 j side are numerous chutes that are! ; filled with ore, and Manager Hunter, iuformed us that if tho blasting were J | stopped, the ore constantly on hand j would be sufficient to run the mill for at least three months. Wo soon reach ed two men who were running a drill with compressed air. They had a wall | pretty well peforated. but were still j i drilling in more holes. Two feet was j the depth of the holes they made. .. J

"How much ore will you blow our of i that place?" asked the scribe, j "About thirty tons," was the reply, j "And how far do you go away when ; the discharge takes place?" asked the j News man. "Oh, around the corner a little ways," was the reply. Our judgment was that we would j prefer to be away a half a mile and we haven't changed our mind yet on the | subject. We followed that tunnel some four i hundred feet until wo came to a hole j that Manager Hunter told us was 100 I feet deep. It extended clear across the tunnel and we had no desire to go any ; further, and Mr. Hunter no doubt ; viewed the situation in the same light: 1 we did, for we turned and cut across \ into another tunnel that is still longer and where the cross sections are as nu- i merous. We traveled over 1100 feet j through the tunnel, and think of it, from the surface down hundreds ot feet through solid ore. This vein is more than 400 feet wide, but just how far it extends in downward course, no | one knows, bnt for more than 500 feet: is known to a certainty. Six or seven little cars are constantly I running from the chutes down to where the ore is hauled up to the crusher, which we will see later on. The load- j ing of these cars is done by a man who raises tho trap door to the mouth of I tho chute. The cars are at present run by hand to the place where the ore is ; dumped into the big bin before men-; tioned, but the company is arranging to run these cars by electricity. Here : the man oowor stops short. From

; there the ore is all handled by ma- i chinery, and how much do you think | the stamps will use in a day? 250 tons, i i Just think of it, 250 tons of ore is; I 1 J mined, crushed and ground as fine as : Hour every twenty-four hours. i We wandered around the caverns for j some time and returned to the shaft: i I : and soon we were up in the hoisting; engine rooms and from there we climbed > up flights of stairs until we reached j the room in which two crushers get in their awful work. We expected to find a mill, a great big strong iron mill! built on the same principle of those , i i

little domestic machines we grind, or used to grind coffee in, and we thought the teeth would be even larg er than a Tacoma girl's foot, but the crusher is a most harmless looking ma chine, and just the opposite of what we expected to see. In the center of the room are two concave disks or hoppers we should probably cell them. The ore comos down an incline chute from the hoisting boxes where thoy are automatically emptied. In the center of the disk is a round opening some three feet wide, and in the center of this opening, a little lower down is a round cylinder two or three feet long that revolves and moves laterally at the same time. The ore falls between this disk and the basin iu which it is set and tho disk just crushes it into small pieces, and when broken to a cer tain size it drops down into a bin below. Two men are in tho crusher room to keep tho large pieces of ore from clog ging the hopper. The ore as it comes down the chute is sometimes in large pieces and those employed at the crusher are constantly on the watch to keep out of the course of the heavy

We next go down several flights of 6tairs into the room whero the stamps are running. Have you ever been in a stamp mill ? If you haven't, you never beard any noise. You may think you havo but my friend you are mistaken. This mill has 240 stamps, all going at the same time. Talking in there is never thought of. Stampmill language is by means of signs. We were only too glad when Fore man Hunter conducted us into a side room, whero we could think and talk. It proved to be the office of Mr. Win. M.Hale, foreman of the stamp mill, who is a genial, pleasant geutloman. Wo were also pleased to moet Mr. Nick King who is employed in the amalga mating department. Here wo bade Foreman Hunter goodbye for the duy. There is much to be seen and a great deal to be said as we follow the course of the precious metal at the Tread well and a future issue will contain more upon this subject. Saturday was a cold dreary day and our stay at the mines was limited. The new stamp mill which is neariug completion is larger than the one we visited and will contain 300stamps, but we did not go into the building. We also made no mention of the tunnels one hundred feet below the one we wore in, the "glory hole" and the many other places of interest. When ono considers the magnitude of the Treadwell mines, ono naturally wonders what master mind is superin tendent of this groat plant and others, as well as the writer, will be surprised to know that a young man, less than forty years of age, has charge of these works and successfully conducts them ?an enterprise that employs some 700 men?included in which is also ono of the greatest general stores in Alaska, and equal to those on the Pacific coast. The name of this man is J. P. Corbus.

piCWUO UL U1U. From the crusher room we go just below, where we see a train of small cars backing up under the chute that holds the crushed ore. Thore are five or six of the cars to which is attached the cutest little engine you ever saw. It is a little bit of a thing, not over three or four feet high, and is minus a cab and tender. One man runs this little locomotive. The diminutive size of the machine makes the man that runs it look several sizes larger than the ordinary man, in fact we thought he must bo betwoon sevou and ten feot tall. We didn't get the best kind of a look at him, but we thought he rode the engine liko the girls did the old gray mare, when the writer was a boy, ?a-straddlo, but we might have been mistaken. When the cars are loaded the litilo engine pulls them into the mill where they empty into bins far above the stamps,into which it is fed automati cally.

A Good Chicken Story. A story is going the rounds of the papers about a man who tried the ex periment of mixing sawdust with his chicken feed. The results were so sat isfactory that he discontinued the uso of meal altogether and fed his chickens entirely on sawdust. Soon after adopt ing the scheme he set a hen with fif teen eggs. She brought off thirteen chicks. Twelve of them had wooden legs and the thirteenth was e wood pecker. Subscribe for the News. / m

jThe Northland The Latest News, from Reliable Sources, Concerning the Great North, Condensed. ; Information for Everybody. . Valdez has a lumber famine. A fish cannery is being built at Yak utat. Over 3500 people have left Seattle for Nome this spring. The White Horse Star has become a j tri-weekly publication. The Methodists are endeavoring to organize at White Horse. The miners of the Klondike are tak | ing steps to organize a union. Packing from Circle City to the Tan ana pays at the rate of $1 per pound. Musicians of White Horse propose to open a concert hall if a license can be j secured. i A $1020 nugget was found on No. 2,! Eldorado, a claim owned by Prank \ Phiscator.

Charles Hinchcliff, a cook oil the steamer Lear, was drowned at Dawson on June 5th. : Up to June 15th 57 vessels of all de j scriptions had cleared from Sound j points for Nome. | A rich placer strike is reported from | Alder creek, a pup of Nome creek, in the Tanana district. W. I. Warner has undertaken the contract of building a railroad from j Yakutat to Dry Bay. > | June 5th there was said to be $7,500, 000 on deposit in Dawson banks from the spring clean-up. W.T. Uiff, a sawmill man of Skag way, formerly of Douglas, died at ; Skagway last week. r j , A $22 nugget of curious shape was J picked up on No. 4 below discovery on Eureka creek, Klondike. The steamer Rock Island left Daw-1 i! son May 27th with passengers and 1 freight for the Koyukuk. I

The House committee on rivers and ! harbors is expected to visit Alaska j ! about the middle of next month. t It is believed that it will be July 10 before the first steamer from St. Mi chael will be able to reach Dawson. Victorian Day at Dawson was cele brated with great pomp and splendor, Americans and British alike participat ing. New placer discoveries are reported from Dicer and Sylvia creeks, in the Big Salmon district, near Livingstone creek. Martin Clair, a miner in the employ i of the McDonald Bonanza Klondike j | company, was found dead at the foot | of a twenty-five foot shaft, where he i had evidently been for hours.

The Yukon telegraph line from Port I Simpson up the Skeena river is com pleted and the first message was sent June 15th. The discovery of a quartz ledge 300 feet wide is reported from Livingstone creek, between the Hootalinqua and Big Salmon. A writer to the Port Townsond Lead- i er profanely remarks that "Christiani-j ty and civilization are raising hell with i the natives at Yakutat." Gold to the value of $2000 was taken from the office of Crown Mining In spector Robinson at Grand Forks, Klondike, May 30th. No clue. Eighty witnesses for the Crown have been summoned to Dawson to testify in the O'Brien murder trial. O'Brien has elected to conduct his own case. The Flora made a record-breaking trip to Dawson. She left White Horse : early Tuesday morning, the 11th, and : arrived at Dawson on the evening of the 12th. The bark Shirley, in tow of the tug Wallowa, sailed from Seattle June 16th for Nome. She carried 1335 head of live stock and 1500 tons of general mer chandise.

The miners of Atliu have formed a union which will be a branch of the Western Federation of Miners. The ! scale of wages adopted for one day's work of 10 hours was So. The remains of Randolph Percival, I the 5-year old child of Prof, and Mrs. i T. S. Lippy*, who died at Forty Mile in I August, 189(5, will be disinterred and taken to Seattle for burial. According to a late Ottawa dispatch ' Mr. George Taylor of Bothwell, Ont., j has been appointed police magistrate! for the Southern part of the Yukon Territory, with headquarters at White Horse. Another discovery of gold is reported in the beach sands at Yakutat and con siderable excitement has been occa sioned in that vicinity thereby. There was an excitement there of the same nature in 1887. The Mounted Police service at Daw son will require 800 cords of wood, and the White Horse contingent 500 cords, to keep them warm next winter. Sealed bids were advertised for and the con tracts were awarded the 22nd inst.

Milo Kelly, of Douglas, who located j discovery on Summit creek in the Big Salmon district, believes pay follows along the left limit in both hillsides and creek and will pay particular at tention to that side of the stream this season. Reports from Copper river bring in telligence of a strike on Excelsior j creek, a branch of the Gokona. Water stopped the work at the depth of seven feet.. The gold was very evenly dis tributed throughout this depth, but no great values were found to the pan. Quite a rush from the neighboring camps has been made to the Gokona and its branches as a result of this strike. The locality is about 215 miles north of Valdez and about 25 from the Slate creek diggings.

Ketchikan has a new watchmaker and jeweler. New Town at Ketchikan has a new meat market. A 1'2-foot shark wa9 captured at Skag way Oct. 6th. Olympic flour sells at S8 per sack at Council City.

Co. boats will carry mail after Oct. 15th. i Slush began to run in the Copper I river on Sept. 26th. Sitka merchants are kicking over poor freight service. ? - - ? ? i - _ i- _ .1 j

Moosemeat sold at Slate creek last season for $1 per pound. The Ketchikan mining district em braces 7200 square miles.

PASSING Kasaan Bay on Prince of Wales ] Island will ever be known as the home of the gigantic totemic columns of Alaska. Although totem poles are found from Puget Sound to Bering Straights no where did the people give as much attention to th?m as in the Hydah country.

In the fall of 1901 Chief San - I - Haat of the Hydahs presented to the U. S. Government an old house belonging to his family and a large war canoe. It is to b< remembered that the old Alaskan house was built of hewn planks and that the large totem pole was set against the center of the front of the house, the door being a hole through the lower end of the pole. The four tK)les that held up the corners of the roof were carved on the inside and served as interior decorations. The house was to be removed to Sitka by the U. S. R. M. C. Rush but the elements had so thoroughly done their work that only the five carved poles of the house would stand transporting. These were brought to Sitka and after being repaired and painted were erect ed in Indian River Park on the supposed site of the Kakesette fort where Kathlean and his men made their last stand against Baranoff and his fleet of Russian Gunboats in 1804.
The pole3 stand in the same position they occupied in the house and the war canoe former ly stood near them. The tall pole is sixty feet hiph and three feet

wide. The canoe was forty seven feet long with a six foot beam. These relics will soon exist only in history. The old canoe is gone, a few pieces of rotting wood represent the once proud ship of war. The pole that records the glory of the ancient Hydah is bowing before the ancient enemy of its original owner. San-I-Haat is the Hydah name for the south-east wind and was taken in revenge by this

chief because this wind had wrecked his canoe on the shore of Kasaan Bay. It is only a question of time when this same south east wind will revenge its self by laying low the totem of San I-Haat. As each year marks the passing of an ancient landmark likewise it marks one more step toward Christian civilization among the people. This year is no exception. The people are in the midst of a great struggle
THE ALASKA DAILY EMPIRE VOL. 1. NO. 50. JUNEAU, ALASKA, THURSDAY, JANUARY 2, 1913. PRICE TEN CENTS

Gov. and Mrs. Clark were at homo to the public yesterday afternoon be tween the hours of three to five, the occasion being the customary recep tion held on New Year's Day. The receptiou was held iu the new Gov ernor's House, which is the official residence of the governor. A goodly number from Juneau, Douglas and Treadwell availed them selves of the opportunity to call and pay their respects to Alaska's chief executive. Between the hours men tioned the halls, drawing room, library and dining room were thronged with pioplc who had come to exchange the season's greetings with Governor and Mrs. Clark. Light refreshments were served by Miss Green, a charming young lady, of Washington, D. C., assisted by a bevy of pretty Juneau and Douglas young ladies. On this occasion the doors of the new building were thrown open for the first time. Many had looked for ward 'o the pleasure of viewing the interior of the splendid edifice. The perfect harmony, and substantial sim plicity of the finish called forth many admiring remarks. The Building. The Governor's House is a two und -a-haif story frame structure, built over a full-sized cellar on con crete walls. The general dimensions are approximately 58 by GO feet. The principal exposure is ou the south and east, commanding a full view of the southern end of Gastiueau Chan nel. as well as Douglus and Treadwell towns. In order that light and out look might not be impaired from that side, no entrance or hallway was pn> vided. but the southern exposure equipped with a broad terrace extend ing the full length of the building, covered in the center to a height of two stories by a pillared porch or balcony. Then entrance is on the northeast side, and is covered with a smaller pillared porch, approached by concrete semi-circular driveway and sidewalk and stone steps.

The American colonial type of ar chitecture characterizes both the ex terior and the interior construction, the colonial expression being carried out to several of the smallest details! in inside finishing, furnishing and decoration. A liberal interpretation, however, of the New England colon ial motive was executed: the build ing is not a pure example of the type referred to. The basement of the new house contains ample storage and fuel' rooms and a well-equipped laundry, | and the basement rooms are well light ed by several half-length windows. The first floor is divided into six prin cipal apartments, as follows: recep tion hall, drawing room, library, din ing room, office, and kitchen. There are also two large pantries, and a back hall: while a vestibule and stair hall are situated between the front entrance and the main reception hall. Each of the four principal rooms on the first floor has a fire-place. A high wainscot in wood panels, and a beam ceiling are the striking features of the reception hall and the dining room. A lower panelled wainscot is shown in drawing room and library. The woodwork throughout the entire house is painted uniformly in old ivory, var iations in color depending entirely upon mural tints, draperies and up holsteries Furnishings of Principel Rooms. The drawing room draperies are of yellow figured silk, while the side walls are in light green. This apart ment. which is 20 by 30 feet in size is finished and furnished for use as a music hall or ball room, among the furnishings being a small grand piano

and a number of Austrian bentwood chairs. The handsome fireplace man tel is decorated with a wood carving of the seal of the Territory of Alas ka. The library or living room is furn ished iu crimson damask overstuffed chairs and divan, with mahogany ta ble and reading lamp. The small con servatory is seen from this room as well as from the dining room through large glass doors. The dining room, which is 18 by 2t> feet in general dimesnions, is furn ished with Sheraton table, chairs, side board and serving table. The window and door draperies are in old blue and a cushioned window-seat extends around the entire west side of the room. The lighting fixtures not only ou this floor but throughout the build ing are artistic in design, conforming strictly to the generally colonial treat ment of the house and furnishings. A small office is situated in the northeast corner of the building on this floor, the furniture being up holstered in brown leather, the win dow draperies being also in brown. Upper Floors. The second floor contains four large bedrooms, a sewing room, and three bath rooms. All the rooms on this floor are entered from a spacious hall which is reached by a handsome main stairway from the first floor. The third floor Is chiefly devoted to servants' quarters. The billiard room on this floor which was provided in the original plans is left uncompleted for the present lack of funds. The whole buildings is heated by steam and lighted by electricty, the electric wires being in all cases en Closed in iron conduits or pipes bur ied in the walls. Practically Completed.

The building is substantially com plete, but a few details of Interior fin ish, furniture and decorations are still lacking. The roof cannot be painted until spring, and a few other items of outside work, including grad ing the grounds, must be deferred un til more favorable weather comes. The work of two or three days by carpen ters and painters is still required on the interior, and a few articles of furniture remain to be supplied within the next week. The new building, however, pre sents a habitable appearance. The construction of the house was author ized in the public building act of 1910, when Governor Clarke made urgent representations to the President and to Congress that permanent and suit able buildings should be provided for the resindence and for government offices in Juneau. The appropriation was $40,000, which sum was to include furnishings. Why "The Governor's House." Governor Clark says that personal | Iv he does not believe that the new otticial residence should be known as executive mansion, but simply as "Governor's House." A mansion, strictly speaking, cannot be "execu tive." "There is every consideration of good taste in favor of the simple term Governor's House," said the Gov ernor. "and moreover, this is the term of common parlance. Soon after Mr. Roosevelt was elevated to the presi dency he must have has this consid eration in mind for he Immediately changed the name of the President's residence from 'executive mansion,' to 'The White House.' He argned that the latter term was much simpler as well as really more dignified and in better taste. Whatever justifica tion there may be for the term 'exec utive mansion' seems to rest rather upon hackneyed usuage than upon good grammar or common sense."

DEMOCRATS BRING GOOD TIMES John Keller, of the Skagway Alas kan, is aboard the Princess May en route to his home from an extended visit throughout the East. Mr. Keller says that times are al ready getting better all over the coun try and that everybody is hopeful and cheerful over the outlook for the fu ture on account of the splendid Demo cratic victory. President-elect Wilson has inspired the greatest confidence in the people generally and the changes politically are having a salu tary effect?at least such is the case from Mr. Keller's point of view. MOOSE MASQUERADE A GRAND SUCCESS Despite the fact that a very strong counter attraction across the channel, the grand ball by the "Cyanide Boys," of Treadwell, drew many people away from Juneau on New Year's Eve, the grand mask ball by the L. O. O. M. was a marked success in every par ticular. The dancing floor of the Elks' large hall was crowded witli merry makers in all sorts of fanciful garb. Excellent music and a smooth floor with the crowd that was present certainly as sured a good time to everyone, and everyone surely had a good time. There was a iarge number of prizes awarded for those who attempted to represent special characters for which prizes were offered: also for those who excelled in waltzing. The party did not break up until two o'clock?but all were happy and wishing that it might be so with every body. WILSON GETS A BOX OF APPLES PRINCETON, N. J.. Jan. 2. ? The first parcels post package delivered here under the new law, was a box of apples for President-elect Woodrow Wilson. MATERIAL FOR BANQUET.

The Alaska Meat Company, John Reck, manager, received on the last trip of the Humboldt 500 pounds of turkey and one beef weighing 1,000 pounds, which President John Reck, of the Commercial Club says will be served at the Commercial Club ban quet on Jan. 14. SCHOOL BOARD WANTS ATTENTION There is a very grave problem fac ing the school board and the people of Juneau in the matter of providing additional rooms for the children of the public schools. Recently the matter was taken up by the Commercial Club and a plan was devised to build a new structure. It is is now up to the people to carry out this idea successfully or to adopt something better immediately. The school board is very anxious that there should be a large turnout at the mass meeting called by Mayor H. A. Bishop for tonight in the city council chambers that steps might be taken to get immediate action. That the necessity of getting addi tional school rooms is very urgent is not contradicted by anyone. It is am solutely necessary to have a new building finished before the fall term of school begins, and it is up to the people of Juneau to provide the ways and means. The school fund is prac tically exhausted and outside resources must be found to meet the necessity. Temporary quarters were secured at the beginning of the last semister for a part of the overflow but it is not sptficient for present needs and besides be surrendered at a moment's notice. The great influx of people during the coming summer will likely double the school population of Juneau. Some thing must be done and that right sud denly Is the cry of the school board. Everyone having interest In school matters is urged to attend the meeting tonight. [WOULD SAVE THE I CANNERY WASTE Dr. J. \V. Turrentlne, who is con-' nected with the fertilizer division of the department of agriculture, with headquarters in Washington. D. C.. ar rived in Juneau on the City of Seat tle from Skagway. Recently Dr. Tur rentine has been to the Westward hav ing gone to Kodiak on the last trip of the Admiral Sampson. The particu lar duty that has called him to this part of Alaska at this time is to in vestigate the possible fertilizer re sources of the country. There are two expeditions in the field now, one un der Prof. Kigg, the other under Prof. Frye. both of the University of Wash ington. These gentlemen have char tered the cruising launches Gjoa and Znrembo and are accompanied by a party of scientists on each boat. The expeditions are for the purpose of investigating the kelp forests or fields in Southeastern and Southwestern Alaska for the purpose of determining their value and possibilities in pro ducing fertilizer. The task Dr. Tur rentine has set himself is to find a means of consuming the fish cannery waste in conjunction with kelp in the manufacture of fertilizer. Dr. Turrentine says that he has found possibilities of getting results from the canneries in the Cook Inlet country, but has not yet fairly started on his investigations. He will remain in Alaska during the greater part of the summer making invesigations along this line, lie says it is rather too early to get a practical idea of what may be accomplished. The fish ing season is not yet far enough ad vanced to give a clear idea of the ma terial that is at hand. o?o?o

OYSTER BAY. May 22.?Col. Theo dore Roosevelt, when asked if he would be a candidate for the Presi dency in 1916 on an opposition ticket, replied: "I cannot tell if I shall run until later developments, but If 1 do run. The small situation at Hoonah baa become serious, according to Informa tion received by acting Gov. Charles E. All the physicians of Southeastern Alaska have been notified to be on the sharp lookout for the appearance of smallpox, that any suspect and those exposed by him might be placed In immediate quarantine.

DELEGATE . MISQUOTED PLATFORM ?t? Wednesday night at his Kink meet ing Delegate James Wickersham pre tended to quote from what he repre sented to be the Democratic 1912 plat form. He pretended to read there from a declaration in favor of State hood for Alaska. With that as a basis from which to start, he declared that the Democratic party of Alaska is re actionary because its Skagway con vention declared for "full Territorial form of government." and Democrats la the Legislature and The Empire have supported a memorial asking Congress for "full Territorial form of government." There was no available copy of the platform in Juneau. Friends of Dele gate Wickersham had been searching for a copy of the platform because, it was said, someone had told him that it had declared for Statehood. The Empire, knowing of the Dele gate's habits when "quoting" in pub lic and knowing of his intention to try to make a point on the alleged infor mation. also made a search of the town for a copy of the platform. The Empire was unsuccessful, but the Delegate "quoted" as stated. Yesterday morning The Empire, still mindful of the Delegate's habits, sent a telegram to the Yaldez Prospector, published at the town where the 1912 convention was held, asking thut it telegraph The Empire the plank in the platform on Statehood for Ataska. DEMOCRATS DECLARED FOR TER RITOR1AL GOVERNMENT IN 1912

The Empire received this reply: VALDEZ, April S.?The Home Rule plank in the Democratic platform of 1912 was as follows: "The power to make laws to govern local affairs is but the application to Alaska of a right sanctified by the blood of our fathers and Justified by more than a century of actual exper ience. Every Democratic convention held in Alaska has insisted upon that right, and we do but reiterate the ut terances of these conventions when we again represent to Congress: (1) That the people of Alaska want home rule. (2) That the people of Alaska ought to have home rule. (3) That until the people of Alaska get home rule they will never cease demanding it as the right of American citi zens. "We pledge to the people of Alaska that, if elected, our candidate for Dele gate will use every effort to secure the enactment of a law giving to Al aska a local Legislature, elected by the people, with power covering every rightful subject of legislation not Na tional in character." (Signed) PROSPECTOR. NO STATEHOOD DECLARATION Upon receipt of this telegram, think ing that perhaps the Prospector had not understood the request. The Em pire sent this wire to the Prospector: "Did the Democratic 1912 platform contain any reference to Statehood for Alaska. If so. please wire it to The Empire." The following reply was received last night: VALDEZ, April 8.?Nothing in plat form regarding Statehood. Mailing you copy of platform on tonight's st earner. (Signed) PROSPECTOR.

"Our work will be steady, but gradual." Richards decided to go ahead with the double-tracking of the old tunnels. The amount offered for the claims was $25,000. The com pany wanted the property as a right of-way. for a proposed new tunnel, and not as a mine, it was said. 1.000 TONS IS CRUSHED DAILY Four thousand tons of rock is be ing crushed every twenty-four hours iu the Alaska Oastinoau company's mill ai Thane, acocrding to ofilclals of the company. President Woodrow Wilson to! : the members and guests at tiu Gridiron Club dinner Saturday I night that America ought ;to keep out of the European war id the "sacrifice of everything ex cept this single thing upon which her character and her history are fou ided, her sense of human ity and justice." The President spoke of the na tion's affairs with unusual grav ity. His hearers included scvc;: - al hundred members of Con gress, government officials, busi ness men and correspondent Every person present jumped lo his feet and cheered for sev eral minutes when the President concluded with the following words of his speech: "I would be be just as much ashamed to be rash as I would to be a coward. PRESIDENT ASKS I PEOPLE TO VOTE FOR DEMOCRATS A/ilson Wants Democratic Congress as Endorse ment of Administra tion in War. WASHINGTON, Oct. 26.? Realiz ng the great necessity of undivided .upport in the face of the great vorld's crisis on the event of elec ions at home, President Wilson to lay issued an appeal to the public, jrging the people to return a Demo iratic Congress at the November elec ions if they approve his course in his critical period. He said the re urn of a Republican majority would certainly be interpreted across the vaters as disapproval of the admin stration policies. He said he would iccept the verdict of the people with >ut cavil, but added that an adverse verdict v/ould seriously interfere with lis power to administer the great rust imposed upon him. The statement says: "Congressional elections are at land in the most critical period the country has evtr faced, and is ever ikely to face. "If you approve my leadership, if (ou wish me to continue to be your embarrassed spokesman, I beg you :o express yourselves unmistakably ;o that effect by returning a Demo cratic majority to Congress, because to many critical issues depend upon four verdict. "I frankly tell you the great trust issigned me by the Constitution vould be seriously impaired, should four judgment be adverse. ?'I am your servant and will accept four judgment without avail. "I have no thought suggesting any party is paramount in patriotism. "The difficulties and delicacies of the present task are such that the Nation should give undecided sup port to the Government for a unified leadership.

"A Republican Congress at this time would divide the leadership. The leaders of the minority of the present Congress unquestionably are pro-war supporters, but anti-adminis tration. They seek to take the choice of policy from my hands, and put it under control and instruments and instrumentality of leaders of their own choosing. "This is no time for divided council and leadership. Unity of command is necessary at home as on the bat tlefield. "An opposing majority could as sume control of legislation and oblige me to take action amidst a contest of obstruction. On the other side of the waters they would interpret the return of a Republican majority as a repudiation of my leadership. "The Republican spokesman is urg ing the election of Republicans to support the President. They des're not to support him, so much as to control him. '?The Allies would find it hard to believe the American voters had chosen to support the President by [the election to Congress a majority | of those not in fact in sympathy with the attitude of the Administration and its policies. "I am not asking support for my sake or the party's sake, but the Nation's sake, in order that its in ward unity of purpose may be evi dent to all the world. "In ordinary times I would make no such appeal. "In ordinary times divided councils can be endured. "If, in these critical days, you wish to sustain with undivided minds, I beg of you to say so in a way not possiblo to misunderstand, here or abroad. "I submit my difficulties and hopes to you." TERRIFIC STORM DRIVES PRINCESS SOPHIA OVER REEF, ONjljWHICH SHE HAD SPENT TWO DAYS, AND SHE Sflfe WITH ALL ON BOARD; EMPTY LITE-BOATS INDICATE THAT CHANCE THAT ANY SURVIVE THE DISASTER IS VERY REMOTE-ONE BODY EOUND

The Canadian Pacific passenger liner Princess Sophia sunk at sometime between 8 o'clock last night and 7 o'clock this morning, and in all probability every one of the 343 souls on board met watery graves in Lynn Canal. The only possibility that some of those on board were saved is the chance that life boats were launched during the night and reached shelter with their human cargoes. This possibility is regarded as remote by those familiar with the storm that was raging all last night in Lynn Canal. The fateful message bringing the news of the greatest disaster that ever has occurred in northern waters was received at Juneau at 9:25 o'clock this morninig. It came from the United States Lighthouse Tender Cedar, and it held out no hope for those on the ill-fated Canadian liner. The message, referring to the Prin cess Sophia, said: "Driven over reef during night. Only masts showing. No survivors." With the King and Winge the Cedar immediately began the search for the passengers?the living, if any, ihe dead if none survived.

LITTLE HOPE EXISTS THAT ANY LIVE. This afternoon a wireless dispatch says the Cedar had picked up four empty, and capsized life boats from the PrihceSs';;,$8phih, and tne^ijjlrig and Winge one. The King and Winge had recovered one body?a woman, unidentified. | t The Princess Sophia ran ashore on Vanderbllt reef, four miles from Sentinel Island, at 2 o'clock Thursday morning. Since that time the weather has been too rough to transfer passengers. Boats have been lying by all the time. Yesterday the storm became terrific. Boats that were lying by sought shelter at night. At 8 o'clock Capt. Locke of the Princess Sophia sent a wireless dispatch to General Ageni Lowle which said the passengers' conditions were normal, that the vessel was not taking water, but that it was too rough to transfer passengers. That is the last that was heard from the scene until 7 o'clock this morning when the Cedar, which had been compelled to seek shelter, wired that she was leaving for the Princess Sophia. About two hours later came the fateful wireless dispatch saying that the vessel had sunk and that there were no survivors. The circumstance that the Princess Sophia was blown over the reef leads to the conclusion that the cli max of the disaster came at high tide, about 4:30 this morning. The story, of the last hours of the doomed vessel and her hundreds of human souls will probably never be told.

The disaster is probably the worst that ever has occurred in northern waters. There seems hardly a chance that a single life has been saved to tell the tale. RECOVER LIFE BOATS. % At 3:20 this afternoon the customs house received a message from the lighthouse tender Cedar that four capsized boats had been picked up. The King and Winge picked up one unidentified body of a woman. The mes sage said the boats were still cruising around Sentinel and Lincoln islands in the hopes of finding some survivors. EVERY AVAILABLE BOAT TO THE RESCUE. Every available boat at Juneau and vicinity has been sent to the scene of the disaster. The Princess Alice will be due here at 8 o'clock, and she will leave immediately. Among those who will leave on the Princess Alice for the wreck will be Gov. Thomas Riggs, Jr. )

TOD A Y and The Future Day — by Arthur Brisbane —— ^ THE POWER OF SILENCE , We talk too much, think too little. ! We are a talking nation. We are a nation of speechmakers. Our political campaigns are cam- ' paigns of talk. Talk is our eter- t nal occupation and if we stop' talking, by chance, we rush off to meetings or theatres to hear others talk. * * * It is not necessary to say that speech is man's most valuable physical accomplishment. Tru speech and writing we hand knowledge from generation to generation. But with us Ameri cans talk needs no defence. It is the gift of silence that our peo ples lack. How hard it is to THINK CONSECUTIVELY EVEN FOR THREE MINUTES. There is not one man in a thousand capable of keeping his thought steadly upon one subject even for a few minutes at a time. * * * There are two kinds of silence PASSIVE and ACTIVE silence. The type of passive indolent si lence is the village idiot, nodding in the sun at the poorhouse door. And the type of ACTIVE silence may be seen in one of those stu dies of Napoleon digging up si lently OUT OF HIS OWN DEEP MIND the solution of his world problems. The silence that is mere cessation of noise is as use less as the noise itself. w + w There was a wise man that took crae of dogs. All those that were ill he cured in one woy. He put the sick dog in a barrel with' a supply of water for twenty four hours and the dog was all right. Foolish and careless eating had made him sick. Water, soli tude and rest made him well again. Our tired, sick minds need the cure of solitude. We are sur feited with talk, chatter, noise, aimless gossip. Many of us could cure our minds as the wise man cured his dogs. In any of our big business houses you can tell almost at once who the USEFUL man is, who the COMJNG man is. Nine times out of ten, he is THE Sf- { LENT MAN. t

There are actually many that have achieved moderate success ' by a mere PRETENCE of solemn silence. Talk without meaning is a ha bit hard to overcome. Listen to others, listen to your own thoughts. Think ahead a little ^ and as the flow of words is about j to start, ask yourself if it is worth while and stop it. * * * The great Dante is history's ' best proof of the value of solitu- * de and silence. Happy, talking, busy, honored in his native city, Dante might have done nothing worth while.) But turned adrift by an ungra-, teful people, forced into solitude ! with non companions but his THOUGHTS he wrote his DI VINE COMEDY that has cut lasted centuries.

La fiducia ! dei banchieri e degli investitori americani nei titoli industriali i taliani è riflessa in un aumento medio di quotazioni del 10 per cento. L'energia idroelettrica dalle Alpi agli Apennini occupa una parte sempre piu' importante nella rinacsita industriale italia na. Le filovie che una volta por tavano carbone oggi portano ma teriali e apparecchi per la produ zione della energia elettrica. I Con la stabilizzazione della li ra e il ritorno alla base aurea il 1927 fu un anno di difficoltà per l'Italia industriale superate tuttavia con la piu' ferma disci

plma. [ Pure ne! 1927 !e costruzioni i droe!ettriche progredirono circa de! 31.2 per cento. I! calcolo di un consumo annua le di 24.000 kilowatt all'ora per chilometro quadrato rivela il suc cesso delle compagnie italiane nella elettrificazione rurale. L'Italia — scrive il Wall Street Journal — occupa oggi il primo posto non solo nello sviluppo del la energia elettrica ma anche nel la elettrificazione delle ferrovie. 3785 chilometri di ferrovie su un totale di 26.588 in Italia sono state già elettrificate. Nelle regioni industriali — scrive il Wall Street Journal — e cioè in quasi tutte le provnicie dell'Alta Italia le compagnie idroelettriche sono raggruppate nella Edison General Italian Electric Co., che produce il 30 per cento di tutta l'energia elettdica che si vende in Italia. In cinque anni le somme investite da! gruppo. Edison sono salite da lire 907 mi lioni a lire 2,440,000,000 mentre l'energia trasportata sulle linee del gruppo è cresciuta da 1,384. 000,000 kilowatt all'ora a 2,396, 000,000 kilowatts, l'energia for nita da 364,000 kilowatts a 619 mila kilowatts e i clienti da 514 mila a 851 mila. Il "Wall Street Journal" con clude rilevando che gli ingegneri che hanno studiato gli impianti i taliani per incarico di banchieri americani, hanno la piu' alta sti ma de! valore tecnico degli inge gneri idraulici italiani e della ec cezionale competenza ed abilità degli operai italiani specializzati per questa industria.

i LA TURCHÌA Sì MODERNIZZA I! Presidente Kemal Pascià è deciso a trasformare compieta mente la vecchia Turchia e non ha esitato a portare le riforme anche nel campo religioso, che costituisce il punto debole delle innovazioni in quanto i riti sono tradizioni antichissime e sacre ad ' ogni mussulmano. Kemal Pascià ha messo il dito anche in questo campo e le riforme sono già sta te annunziate. Tutti i mussulmani che d'ora in poi si recano nelle moschee dovranno calzare le scarpe e se dersi sui banchi che saranno di sposti in Ale come nelle chiese cristiane. Non sarà piu' permes so ai fedeli di entrare in una mo j schea a piedi nudi, nè di pregare stando accovacciati sulle gambe incrociate, alla maniera proprio degli indù'. Oltre ai banchi saranno instal lati nelle moschee altari, cori ed organi che rimpiazzeranno con le loro dolci melodie il monotono salmdiare del sacerdote mao mettano che recita il Corano. Questi cambiamenti radicali sono considerati a giusta ragione di grande importanza e senza dubbio molto piu' radicali del provvedimento adottato qualche anno fa il quale aboliva il carat teristico "fez". Il Presidente Ke- ' mal Pascià vuol modernizzare a ' qualunque costo la vecchia Tur chia, e non ha avuto un momen to di esitazione neanche innanzi a queste ultime riforme che per il loro carattere religioso si pre stano ad una facile critica ed al la ribellione dei vecchi mussul mani attaccati alle tradizioni del Corano piu' che al governo. Ke mal Pascià è fermo nella sua at titudine e vuole educare la gio ventù turca aPa maniera occi dentale.

Morso da un serpente a sonaglio HARTFORD — Nei pomerig gio di lunedì scorso ritornava a casa dopo una passeggiata Victor Gronda di anni 35 di Matson Hill Glastonbury in compagnia di Ja mes Quagliaroli. Ad un certo pun to, camminando per un viottolo di bosco, scorse sotto un grosso macigno un serpente a sonagli. Punto da una cattiva tentazione, a gradi sforzi riuscì a rivolgere il macigno, il serpente gli si slan ciò contro e gli affondò nell'avam braccio i suoi acutissimi denti. Gronda gridò aiuto al compagno che s'era di poco allontanato e questi corse subito. Il serpente aveva lasciato la sua vittima ma aveva iniettato il suo veleno. Qua gliaroli cacciò di tasca un col tello, allargò la ferita, indi ne suc chiò il sangue. TODAY (Arthur Brisbane.) Our brain, the spirit of thinking power which works through the brain, must work through genera tions to come witr a very defective instrument. We have only recently risen above the plane of animal life. A hundred thousand years ago we were ail howling, murderous can nibalistic savages. And two hun dred and fifty thousand years ago there were only a few of ua on this earth—and we were actually ani mals, with huge teeth and jaws, with the faintest signs of humanity about us. We had big muscles, big bones, big appetites, great voracity^-FEE BLE BRAINS AND FEEBLE IN TELLECTS. And we still have feeble brains and feeble intellects. All of our physical impuses are stronger than our mental impulses. To rest, to sleep, to eat, to in dulge the various attractions we have within us—shch is the in heritance that we get from millions of years of animal life back of us. It is a difficult thing to teach the brain—now in its infancy—TO CONTROL THAT LONG HEREDI TY OF ANIMAL LIFE. Emile Zola, the Frenchman, wrote, “Every man has within him a hog asleep.” | That may not be literally true of every man. But it is certain that every niSta has with in him various animals, very much awake. Every man has in him something of the monkey—and the monkey never sticks at anything, if he can avoid it. We all contain remnants of the various animal forms through which we have passed during the millions of years that stretch behind us. And all of these are constantly working to overcome the activity of that recently acquired power, THE FACULTY OF THOUGHT.

UNEMPLOYMENT The miseries and trials of the un employment are worse than pictur ed. It takes more than a casual ob server to detect the real situation brought about by the long period Of depression. The tragedies that are enacted in the privacy of the strick en hearth seldom come to the sur face. The occasional tear of the care-worn housewife, the pale and haggard child and the sullen husband whose face bears traces of worry and discourgement, are but faint re flection of what takes place within the homes of these unfortunates. Day in and day out the victim of unemployment goes about in search of work. At an early hour he leaves his home with the faint expectation that the dawn of the day will usher in new hopes. He follows the same routine and walks the same streets. He goes from shop to shop but the monotonous and unpleasant reply greets his plea. The gloom of dark ness marks the end of another day. With weary feet, empty stomach and sinking heart, he returns home to And further sorrow. The sight of shivering, unfed and scantly cloth ed children is more painful than the pangs of hunger; The very thing that society calls honorable is again de nied him. Work and not charity is what he asks. How many read the tragic news of the unemployed whose entire family was the victim of the present state affairs, without realizing the nonag gressive, silent cruelty and ruthless ness that prevail in our midst? The episode will undoubtedly re main a libel upon our civilization and a stigma upon our social system, and will be recalled by future gene rations, in the same manner we re call deeds ascribed to ages of bar barism. The unfortunate unemployed was the father of a family who absented himself from his wife and three children for a few days, in search of work. His sense of duty and love for his half-starved wife and children brought him beyond the limits of this city. His plight was not understood and his pleas found no response in our civilized and so-called self-suffi cient social system. He returned un successful, empty handed and dis heartened, perhaps beating his weary brains to And a tactful way of break ing the news of his failure to hi? wan and suffering wife. But antici-j pating perhaps the unpleasant tid ings, she hid herself and the children under the cloak of death. A mental aberration, suddenly affecting the despairing and needy mother, pre cipitated the bloody act of self des struction and Alicide.

This is only one instance of the human miseries, the product of un employment that rise to the surface with all the attending circumstances. Untold host of others never come to light and remain buried in the sands of time. We cannot but blame society for the present blight in the very midst of civilazation. That some of the members of the social organization are intefering with the functioning j of its wheels, is obvious. The malad justment that is so much spoken of is not natural but artificial. 11 there was ever a time when a concrete example of a human "par adox" was more clearly reflected, it is now. While banks overflow with money, hundreds of people are com pelled to give up their equities in properties which are calculated to represent ^fheir lifelong savings. Products and food supplies, in large quantities, have been burned or dumped into the sea to safeguard the market. In the midst of depression, hardship and want, we And more re velries, sumptuos banquets, orgies and dances, than at any other time. The exceedingly unequal distribu tion of wealth, resources and oppor tunities, are the cause of the socalled frozen assets. That which has been looked upon as essential to the pro gress of prosperity seems now an ob stacle to its continued existence. Green, selfishness and inordinate hoarding are the social blight and plague that exact more victims than famine itself. "The army of the foe", says Mr. Phelps," is made up of money grubbers and money grab bers, self-lovers, and selfish, deprav ed, degenerate, cruel, cold hearted children of this world". How can any individual with hu man limitation cleave to his enor mous ill-acquired fortunes and look upon the present situation with in difference? Who is responsible, if not the money "hug" for the increas ing number of radicals and law breakers? Dodn't they realize that they are stewards of all the excess that flow from the substance of their possessions and that they are bound in justice to pass it ou to the ones in need? What would the merry makers, who revel in constant sum ptuos feasting say?, if they were told that within a stone's throw, stood the shivering needy in the slow moving breadline? What will they say, of the hundreds of inno cent children that languish and pine away emaciated and undemourised? Would they try to rationalize and justify their conduct? This is what we call civilization. We denounce a former age of some instance of cruelty of injustice little knowing that the very brutali ty and uncivilized acts that are the subject of our demagogic denuncia tions are constantly enacted in our very present time with greater cruel ty and ruthlessness. atty. Prominent men in various part: of the world are quoted as saying that there cannot possibly be wai between the United States and Japan. That is exactly the kind of talk that preceded the World war. Every body said war among civilized peo ples was unthinkable. The historians had made a diagram of civilization & proved beyond a doubt that the long dreamed-of Golden Age of Univers al Peace was just around the corner. The economists had made other dia grams and proved that war was no longer profitable and hence it could not occur. It was believed that the influence of the churches alone would make war impossible. A writer was in Europe as the World war started. The news dis patches told that the Austrian arch duke had been assassinated at Sara jevo. At that time nobody had never heard of Sarajevo. No American had even been to Sarajevo. Even President Wilson was foggy about the location of the place and in one of his state papers he put it in Serbia. As a matter of fact it was in what was then the province of Bosnia—a part of the Austro-Hungarian mon archy—now Yugoslavia. It was real ly a small and unimportant city of oriental type which had been taken from the Turks—the last place in the world which anybody would think could start the worst war in history.

A aeroian patriot irom over tne border in Serbia had kiHed the arch duke. Austria-Hungary made this assassination the excuse for declar ing war on little Serbia—and from that moment the fat was in the Are. Russia got in because the Serbs were of their race. Then Germany, France Britain and the other countries jumped in—each one having the best reasons possible ofr their action. It took three years more to bring the United States in—and when the war closed, more than a score of na tions had been forced into the hos tilities, and ali the neutral nations were also heavily involved. So let nobody say that war with Japan is impossible. The Japs are a nation of Aghters, and they have a long list of grievances against us. It was Uncle Sam who woke them up out of their feudal sleep, less than a century ago, when our navy went over there and made them open up. The Japs want what they want when they want it, and their religion com mands them to go out and take it— somewhat as the religion of the fol lowers of Mahomet does. History will tell you how fast and how far the Turks went in their conquests. In fact it was that same little old Sarajevo that marked the western-most point in Europe to which they pushed their conquests. The Turks didn't win all that terri tory in a year, or even a century; it took them several centuries to spread out from their home country in Asia. The Japs have a lot of historyJ from which they can pick models for their plans—which we can assure you are most ambitious. "Do you believe there are mi crobs in kisses?" "Yes. That's what the scientists say." "What disease do they cause?" "Palpitation of the heart".

La povera vitti ma e' tale Ralph Ruby il quale nel mentre si trovava a spolverare la sua automobile in fronte della casa del Trotta si vide avvicinato da co stui e senza alcuna parola si ebbe il viso sfregiato con una lunga ferita dall'orecchio alle labra e che richiese la sutura di ben 10 punti all'Ospe dale, dove dichiararono che resterà' sfregiato. He Great Drive The great drive for November votes is beginning — and both ma jor parties are throwing themselves into the job of getting them with more force than they have shown for many years. The Republicans, who have been dormant for the last year and a half, are emerging. Definite, reason ed opposition to the Roosevelt pro gram is springing up. In a recent magazine article Senator Dickinson, who proposed Herbert Hoover at the convention wh'ch nominated h'm, made these definite criticisms of the present administration: That the Democratic party has been leading us toward a dictatorship; that its rate of expenditure of public funds if continued, will result in national bankruptcy; that it is destroying in dividualism and private initiative; that a return to Republican princi ples is essential to the preservation of the constitutional government and our ancient traditions. Mr. Dic kinson's points are generally in com- t plete accord with those of Chair man Fletcher of the Republican Central Committee. The Democratic party is not tak ing criticism "lying down". For ex ample: Recently only cabinet offi cers — Hull of the State Depart ment and Perkins of the Labor De partment — were in Washington. The rest of them were about the country, making speeches and look ing things over. Less important of ficials, such as the sub-cabinct mem bers, were likewise in far places, and it would have been hard to find astate not vis ted by some Adminis tration official. Gist of the talks made by these men is that the New Deal, for the most part, has been successful; that we are in the mid dle of the stream now and that changing horses would spell ruin; that if Mr. Roosevelt is permitted to carry on his policies, with full Congressional support, for two ye ars more, he will succeed in ring ing prosperity back. The ordinary voter is obviously in a different position when it comes to making up his mind. He has no means of knowing how much re covery has actually been achieved — almost all the reports he receives are prejudiced in favor of one par ty or another. He is aware that neither party is above doctor ng the facts to prove a point; that when election time rolls 'round, political considerations are para mount. Most forecasts lead to the belief t!%t the Administration has lost considerably.

It was then, in the words of Time, that, "13 months be fore he was to defend his Presiden tial title against an as yet unnamed Republican challenger, Franklin De lano Roosevelt jogged out of Wash ington fur a 3,000-mile stretch of po litical roadwork. Champion Roose velt felt it was not too early for him to go through his paces for the benefit of some 50,000,000 voters who will turn thumbs up or down on him in 1936." Lesser lights had played their parts - it was time for the chief to lead his legions into battle. The President's speeches on his trip constituted direct, non-apologe tic defenses of what he and his Ad ministration have done. First address for example, was at Fremont, Ne braska, in the heart of the farm belt. There Mr Roosevelt stood four square for one of his most import ant legislative pets, the AAA. At Salt Lake City, he praised Philippine independence, one of the major acts of his Administration in the field of foreign affairs. At Boulder City, Ne vada. he dedicated the great Bould er Dam - and spoke aggressively in defense of Federal Public Work? spending, and government-in the power-business. Thus it went, in set and informal speeches made all a long his route. It is significant that he said nothing concerning a new constitutional amendment, a much debated issue. Most experts now think that he will continue to say nothing about it in. the future - it is too dangerous and might become a boomerang.

And, shortly af ter the Pretident had gone to the sea on the Cruiser Houston, it was ! met by the head of the party-out-! of-power, Mr. Hoover, who appar ently opened the Republican cam paign of 1936 with a ringing speech at Oakland California. This speech by the only living ex-president, was more thqtn usually important - in it, i for the first time since he went down to defeat in 1932, Mr. Hoov er directly attacked, by name and by inference, definite acts and poli cies of the President. Even when he was campaigning in 1932, Mr Hoo ver, if this writer's memory is cor rent, stuck to principles, steered clear of personalities, and on only one occasione in that bitter fight spoke the name of Roosevelt. Mr. Hoover said that the Roose velt administration "is now clutched in the meshes of the gigantic spend ing bureaucracy it has created." He went on to say that unless the bud-! get is balanced, "we shall see one of! these three horsemen ravage the land - taxation, repudiation or infla tion." He denounced the New Deal's relief program, and said that the * last Republican administration (his own) had provided sound economi cal relief for the needy, and that the Roosevelt administration had undone the good work achieved then In effect, his speech was a clarion call to Republicans to join shoulder to shoulder in a fight to bring back into government the principles of their party. These recent events have done much to clarify vagueness surround ing the political situation, are help ing to bring the issues into bold re lief. One news magazine has obser ved that the forthcoming battle will be the greatest since 1896, and that the main issue will be the same one that McKinley and Bryan fought o ver - sound money.

Slips It was only recently that the late Huey P. Long- was winning no toriety, if not fame, with his “Ev ery Man A King” idea. Before he died he had promised every man an income of $5,000 a year. Everybody, including Long, knew his shase-the-wealth scheme was im practical. But Huey was a smart pol itician. He knew he could win foll owers by promising something they didn’t have. As his audience grew, he ra sed his ante. Now it appears that he left a cou ple of disciples behind - President j William Green of the American Fed eration of Labor and President John L, Lewis of the United Mine Work ers.

In their fight for the control of labor, Green and Lewis have been bidding r|giht anld left. On Labor Day, Lewis pulled his bushy eye brows together, puffed up 1 ke a vol cano getting ready to erupt, and promised a $2,500-a-year for all. Green was a little surprised. But he pondered. And on Christmas day he upped Lewis $1,100, promising $3,600, As the New York Times remarks, “it would be very desirable if each family could have a minimum income of $3,600 a year, but still more de sirable, for that matter, if each fam ily could have a nrnimum of $5,000 or even $10,000.” But the way to achieve that income level is not, as Lewis and Green propose, to shorten the work week and raise wages arbi trarily, thus increasing the cost of living. It is instead, as The Times points out, “to improve labor skills, machine efficiency and industrial or ganization - in short, to increase both individual earning power and nation al production.” WHO PAYS? The great majority of American workers attend to their own affairs, strive for the fullest possible pay envelopes and are happy to live in a country in wh'eh they have helped to develop the highest living stand ard in the world. But occasionally groups of American workmen are persuaded to go on strike. What happens then? Who pays for strikes? First of all, the investors pay. They may lose dividends; their plant may lose contracts to a competitor; their investment is jeopardized. But usually, , the investor has other sourc es of income and manages to get a long reasonably well. Secondly, the community where a strike occurs pays. The earning pow er of those who make up the com munity is reduced and therefore con suming power is cut down. The groc er, the butcher, the baker, the doct tor the motion picture manager, gas J stations and every other form of lo cal business suffers in a strike. Thirdly, relatives of the strikers pay. Often they have to pull in their belts another notch to help the fell ows who are running short. And then the wives and ch'ldren of the work ers pay - not only in reduced food and clothing and opportunity but pay the heavy mental costs of wor- ! ry and fear. They fear prolonged poverty. They worry over debts. They fear the physical consequences of violence so often resorted to by strikers And finally, the strikers themselves pay the heaviest bill of all. They lose time. Pay envelopes vanish. Ha treds are engendered and often the job itself is lost. Time lost in a strike may not be made up in a year’s work. It is a fair quest’on to ask: “Is a strike worth the price?” Or isn’t peaceful discussion of employees and employer the better way?

What About Big Business? One hears a great deal of talk these days about BIG business and SMALL business with the intimation that "Big" business is something to criticize. Before we accept too readily the ready made phrases of the critics of big business let us examine a little further into the question of what and why is big business. Why are some businesses big and some small? Simply because the work to be done either is of such scope that it cannot be per formed on a small scale or it is of such nature that large scale production gives the public bet ter goods or services for its mon ey. Let us take one simple illustra tion. If you are going to make a toy boat for a child you can do . it yourself with a few pieces of wood and the simple hand tools found in most any*Househo!d. But if you are going to make a boat to carry passengers and freight across the ocean, you must have enormously expensive tools, a vast labor force and the most ex pert technical direction. A big job to be done requires big bus iness to do it. In the matter of taxes, invest ment, etc., the problems of "big" business and "small" business are exactly the same. There is no dif ference. The only difference be tween the two is in the type and character of the job. You can t attack one without hitting the other. But there is one other thought about big business. Did you ever stop to think how small businesses - the corner gro cery, the gas station, the repair shop - that big business makes possible? It all boils down to this- Here in America we want to make ALL business prosper ous - big and small.

Which Way? There are two ways of inter preting the fact that throughout this world some people have more than others. There is the interpretation that is prevalent in some quarters This is that because .some people have more, others have less. And in these instances the effort is to take from some and give to oth ers. The net result of this process and this philosophy is a general downward level of living stand ards. Then there is the other inter pretation which has been for years accepted in this and other progressive countries. This inter pretation is that the fact that someone else has a better home or a beter car indicates that oth ers have an opportunity to a chieve the same position. Success by some means that success is possible for others. In this coun try we call that "opportunity" and it is one of our most cherish ed possessions. It has a direct influence on the way all of us live. It is largely responsible for our high Ameri can living standards. The pressure of men striving - not to tear down what someone else has achieved - but to get a head himself, to achieve and pro duce, has been a mainspring of American progress. Between 1790 and 1930 the A merican standard of living was raised 400 per cent.

PER UNA NUOVA EUROPA II discorso del Cancelliere Hitler non puo’ e he’ dev’es sere cestinato aprioristicamente, senza una onesta e congrua considerazione. II discorso stesso, nell’ora burrascosa che volge, non so lo rappresenta una tappa storica di notevole importanza, ma sintetizza ancora uno stato spirituale, molto diffuso in quasi tutte le Nazioni del Vecchio Continente.; Ignorare per deliberato proposito, per solo impulso fa zioso, le parole del Capo della Germania Nazista, puo’ essere addirittura pericoloso e rovinoso; perche’, oggi, non sV piu’ davanti ad un tavolo dove si muovono le carte diplomatiche, in un’atmosfera di pace e di semplice rettorica verbale; ma milioni di gente si trovano in pieno assetto di guerra, in im minente pericolo di guerra, in imminente pericolo di vita. Romba insomma il cannone; sono in pieno atto i sottomari ni e da un momento all’altro, i velivoli potrebbero seminare stragi incalcolabili e masse di eserciti, nell’urto tremendo e micidiale, potrebbero trascinare nell’abisso della distruzione, anche tutta la civilta’, tutta l’esistenza europea. Si puo’ non condividere i sistemi di Hitler, si puo’ nu trire per lui una cordiale antipatia; si possono nutrire dei so spetti sulle sue promesse; ma in questo momento, il destino pericolante ed in pena di Nazioni piccole e grandi, di tutto un Continente e forse del mondo, impone una severa ponderazio ne anche a coloro, che sono infatuati di bellicismo ed inse guono delle chimere, che domani, i fatti e la realta’, potreb

bero rivelare disastrosamente fallaci. Senza dubbio, il Cancelliere del Reich, con un insolito linguaggio di moderazione, ha offerto il ramoscello d’olivo; ha offerto un piano di pace; ha dette delle grandi e roventi verita’; ha dimostrato d’essere disposto a deporrre la spada, che e’ vittoriosa, per iniziare delle conversazioni, che pero’ debbono partire da un tremendo presupposto, quello dell’av venuto decesso del Trattato di Versaglia. Il che significa, che una possibile adunata di grandi Po tenze, dovrebbe verificarsi, in un clima storico, che non ri cordi piu’ la mentalita’ versagliese; che non sia piu’ intossi cato dai ricordi terribili del 1919. Perche’ con lo spettr-o sinistro di quella mentalita’ e di quei ricordi, sarebbe difficile far sbocciare dalle possibili con versazioni la nuova Europa. Cioe’ la nuova Europa preconizzata, intravveduta, acca rezzata, desiderata dal Duce dell’Italia Fascista. Percio’ la storia d’Epropa, si trova di fronte ad un for midabile dilemma e di frcnte ad una svolta solenne e deci siva. Bisogna seppellire il passato con tutte le sue odiose in giustizie; con tutti i suoi acrimoniosi rancori; con tutte l'e sue paure, i suoi sospetti, i suoi perfidi sistemi; con tutti i suoi tradimenti, le sue egemonie e sopratutto con la sua cor sa pazzesca e suicida verso gli armamenti. Sul cumulo di tutte queste rovine e di queste tombe, bi sogna daccapo, dalle fondamenta, ricostruire una nuova Eu ropa, in una ossigenata atmosfera di fiducia reciproca, di se rena e chiara comprensione dei bisogni materiali e spirituali delle singole Nazioni; di equita’ e di giustizia per tutti. Sono molteplici i delicati e spinosi problemi, che e’ uo po risolvere; ma tutte le difficolta’, tutte le angolosita’ sono facili a superarrsi ed a spuntarsi, quando dominano la fiducia e la buona volonta’; quando prevalgono le preoccupazioni sui destini dei popoli, che odiano essenzialmente la guerra, che la detestano; che amano invece la pace, che e’ il migliore e maggiorq bene, che la Provvidenza abbia regalato ai mor tali, perche’ ne usufruiscano in tutta la sua grandiosa benefi cenza ed in tutti i suoi innumeri e santi frutti. Le cosa piu’ difficile fra gli odierni awenimenti, e’ il disar mo spirituale. La parola autorevole del Capo e giunte opportuna ed era atte sa. Come sempre Egli ha parla to con chiarezza, efficacia, preci sione. Ha parlato all’intelligen za degli italiani, ha detto che ha fiducia nella loro comprensione e nel loro amore alia Patria. II breve suo silenzio ha significato lavoro tutto rivolto ai gravi pro blemi dell’ora. Quando ha cre duto opportuno e giunto il mo menta di esporre quanto stima va necessario alia vita della Na zione e all’altissimo posto che occupa nel consesso delle Nazio ni tutte, Egli ha messo i punto lini sugli i. Tutte le vociferazio ni di piccola gente, che non in tende l’importanza dell’azione del Capo, tutta rivolta, con grande visione, alia grandezza italiana, Egli le ha sdegnosa mente lasciate cadere... Xi fedeli di Bologna ha volu to rivolgere, pe’ primi, il suo detto preciso e conciso. Era una importante manifestazione del suo pensiero e della sua volon ta: intenderla bene, dunque, conviene... Noi siamo in un’ora solenne della Storia del Mondo. Benito Mussolini vuole la pace secondo giustizia ed i diritti di ogni Na zione in Europa. La parola del Capo e stata, quindi, di monito e di indicazione agli italiani. La vorare con serenita, in silenzio, ma essere pronti. Ecco la preci sa direttiva, ecco la significativa e buona indicazione. Il diScorso d£l Duce, per la ri presa dei suoi contatti con le gerarchie del Partito, e fra i piu rilevanti. Quando ha detto U Duce: “II popolo italiano sa che non bisogna turbare il pilota. specie quando e impegnato in una burrascosa navigazione, ne chiedergli ad ogni istante noti zie sulla rotta”, ha indicato il dovere di tutti e dj ognuno. Il pilota e lui, il pelago tempesto so e il presente nel quale la nave italiana procede serena, per l’abilita e la saggezza del pilota, sulle acque irte di sco gli. Non si turba il pilota, e giu sto. Lo si segue con fiducia. La nave cosi evita i bassi fondi, e

vita ai urtare in uno scogno, e dalla difficile navigazione esce vittoriosa. Fede bisogna avere, e credere e saper tacere ed obbe dire. La parola di Lui e precisa al lorche scandisce il suo proposi to: “Se e quando io appariro a) balcone e convochero ad ascol tarmi l’intero Popolo Italiano, non sara per prospettargli un e^ same della situazione, ma per annunziargli — come gia il 2 Ot tobre 1935, e il 9 Maggio del 1936 —, decisioni, dico decisioni. di portata storica”. Anche quelle due convocazio ni del Popolo Italiano da Lui ri cordate incisivamente furono vere DECISIONI. Si chiamo il Popolo a raccolta per resistere alle sanzioni, per il diritto deirimpero, si chiamo, a vittoria conseguita, il Popolo ancora per la decisione della fondazione av venuta deH’Impero. Gli avveni menti storici furono segnati. Ora Egli preannunzia che, se e quando apparira al balcone, un novello avvenimento storico si compie. Il Popolo Italiano ri spondera, come allora, con quel significativo “Si” che risponde alia fiducia nel Capo e alia grandezza e agli interessi del Paese. E’ vero che ha aggiunto: “Per ora non e il caso!”. Ha soltanto

due pericoli tremendi: la mi naccia della guerra e la minac cia di Mosca. La prima e piu fa cile ad elTminarsi, dati gli umo ri ostili dei popoli, alia conti nuazione del conflitto; ma la se conda e piu difficile ad elimi narsi, perche implicherebbd la concordia di tutte le Nazioni di Europa e del mondo. E’ l’Euriopa capace di tanto? Questa sara la risposta di do mani. XXX.

Uno degli eventi politici piu prominenti e di particolare si gnificato, verificatosi in Europa in questi ultimi giorni, è costitui to dal nuovo atteggiamento del la Iugoslavia, nel quadro della situazione odierna nel Vecchio Continente. Le dichiarazioni del Primo Mil nistro iugoslavo, hanno avuto u na tremenda e profonda riper cussione internazionale; in quan to hanno rivelato un nuovo sta to d'animo subentrato nella na zione balcanica, che sino a qual che tempo fa, non aveva chiari ficata la sua volontà e nè presa posizione decisiva alcuna nei ri guardi degli attuali belligeranti. Che anzi, erano ben note le correnti anglofile e francofile e sistenti nella Iugoslavia, aventi maggiore autorità, anzi predo minanti addirittura. Correnti che d'altro canto, per logica coiy seguenza, erano ostilissime alla Asse Roma-Berlino ed in ispe cial modo verso l'Italia, contro la quale s'è sempre aizzato il po polo serbo; quello stesso popolo, che durante la Grande Guerra, fraternamente venne aiutato da l'Italia, allorché in disastrosa rotta, dovette allontanarsi dalla Patria, invasa dalle forze nemi che. C'è voluta tutta la saggezza politica di Mussolini, per evita re degli urti sanguinosi fra le due Nazioni, che invece hanno tutto da guadagnare stando ami che e cooperando iniseme. Senza dubbio, il Primo Mini stro iugoslavo, quando qualche giorno fa, ha fatto le sue chiare

ed importanti dichiarazioni, s'è ispirato a tali sentimenti ed ha avuto la visione di una politica profìcuamente Realistica. L'emi nente uomo politico ha detto che è venuto il tempo opportuno per la Iugoslavia di guardare in fac cia la realtà e di partecipare al processo storico, che sta per tra sformare l'Europa, non con le braccia al sen conserte e da spet tatrice, ma come dramatis per sona. Ha aggiunto che il suo Paese deve orientarsi definitiva mente verso l'Asse e dividerne le fortune; uscendo dalla posi zione di attesa in quella dell'a zione, per evitare di rimanere superati dalla corsa irresistibile degli avvenimenti. A prescindere dalle conse guenze cospicue derivanti dal nuovo atteggiamento iugoslavo, in quanto concerne la situazione odierna nei Balcani, l'atteggia mento stesso dimostra con una terribile chiarezza, che la Jugo slavia oramai è più che sicura dell'esito finale della guerra e si affretta a prendere posizione, ac canto alle Potenze, che possono contare su maggiori probabilità di vittoria.
