DOAM A7/ Una parola ed una visione paurose, cominciano ad affac ciarsi e ad insinuarsi nella mente e nel senso di responsabilità' umana delle genti. Domani! , t Panorama apocalittico di rovine materiali e spirituali; di tremendi dolori, di incommensurabili miserie, di pianto, di lutti, di strazio.

ranorama feroce e dolente di resti umani ; di una civiltà sconquassata; di una vita ridotta d brandelli, e di una troma di superstiti, brancolanti nel buio del destino, senza speranze, forse senza nemmeno piu' desiderio di vivere, per non sop portare piu' dopo la tragedia della guerra, quella della pace. Perche' la pace di domani, dopo che sono scorsi fiumi e fiumi di sangue; dopo milioni di caduti; alla presenza di mi lioni di feriti e di mutilati; alla presenza di selvagge devasta zioni di citta', sara' anche una grande e terribile tragedia per coloro, che sono stati risparmiati dal ciclone della guerra. E si dovrà' rivivere in tutta la sua immensa pena, la tra gedia della pace, che almeno spunti sulla terra scombussolata, con carità' e con giustizia. Spunti almeno sull'umanità' esterrefatta ed ansiosa, non piu' suggellata ed avvelenata dalla tempesta delle passioni e degli odi, col predominio della forza brutale del vincitore in sensibile e prevaricatore, ma illuminata da quel senso di so lidarietà' umana, che davanti all'atroce sventura, che tutti ha colpiti, vinti e vincitori, affratelli, spezzi il gelo delle ostili tà' e faccia tendere la mano del pentimento e del reciproco per dono. Riconoscendo al conspetto di tante distruzioni ed al ri cordo fresco di tante inenarrabili dolori, che soltanto un mo mento disperato di follia criminale, ha potuto provocare la tragedia della guerra. Pentimento e reciproco perdono potranno domani, sal vare i destini del mondo ; potranno evitare le tremende ingiu stizie del passato; rimuovere per sempre le cause perturbatri ci di altri conflitti nell'avvenire e rendere meno amara e meno pesante la tragedia della pace. Perche' il pentimento e' un implicito riconoscimento del la propria colpa ed il perdono, sotto la dolcenza cristiana del la comprensiope, fa dimenticare le colpe, per ridiventare una volta ancora, all'ombra della Croce santa p gloriosa, fratelli di una stessa patria, che e' tutto il mondo e di una stessa im mensa e luminosa speranza, che e' tutto il cielo. Questa dovrà' essere la missione, questo il messaggio del domani; del domani della pace vera, della pace giusta, della pace umana, della pace fraterna; della pace, che pur non po tendo distruggere le tormentose risultanze della guerra e non potendo completamente cicatrizzare le profonde ferite scava te nella materia e nell'anima dalla guerra, almeno le attenue rà', le renderà' piu' sopportabili, fintanto che il tempo ed i nuovi avvenimenti le rimargineranno, non per la sola gene razione, che n'e' stata la martire lacrimevole, ma per tutte le generazioni future, che saranno comprese ed assalite da or rore al ricordo.

Tanto sangue sarebbe scorso invano, scorrerà* invano, se esso non rappresenterà* domani, un salutare lavacro per tutta l'umanità* ; se esso -fara* rimanere ancora aride le zolle, che ne rimangano bagnate e santificate; se da queste zolle e da tutte le presenti rovine e da quelle che ancora la guerra produrrà', non spunterà' l'alba di un nuovo mondo morale, di un nuovo ordine sociale, d una nuova esistenza per tutti, per vinti e vincitori, per belligeranti e per neutri, se ancora, alla fine del conflitto, delle nazioni e dei popoli saranno ri masti nella privilegiata e miracolosa posizione di neutralità*. Citta' distrutte, beni despersi, tombe innanzi tempo schiuse, cimiteri pullulanti di croci, ospedali gremiti di feriti e di mutilati, milioni di vedove senza marito, milioni di madri senza figli, gli eserciti interminabili di raminghi, rappresente rebbero la piu* feroce beffa del destino, dopo quella della guerra, se i morti non venissero illuminati dalla novella auro ra di resurrezione umana ed universale, se le turbe dolorose di vittime non fossero sorrette dalla speranza di una piu' gran de giustizia e se sulle immense rovine, non risplendesse do mani, il sole di una nuova civiltà'. Civiltà di amore, civiltà* di carità e di giustiziai La storia di ieri e di oggi s e' dimostrata inetta ed impa ri, ad evitare le cause generatrici di conflitti; l'esperienza de! passato non e' valsa a nulla; e* segno evidente che l'organiz zazione umana si trova, s e* trovata sempre sulla falsa strada: e segno piu' che evidente, che nella struttura della presente civiltà , vi sono delle ruote di vitale importanza, che non fun zionano, o funzionano a ritroso; che tremende sperequazio ni sociali, di ricchezze naturali e geografiche sono in pieno at to; che esose ingiustizie ottenebrano gli orizzonti della storie e della terra e che tutto l'edificio umano e' stato costruito con una architettura fondalmente errata. Le guerre non sono uno sport, ma sono l'esplosione di un cumulo di cause, che si sono accavallate e che non si sono sapute o volute evitare dai pochi, avvicendatisi nel governo dei popoli e delle nazioni. L alba di domani arrossata dal sangue ed in gramaglie, dovrà' disperdere ed incenerire, con le fiamme della nuova giustizia e della nuova pace, questo cumulo di cause; dovrà' fare piazza pulita di uomini e di cose e sulla croce del dolore e della espiazione, salutare l'avvento di una novella etade. ; IL CORRIERE

Le notizie che pervengono dal Vecchio Continente, informano òhe dopo due mesi di assedio, la Capitale deirUcraina, Kiev, è caduta in mano dei Tedeschi. Quantunque tale notizia fosse attesa, pur tuttavia ha prodotto una viva impressione ed in mol ti ambienti più interessati, una vivissima preoccupazione, per le immediate conseguenze, che ne possono scaturire nei riguardi della guerra, che si sta combat tendo sulla fronte orientale e dalla quale dipendono altri svi luppi, anche su altre fronti. La caduta di Kiev deve rite nersi senza dubbio, un gravissi mo colpo per i russi, che si vedo no inesorabilmente scacciati da una delle zone più ricche di tut ta la Russia ed in procinto di perdere una delle fonti più co piose, per rifornire le truppe ed alimentare tutto il sistema di ri fornimenti indispensabili. Perciò la caduta porta con sè un signiAcato militare, politico e spirituale. SigniAcato impor tantissimo in tutto il suo vasto complesso, che potrebbe addirit tura segnare il principio di quel la debacle bolscevica, che non sarebbe più soltanto di caratte re militare; ma anche di caratte re morale e politico. Kiev, nel bilancio dell'attuale guerra, non rappresenta solo la capitale dell'Ucraina; ma anche una chiave strategica di primo ordine ed anche un punto sensi bile del prestigio spirituale del bolscevismo; tanto più che il Kremlino, pochi giorni dietro, faceva sapere al mondo che Kiev è stata la capitale dell'Ucraina, è la capitale dell'Ucraina, e ri marrà la capitale dell'Ucraina. Oggi Mosca è costretta a riman giarsi la spacconata di ieri e que

sta tortuosa operazione, non è la più adatta a ribadire la fiducia nelPavvenire delle armate russe e nella futura vittoria bolscevi ca. Kiev è la terza città russa più grande, viene dopo Mosca e Le ningrado; conta 846,293 anime ed in questi ultimi decenni, ha rea lizzato uno sviluppo cospicuo, raddoppiandosi. Quantunque non si conosca la data precisa della fondazione di Kiev, si sa che nel 988, era una città principale; che venne di strutta una prima volta nel 1240 dai Mòngoli, passando dopo di mano dalla Lituania alla Polo nia, sino a che nel 1654, venne annessa alla Russia. La storia di Kiev comincia a ritornare sulla scena europea, allorché nel 1918, dopo l'uccisio ne del Generale Eichorn, passò dalle mani dei Russi Bianchi a quelle dei Bolscevisti. Ciò av venne il 3 Ottobre del 1919. Ma nel 1920, truppe di Russi Bian chi e di Polonia occuparono la città e l'Ucraina venne dichiara ta Indipendente, col Trattato di Riga del 1921. Ma nel 1923 diven ne una delle tante Repubbliche dell'Unione Sovietica. Senza dubbio, TUcraina è sta ta sempre una delle principali mire della Germania e si crede che il conflitto attuale tra Berli no e Mosca sia scoppiato appun to par l'Ucraina, p cui possesso Hitler avrebbe domandato a Èta lin, che l'ha rifiutato. ^ Oggi Kiev è in mano delle truppe tedesche, che avanzano verso il centro industriale di Charkow; mentre Leningrado s'avvia a diventare un mucchio di cenere e di sanguinose rovine. Z)<%w %% E* trascorso un anno da Pearl Harbor' Durante questi dodici mesi tremendi e grandiosi, il mondo ha assistito ad un miracolo terreno, che giammai si sarebbe immaginato, anche all'ombra delle piu' ottimistiche previsioni. 11 miracolo cioè' deH'invitta e sempre piu' invincibile po tenza degli Stati Stati Uniti, .che sono riusciti a capovolgere la situazione, a dare un nuovo corso alla storia della presente guerra ed a rialzare i penitenti destini degli Alleati. Tale miracolo s e' compiuto e continua meravigliosa mente a compiersi fra lo stupore degli amici e quello piu' an sioso e doloroso dei nemici, che nella sfolgorante e travol gente potenza dell'America, hanno già' scorto le colonne d'Èrcole, che hanno chiuso loro inesorabilmente la marcia verso la vittoria. **133 Si tratta di un miracolo decisivo e definitivo, compiuto nel giro di un anno; brevissimo lasso di tempo, in considera zione del già' fatto, di quello che si sta facendo e di tutto ciò', che e' in preparazione per il prossimo futuro. Basta dare uno sguardo al panorama mondiale del 7 Di cembre 1942, per avere una piu' o meno esatta percezione e visione dello sforzo americano, che e* unico nella storia di tutte le Nazioni, di tutte le genti e di tutte le guerre umane. Un anno fa, quando i gialli del Sol Levante commisero l'infame e proditorio gesto contro le navi e contro i possedi menti, su cui sventolava la Bandiera Stellata, il corso del con flitto era decisamente avverso e pericoloso per la causa al leata.

H gesto di Pearl Harbor doveva certamente avere i suoi logici e fatali sviluppi iniziali, che per un cumulo di ragioni volontarie ed involontarie, si sono piegati a tutto favore del l'aggressore, che e' passato da un successo all'altro; da una conquista all'altra e da una aggressione all'altra, con una cer ta facilita', ma con rilevanti perdite. Intanto l'America, vinta la prima impressione, che segue tutte le piu' insigni e piu' solenni infamie della storia; vinta la ripulsione morale provocata dal proditorio attacco nel Pa cifico, in una atmosfera di rinsaldata concordia e di travol gente unita* spirituale, nonché*^ di fède nella propria forza e nella giustizia della propria causa, si buttava anima e corpo in una preparazione ed in una organizzazione bèllica senza precedenti, spianandosi il cammino verso la rivincita, verso la riscossa, verso la giusta punizione. All'indomani di Pearl Harbor ed all'indomani delle di chiarazioni di guerre, che ne sono scaturite, ha avuto inizio nella Repubblica il miracolo, che s e' andato sviluppando giorno per giorno, costantemente e vittoriosamente. Oggi e' nel suo pieno e formidabile splendore e manda i suoi fenome nali riflessi sulle acque dei due Oceani, dove sono in terribile e tragico giuoco i destini non solo del nostro Paese, ma di tutto l'avvenire del mondo. Esplosione e conclusione piu' grandi di questo miracolo, e' la conquista rapida, che ricorda quelle di Cesare, dell'Afri ca Settentrionale Francese da parte dell America. Conquista che si deve considerare come un autentico capolavoro di pre parazione diplomatica, politica e militare; che ha rivelato di quale arcane e dinamiche forze creative ed organizzatrici, siano capaci gli Stati Uniti; di quali sforzi di volontà' siano capaci, quando si siano messa in testa una mèta da conse guire.

Della volontà* americana e' prudente avere la debita paura, perche* può* diventare all'occorrenza, piu* dura de! piu* infrangibile macigno ed i nostri nemici cominciano a constatarne i tremendi effetti, che sono ancora all'inizio. Quelli di domani saranno terrificanti e distruttivi addirittura. Sui Pacifico infatti, il nemico giallo e' sulla difensiva e da Midway, sta avendo ed incassando tali e tante batoste, che hanno cominciato a cancellare varie pifre de! conto americano di Pearl Harbor. Da Guadalcanal alla Nuova Guinea ed a Burma, i giap ponesi sono stati afferrati per la gola e mantenuti inesorabil mente in tale posizione dagli Alleati, ma in ispecial modo, dalle forze terrestri, aereee e navali americane, che non dan no oramai piu* loro tregua, sottoponendoli a perdite sangui nosissime e rendendo precarie alcune delle loro conquiste. Senza dubbio, nel Pacifico la situazione s e* capovolta; i giapponesi non sono piu* capaci di muovere un passo in a vanti, costretti ihvece a farne parecchi indietro. Nel Mediterraneo, il capovolgimento e' ancora piu' co lossale e piu' impressionante, e può' essere fonte d'impreve duti e straordinari sviluppi, che potranno avere una imprevi sta portata storica. La marcia delle legioni di Uncle Sam hanno assicurato agli Alleati, posizioni e vantaggi strategici e tattici d'impor tanza capitale ed hanno reso possibile la furiosa offensiva russa sulla fronte orientale, da Leningrado alle anse del Fiu me Don. Quello che il Presidente Roosevelt, con cauta modestia, ha voluto chiamare "Piccolo Secondo Fronte ', e* invece un Secondo Fronte di proporzioni gigantesche, che ha richiama to sulle sponde africane l'attenzione degli Dei vecchi e nuovi ed ha scombussolato tutti i piani avversari, iniettando nello stesso tempo, coraggio e fede a tutte le Nazioni Unite, che nella Marcia delle Legioni Americane, finalmente, scorgono l'alba di una nuova Era ed il prodromo della finale riscossa. N. H. Council1 Urges Defeat Of Strike Bill Committee Asks Senators To Vote Against Con nally Measure

The legislative committee of the New Haven Central Labor Council this week urged Senators John A. Danaher and Francis Maloney to vote agaisKt and to work to prevent the passage of the repressive anti strike bill passed by the House of Representatives last wek. Letters on the Smith-Connally Anti-Strike Bill were received at the last meeting of the Council. Dana her’s communication merely acknowl edged the receipt of the letter sent him by the C.L.C. urging him to vote against the bill when it returned to the Senate and to work for the defeat of the Poll-Tax. Maloney’s reply, however, stated that he voted for anti-strike bill as it passed in the Senate, and that he did so in the spirit of friendliness to labor. He further stated that he had received letters from other labor organizations urging him to oppose the measure, and that he asked these organizations to point out to him parts of the bill which they felt were unfair to labor. Delegates attending the meeting unanimously instructed the legisla tive committee to inform the Sena tor why they were opposed to the BUI. In the meantime the House, under the pretext of “curbing” John L. Lewis, passed the drastically amended Connally Bill, which included many of the worst proposals of the anti laborites in Congress. Only one of Connecticut’s rep resentatives was listed as voting for this measure—John D. Mc Williams, Republican, of the Sec ond District. Representatives Clare B. Luce, William J. Miller and B. J. Monkiewicz, voted against the biU. Major Ranulf Compton and Joseph Talbot, did not vote on the measure. All of Connecticut’s rep resentatives had been urged by the Conn. Federation of Labor, the Hartford and Bridgeport Central Labor Unions and the New Haven Council to vote against the Con naUy BUI in the House. Maloney stated in his letter to the New Haven C.L.C. that he was among those favoring the aboli tion of the poll tax. Danaher, who with Maloney voted against the poU tax in the Senate last year, is a member of the Judiciary sub-com mittee which received the House anti-tax poU tax biU, this week.
Vice-Pres. To Be Elected At Next Council Meeting

The New Haven Central Labor Council will nominate and elect a vice-president at its June 17 meet ing to fill the vacancy caused by Sen. Joseph T. Rourke’s enlistment in the Seabees. Rourke, in a letter to the C.L.C., thanked the Council for the farewell party it gave in his honor and for the going-away gift it presented to him. At the next meeting, Pres. Harold V. Feinmark will name a committee to revise the bylaws of the central body. This committee will submit proposed amendments to the Council at a future date. David Strauss, of Local 404, Hotel and Restaurant Employes, brought to the Council’s attention the matter of changing the by-laws. He pointed out that the laws made no provisions for electing successors to officers who re sign. The C.L.C. decided at the last meeting that it will go on the same schedule this summer as last. There will, therefore, be only one meeting each in July and August. The July and August meetings will be held on the first Thursday of the month. The September meeting will be held on the third Thursday. Mrs. Mae Grinnel and Miss Marie Frabisso were obligated as delegates from Local 20267, Office Employes. Hundreds of Bradley Field non coms of the three upper grades are planning to take advantage of the new amendment to the Service men’s Dependents Allowance Act which permits their dependents to receive substantial government benefits previously available only to family members of the other grades of enlisted men. A new simplified one-sheet de pendency certificate will help speed the monumental task of converting family allowances to larger sums as authorized in the amendment. More than 3,000,000 allowances now in effect will be re-examined to determine the extent of the de pendency and whether allowances will be increased. Dependents are receiving the new forms (WD form 630) and should fill them out as quickly as possible as they are regarded as evidence of dependency by the ODB and will furnish the information for author ization of increases to which they may be entitled under the amend

mem. Meanwhile, it was announced by Brig.-Gen. H. N. Gilbert, director of the Office of Dependency Benefits of the War Department, that checks will continue to be mailed to those who have been receiving them in the past, while the neces sary conversion will be effected through a streamlined procedure which has cut the time period from 36 to four hours. Checks will be for the old amounts until new accounts can be set up but any sums accrued (rep resenting the difference between the old and new amounts) will be included in the check starting off under the increased allowances. It

will take several months to com plete conversion of the millions of accounts. Dependents already receiving a family allowance need not make application for the increased bene fits. The ODB has already set up procedures for converting accounts of those eligible for the increased amounts. Unnecessary letters and inquiries will only delay the work, Gen. Gilbert explained. Under the old arrangement there were two classes of dependents, class A, which included wife, child and former wife divorced to whom alimony was being paid, and class B, which included dependent par ents, brothers, sisters and grand children under certain conditions. Class A remains unchanged. A new class B-l includes parents, brothers, and sisters who are de pendent on the soldier for their chief support, and class B, which includes the same persons when they are dependent upon the sol dier for only a substantial portion of their support. Payments under class B is fixed at $37 while al lowances for B-l dependents varies.

Staff, technical and master ser geants who had been receiving monetary allowance in lieu of quar ters for their dependents may choose either to continue the al lowances in conjunction with a class E allotment of pay, or to dis continue them in favor of a family allowance. In either case the money will be sent direct to the depen dents by the ODB. From now on, however, no monetary allowances in lieu of quarters will be author ized.

In queste ultime settimane, il mondo ha potuto assistere a degli improvvisi mutamenti di scena deH’undecima ora, in alcune Nazioni sino ad ieri spalleggianti il regime nazista e fonte non indifferente, di aiuti materiali alia Germania, a tut to detrimento degli Alleati. I mutamenti di palese opportunismo, e non di sincera Conversione o convinzione, sono valsi pero’ a farle ammette re alia prossima Conferenza delle Nazioni Unite di San Fran cisco, che avra’ inizio il 25 Aprile. Codeste Nazioni nulla hanno fatto a favore della causa alleata, per ricevere il dono di tanto cospicuo privilegio e po tervi sedere accanto a quelli altri Paesi, per ricevere benefici ed autorita’, che non hanno mai meritati; che anzi, hanno de meritato, allorche’ con gli aiuti ininterrottamente fatti afflui re in Germania, hanno causato la perdita di molte vite nelle file armate degli Alleati. Cio’ facendo, si sono avvalse del velo di una neutralita’ non neutrale, per nascondere uno stato di guerra alimentato alia macchia. Eppure il tardivo gesto di contrizione e’ stato preso co me oro di diciotto carati, e domani si metteranno nelle condi zioni favorevoli ed appropriate, di far sentire la loro voce e di fendere e'propugnare i propri interessi nella futura organizza zione della pace e nella sistemazione del* mondo, che emerge ra’ dalla guerra. Mentre pero’ Ie porte della Conferenza di San Francisco si sono aperte per farvi entrare anche le Nazioni di cui sopra, si vogliono invece tenere serrate per 1’Italia co-belligerante, che dal 1943vs’e’ acquistati cospicui e pogitivi titoli di bene merenza nei riguardi degli Alleati. L’Italia, e’ storia di ieri, e fltata la prima Nazione legata al carro di Hitler, che con vindi i cc gesto liberatore, ha tagliato la catena della servitu’; ha a perto le sue porte e le sue braccia agli Alleati, dando la piu’ chiara e piu’ lampante prova della sua buona volonta’ di rifar si moralmente e politicamente, e di diventare un efficace fat tore di cooperazione sper la causa alleata, che e’ diventata la sua propria causa. L’ltalia ha compiuto tale solenne gesto in una epoca in cui le fortune militari della Germania erano in piena possan za, ed Hitler era ancora padrone di quasi tutta l’Europa con tinentale. Altre Nazioni invece, si sono affrettate a cambiar faccia, ora che i fati del Nazismo sono irrevocabilmente segna ti, ed il suo crollo e’ ormai quistione di giorni. L’ltalia, favorendo la marcia alleata e passando nel cam | po opposto da quello iniziale, ha inferto alia potenza della Germania il primo grave colpo, che e’ riuscito fatale, e dal ^ quale non s’e’ piu’ potuta rialzare, se non per cadere nell’abis j. so della sconfitta.

II tramPnto della Stella di Hitler, e’ cominciato appunto dal giorno, in cui le forze degli Alleati sbarcarono in Sicilia; in quel giorno un nuovo capitolo s’iniziava nella storia di questa Seconda Guerra Mondiale, e lo aveva iniziato Thalia. La qua le col suo cambiamento, aveva cancellato le stigmate del suo passato recente, rendendo alia causa della democrazia i'l pm’ segnalato dei servigi ed alia vittoria delle Nazioni Unite un al tro grande servigio. Che sarebbe piu’ che ingiusto ed inumano non ricordare oggi, in cui T Italia ha bisogno di giustizia e di comprensione, ed ha bisogno di un trattamento migliore e del riconoscimento equo di quel che ha fatto e di quel che sta facendo, per aprirsi il varco nei ranghi delle Nazioni Unite.

Coloro che oggi perorano la causa dell’Italia al cospetto del tribunale della storia, non chiedono privilegi di sorta; non domandono cose impossibili o irrealizzabili; domandono sem plicemente e modestamente un po’ di giustizia; domandono un po’ di umanita*; domandono che nel rigurgito delle passio ni, non debbano soltanto prevalere gli egoismi eccessivi; gli odi vecchi e nuovi; lo spirito feroce di vendetta e le idiosin crasie delle sistematiche persecuzioni verso i piu’ deboli. Ecco perche’ i maggiori appelli vengono fatti all’Ameri ca; ecco perche’ tutte le speranze per una piu’ equa giustizia all'ltalia, si concentrano verso 1’America; perche’ 1’America e’ la sola Nazione nel mondo caotico e disorientato dalle pas sioni, che e’ libera nei suoi giudizi; che e’ esente da passati compromettenti; che e’ immune da pericolosi preconcetti e da viete pregiudiziali. L’America ha ben delineato il suo idea le, e ben precisata la causa che sta difendendo e deve far trion fare; e ne’ e’ consumata da appetiti che devs soddisfare, o ac~ cecata da altre mire egemoniche da imporre. II nostro Paese, fortunatamente, si sa mantenere sereno. imperturbato ed imperturbabile in tanto disordine spirituale del mondo; la sua feconda calma e’ la stessa; il suo giudizio e la sua comprensione piu’ eccelsi e piu’ universali. Codesta pre rogativa dell’America in questo turbinoso momento della st > r’a, e’ un buon augurio ed e’ una salda garenzia per tutti i po poli della terra di buona volonta’, e che desiderano davvero iniziare la loro resurrezione all’ombra della Democrazia. Tra questi popoli, quello italiano e’ stato uno dei primis simi a dimostrare la sua buona volonta’ di ripigliare le sue tra dizioni democratiche e di riallacciarsi sinceramente alia sua storia. GOPS SWEEP ELECTION INAUGURATING TOWN CHARTER FORM GOVERNMENT
BESTOR MADE CHAIRMAN TOWN’S FIRST COUNCIL

Dr. Eugent L. Bestor of Mount ain Avenue, for several years chairman of the non- existent Board of Finance, was elected chairman of Bloomfield’s first Town Council at an organization meeting of the new board’s mem ber’s Monday evening, September 8. At the meeting Town Manager W. T. Williamson was re appointed to his position. Attorney Ernest W. McCormick of Kenmore Rd. was appointed towns attorney, suc ceeding Attorney John P. Faude. Andrew E. Carr of Marguerite Ave. was re-appointed tax col lector. The firm of Hadfield, Roth well, Soule and Coates of Hartford was reappointed town auditors. Town Manager Williamson was named acting town treasurer, pending the appointment of a per manent appointee to the position. The council voted to hold meet ings on the third Tuesday of each month. These meetings, it was an nounced, will be open to the public.

SGT. BEAUPRE GIVEN NEW FLIER AWARD Technical Sgt. Ralph E. Beau pre, Jr., was one of the members of the 6th Bomb Group based on Tinian, recently awarded Oak Leaf Clusters to the Air Medals. The organization participated in every major B-29 effort against Japan, including daylight precis ion strikes, incendiary attacks, technical blows in support of the Okinowa campaign, and mining efforts which bottled up Japan’s Navy and Merchant Marine. Sgt. Beaupre, son of Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Beaupre, Sr., 769 Blue Hills Avenue, has been in the service since August 3, 1943.

TWO REGISTRANTS ARE INDUCTED INTO ARMY William Vincent Starr, of Dud ley Town Road, and Edward David Boudreau, of 486 Tunxis Avenue, were inducted into the Army in September and are now receiving preliminary training. Donald Reid, son of Mr. and Mrs. Lorin H. Reid, of Bloomfield Ave., has enlisted in the Marine Corps and is undergoing training at Parris Island, N.C.

Una Guerra Necessaria E' quella contro la fame; contro la obbrobriosa ed umi liante schiavitù' della fame, che e' la maggiore e peggiore ne mica dell umanità, ed e un solenne e tremendo affronto con trq la civiltà', ed una feroce rampogna contro coloro che na vigano nell'abbondanza. In questo momento nero della storia del mondo, a causa della guerra teste' chiusasi, vi sono decine di milioni di esse ri umani, innocenti e disgraziatissimi, che muoiono letteral mente di fame, vittime del piu' atroce e piu' detestabile de stino. Contro la fame c'e' un solo rimedio: la carità' degli al tri; il senso della solidarietà' fraterna. Se queste due forze non agiscono a tempo ed adeguatamente, l'olocausto, l'im menso, doloroso olocausto e' sicuro, e sempre in piu' grandi proporzioni. Codesta e' la terza guerra necessaria, che i piu' fortunati su questa terra debbono saper combattere e vincere, a favore dei meno fortunati; a favore delle interminabili schiere di af famati e di sofferenti, piombati senza loro colpa, nella piu' deprimente delle degradazioni umane, che avvilisce il mora le, come fiacca il fisico. Non si possono leggere e ne' ascoltare le notizie, che pro vengono d oltre Atlantico, dal Vecchio Continente, culla del la civiltà' del mondo, senza sentire una! forte stretta al cuore, e senza essere oppressi dalla paurosa visione di quello che di tragico vi si sta verificando. L'America grande, potente, cavalleresca e generosa, che non e' rimasta mai insensibile al grido di dolore ed agli ap pelli di soccorso, attraverso la sua storia, non può' permettere in nome dell'umanità', che l'olocausto diventi addirittura una strage, e che si compii sino all'ultimo. L'Ameiica sino ad oggi, ha dato generosamente e cospicuamente! a tutte le popolazio ni affamate della terra, evitando maggiori disastri e piu' este se ed intense sofferenze fisiche e morali. Ma l'entità' delle vittime e dei loro immediati bisogni e' tale, che non e' sufficiente l'opera già' svolta. Bisogna ed ur gentemente, aumentare la generosità' e gli aiuti, e prima che fosse troppo tardi. L'alimentazione in certe Nazioni europee e scesa all'ultimo livello della deficienza; non può piu essere abbassata, senza togliere al simulacro della vita rimasta, il suo estremo anelito, quello che costituisce il solo transito dal la vita alla morte. Questo e' il quadro doloroso ed asfissiante, che in questi giorni ha richiamato in modo piu' particolare, l'attenzione e la considerazione del Presidente Truman e di altri alti esponenti del Governo Federale, che hanno lanciato attraver so il Paese un vibrante grido di allarme, richiamandolo ai do veri umani, che bisogna assolvere, per non venire meno alle piu' sante tradizioni, che hanno sempre fatto piu' grande, piu' benemerita e piu' luminosa la storia americana. Le condizioni portate alla considerazione degli ambienti ufficiali di Washington, sono cosi serie, che il Presidente s e rivolto all'ex Presidente Hoover, un esperto in materia, per che' si rechi in Europa per un sopraluogo, mentre nello stesse tempo, ha raccomandato agli Americani di prepararsi per qualche lieve sacrificio, che deve tornare il piu' gradito, per che esso saivera delle vite umane e renderà meno paurosa e meno tragica la situazione in certe nazioni europee. Codesta e' una crociata, che innalzerà' ai piu' eccelsi fa stigi la grandezza spirituale dell'America; ed e' anche una cro ciata, che non costa troppo agli Americani, i quali rimangono sempre nell abbondanza e nella posizione privilegiata di esse re oggi i piu' fortunati sulla terra. E la vera grandezza morale di un popolo si rivela, allor ché' tra il fulgore della sua ricchezza e della sua potenza ma teriale, sa stendere la mano fraterna agli altri popoli meno fortunati e colpiti da una immensa sventura. !L CORRIERE

Quick Picture Of Taft-Hartley Law Almost Every Phase Of Labor-Management Relationship Changed — Read This In Conjunction With Leading Story On This Page Here is a quick picture of how the Taft-Hartley law invades or ganized labor’s traditional rights and restricts its activities and operations:

“FREE ENTERPRISE 1— Bans the closed shop. Con tracts in existence before June 23 providing for a closed shop con tinue in force and may be renewed before the 60 days following June 23 but only for one year. (Effec tive Aug. 22.) 2— Bans the union shop unless a majority of workers covered by the contract—not a majority of those voting—vote in favor of it. (Effective Aug. 22.) 3— Bans the expulsion of a member from a union except on the grounds of non-payment of dues or fees. This is seen as an open invitation to company spies and restricts the union’s right to discipline a member who provokes trouble. (Effective Aug. 22.) 4— Bans a dues checkoff under threat of $10,000 fine and a year in jail against the employer unless he receives a written request by the em ploye authorizing the deduction. (Ef fective Aug. 22.) 5— Bans maintenance of member ship except on the same terms as the union shop. (Effective Aug. 22.) 6— Bans preferential hiring. This prohibition, however, will probably be open to court interpretation. (Effec tive Aug. 22.) 7— Bans collective bargaining by foremen. (Effective Aug. 22.) INJUNCTIONS COMING 8— Bans all forms of secondary boycotts and nullifies the Norris-La Guardia Act which has been inter preted to uphold the right of a union to tx>ycott where the intention is to compel collective bargaining, better wages, hours, etc. (Effective Aug. 22.) 9— Bans jurisdictional strikes and requires the NLRB to seek in junctions against jurisdictional strikes, secondary boycotts, and strikes to obtain union recognition. An employer can more easily ob tain an injunction when the NLRB, a federal agency, asks for it than if he applies for one himself. (Ef fective Aug. 22.) 10— Bans union expenditures or contributions in connection with either Presidential or Congressional elections. This is the section which would prohibit a dues-supported union paper from supporting or opposing a particular candidate, political policy or platform. (Ef fective now.) 11— Permits the Attorney General 'to obtain 80-day injunctions against so-called national emergency strikes which could endanger the national health and safety. Picketing and strike benefits would be banned during the injunction. If mediation is unsuccess ful the workers would vote on the em ployer’s last offer. (Effective now.) 12— Bans strikes against the gov ernment under penalty of losing civil service status and become ineligible for federal employment for three years. (Effective now.) “MADE WORK” 13— B a n s “featherbedding” or “made work.” This section could be construed to prohibit a guaranteed work week, paid vacations or even rest periods. It could permit an em ployer to claim that the work done by 20 men could be done by 15 and there by fire the “extra” five. (Effective Aug. 22.) 14— Bans strikes within 60 days of contract expiration. This could invite employers to initiate the worst kind of anti-union activities during the las1 60 days because the union could not walk out in protest. (Effective Aug. 22.) (Continued on Page Two)

High Living Costs Compel Workers To Use Up Their Savings WASHINGTON (LP A)—Indus trial profits continue to hit all-time record highs; workers’ wartime sav ings have been depleted by more than 50%; unemployment is growing. That was the ominous picture of the state of the nation’s economy given by government and private economists last week. A survey of the consolidate net in come of 228 industrial manufacturers made by the N. Y. Times showed that for the first quarter of 1947 the net income rose 305% from $147,665,103 for the first three months of last year to $597,553,217. At the same time the U. S. Com merce Dept, announced that “pub licly reported cash dividend pay ments by U. S. corporations amounted to a record high of $1 117,500,000 for the first quarter of 1947. This is 21% more than the $920,800,000 paid in the first quarter of 1946.” The report ac counted for only 60% of all cash dividends paid; corporations like Ford Motor Co. made no public an nouncement of their dividends. Individual savings in liquid form dropped sharply durifig the first quar ter of 1947, the Securities and Ex change Commission discloses. Indiv iduals saved $1.4 billion during the three months. “This rate of saving was less than half that in the last quarter of 1946 and the lowest since 1940,” said the SEC.. 80th Congress Driving Nation Without Brakes Rep. Douglas Analyzes Record, And Finds People The Losers WASHINGTON — (FP) — The 80th Congress has utterly failed the American people and is riding along without brakes on the roller coaster of inflation, Rep. Helen Gahagan Douglas (D, Cal.) told the 38th an nual conference of the Natl. Assn, for the Advancement of Colored People last week. The California progressive as sailed the GOP-controlled Congress for its program of making the rich richer and the poor poorer, which she summarized as: “1, cut taxes for the rich, 2, break the back of labor, and 3, destroy the agencies of government set up to protect and promote the welfare of the people. “Rising prices, housing, FEPC, health, education, development of nat ural resources, anti-poll tax law, anti lynch bill and civil liberties are not the concern of this Congress,” she continued. “But they are the concern of every family in America. They particularly affect the Negro family. “An economic slump will come down on the Negro people like a ton of bricks for they are among the first to be discriminated against.” Mrs. Douglas attacked the hyster ical red-baiting in word and deed by the 80th Congress, saying: “This Congress, while creating a frenzy of fear over communism, shows in amendment after amendment, attached to legislation which it passes, that it has no real understanding of totali tarian methods and rushes often with arms outstretched to embrace them in its frenzy.” Housing Bill Still Stymied WASHINGTON—(FP) — Some 700 delegates representing 35 national organizations lobbied on Capitol Hill last week for passage of the Taft-El lender-Wagner long-range housing bill, and heard Sen. Robert A. Taft (R, O.) suggest the bill might have to be modified in order to clear the 80th Congress. Delegates from both AFL and CIO were among the hundreds buttonholing senators and representatives during the day, set aside as Fight For Hous ing Day by the sponsoring groups, to seek passage of the bill. It was model ed on the measure which passed the Senate unanimously a year ago but was bottled up by the Housing bank committee in the dying days of the 79th Congress. Taft and Sen. Allen J. Ellender (D, La.) said builders and real estate groups had slandered the bill with “misleading propaganda.” that soaring living costs have com pelled workers to exhaust their sav ings.

Report of Joseph M. Rourke, Secy-Treas. Of The Connecticut Federation of Labor

It is a pleasure for me to report that the Connecticut*'* Federation of Labor is growing day by day and that dur ing the past year several thousand wage earners in the State of Connecticut became a part of the American Fed eration of Labor. There is absolutely no reason why the Connecticut Federation of Labor cannot double its mem bership if every officer of every local union would take an active part in the organization of workers into A. F. of L. unions. Although we are, slowly but surely, adding new members to our ranks, it must be borne in mind that as our membership grows our problems grow too- As these local unions are organized they must be properly serviced; effective grievance and negotiating committees must be set up to take care of the needs of these workers- I urge each and every one of you to take a more active part in the; growth of the American Federation of Labor in Connect- ; icut. Do not be satisfied by taking care of your own local j union. Give a helping hand to others. Preach the gospel j of the A. F. of L., and make every effort to see that every worker in the State of Connecticut is organized.

The 80th Congress does not rep resent the working men and work ing women of America. They have failed to curb inflation. They have weakened our Social Security law. They have failed to provide ade quate housing. They have weak ened the labor movement in general and it is up to each and every one of us to go out and work for the de feat of the six Congressmen from

Connecticut who voted for the pas sage of the Taft-Hartley law and other legislation that represented the views of the vested interests in this country. The failure of the 80th Congress to enact various pro gressive measures sponsored by the American Federation of Labor, in the long run. will play Into the hands of the reactionaries and the Communists. The record of the 80th Con gress on price control is one of complete inaction, in spite of the fact that wage increases have been ' Wiped out by the uncontrolled rise iri living costs, and the pressure is continuing to mount. As finally passed by Congress the measure to admit 200,000 dis placed persons from Europe dis criminated grossly and unjustly against the Catholics and the Jews.

If there is to be no repetition of the 80th Congress’ record, organized labor must take an active interest in the 1948 national, state and local elections. The 15 million members of organized labor and their fam ilies and their friends must exer cise their democratic right and ob ligation to regain the rights which the Congress and various State Legislatures have taken from them. Labor can and must make itself felt in the coming general election. Central Labor Unions In my report at the 1947 Conven tion of the Connecticut Federation of Labor, I stated that in order o have a strong State Federation of Labor, it was necessary to have equally effective central labor unions. I am sorry to report that from what I can observe, our cen tral labor unions have not been strengthened since last year. It is my humble opinion that we must do everything in our power to build up our central labor unions if we expect to be a strong force in our various communities. I say

without tear of contradiction that all local union officers who do not see to it that they have delegates from their local unions in attend ance at central labor union meet ings are derelict in their duty. The strength of our labor movement lies in our Central Labor Unions. It may well be that certain officers of local unions for some reason or another do not wish to affiliate with or send delegates to central la bor unions. This is a gross mistake. There is no valid excuse. Every A. F. of L. local union in Connecti cut should become a part of the Central labor union in its respective area. For that reason and others, the Executive Board of the Con necticut Federation of Labor is bringing in a recommendation that there will be a vice-president from each central labor union area in Connecticut. I hope that if this amendment to the Constitution goes through, the particular officers elected will do everything in their power to build up the strength of the Central Labor Union in their {Articular area. I

We should have central labor] unions in the Derby, Ansonia, Shel ton area; Bristol, Willimantic, Dan ielson and several other cities. There is no reason why a few offi cers of local unions and the State Federation of Labor should carry the entire burden of the labor movement in the State of Connecti cut. I beg of you, if your local union is not an active participant in your central labor union area, please make a pledge that you will become a part of the central labor union in your city or town.

Mary A. Cannady obtained a ver dict of $5000. vs. Mathew and Lydia W. Lynch, at the rccent term of court in McLeod Co., as damages for inhuman and cruel treatment at their hands. The plaintiff, who is only eighteen years of age, was to ken from the ^Orphan's Asylum at St. Paul in 1871 by the Lynch's, and stayed with them two years when she ran away. While she was with them she was kicked, beaten, bruised, wounded, struck with stove lifters, compelled to work at improper labor at unseasonable hours and was so crippled and broken down in health that she became insane and was con fined in the asylum at St. Peter for two years. A State Farmers' Institute will be held in this citj on Friday and Satur day, Feb. 4th and 5th, commencing at 10 o'clock a. rn. Supt. O. C. Gregg, with his entire staff of assistants, in cluding Prof. Shaw, Prof. Carlyle and Theo. Louis, the well-known hog man, will be present.

This is a meeting in which every body is interested, because there is no question of such vital importance to the business interests of the county as agriculture. Everything depeads on the productions of the soil.

The fact that prices are low and profits are very small in almost every line, is what calls for better methods and more skillful practices to enable us to compete with conditions before us. The Farmers' Institute is the medium through which improvement, skill and enterprise, can prepare us to meet the emergencies of the times.

The Institute instructors are those who have faced the difficulties they have overcome the obstructions that so often meet us at every turn, and are therefore able to render assistance to the discouraged, give valuable advice to those seeking information and put up the danger signals for the venture some so that our agricultural meth ods may be improved to the degree of all other branches of business at the present day.
The following are some of the many features of the Institute work this winter:

Cultivation and care of the soil. Ro tation of crops. Conservation of moisture in the soil. Clover for stock and the farm. Manure and how to get the benefits. Growing corn and potatoes, and many other products on the farm.
Feeds and feeding of dairy stock. Butter making and creamery talks. Handling a dairy herd in winter. Stables, ventilation, stalls, etc.
Stock breeding, feeding, handling and marketing. Selection of dairy stock, by an expert. Learning how to know the good dairy cow when one sees her.

Christopher Wiik, 50 years old, a blacksmith at Belview, and residing with his family of nine children on the farm of his son one and one half miles south of Belview, turned up missing at his home last Thursday morning. An hour later his body covered with mud, and his face covered with the same kind of earth, was found on the farm of A. D. N. South worth half a mile south of Belview. Wiik was very dead.

The demise of Wiik will be point ed to by temperance orators as a horrible example of the foe which they are combating. Wiik, with his son-in-law, Andrew Harried, who had come over from Swedes Forest, had been drinking nearly all of Wednesday, and late in the afternoon the former was badly in toxicated. Shortly after 8 o'clock that night Wiik succeeded in getting two bottles filled with alcohol and started for home with his son-in-law, whose team was to convey the two men. The team was started on the jump, and when but a few rods from the village windmill the whiffle trees became detached from the wagon, Harried was pulled out of the vehicle by the running team, and after he had lost his hat and ploughed a long furrow in the road with his body, all trace of him for the time being was lost.

DUKE AND HEIRESS COMING WEDDINC OF MARLBOROUGH AND MISS VANDERBILT. ENGAGEMENT INTERESTS ALL Lineages Compared—Both are Sprang Front Strong Men—-John Churchill And Cornelius Vanderbilt Sit Side bv Side—Lead ers in Their Time.

The news of the day yesterday for all studients of history, as well as for all lovers of the doings of the great and wen.lty. was the an nouncement of the engagement of thegreal-grand-daughter of Cornelius Vanderbilt to tin* descendant in the ninth generation of Johu Churchill, conqueror of France, ruler in all but name of England, and the first Duke of Marlborough, says the Philadel phia Times. The two young people themselves were presumably less in terested in the various reflections which the event will call forth than other people; but there can be little denying that a more noteble en gagement has not byen announced in America since Jerome Bonapart told a surprised and excited world that he desired to take to wife Miss Ei z.-ib'oth PiittCH’on, of Bs.ltiniorp To begin with, the destination of the great American fortunes is be coming a matter of public concern, especially on account of. the tendency of their Inheritors, when women, to marry foreginers of noble birth— which suggests that in a few years from now political economists and sociologists will probably be study ing some new tendencies which have established themselves in counter balance of this tendency, for it is the inevitable law of human affairs that they prepetuallv seek to establish a stable equilibrium and never suc ceed. An.1 now that an enormous slice of the Vanderbilt money will go to England to restore and maintain

the State of Blenheim, it begins to look as though it were time for the first indication of reaction to set in. But that apart, the contrast and comparison of the great statesman and general of Queen Anna’s reign, and the great railroad man of the nineteenth century, is most inter esting. There is not space to make it here in full, but it has no end of suggestions. CHt RCHII.n ANI) VANDERBII.T For Cornelius Vanderbilt is not altogether dwarfed when he is placed beside John Churchill. True, Churchill was much the greater man. Not only lmd he the advantages of figuring in battle and parliaments and cabinets which provides the whole magnificent pageant of the history of a. time for a back-ground —and not only was he cast as a chief actor in an epoch of peculiar dignity and splendor—but in spite of his avarice and his time-serving qualities he did have that greatness of soul which distinguishes the few majestic figures in the world’s rec ords. Cornelius Vanderbilt, on the I other hand, was scarcely a figure in j history at all, as it is written by the j drum and trumpet historian, and, as f >r greatness of soul, if he had if he was never given a chance to show it Yet lse had one faculty that Marlborough had, and it was what made him the first master of the science of transportation that the world has seen, and but till the present time the greatest—the faculty of altering and ordering condition according to his far-seeing sense, disregarding the objections and intepositlons of smaller-minded men. Vanderbilt, in a material way, had genius—and genius means imagination. And John would not have been ashamed of Cornelius— not by any means. He had most profound respect for money, had John. He took it from women, which is what Cornelius, with his

manly Dutch blood, wonld never have done, even in John Churchill’s depraved day, not if he had died a pauper for refusing it. And then, too, though he was born a gentle man, John Churchill had a very bare outlook of it at first us a young man, and if he had not had a sister whom tlie Duke of York peculiarly delighted to honor—which, by the way, in those days was not thought so much discredit to a lady ns we now suppose—he -might never have worn a sword. So that he knew what it was to rise in the world. And in fine one thing is probable: that Cornelius Vanderbilt could have commanded an army better than John Churchill could have built up the New York Central Rail road. i HE VOT'N’O PEOPLE. But now to look at the young people—Miss Consuela Vanderbilt is the daughter of William K. Vander bilt and the grand-daughter of the late William H. Vanderbilt. She is about 18 years old, vr-’ tall, very vivacious and quite good looking, with dark hair and a pronounced brunette complexion. She is heiress to one of the greatest fortunes in the world and has only one care in life, that her father and mother are divorced. Of course it can scarcely be expected that so young a girl should have as yet pronounced character istics, but her friends say she has much sweetness of disposition and charm of manner, and her executive ability lias already been tested. As is always the case with children of parents with great fortunes, she has been most carefully educated and trained to understand the responsibilities of her station, and to act as the mis tress of a grea t establishment. The young Duke of Marlborough is really one of the most promising of the young noblemen of England. Far from following in the footsteps of his father, whose reputation need not be recalled, he lias already made his entry into politics, and intends to devote himself to a public career. He was made Hie mover of the ad dress of the Lords in reply to the Queen’s speech on the opening of the

present Parlament,an honor general ly conferred upon the most distin guished and promising of the young er members of the party in power. He is very young, having been born on November 13, 1871, so he is still short of his 24th birthday; his school was Eton and his university was Cambridge, where he did very well at his books, and also polo and cricket in a manner to satisfy con- { temporary requirements. He is also said to ha ve—heought to have—good taste in pictures, books and china, altogether he is likely to do himself and country credit. He is not likely to turn out a new Benconsibid or Salisbury, but he may do as ivell as his grandfather, who was Lord Lieutenant of Ireland under Beacons- ; field, and that will be doing infinitely , better than any member of the four hundred whom Miss Vanderbilt might have married would ever have dreamed of doing. < THE SPENCEIt-CUUKCIin.I.S The young Duke, Charles-Kichard John Spencer-Churchill his name is, the ninth Duke of Marlborough and twelfth Earl of Sunderland, is really a Spencer by decent and Churchill 1 only by royal warrant. THE GOLD BRICK SCHEME A FORMER RESIDENT OF PINE BLUFF ARRESTED IN ST. LOUIS. Allen J. Wine and His Wife, Known Here as Mrs. Peters, Charged with Attempting to De fraud in the Old Way.

Thursday’s Republic gives a rather sensational account of the arrest of Alien J. Wine and his wife, who was known here as Mrs. Peters, and for some time was the trimmer in the millinery department of the Kauf man Bazaar. After leaving here Mrs. Peters married Wine and they rented a small house in St. Louis and lived there until the cyclone de stroyed it and a part o‘f their be longings. They afterwards met J. C. Kallal, who runs a furnishing goods store and there the Wines traded occasionally. To the pro prietor of this store was unfolded a mining scheme that rivaled the most dazzling ever loid in the Arabian Nights. The story teller owned a mine in Alaska,and through the kind offices of Black Antelope, whom he at one time had befriended, he was enabled to bring away from the great Northwest untold wealth. The miner refused to pawn these treas ures, consisting of ore and precious stones, because he feared that it would give the snap away, but took the merchant into his confidence and wanted $165 for the purpose of re turning, to the land of Black Ante lope and being allowed to pick up millions in diamonds. They showfed their wealth to the intended victim. It was in a tin box and looked re markably like a gold brick and a variety of precious stones. 'j» The store keeper had advertised to sell his store and expected to start for Alaska when he told the police about the scheme and they investi gated the matter. Wine’s wealth was worth about $4.50. Both hus band and wife were arrested and placed in jail. Mr. Kaufman, of the Bazaar, was seen this morning by our reporter and stated that he had nothing to say except that he believed Mrs. Wine is insane. It is understood that her mother has been in an asylum for years. STOLE A PASS BOOK

INQUIRY REPORT, OFFICIAL DOCUMENT SAID TO HAVE BEEN DELIVERED TO ADIMIRAL SICARD YESTERDAY. Thought the Admiral Will Examine the Document and Forward It to Washington Today. Key West, March 21.—Judge Ad vocate Marix, of the court of inqui ry, came ashore at 3 o’clock this af ternoon, accompanied by an armed orderly, from the Iowa, who carried a bulky package of the documents, which was handed over to Rear Ad miral Sicard. It is believed the documents are the full findings of the court of inquiry. Lieutenant Commander Marix, when questioned on this subject, refused either to deny or confirm, but an officer from the Iowa said the documents were the long-expected report on the Maine disaster. It is presumed that if these docu ments are the anxiously-expected report they will be taken to Wash ington tomorrow by Lieutenant Commander Marix. Alderman Meyer gave notice that in future he would vote to sustain any veto the Mayor should present on tiiis question until the Water Companycomplied with itscontract, that in the future, uuless its water service was much better, he would not vote to pay its hills, or scarcely any part of them. USE OF BICYCLES IN CHINA.

Much Hied toy Foreigners in the Cit ies on tbe Coast. Consul General Goodnow at Shang I jhn,i reports tb.s.t ttie tr&ds in bicycles in China increased very rapidly during the past season and gives promise of even more rapid expansion during the season now opening. Prior to 1897 very few bicycles were in use on the Chinese coast, while now, in all ports where cycling is possible, the habit is becoming almost universal among for eigners. “Society here,” says the consul gen eral, “is dominated by the English,who claim that no man or woman can hope to endure this climate unless they de vote considerable part of each and every day, rain or shine, to outdoor exercise and sportn. Horseback riding has been universal among those who can afford that luxury; others take long walks daily. The bicycle appeals to all—rich, middle class and poor— and all classes are using it. The city of Shanghai is perfectly flat, and some of the roads in and immediately around the settlements are good. Each na tionality has generally bought wheels made in their own home country, and at first the English wheel, with brake, mud guard and heavy tubing, predom inated. I believe that now the more graceful and lighter American wheels have the larger sale. “No wheels are maeje in China, nor do I believe they can be made here. No wheels are brought in on a less rate of duty than tho#e from the United States. There are no native roads, as we understand that term. There are narrow paths for the pedestrian or the horseman, but generally not wide enough for vehicles; dusty in dry weather, muddy ic. wet, and rough all the time, they are practically impossi ble for wheeling. “Few Chinese have as yet taken to the wheel. Their clothing is not adap ted to exercise, and especially not to the wheel. No man above the coolie class, in middle and northern China, appears in public otherwise than in long clothes—i. c., an outer petticoat reaching to his angles. The few young Chinamen who rt£e here either leave oil this outer gafiaent temporarily or turn it up and fasten it at the waist. They also bring thj long queue of hair over the shoulder and fasten it at the waistband. Their trousers are as long and full and baggy as the average woman’s divided skirt in America, and I havo not yet seen a Chinaman ride without a chain guard to keep the trousers from catching and tearing. No Chinese women ride. I have seen it stated in American and English pa pers that it is now common in Shang hai for Chinese ladies to ride in the streets. Nothing can be farther from the truth. The Chinese women of the better class are kept in absolute seclu sion from men other than those of their family. This rule has not been broken in the slightest degree. Even in the missionary schools, where the daugh ters of the merchants and mandarins are educated, no man Is allowed to see the girls. “The customs report of 1S97 shows that in many Important products the imports from the United States have Increased at the expense of imports fiom other nations. We are nearer to the market, freights are lesstaecording ly, and the feeling of the Chinese peo ple is more friendly to Americans than to the people of any other nation. Now is the time to push our trade on this roast. I do not believe that any other method will give better or more per manent results than an exposition of United States products at Shanghai.”

The American Ragle voiced his sen timents on the 4tli of July, 1776, in tho great and only Declaration of Inde pendence, but he did not take shape for several weeks after that day. Immedi ately after the declaration had been, read to the Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia at that time, ;; resolution was passed creating Benja min Franklin, John Adams and Thom oa Jefferson, all woll-known gentle men, to be a committee to prepare a seal of the United States. On the 10th day of August they reported, bringing in a combination consisting principally of a Goddess of Liberty, a Goddess of Justice, and an Eye of Providence with a very small and insignificant eagle in one corner of the device. Incidentally also on the device was the legend, “E Pluribus Unum.” Although the eagle at this time was not much of a bird, It still seemed to the Colonial Congress men that something was wrong with the report of the committee,, and the seal had such a bad effect that the re port was laid on the table, where it stayed until 1779. In March of that year it took a fresh start with a new committee, but nothing was done until 1781, when among several designs sub mitted was one from William Barton of Philadelphia, who made the eagle prominent, and described the bird as emblematic of sovereignty. Another design was furnished by Charles Tom son, secretary of Congress, and the last design, and the one finally adopted, was endorsed “Mr. Barton’s improve ments on tho secretary’s device,” which made some changes in Mr. Tomson’a designs, and this was adopt ed June 20, 1782, at which time tho great American Eagle made its first and genuino appearance In the history of the great republic ho is under a pci • potual engagement to scream for.

Most of the army mules In Cuba were fitted with the Mexican aparejo, which Is to be preferred to the saddle with "tree and sawbuck.” It consists first o1 two or more thick felt blankets, folded large enough to nearly cover the mule from shoulder to rump. Over this la placed a huge pair of leather bags united by a broad band of the same material, tho cavi ties stuffed with soft hay. This is girthed to tho mule by a cinch nearly a foot in width, which la drawn as tightly as possible by* a strong man, pulling with both hands, and with a foot against the a^Jpial’a ribs to give him a greater purchase. On each side of the spine tho articles to bo carried are placed and lashed by a ropo about fifty feet in length, which has at one end a broad webbing belt to pass under the belly as was done with the others. Anothor “squeezing" Is given and the rope is crossed In dif ferent directions over the load, tight ened at every crossing, and finally fas tened in a knot loosed by one pull. “Packing" is a science, and as such commands good wages. I have known a “chief packer” to be paid a salary of $150 per month on the frontier, and his services were worth the money paid. The duty is taught to cavalrymen as part of their drill, and many of the soldiers become very expert at it. At a pack drill of tho Ninth Cavalry a few days before it left Montana one com pany packed its mule In 1 minute and 54 seconds, and others were but little slower. Thirty mult's generally constitute a "train,” and are managed by three men. They are trained to follow a bell, worn by a horse, white preferred, as being more readily seen. They are not confined in any way except when first put Into the train; then, any straying from It is punished very severely and Mr. Mule soon learns his place and that It is best to keep it. Each man with the train carries a diamond-shaped leather blind with leather cords attached to the ends and knotted together. If ^ pack becomes disarranged two of the men lead tho mule out of the trail, blindfold him with thl3 blind, rearrange his load, re move the leather and allow him to re join his fellows. He Is never struck when started, and pack mules are never • misused by good packers.

THE WORLD’S PRAYER. A New Mexico Editor Has It Figured Out About Right. O! Almighty Dollar, our ac knowledged governor, preserver and benefactor, we desire to ap proach thee on this and all occa sions with that reverence which is due of superior excellence, and the regard which will be cherished for exalted greatness. Almighty Dollar, without thee in the worl-t we can do nothing, but with thee we can do all things. When sick ness lavs its paralyzing hand upon us, thou canst provide for us the tender nurses, the most skillful physicians, and when the last strugle of mortality is over and we are being borne to the last resting place of the dead, thou canst pro vide a band of music and a military escort to accompany us thither, and last but not least, erect a mag nificient monument over our grave, with a living epitaph to perpetuate our memory. And while here, in the midst of misfortunes and temp tations of life, we. perhaps, are ac cused of crime and brought before magistrates, thou Almighty Dollar, canst secure us a feed lawyer, a bribed judge and a packed jury, and we go free. Be with us.we pray thee, in all thy decimal parts, for thou art the ^nly one altogether lovely and chief among ten thousand. We feel there is no conditions in life where thy potent and all powerful charms are not felt. In thy ab sence, how gloomy is the house hold and how desolate the hearth stone, but when thou, O, Almighty Dollar, art with us, how graceful the beefsteak sings upon our grid iror, how genial is the warmth that anthractie coal or hickory wood diffuses throughout the apartments, and what exuberance of joy con tinues to swell our bosom! Thou art the joy of our youth and the solace of our old age; thou canst adorn the gentleman and feed the jackass; thou art the favorite of the philosopher and the ideal of the longhead. When an election is to be carried. 0, Al mighty Dollar, thou art the most potent argument of politicians and demagogues, and the umpire that decides the contest. Almighty Dollar, thou art worshipped the world over, thou hast no hypocrites in thy temple, no false hearts at thy altars; kings and courtiers bow before thee and all nations adore thee; thou art loved by civil ized and savage alike with unfal tering affections; we continue to r'gard thee as the handmaid to re ligion and the twin sister of chari ty. O, Almighty Dollar, be with us, we beseech thee, attended by an inexpressible number of thy ministering angels made in thine own image, even though they be

but silver dimes and quarters, whose gladdening light shall illumi nate the value of penury and want with heavenly radiance, which shall cause the awakening soul to break forth in acclamations of joy. Al mighty Dollar, thou art the guide of our footsteps and the goal of our being. Guided by their silvery light, we hope to reach the pearly gate and triumphantly enter gold en street. Let us join in singing the follow ing: Almighty dollar, thy shining face; Bespeaks thy wondrous power; In my pockets make t^y resting place, I need thee every hour! And now, Almighty Dollar, ir closing this invocation, we realize and acknowledge that thou wact the god of our forefathers, the two fold god of their grandchildren. Permit us to possess thee ir, abundance and all thy varied ex cellence is our constant and un wavering prayer.—News, Elida. New Mexico.

The Mosquito. The mosquito is here. He is here with both feet, and then som°, He also brought with him his bill. The mosquito always has a bill with him. He introduces it indis criminately, and without recogni tion from the speaker. But the speaker recognizes him sooner or later. When he does recognize him it is quite often in language that would not be fit to publish in a Sunday school paper. But the mosquito don’t care. He hasn't got any manners. But he has feelings. He is always feeling for a soft place in which to insert his bill. The mosquito is a hero. He is worse than that; he is a borer. His principal business is to bore people. He is also a collector. When he introduces his bill he collects some blood. He has had in his veins, or somewhere about his anatomy, the best blood in the world. The mosquito has no blood of his own; he has to borrow his blood. He has been 1 nown to borrow the blood of Kings. But he don’t seem to appreciate it. and it don't make him any better. He will go away from a King, when chased off. and mix the blood of the King with that of a measly yellow mule. The mosqu'to has six feet, four to walk with and two to rub together, like a Jew rubs his hands together when he has sold you a $5 suit of clothes for $14.90. The mosquito does this when he has struck a pay streak some where in your anatomy. So does the Jew. The mosquito can sing when he is empty, and he’s nearly always empty. In this respect he's like the organ grinder; gives you the music first and collects the toll afterwards. Whenever you hear a mosquito simr you may know that he is hollow—hollow and hungry. You never know just where he is going to dig a hole in your anatomy until he sets his augur to work. Your Uncle Tobey has been bored by mosquitoes until he understands all their habits. If

there's a dozen persons in the house and only one mosquito it will sink on him. His blood seems to be especially prepared to suit their taste. This, however, is the only discrimination I know them tc be guilty of. The doctors say that mosquitoes peddle the ague about from place to place. 1 don't know how true this is, but the mos quito is mean enough to do it. He has been known to trade a case oi yellow fever for a drop of blood and not ask any boot. He don't seem to know much about the value of anything but blood. That seems to be his theme and he goes after it like a swarm of bees after a meddlesome dog. People who have no mosquitoes of their own can have a good brood hatched out by leaving some ’dirty water in a rain brrrel. A brood thus hatched will give satisfaction cn a sma'l scale. The size of mosquitoes differ in localities, but any of them are big enough. Their intelligence has been the subject of some consideration. Your Uncle Tobey has seen them on the hotel register as it lay on the coun ter open It has been charged 1 that they were looking to see what j rooms were occupied, but that is ! merely guess work. However, the mosquito is mean enough to do it. It is more probable that they were waiting for a victim to come 'along and register. They have been i known to find their way into rooms | of hotels that l ept no register. i Home and Farm.

A dog Eating People. The hog crop of the country amounted for the year 1908 to , $438,000,000. This is a con servative estimate for the packing houses paid to the hog raisers fot the hogs slaughtered the enormous : sum of $358,000,000. The total ! number packed by all the packeries was about 35.000.000 head. In weight the total product was about 950.000.000 pounds, or about 1 1 6 pounds for every inhabitant of this country. This may appear monstrous, but it is about as near correct as estimates can be made. The American people consume the bulk of the pork manufactured in this country and we are therefore forced to the conclusion that we are a hog eating peoole. An industry that brings to the farmers annually $558,000,000 is an industry wbrthy of being fost ered. Did you ever stop long enough to consider what this means? It means a little less than $5 per capita of the tctal popula I tion of the United States. Then you can’t blame the hog fancier i from going a little hog wild. And yet with this vast sum being real ized in the hog industry we are not living up to the full opportunities in hog production.* The South is much behind the North and West in the rearing of improved varieties and the production of pork. Our system can and should be greatly improved and our production in creased. Our Southern farmers give entirely too much attention to cotton. They should add hogs, cattle, fruits, vegetables, grains, alfalfa, pou'try, sheep and goats. But we should start out with the determination to grow the best of everything. When this is done our rich States will become richer and our people happier and more prosperous. Texas Farm and Fireside. i

T. R. CARTER KILL SELL former Resident of Huttig, Committed Sulcidi at Siloam Springs Last Friday. Word was received here last Saturday by the secretary of the Odd Fellows’ lodge that Thomas R. Carter has committed suicide at Siloam Springs last Friday by swallowing poison, and that the Masonic order had taken charge of the remains. The deceased was a machinist by trade and worked in the ma chine shops here for several years, up until about two years ago, when he moved to Argenta where he worked at the Baring Cross shops until recently. He moved his membership in the Masonic lodge from here to Argenta about one year ago. but was still a member of Huttig Lodge, No. 348, I. O. O. F. He was an industrious worker and well liked by all who knew him. He lost his wife last winter and the fact that he was out of employ ment caused him to become de spondent, as the following note found on him explains: ”1 am despondent and can't get work. 1 am not happy and want to go with my dear wife, who went on February 23. “My receipt will tell who I am. 1 am a member of the Royal Ar- j canum of Little Rock and carry! $ 1.000 insurance in that lodge. I am a member of the F. and A. M. and the I. O. O. F. After my funeral expenses are paid please | pay my step-son, Lloyd Carter, j Kearney. Ark., the balance of my insurance. Please say a little prayer at my grave. Tell all my friends in Little Rock good-bye. “Your departed friend, “T. R. Garter. “Please bury me under Masonic order. Gocd-bye, everybody."

Each contestant for the above prizes must list at this office not later April 15, the patches of ber ries that they wish to enter in the contest, so that they can be measured by a committee ap pointed for that purpose.

The grower may list in this contest a single acre of any Va riety or may list the entire patch net returns per acre will be de termined by dividing total net leturns by hhmber of acres in patch. - All contestants must furnish affidavit and satisfactory proof to the board hf directors of the amount of berries shipped from the patch listsd. Each contestant will be furi^ ished separate book and stencil number by which to keep ac count of all cases shipped from patch entered in contest. Any evidence of frand will be investigated hnd if found the contestant will bCi barred from participation in the feward. No member Of the board of di rectors will be awarded a prize in this contest. Each winner will be required to give a detailed statement as to I the kind of land, preparation, fer | tilization, setting of plants, and | mode of cultivation that it may j be published. i There will also be prizes award [ ed on the first and second best 1 acres of corn and cotton. $17.50 for the best acre corn or cotton, and $10.00 for second best. WILSON SIGNS DAYLIGHT BILL ('locks To Be Moved Forward One Hour This Month. Washington, March 19.— The | daylight saving bill was signed today by President Wilson. It puts all clocks forward an hour on the last Sunday in March and turns them back again the last Sunday in October. The daylight saving plan will go into effect and be observed without the slightest disorgani zation or impairment of existing conditions. Trains will run as usual and every feature of daily life into which the element of time enters will remain unchang ed. Before retiring on the last Saturday of this month the A merican householder will set his clock an hour ahead and then | may go to sleep and forget en I tirely about daylight saving un ; til the last Saturday of October. ! On that date he will reverse the I process, turning back the hands of the clock an hour, and the next day the nation again will run on “sun” time. In the summer time the Amer ican man actually will rise trans act his daily business and retire an hour earlier than has been his custom, but with his clock an hour fast, he will not know ! the difference. The Plan’s practicability and | efficiency have been effectively demonstrated in 12 European countries. BRYAN REGARDED AS “SLACK ER” BY WILSON President Will Not Quit to Please Commoner Washington, Nov. 5.—Several im portant facts were made clear here today. One of them is that President Wilson will not resign at the request of William Jennings Bryan, who is described by indignant administration Democrats as a “slacker”. Another is that leaders of the defeated party are not going to turn the organiza tion over to Mr. Bryan or any other person. or persons who sulked through the campaign and never turned a hand toward electing the ticket. A third development was that. President-elect Harding will have to do the goose-step for the old Dis trict of Columbia contingent that used to make money out of inaugu rations in various ways. He has al ready been asked to revive the inaug ural ball that President Wilson promptly vetoed when he came in eight years ago. Among those senators who will be on hand to thwart any plans of Mr. Bryan to embarrass or humiliate President Wilson, or to take charge of the party machinery, are Carter Glass and Claude A. Swanson of Vir ginia, F. M. Simmons and Lee Slater Overman of North Carolina, Oscar W. Underwood and Thomas Heflin of Alabama, Duncan U. Fletcher of Florida, John Sharp Williams and Pat Harrison of Mississippi, Gilbert M. Hitchcock of Nebraska, Thomas J. Walsh of Montana and Atlee Pome rene of Ohio. . Southern Democrats Angry Southern Democrats are very an gry with Mr. Bryan. They think that he should ask for no more fa vors at the hands of the Democratic party after his failure to help in the campaign for Gov. Cox. His old pop ularity there is gone, and he will be told where to get off whenever he starts his proposed reorganization movement. Democrats charge Mr. Bryan with “slacking” at a time when his coun try needed him, when he quit the State Department and after the San I Francisco convention. For these and other sins he is not to be taken seri ously. President Wilson has no idea of quitting his duties at the White House because Mr. Bryan suggests it. WE CAN DO IT Our people are taking a more opti mistic view of conditions every day and we believe they are justified in so doing. Conditions have always been depressed prior to national elec tions and have never failed to revive and produce better times after the po litical atmosphere clears up and the people get down to business again, if we would just take a second thought we would readily see that it is useless to sulk and lie down on the job. Get busy at something and busi ness will get back to normal before you realize what has happened. The continual talk of bad conditions and bad business will eventually make bad business. Think a moment and then begin to talk the other way and you will soon begin to see a change for the better. We never gain any thingby looking on the dark side of anything. Let’s look on the bright side for awhile. Let’s make condi tions better. We can do it, if we will only think so. Many of our people have passed through conditions ten times as strenuous as today and come out on top. The only trouble at this time is that we have had a few years of exceedingly good times, and it is hard to get back to the old grind, but we believe we will get back with but few scars and no fatalities. Let’s cut the word "can’t” out of our vocabulary and make good conditions anyhow. We can do it.
