Some Important Happenings in the South THAT MAY PLEASE OUR READERS An Assortment of Newsy Events That Occurred In our Midst That Cannot Fail to Interest. Work has begun on the depot at Randsburg. Ventura's new city government has assumed office. Riverside banks have nearly $1, 000,000 on deposit. A White Cross society "has been organized at San Diego. Over 100 Pasadenans have organizéd a "Better Roads" society. San Diego has sold its $260,000 worth of refunding bonds. San Diego has over 3000 pupils at tending her public schools. The postoffice at Newport has been made a money-order station. The Western Union has purchased the new Kramer-Randsburg telegraph line. The First National Bank of Santa Ana has declared a t per cent, divi dend. The Riverside Supervisors have placed a 5-cent bounty on rabbit scalps. Leonard W. Head has been ap pointed postmaster at Bolsa, Orange county. The gunboat Pinta is to be assigned to San Diego for the use of the naval reserve. San Luis Obispo is contemplating putting in an eight or ten-box fire alarm, system. A new lemon pest has appeared in Los Angeles county, and orchardists are worrying. During 1897, 257 marriage licenses were issued in San Diego county and 209 in San Bernardino. The townsite if Oxnard is to be laid out in the vicinity of Ventura county's new sugar factory. It is reported that Gov. Budd will attempt to reorganize the Board of Trustees of the Whittier school. It is stated that the California Eastern Railroad is to be extended from Manvel to Good Springs, Nev. The passenger train over the Oceanside and National City road has been supplied '-vith a mail coach. The Santa Ana City Trustees have called an election for February 5 on the proposition to issue $65,000 sewer bonds. The Santa Fé Pacific has named two of its stations where it gets warmest on the Mojave 'Desert, Klondike and Siberia. There have been 626 mortgages can celled in San Bernardino county dur ing the past year, representing $1, 492,137. The Glendora Fruit Association will erect a one-story basement packing-house in Alosta this month, to cost $1345. The San Diego Garbage Crematory Company, with a capital of $10.000, has made a proposition to dispose of the garbage. Santa Barbara Supervisors have adopted an ordinance granting a bounty of 2 cents lor squirrel and gopher scalps. The San Diego Aldermen have de clined to accept the crematory as it was not constructed according to plant and specifications. The Redlands Record on January 1 enlarged from four to eight pages. It is now one of the neatest little dailies in Southern California. Col. Harrison Gray Otis, editor of the Los Angeles Times, has gone to Washington, where he will oppose the Hawaiian annexation treaty. It is said that a Los Angeles capi talist is contemplating the building of a new theater in that city for Gus tave Walter of the Orpheum circuit. A franchise for a telephone system has been granted John B. Wright by the Yuma City Council. The line will be in operation on or before June 1. At Fresno, recently, Capt. W. A. Johnson of Stockton was elected lieutenant-colonel of the Sixth Regi ment, N.G.C., to succeed Col. Chis holm. George Lord of San Bernardino.aged 98 years, now at the point of death, is ' the oldest Mason and Odd Fellow in years and service in the United States if not in the world. An effort is being made to cancel the electric lighting contract recently let by the San Bernardino City Trus tees. It was made for a term of years and is illegal. The first California mission was

San Diego, founded in 1769 by the very Reverend Father Junípero Serra, who walked i,up from Loreto,' over four hundred miles. The Union Land and Water Com pany's canal will be ten to twelve miles long, and will head at West Yuma, where the water will be pumped from tfie Colorado. The new board, of directors of the San Diego Chamber of Commerce has organized by electing R. A. Thomas president, R. V. Dodge, vice-president; George W. Marston, second vice-president.

At Poloma, in San Diego county, only forty miles from the city of San Diego, there was good sleighing on New Year's. There was eight inches of snow, and the mercury was down to 18 deg. Los Angeles is something of a place for securing divorces itself. A record of about four hundred cases instituted and over two hundred and fifty de crees granted, puts the city right in the lead. Charles Cassat Davis, the represen tative of the Fourth Ward in the Los Angeles Board of Education, is now president of that body. He was elected by a vote of 4 to 2 over Di rector Poor. The contract for the construction of a bridge across the arroyo to the Campbell-Johnstone tract has been let -to Sawyer & Arthur of Los Ange les, who must build the bridge in ninety days. C. L. Sturgis of Escondido has in vented a balloting machine after many years of study and work. The ma chine is ingenious and Is far ahead of the several voting machines that have been invented. The remaining two contracts for the completion of the new Courthouse at San Bernardino have been awarded that for hot water beating to Hol brook, Merrill & Stetson, $2645; mar ble work, Stone Bros., $4320. The Colton, Cal., cement works are getting out 170 barrels of cement per day, and the daily shipments are now averaging three carloads. A sale of 6500 barrels was recently made to the San Gabriel Electric Company. W. L. Moore, chief of the Weather Bureau Service, has notified Con gressman M. A. Smith of Arizona that a second service-station will soon be started in Arizona, probably at Flag stafT, in the high plateau region. A new water system for the foothill suburb of Santa Barbara has ' been inaugurated. Twenty thousand feet of pipe has been ordered, and water will be piped from J. L. Barber's tun nel over a thousand-acre tract. A submerged rock is reported on the further side of Catalina Island. The rock is said to be situated on the southerly side of the island, at a point opposite Avalon, or nearly so. it is said to be covered with about six feet of water, and therefore in a position highly menacing to vessels navigated in that locality. The contract has been let for the new building for Occidetal College at Highland Park, between Los Ange les and Pasadena. The architecture is of the Mission Renaissance style. The main building will be two stories and basement, with a tower equiva lent to four stories, it will occupy an area of 89x72 feet. Los Angeles will probably have a glass factory in the near future. The Atlantic Coast Glass Company of Bar nezat, N. J., has written a letter of inquiry to the Board of Trade. If good glass sand is obtainable, a plant will be at once erected. This company is one of the largest glass manufac turers in the United States. Game Warden Dunn of San Diego has received a crate of six Mongolian pheasants from the State Fish Com missioners, for breeding. Only three crates of the pheasants were sent by the Fish Commissioners to South ern California, the other two coming no further south than Los Angeles. The 10-inch mortar oresented to the Grand Army posts of San Diego has arrived. The barrel is 3 feet long and the gun weighs 3800 pounds. At Ballast Point the huge coast defense guns are being placed in position. One of the guns weighs 67,000 pounds. It will be placed in a disappearing gun carriage weighing 245,000 pounds. Count von Goetzen, military attache of the German embassy, was married in Washington to Mrs. Mary Stanley at the residence of his bride. The Count and his bride have started for a trip across the continent. They will stay for a time at Los Angeles, and will then go to Berlin, where Count von Goetzen will rejoin his regiment, now at Potsdam. The latest report of the postal re ceipts at the Los Angeles postofiire shovji some interesting figures, as compared with the receipts of last year. For the quarter ending Decem ber 31, 1896, the receipts were $49, 995.27; for the quarter ending Decem ber 31,1897. $56,785.27, Ehowing an in crease of 13.57 per cent. For the year ending December 31, 1896, the receipts were $186,103.80, and for that ending December 31, 1897, $200,941.03, show ing an increase of 8 per cent.

Coal has been discovered on James Tong's place, near Duncan, Ariz. There are a total of 240,952 school children in the State, and the total apportionment is $2,035,483.44. The shingle mills of the State will be closed until Fsbruray 1. An ad vance in rates of about 10 cents per 1000 has been inaugurated. The Supervisors of Fresno county have resolved to .-naintain an exhibit of that county in ihe State Board of Trade at San Francisco, and have voted $15 per month to keep it up. McCord has requested a confer ence at Phoenix, on the 24th, of county assessors and representatives of the boards of supervisors of the Territory, that a more uniform tax rate may be arrived at. It is authoritatively stated that the Valley road will be in operation be tween Bakersneld" and Stockton by the first of March. Byron Waters has gone to Washing ton, D.C., to appear before the Su preme Court of the United States in two Mexican land grant case. In one he represents Mrs. Hearst of San Francisco, and in 'he other a gentle man from Arizona. Ex-President Cleveland has ad dressed a second communication on the subject to Gov. Budd, urging the exercise of executive clemency in the case of Salter D. Worden, convicted of murder in connection with train- wrecking during the great railroad strike of 1894, and sentenced to be hanged February 11. The amount of the contract of the Valley road tunnel near Rodeo will be something like 450,000 or $500,000. This new tunnel is to be 5700 feet in length. It will be the third longest tunnel in California. The longest is that of the Southern Pacific near San Fernando, which is-7200 feet long; the next, that on the Southern .Pa cific's road to Santa Cruz, which is about six thousand feet long, and the fourth, :tUat on the Southern Pa cific's coast extension between Santa Margarita and San Luis Obispo, a tun nel of 4000 feet. The Santa Fé Pacific is preparing to enlarge its shops at San Bernardino An entirely new car building and re pairing shop will be erected, that in floor space will be larger fhan all the floor space of all the various de part.ments combined; the present blacksmith and boiler shop will be all one vast blacksmith shop; a new boiler-making plant will be erected in which this branch of railroad work will be carried on. There are now on the way fifty-nine cars loaded with lumber, with which to commence the building, and it will only be a few days now when the preparatory work will commence. James H. White, representing the Edison company, -was in Riverside re cently, and was taken to the packing house of Riverside Heights, No. 10. by A. S. White, and got some splendid views of the packers at work. The process by which these views are taken is little short of marvelous. In thirty seconds 1800 pictures can be taken, and Mr. White announces that the conditions were very favorable to securing some very choice "living pictures" of an important feature of the orange industry in Southern Cali fornia. Mr. White is taking a se ries of interesting scenes represent ing life and industries in Southern California. These views will be used in Edison's kineoscopes, cinemato- scopes and animatoscopes, and will en lighten many an easterner in regard to features of life in the new Italy.

What the San Frnnclxeo Minera' As- Moeiatlon Propones to Do. The Golden Jubilee and the ereat mining exposition which will follow it are absorbing all the energies of the San Francisco Miners' Associa tion, which gave the semi-centennial us nrst impetus, but when these af fairs are over the association will take up other lines of effort, and promises to be a very great aid to the prosperity of the industry in many ways. The active president of the asso ciation, T. J. Parsons, gives the fol lowing general outline of the new ca reer which is planned for the organ ization: The San Francisco Miners' Asso ciation has started an effort to stim ulate the growth and prosperity of tne mining industry in California, mainly by advertising its possibilites and greatness to the world. The plans for this work are yet very general. They will develop in detail as we go along, and will, 1 hope, grow as we progress, as the plan for a semi-centennial of the dis covery of gold grew out of the idea of this association to celebrate the event with a large parade and other suitable exercises, and develop into a plan for an exposition in connection with a great Golden Jubilee. The jubilee and exposition will command all the energies of the as sociation until they are over, and then active steps along other lines will be taken, plans for which will be considerably developed meantime. The first work will be to get the associa tion thoroughly organized and strengthened. Its membership is now about 265, composed mainly of manu facturers and merchants directly in terested in the mining trade, and hence in the prosperity of the indus try. Individuals pay dues of $5 a year, commercial and manufacturing firms $50, and mining companies $25. We wish to largely increase the mem bership from among all who have an active or a merely friendly interest in mining. We will show many busi ness men the direct benefit of identi fying themselves with the association and helping it along. We want to establish a headquar ters supplied with publications, etc. of interest to miners, and to make It a rendezvous for mining men when they come to the city. It is our idea to maintain there a bureau of mining information which shall do the statis tical and scientific work of the Min ing Bureau, which will afford ready practical information to mining men and to strangers. A permanent exhibit may be main tained, displaying as well as possible the mineral resources of the State. This exhibit would correspond to that of the horticultural and agricultural resources of the State by the State Board of Trade. One purpose of the association is to advertise San Fran cisco as the mining center of the Pa cific Coast, and manufacturers cf mining machinery and supplies might maintain private exhibtis there. What this institution will become depends on developments in the near future, but we hope to make it a grand advertising bureau for the in dustry. From it literature might be circulated all over the world. All these plans will be discussed during the preparations for the jubi lee and interest in them developed. So many have already become deeply interested in our plans that I am con fident that we will find the enthu siastic cooperation needed. The en tire State is interested in the mining industry and wishes to see it flourish. T. J. PARSONS. From the data at hand it is esti mated that the output of the precious metals in Washington for the year 189V will amount to about one and one-half millions of dollars, which is a substantial increase over any pre ceding year. Canadian )IInra. The detailed report of the geological suivey upon statistics of mines and minerals for the year 1896 has been issued. It gives Canada's total min eral production for the year at $22, 000,000, an increase of 125 per cent, in ten years, the production in 1886 having been $10.000,000. The increase of mineral production for the same decade was 40 per cent. The annual production per capita is $8 in the United States, against $450 in Canada. In the production of gold, British Columbia stands credited with over 64 per cent., and Nova Scotia with over 18 per cent. The Northwest Territories, including the Yukon dis trict, come third, with 10 per cent., and Ontario fourth, with about 5 per cent., while Quebec contributes much, under 1 per cent. Fitz Boy Dixon tells of a baby elephant that was cap tured by friends of his in Ceylon, after the death of its mother. Mr. Dixon says: When Sidney was first brought over, virtually in order that she might be fed, the question naturally arose as to how she would take her nourishment Of course the proper way for an adult elephant to take in water is by means of the trunk, which is furnished with two tubes running its whole length. But when a bowl of milk was placed before the baby elephant she did not know what to do with it. She dipped the tip of her trunk into it, and the lookers on thought that there would be no difficulty about her drinking at all, since she recognized the scent of the nourishment the bad been accustomed to. But she was quite at a loss and set up a roar which seemed quite natural under the circumstances. Then some one suggested pouring it down her throat from a bottle, and this was ac cordingly tried, and after one or two in effectual attempts she understood. She was half starved when this was done, for she bad bad nothing to eat since the death of her mother, and her delight at being fed was most amusing. The dearth of servant girls in Los Angeles may result in. importing a number of young Russian maidens from Canada. The girls want to come and have communicated with a Russian lady asking for advice. Some time ago a Russian colony was started in Canada peopled by religious enthusiasts from the south of Russia whose views did not meet with the ap proval of the czar. They fled from the terrible tyranny of their native land and established . an Edward Bel lamy kind of a town across the Cana dian border. It was about as successful as most such colonies, which is another way of saying that it was a dismal, flat fail ure. The money is all gone and the colony is about to break up. Being thrown on their own resources to a certain extent, the Russians turned to the wife of an exiled Russian no bleman who also had views to his own undoing. His estate reverted to the crown during his lifetime and on being banished from the Russian borders, the nobleman, as everybody knows, cut a few slices off his impossible name and came to Los Angeles to live. To his wife, the Russians appeal. They want to know if work cannot be had for the maids of the colony. It is understood that she has not replied, and is consulting with American la dies of her acquaintance as to the ad visability of sending for the girls to come. They do not speak a word of English." The people of whom they are a part are said to be faithful, strong, sedate and deeply religious.

Republican. Tucson may fo'low the lead of Los Angeles and establish a stockade in which to confine hoboes. Marshal Hopley stated to the Citizen that if the hoboes continued to arrive there it would be necessary to make some special provision to care for them as the city jail is already overcrowded. Tucson appears to be a favorite stopping place for hoboes as it is the largest city between Los Angeles and El Paso along the South era Pacific. Citizen. The Phoenix local of the Inter national Typographical Union held a meeting, at which it was decided to continue the agitation of the matter of the establishment of a home for tuberculosis members of the union somewhere in southern Arizona. Arizona's delegate to the printers' convention last summer brought the question up, but at that time the ot her delegates had not bad time to meditate upon the matter, and so nothing was done. Since that time the Phoenix local has received a number of letters from different parts of the United States, in which print ers declared themselves in favor of tíie home. A committee was ap p (inted to communicate with the o ber five locals of the territory, urging them to send delegates to the c invention in Boston next August pledged to push the project through if possible. It is believed that some thing may be accomplished at that time. The Savage Gold and Copper com pany is to be more aggressive than ever in its policy. Owing to the nature and magnitude of the new .lans contemplated, it must needs be some little time before the force will be increased. But we are glad to be able to state authoritatively that no shut-down will occur in the mean time. At the same time that the new vertical shaft on the Snowball claim is, with the aid of machinery, being sunk, ore will be shipped to the Copper Queen smelter at Douglas. Shipments will be commenced as soon as the necessary arrangements have been made by the company, or as soon as the ore will be accepted at the reduction works. It is under stood that the Coppor Queen can use this ore to advantage. The ore is a silver-copper ore, running high in silica. The Copper Queen can use the silica (which is ordinarily ob jectionable in large quantities) as converter linings. Careful analysis of the ore also convinces the Savage company that shipments will pay and bring some money into the treasury. And there is considerable ore in sight quite easily mined in drifts from the shaft, as well as elsewhere on the property. Work on the new road is progressing favorably. Southwestern Opportunities and State hood for Arizona. Thirteen American territories were born to statehood. Most of the others achieved statehood. Only a few had statehood thrust upon them. Last year Arizona declined to be thrust, when the process called for a union with a foreign territory under a single star. Oklahoma found her affinity in the person of her stalwart Indian neigh bor and the two entered the union as one state. New Mexico sees a clear way before her, and the outlook is for Arizona to remain a lonesome territory or to proudly place her own star upon the flag. Such is beyond doubt the will of her people. Until the star can take its place upon the azure of our ban ner, it will remain in the care of a grand people. As a territory, Ari zona is rich. No amount of imported federal supervision has held her in serious check. There have been questions in the national congress of great moment to the nation, in the decision of which the whole west would have liked the aid of Arizona. There are obstacles to her own pros perity which she will never overcome until her own people rule. But still she is grand. From the marvelous canyon in the north, southward through the great pine forests, past Prescott, Mayer, Jerome and the Bradshaw mountains, with their wealth of gold and copper, past Globe witL its metal and the Salt and Gila rivers with their setting ot green fields and shaded groves of fruit, down into the southern deserts where the surplus wealth of the world is buried a thousand feet below the sur face from north to south, the terri tory is all magnificent. In Phoenix, Morenci, Tombstone, Douglas. Bis- bee, Nogales, Tucson, Clifton, Solo monville and in thirty more rushing, growing, prospering western cities the American language is spoken, clothes like those of civilized human beings are worn, tall-spired churches stand on many street corners, schools and colleges exist and are patronized by sturdy American boys and dainty little girls who can trace their line age back to the proudest families of old Virginia or the proudest of Pil grim dames. The carrying of fire arms is prohibited and the saloons are closed on Sunday. Burdened with the care of the invalid of half the English-speaking world, they are still a people hospitable in the true old western way. From the mines of Arizona comes a steady flow of eold to sustain American commerce and a supply of trade metals without which eastern enterprise would languish. Her fields are not so broad as the fields of Illinois, but her harvest is rich and her produce helps to feed other than her own people. In time of peace her men add more to the wealth of the world in propor tion to their numbers than the men of any state. In time of war a larger proportion of her men volun teered than the proportionate volun teer and militia force of any state. The statesmen, who stand in the way of admission when Arizona knocks at the door are the men whose public position depends, and ever must depend, on the votes of the self-exiled from the serfdom of Europe. The congressman who repre sents the jungle in the stockyards district has for his constituents a people whose language is Labe', whose religion is the superstition of twenty centuries of ignorance, whose politi cal ideas were gained in the realm of the czar or under the rijtous rule of the Austro-Hungarian combination. Yet this congressman may be depend ed upon to vole that the people of Arizona are not yet ready for state hood Arizona or the Philippine islands, which ever happens to be up for consideration. New York City congressmen calmly declare Arizona incompetent, and go back and boast of it to constituents who never had an ancester who could read or write. An Indiana senator, coming from near the site of old Vincennes, where the freedom of the west was won by heroic men, used an interpreter to talk to the people of Phoenix, because he could not under stand Spanish! The effect of the translations thus obtained is said to have had a startling effect upon some of the intelligent members of the caucus. Arizona rightly declines to pledge her heart to either of the political parties. She will not put her state hood in pawn before she gets it. ; Within her borders, proud southern (families meet the sturdy men of the north on common ground and unite with them in single hearted devotion to Arizona. The entire west joins in the demand that Arizona enter into the councils of the nation. Politicians with their ear to the ground will do well not to mistake the meaning of the rumbling that is heard from the great south west. Southwestern Opportunities, El Paso.

United Verde in Big Suit. In the district court at Prescott the respective attorneys in the now famous case of the Territory and Yavaipa county, through the tax col lector, vs. the United Verde Copper company for the collection of $1,250, 000 assessment, agreed on a state ment of facts in the case, which was submitted to the court, who took the matter under udvisement, a decision

Sheriffs Who Go Out of the Territory Will Get Allowance. At Prescott after several days of consideration Attorney General Clark and District Attorney Morrison have reached a decision in the matter of the payment of sheriff's fees and ex penses in extradition cases. The question was referred to the district attorney by the Yavapai sheriff's office after the extradition of J. H. Fry from La Junta, Colo., a few weeks ago. District Attorney Morrison con. suited the attorney general and a correspondence also ensued between Governor Kibbey and both attorneys. I The law bearing on the payment of : extradition fees has been construed one way and another by different dis l trict attorney, in the past ten years, some holding that the territory should pay all extradition expenses and others that the county where the crime is committed should stand the entire expense. Governor Kibbey was asked for an opinion in the matter by Attorneys Clark and Morrison. The governor takes the position that the territory should and will only pay the actual expenses of an officer, incurred in ex tradition cases, outside of the boun dary lines of the territory. His position is that the county should pay the lecral fees to the officer inside the territory. Basing their theory of the law on the presumption that as soon as a sheriff of a county crosses the boun dary line of the territory his author ity as sheriff ends. Attorneys Clark and Morrison agree that where the sheriff is the agent of the territory, in an extradition case, he is entitled to the statutory fees allowed in the execution of a warrant from the place where it is issued to the terri torial boundary line, such fees to be paid by the county. In the case of Sheriff Murphy, of Pima county, who sued the territory for the statutory fees in an extra dition case, Judge Kent decided that the territory was not liable except by order of the governor. E. E. Ellinwood, lormerly district attorney of Yavapai county, gave as his version of the law that the terri tory should pay all expenses in ex tradition cases. It was formerly the custom of the board of supervisors of Yavapai county to pay mileage to the sheriffs in the execution of extra dition matters. Joe Roberts, when sheriff of Yavapai county, demanded payment from the territory for the expenses of an extradition case outside of the boundary lines. Relates Facts Regarding Clifton-Morenci District. The following- interesting article appeared in the El Paso Herald of re cent date: The great copper district of Ari zona calle' the Clifton-Morenci quad rangle by the Onited States geological survey, an elaborate report on which was made by Prof. Lengrene a couple of years ago, and which is the pioneer copper producer of Arizona, was dis covered by Isaac N. Stevens, now a citizen of Clifton, his father and other associates many years ago. The story of the old pioneer days is given in Mr. Stevens's own words. It may be well to add that "Ike" as all the old timers like to call him, was also one of the discoverers of the rich Sabinal silver camp in. northern Chi huahua, Mexico. "This large copper district was first reported to the world by Geo. Coro- hado, a Spanish explorer, so I have been told," said Mr. Stevens. "The next man to report the copper there was a trapper by the name of Weanes, who trapped beaver along the river in the early 50's; also some of the ad venturers of the early 60's who re ported having seen large copper out crops in eastern Arizona. "In February, 1870, a party of seven men, from Pinos Altos, the gold camp near Silver City, N. M., went to the Clifton-Morenci copper field and located some of these mines, but did very little work. This party found what they thought was a very rich gold placer in what is known as Gold gulch, two miles west of Morenci. The Apache Indians being so bad they returned to Pinos Altos, it not being safe for so small a party of men to stay in the gulch. "In July, 1870, some of this party, including myself, got up a party of 46 men and went back to Gold gulch to wash out gold, they expecting that the rainy season would furnish them water to wash gold with, but as it did not rain that season they went back , . ' i turned again to Gold gulch July 13, 1870, and stayed there till the latter part of August following. "In 1872 some of the same men that were after the gold, returned in the month of June and located four mines, called the Copper mountain, Arizona Central. Yankee end Mociazuma. These were the first copper mines ever located in that district, and afterward patented, and have been some of the big producers of the cop per oxide and carbonate ores of that country. "What started the first real work in this new copper camp was a pro position made by E. B. Ward, a mil lionaire of Detroit, the famous steam boat owner on the great lakes, who agreed with the owners of these four pioneer claims, that he would pay them $2300 each for their locations, he to pay all expenses for the work required by law and to obtain patent, after which he would pay them the agreed purchase price, which be did. So you see, the first money spent in the district was Detroit money. "Ward sent a man out there, named Cap Jay, an old steamboat captain of the lakes, who went with a party of men, of whom I was a member, who did the first work in that camp. "While we were doing the work for the patent of these four claims, Mr. Metcalf, came out there and located the Metcalf mountain and the Long fellow mine. The town of Metcalf still bearing his name. "At this time the miners organized and formed the Copper mountain mining district, i. e. in the latter part of August, 1872. Joe Yankee was elected as the first district re corder. The names of the men who first organized that district were: Cap Jay, a Mr. Pierce, Bill Blood, Metcalf, Joe Yankee, Jim Bullard, Webb, Isaac N. Stevens, Stuart Brunnan, Owen Roberts, Joe C. Caldwell and George Parker, the colored cook. "In 187S, the Leszynsky Bros., Met calf and others commenced stneltint; copper ores from the Longfellow mine, Metcalf selling out to Leszynsky Bros, after four months of working, as the company ran behind. They ran in debt to Leszynsky, not having taken out enough copper to pay ex penses. "Leszynsky Bros. paid Metcalf $5000 and the latter had to go to Las Cruces, N. M., as that was the principal place of business in the southwest. "Leszynsky Bros, continued to mine and smelt copper until they sold out to the Arizona Copper company, a THE TWO HORSE BRAND

Scotch corporation, in 1883, for a large sum. The last named company has continued to mine and smelt cop per to this day and is producing 50 tons of copper bullion a day. Charles shannon refused to sell out his tig interests in that district to the new company at that time, at the price offered him. The Arizona Copper company built the railroad from I Lordsburg to Clifton in 1884. The j above isa brief outline of the b is-1

tory of this great copper camp, the j pioneer copper camp of Arizona, with j which I am proud to bestill identified. ; "The Clifton and Morenci cbDDpr 1 district is five by 10 miles in area, lying between the Frisco river on the east and Eagle river on the west, and the Gila riyer 10 miles to the south. 1 he formation is limestone with por phyry intrusions and contacts with quartz-porphyry contacting with granite and granite-porphyry. "The ores which were on the sur face were mostly oxides and carbon ates, with depth contain copper sul phides. The earliest workings were in the.lime and lime-contacts, where the ores were oxidized, and the sul phides were not looked for nor mined until the mines of the camp bad been worked for 18 years. " Today most of the copper is taken from the sulphide zone. The carbon ates and oxidized copper ore deposits in the old lime and lime-contacts, which were first worked, have nearly all been worked out; this class of ore playing out at the porphyry contact or else turning into sulphide. "We have in this district a variety of ore bodies. In some places there occur what one would call fissures, and at other places just immense ore deposits or bodies lying in all shapes. It looks like the country at some time was badly jumbled. Most of the mining has been done above a depth of 500 feet. "The Copper King and the Coro nado mine are working down to a depth of 800 feet. Nobody has gone down to see how deep the ore goes. They are getting plenty of it above tüe depth of 500 feet. So what is j the use of going deeper until this large inland sea of copper ore bodies has been mined out above the water level? "The first smelting of copper in the Clifton-Morenci district was done in Mexican adobe furnaces by a com pany taking their ore from Longfel low mine. This company was called the Longfellow Copper Mining com pany, which, as I have stated began working early in 1873, composed of Henry Leszynsky, Charles Leszynsky, Bob Metcalf and others. The ores were carbonated and oxides of cop per running 25 per cent. One ton ofacopper bullion per day was a big run. Copper was then worth about 30 cents a pound. Now it is safe to say that the output of copper bullion of this district amounts to 110 tons every twenty-four hours quite an increase in thirty-six years. "The ores in those early smelting days, throughout the district aver aged about 15 per cent, copper a ton. Now the average is only about 3 per cent., together with some gold, the amount of which I am unable to state. "I will say in conclusion, that if all the mines in this district were being worked, it would be an easy matter to produce 200 tons of copper bullion 1 er day. You may think I a mtalking through my hat; but I have no hesi tation in saying that copper will be mined for 1000 years or more in this great cuperiferous district, where I can show you copper till your eyes get green." A. N Brown is Promoted The installment of the shakeup in the executive department of the El Paso & Southwestern, which has been expected for some time, came with the news from Chicago that A. N. Brown had been promoted to the system with headquarters at Chi cago. Mr. Brown has been filling the position of general freight and pass enger agent for a number of months, since the resignation of V. R. Stiles. The duties of his new position will make necessary his residence in Chi cago. His salary, it is reported, will be $15,000 a year. T. M. Schumacher, present traffic manager, it is understood, has ten dered his resignation, and will be made a vice-president. H. J. Sim mons, the present general manager according to advices from Chicago, will also advance to a higher place in the organization of the company by being elected a vice president. It is expected that he will continue his duties as general n anager after pro motion. Among the men mentioned as likely to succeed Brown are Eugene Fox and John Mason. Fox is at present assistant to the general freight and passenger agents and Mason was chief clerk to V. R. Stiles, former general passenger agent. Mr. Mason has also acted as chief clerk to Mr. Brown. In the final session of the Arizona postmasters"convention recently held at Phoenix, new officers were elected as follows: A L Smith of Prescott, president; O D M Gaddis of Kingman, vice president; F W Smith of Wil liams, secretary and treasurer. There were a number of technical questions discussed, and several re solutions passed.

Prosecutors in Organization. With nine of the thirteen district attorneys in Arizona present the first steps taken at Phoenix toward the organization of the territorial Dis trict Attorneys' association, which will be completed when the prosecu

tors hold another meeting in Phoenix during the January term of court, when it is expected that every county attorney in .A."-izona will attend. John S. Wil'lams, district attorney of Cochise county, and father of the organization, was selected president and A. G. McAllister of Graham county, secretary. District Attorney Williams, at whose suggestion the attorneys met, stated that the disadvantages at which the district attorneys find themselves in many instances led him to evolve the plan of the meeting and organization. By having the district attorneys agreed on certain important matters relating to form and procedure, Wil liams believes that the efficiency of all the district attorneys' offices will be increased and their work made easier and with less confusion than now results when tne interests of the different counties happen to be mutual in any given matter. A Superintendent to be Raked Over. There promises to be some lively doings within the next few weeks, when a "discipline committee," ap pointed at the recent territorial teachers' institute in Phoenix, will hold a special session at the capital city. It has leaked out that serious charges have been preferred against one of the school superintendents of the territory. The matter came up at the meeting at Phoenix during fair week, and after some considera ble discussion a committee of five was appointed as aboard of inquiry. The charges against the superin tendent are embodied under the one allegation, "unprofessional conduct," though the educators are reticent as to their exact nature, preferring to say nothing until the committee meets and investigates. It is under stood, however, that falsifying is one of them and should the teacher in question be found guilty it will mean that his license in the territory will be revoked. Mohave County to Have Big Smelter. A smelfr and a 20-mile railway, to cost about $475,000 will be built in the southern part of Mohave county by the Evans Mines & Smelter com pany. The smelter will be erected at Evans, where the railway will cross the Bill Williams Fork. It will have an initial daily capacity of JoO tons, and will cost approximately $225,000. The railway will be constructed be tween McCraken Hill mine and Swan sea, and will require an outlay for building and equipment of $250,000. Final suryeys will be finished and construction begun in two weeks. At Swansea, the road will connect with the line now beingbuilt between that place and Bouse, on the Arizona & California, by the Clara Consoli dated. The smelter and railway will be located in the Owens or McCracken Hill district, in which the Evans com pañas owns the Centennial, Van Britt and other mines that produce fluxing ores of a desirable grade which are to be supplied to smelters in the south west. Creel's career as chief adviser, will in real ity be a sort of "training" to pre pare him for the presidency. To Form Organization. The National Indian War Veter ans, an organization formed in Den ver, Colorado, has for its object, to obtain pen-ions for all those who, while serving the government, con tributed their share to open for peaceful settlement of this great Western country.

The men as a rule are old and feeble, by reason of endured hard ships and privations, unable toper form manual labor and on account of age barred from obtaining suitable employment. A government which through its liberality to its veterans of other wars, to its educational institutions and its farmers, ranks' as the very lirst in the civilized world, sbou!d surely not hesitate to give to this limited number of surviving Indian war veterans enough to allow them at least a living for their few remain ing days. These men spent some of the best years of their lives in their country's service, opening up this great west ern empire, fighting undí-r such noted leaders as Custer, Merritt, Crook, Miles, Forsyth. McKenzie and others, and should in their last days receive government recognition. We request all those eligible to membership in this organization to at once send in their application to the National Secretary and Treas urer, C. R. Hauser, 1043 Market St., Denver, Colorado, where they will receive further information. Smelter Will Be Blown In. Wells departed from Knil, on Knib Arm, August . to join his brother Frank Wells in the Taleeetna range. When out four days Wells fell in with wolves, who dared not attack him because he was armed, yet con stantly kept him company until he reached his destination. month. Douglas establishes her claims on the basis of locality, ability to raise the fund necessary to take care of the congress, hotel service to care for the delegates when they come here, perfect autumn climate, side trips to the most famous mining centers in the United States and Mexico, adequate railroad facilities, a people readv and willing to devote themselves to the pleasure of the visiting delegations, and the fact that this city has been foremost in striving to bring the congress to Ari zona in other campaigns for this honor. Presidential Proclamation Changes Area of Kaibab National Forest, Arizona Washington. The president has signed a proclamation adding ap proximately 18,330 acres to the Kaibab National Forest, Arizona, and at the same time eliminating 10,880 acres. These changes are the result of a careful field examination made last summer by the U. S. De partment of Agriculture in pursu ance of a general plan for the cor rection of a'l national forest boun daries. The arei added contains some tim ber, but the addition was made mainly to secure a better administrative boundary. Previous to this procla

mation, the western boundary of the forest had been in the bottom of deep, narrow canyons, locally known as Snake Gulch and Kanab Canyon. Most of the watering places for stock grazing upoi the adjacent range within this forest were within this forest were these two gulches. Sjme outside stock came into these same watering places, which resulted in the constant mixing of-the stock. The new boundary will enable all the stock to be taken care of without mixing. In addition, the fact that the cliffs bordering the western edges of the canyons forms the new boundary line will -make it posssble, by the construbtion of less than a mile of fence, to effectually close the forest boundary for nearly 150 miles, so that the trespass of stock from without or the escape of stock from within the forest will be practically impossible. The petition requesting this addition was signed by practi cally all the local settlers concerned. The elimination consists of seven teen sections of land adjacent to the northwest boundary of the forest. The area eliminated is covered with grass and a scattering growth of juciper and pinon, and is chiefly valuable for grazing purposes. The changes made by this proclamation do not affect the boundaries of the Grand Canyon' Game Preserve or the Grand Canyon National Monument, both of which lie partially within the Kaibab National forest. The lands eliminated by this proclamation will be restored to set tlement and entry after they shall have been advertised in the local papers by the secretary of the in terior. Colorado Engineer Without Food For 57 Days in Seach of Health. A new record for long fasting is be lieved to have been made by Roland Moeller, a young civil engineer, who after going fifty-seven days without food, last week began taking nourish ment in the form of orange and plum juice in Denver. Young Moeller, whose father is a prominent physician of Milwaukee, Wis., began his fast for the purpose of regaining his health as he was suffering from stomach trouble. When he began his fast he weighed 148 pounds. He now weighs 974. pounds. For two or three weeks, one of the four physicians who have been watch ing Moeller has been giving him daily olive rubs and these are be lieved to have given him nourish ment sufficient to sustain him beyond the forty day period of fasting, which physicians say is the limit of safety. Dead Man is Winner of Lottery Prize. Brussels, Sept. 7. A romance has just been unfolded in connection with the recent Brussels lottery. For some time the chief prize of $40,000 went unclaimed, and the identity of the winner has just been established in a remarkable manner. It appears that a young Belgian miner, aged nineteen, had purchased a ticket for the lottery, and shortly after he was killed while at work, through a stone falling on h'm. A few days before the result of the lottery was announced, he was buried, according to custom, in his Sunday clothes. Some weeks passed, and no claimant came forward for the first prize. , Then the young man's friends re membered that he had a lottery ticket in the waistcoat pocket of his suit, and an application was for warded to the authorities for per mission to have the body exhumed. After the usual official delay, the re quest was granted, and as was ex pected, the winning ticket was found In the dead man's clothes. His rela tives are now claiming the money. Big Wire Fence To Separate Countries Douglas. Not since the building of the great wall of China has a barrier been put between two countries of such an extent as that which is to be erected along the international line between the United States and Mexico, extending from Calexico on the pacific coast to El Paso, Texas. TñV fence will be put up to protect the United States ranges against the danger of fever ticks which infest some of the wild cattle roaming the mountains and hills of Sonora and Lower California, which at present have access into Arizona, California and New Mexico. The announcement for the building of this international barrier follows a consultation held in the City of Mexico. At this conference Minister Wilson represented the United States and Minister Creel Mexico. For a longtime the officials of Uncle Sam have been carrying on a rigid war against the introduction of fever ticks and the problem has been one of the interesting policies along the bórder-land. The fever ticks were allowed to get a deep hold upon the cattle and mules of Mexico, for two reason; first because the ticks are not fatal in Sonora as they are in the United States, and second because thy were not treated with the same deep concern as they have caused in this country. The are two distinct districts to which have been affected in Sonora. Oae of these regions lying to the east of the big state, and the other to the west, extending through Culiacan to the coast, and ranging up to the boundaries of Arizona and California. In the north of England It was formerly the custom to punish wife-beating, hen-pecking and other frailties incident- to mar ried life, by a peculiar process known as "riding the stang." It was so called because the leader was borne on a "stang," the north country word for a chair fastened on two poles. In south ern England the process Is called "rough music." The offender was called upon by a company of men, women and children and treated to a loud and boisterous serenade, the Instruments being cows' horns, fire shovels, tongs, frying pans, pot lids used as cymbals, tin pails, and other Im plements and utensils capable of producing loud and discordant noises. Along with the din the serenaders would keep up a con stant hooting and yelling, and make many Jeering remarks to the culprit. If one application was not sufficient, the perform ance would be repeated; some times, In flagrant cases, every evening for a week. This form of punishment Is known to have been meted out to wife-beaters as late as 1862, and there Is some ground for believing that the custom still survives among the lower classes in some parts of England. In this country newly wedded couples are sometimes treated to a serenade somewhat resembling the above ceremony, but it Is always good-natured and does not carry the Idea of punishment.. The Mountain States Tel. & Tel. Co. Sell Their Hold ings In Navajo And Apache Counties

On last Thursday a deal was made here between Wm. B. Woods, Lloyd i;. nenning and Fred W. Nelson and the Moun tain States Telephone & Tele c-raph Co. whereby all of the holdings of that company in Navajo and Apache Counties passed into the hands and con trol of the above named gentle men, they having purchased the property outright from the above name company. A brief state ment describing the property may be of interest to our readers In 1907 F. W. Nelson organized a stock company incorporated under the name of Arizona Elec ric- Telephone Co. it being built and equipped under the manage ment and direction of Mr. Nelson and was the first extensive Tele phone system in this section of Arizona. After its successful operation for about four years the system was purchased by the Overland Tel. & Tel. Co. whose headquarters was at Phoenix. About this time the Overland Company incurred heavy indebt edness on account of installing an entirely new and expensive automatic system in the city of Phoenix, this together with other ill-timed purchases involv ed them in financial difficulties from which they could not ex tricate themselves, so that just at the time the. company was about to go into a Receivers hands, the Mountains States Company offered to take over the entire Overland system at a ridiculously low figure, which owing to the unfortunate condi tion of the affairs of the Over land" Company, its Board of directors and bondholders decid ed to accept rather than to lose all. The Mountain States Tel. & Tel. Co. took charge of the Over land property on July 29, 1912, which incluned the system locally known here as the "Nelson ines". Representatives of the Mountain States Co. made an in spection of their lines in Navajo and Apache Counties, and while they considered the property of good value, it being discounected from their main lines at present made it difficuit for them to operate at long range, and this was principal reason that induced them to sell the property to the above named parties. The exact consideration was not ascestain- ed, but it sold at a sacrifice. The new owners . are all men interested in the building up and development of this section of the country, and they mean to make their new acquisition of this Telephone system connected most all important towns in the towns in the two Counties now, but there are many nearby set tlements and ranches that have for a long time wished to be connected with the system, and those things will be looked into by the new management and everything possible will be done to increase the efficiency of the service and the new owners hope to merit a liberal patronage of the public.

State School Fund Cut Short The. schools of Arizona find themselves in a serious position because the state tax'commission failed to make a levy for the state support of the schools in addition to the amount raised by county taxation. The commission was author ized to levy $500,000 for the sup port of the schools. After de ducting the sum of expense of the state superintendent of in- struction, the balance of the fund was to be apportioned to the counties. The commission has as its . ex cuse the "ambiguity" of the statute relating to the apportion ing of the fund among the coun ties. Another reason is that the school board decided not to put the free text book law into effect this year. Supreme court upholds decision of lower court in case of Dun seath against the city of Tucson for damages. Judgement of the superior court of Pima county was upheld last Tuesday in the state supreme court, snd James R, Dunseath of Tucson may collect $233 51 from the city of Tucson, damages for which he sued in the superior court. The case is of especial interest to the state in that it is the first decision ever handed down by an Arizona supreme court, state or territory, which defines the right of citizens to protect their prop erty against the encroachment of city government. Dunseath filed his suit against the city of Tucson, contending that damages had been done to his premises, especially to his cellar, by water "flowing from city ditches which flooded his proDerty. The superior court de cided in his favor, and the city took an appeal. In the supreme court it was decided that Dun seath was damaged to the extent awarded him by the lower tribu nal, and the decision of the su perior court was sustained. Re publican. Will Distribute Lands The miliitary government of Chihuahua, issued a decree Mar- ch 11, . for the distribution of public lands among the soldiers active in the present revolution, the disabled veterans of the Ma dera revolt and the widows and orphans of the two revolutions. According to a tentative estim ate, each will be given sixty-two acres. The decree provides . that no persons with resources equal to one of these farms shall parti cipate inthe benefits of the plan. The new owner will not be per mitted to sell his farm within ten years, nor shall it be subject to execution for debt. The decree excited .interest as being the first attempt to apply the constitutionalist plan for sol ving the land problem. Two commissioners from Gen. More Men Needed for Lumbermen's Regtment

Six thousand additional men are wanted at once to bring the Twentieth Engineer (Forest) regiment up to full strength, according to officials of the ' For est Service who have been re quested by the War. Department to aid in securing the necessary recruits. This is the second forest reeiment formed by the War Department and will be the biggest regiment in the world The first forest regiment has been in France for j several months, busy in cutting and get ting out of the French forests timber, lumber, and other ma terial for our army. Some bat talions of the .Twentieth have also gone across, and others will follow as their equipment and preliminary training are com pleted. Men who enter this unit are therefore assured, the officials say, of. early service abroad. Men can join the regiment by enlistment if not of draft age and if within the age limits, which are from 18 to 40. Re gistrants under the selective draft law who haye not been no tified to hold themselves in read iness to report tor duty at a camp can be "inducted" into the regiment if they can show that they are qualified for it. Applicants for enlistment or induction may apply by letter to the Supervisor, Snowflake, or to the various listing officers who have been receiving local applications for places in the forest regiments. Letters of application must contain a full statement of experience in any of the various lines of work in volved, with names and address es of employers. Three thousand' of the 'men wanted will consist of lumber jacks, sawmill workers, and men experienced in building and operating Slogging railroads. The other". three thousand will make up threelroadfand bridge building battalions which will serve as'auxiliary to.the logging and sawmill units. For these road-building battalions men who are familiar with the opera tionjof rockierushers., road roll ers, scrapers and Ithe operation of rock crushers road rollers, scrapers and graders, motor truck drivers, and laborers ex perienced in road work are re quired. The lumbering and sawmill battalions will be made up of men skilled in every phase of manufacturing and delivering lumber and other forest products needed in the conduct of the war. Sawyers, teamsters, axe men, tie makers, cooks, and charcoal burners are some of the classes wanted for the woods operations. Graders, tracklay ers, track bosses, locomotive en gineers and firemen, brakemen, machinists and laborers are needed to construct and operate logging railroads. Men skilled in all kinds of work around saw mills, including filers, stationary engineers, boiler makers, trucu and tractor operators and labor ers for lumberyards are required. National Forest Grazing Pri vileges Must Not Be Sold The Secretary of Agriculture is notifying all holders of per mits for grazing livestock on the National Forests that the pay ment of any bonus or allowance for waiver of the grazing privi lege in connection with sales of livestock or ranch properties will be cause for revocation of the permit. This is in accordonce with one of the regulations governing the use of the National Forests for grazing privileges, which provi des that permits will be granted only for the exclusive use and benefit of the owners of the stock and will be forfeited if sold or transferred in any man ner or for any consideration. To protect permittees who may
wish to dispose of their property againest the losses which sacri fice sales would involve, it has

been cuBtomary to allow conti nued use of the National Forest ranges by the new owner. With out some provision for this, the Forest Service grazing officials point out. holders of permits who wish to go out of business would not be able to obtain a fair value for their property. But the procedure has aimed throughout at such a safeguard ing of the situation as would prevent the acquisition of any thing approaching vested rights in the public property by private individuals or companies. Owing to the great and ever growing demand for use of the Forest ranges, which is now in most regions' far beyond their capacity, the grazing privilege is of large value. Upon the Na tional Forests the Government applies a system of regulated use designed to encourage pro duction, promote the upbuilding of the country alone healthv ines, and secure the greatest good to the greatest number, but makes only a "moderate charge for the grazing permits. In the view of those in charge of the National Forest crraziner business, it would be entirely unfair'for the publicto forage a maximum return for the value of use of its"property and then allow those granted the privilege of use to collect this value from others, as the price of surrender- ng their privileges. Such ' a practice would they say, make competitive disposal by the' Go- ernment of the grazing the only logical course. As Secretary Houston says in warning the range users thatthe payment of bonuses or the giv- ng of any consideration to se cure the filing of a waiver of the grazing privilege is prohibited. Such a payment would be a consideration for a privilege the granting of which is wholly within the discretion of the Go vernment and for which no one is entitled to receive compensa tion''. Therefore any such pay ment will be "sufficient cause for the revocation of permit or for feiture of all grazing preferen ces based upon the purchase of permitted stock" School Notes This is Patriotic Week in the Public Schools. oil wells there would be no oil fields, for in every oil district the first well was, strictly speaking, a wildcat. No new fields would be open ed up if wildcatting comes under the ban proposed by the American Petroleum In stitute, which was declared in favor of legislation against the sale or advertis ing of wildcat .oil stocks. Many producing wells today owe their origin to the en terprise and faith of the speculators who were the first on the ground and the willingness on the part of the charter stockholders and owners of the land to permit their money to be used to finance the original venture. Many pioneer operators have listened to the inevit able discouraging prophecies of those who watched in scorn their initial efforts. Many have been the hard ships of the bold adventurer in the untried locality and never has it been easy to finance the drilling of a well where no well has been drilled. The way of the wildcatter, like that of the transgressor, is hard, but that is no reason for as suming that the two have other points in common. It is not clear why any addi tional burden should be im posed in the form of legisla tion,, directed -against wild catting. ' '' . ' Stirring and romantic ex- penences and adventures have been woven into the fabric which constitutes the tremendous oil industry of today. The romance, that always attends the ventures of capital has not been lack ing, and very interesting is the story Of the early deve lopment of such fields as the Pennsylvania, the California "oil coast" ánd the great Wyoming pools. For the. enlargement' of the oil industry that must occur to meet the ever in creasing demands for petro leum and its by-products7 it is absolutely essential that present producing areas be extended cr augmented. To count upon private capital and close corporations for this necessary growth would be to askTtoo much because only a few men are willing to stake their entire fortunes on an uncertainty. The only alternative is to permit the moneyed oil interests to have the sole power to, experiment with new locations, and this would preclude the possibili ty of private capital realiz ing returns from new oil fields. Such profits, have been great. . Here may be the reason for the endorse ment by one of the officials of the Standard Oil Com pany of the proposed law to crub -wildcats. If would leave the big interests an unrestricted field. This is the romance of a man who retained his faith in human nature and found that faith rewarded. Jesse Smith, a shipwrecked sailor, is washed , up on the shores of Southern Texas. The cowboys of the region rescue him from a serious predica ment, and make him one! of them, but not being "city broke" he successively be comes the tool of a crook and the dupe of an advent uress. The latter, to satisfy a whim and to win a ribald wager, tricks the sailor-cow boy into marrying her. But it is not long before Jesse's illusions are shattered arid the true character of his wife is revealed to him. Deter mined to make the best of a bad bargain, he decides to take this wife of his out into the open and try the ennob ling influences of- the great outdoors upon her distorted soul. To carry out his plan, he sets fire to his wife's lodg ings, destroying all her prop erty, so that there may be nothing t ó return to, when once he is removed from her old ' environment. -But the woman, . rather than submit to the enforced moral cleans ing planned for her, feigns suicide, and Jesse, believing her deadsets out for the great solitudes alone. . - There, Jesse encounters Kate Trevor, an opera singer, who has brought her hus band into the. wilderness : in the vain hope that the " out door life may restore his fail ing health. But the wilder ness which adds to the strength of the strong, over whelms the weakling, and Trevor, striving to master his loneliness with strong drink, succumbs' to - his pas sions, his jealousies and weakness. Jesse finds hope of happiness m the love of a good woman, who like him has suffered, but once again the shadows of the past ob trude themselves. The. same crook who had been respon sible for Jesse's matrimonial misstep, stumbles upon his nest in the wilderness, and desiring Kate for himself, sends " for Jesse's supposed dead wife. From this point on exciting events culminate in ' big dramatic situations until the crook's dying con fession finally clears the way for the future . happiness of the lover's m the wilds. We suppose a majority of tho tax-pay ora of this county, like ourselves, know thoro is a County Alms-house somewhere the vicinity of Wilmington, to which are sent tho helpless, the aged, the craz ed, the halt and tho blind who have not tho means of proper maintenance and neither friends nor relatives to render them material aid and sympat hy. Know ing these facts, and knowing no more, resolved to visit the Alins-house and see for ourselves how it was managed.— Our visit was opportune, for it happened the "Quarterly Meeting" of tho Trus tees, and when the institntion was visit by the Boards of Trustees from both Kent and Sussex counties, who were in conference with the Trustees of New Castle county to consider tho propriety —perhaps the necessity—of a separate institution for the care and curé of the insane of the State. We scarcely deem it necessary to «ay that each county in this State has its Almshouse, which is managed by a Board Trustees selected by the Levy Court, one member from each election district tho county. — Tho Almsho '430 property consists of a main building for the Superintendent and family and assistants, as well as the sick, the lame and the aged and helpless, who here have their comfortable rooms. another building devoted to the in sane, and still another removed .. _ some distance and thickly shaded with trees devoted exclusively to case3 of conta gious diseases. There i3 also a farm of about twent acres attached to the Almshouse; a wen managed, well fertilized and productive farm, which the Superintendent assures yields annuul products to the value of near two thousand dollars annually.— This farm is tilled chiefly by the paupers, and tho produce is consumed by tho in mates of the institution. There is also a good garden—to seemed a model garden—crowded aa it was with vegetables, monstrous in size and excellent in quality. This is under the direct management of Patrick, who claims to have been perfected in his art through long servico with the Messrs, Pont. Pat's celery and mushroom beds were objects of especial interest. From our out-of-door inspection, where found so much to admire and com mend, we were summoned to partake, in company with the Trustees and their Kent and Sussex county guests, and the professional gentlemen representing the medical departments of each Board, to good, wholesome dinner, which we dis cussed with appetite while we discussed, tho same time, the expenses and the present condition of the institution. Mr. Barlow, the efficient Superintend ent, informed us that the maintainance the inmates, together with salaries for overseer and assistants, and all other ex penses connected with tho management the house and grounds, amounted to an average of forty cents per day for each inmate. Luring the year there have been about five hundred and fifty inmates. One hundred and ninety to ninety-five is, however, the average num ber in tho house at one time. Of the whole number received during tho past year, one hundred aud seventy-seven were colored; two hundred and twenty one foreigners; leaving only one hundred and fifty-one white American citizens who have availed themselves of the use of this grand charity furnished by the tax-payers oi New Castle county. make a tour of tho rooms, and find the same general care of the wards and cleanliness of tho rooms. With an occasional exception, the inmates are con tented and happy as circumstances will admit. Many of them—expecially the sick und aged—spoke with affectionate interest of the matron who they say makes for them a home with all a home's couifortH. Tho weak-minded aud insane we found to be more numerous than we expected, and the hospital for contageous diseases we declined to inspect. Wo next dropped into the parlor, where wo found Trustees of the several counties in committee of the whole, dis cussing tho propriety of memoraiizing the Legislature for a State Asylum for the insane. So rapid has been tho in crease of this class of inmates in New Castle county that tho available rooms are filled, and the Trustees have been under tho necessity of erecting some twelve new rooms, which aro now ready for the reception of occupants, number in tho institution at present classed as insane, is fifty-two, over one fourth of tho wholo inmates. Some of these cases aro hopelessly crazed, others aro capable of amelioration if not of perfect cure under skillful treatment and cheerful surroundings. Wo are informed that the medical staff of the house have been successful in a remarkable degree in these cases. Many considered incura blo have been discharged as sound in mind. But all the care that can bo ex ercised here, and tho best treatment possiblo under the circumstances, could not bo so effective as would be that of doctors who made disoases of the miud a specialty in an institution set apart ex clusively for such patients. It is not our purpose to report what as said at this conference on the sub ject of a State Insane Asylum. We were surprised at tho ability with which the subject was treated by the speakers. Evidently no application will be made to tho Legislature for relief until such facts can bo presented to our law makers as will convince them of the necessity for tho appeal, bas<*i not only on the fact that tho proportion of insane is too large to bo properly treated in connec tion with the other wards of tho coun ties, but chiefly to give this unfortunate class the benefit of exclusive treatment. Intelligent committees wero appointed from each county, who will collect sta tistics in regard to tho number of insane within the State, the most successful modo of treatment as adopted by the various institutions throughout thecoun try and all matters touching the subject. They will also digest a plan for a State Insane Asylum, all of which will bo duly considered by the Board collectively be fore presentation for Legislative action. The Superintendent appears to be indefatig able in the perfoimance of his duties, and tho Matron appears to bo regarded with affection by many a poor creature for whom she provides the real comforts of a home. An Observatory Near Belmont. An association of Boston gentlemen have engaged in an important enter - f rise in connection with the Centennial, t is the erection of a lofty iron observa tory, from which the thousands of visi tors may obtain an extended view of Fairmount Park, the Exposition ground, the city and the surrounding country The Park Commissioners have granted a site for the observatory on the most elovated point in the Park, and the structure will bo made one of the most substantial and beautiful ornaments of that spacious pleasure ground. The placo selected is near the Belmont mansion, on the west hank of the Schuyl kill, and a short distance north of the Centennial grounds. The base will bo 310 feet above the river, and the column will rise to a height of 200 feet, which will give the look-out gallery an eleva tion of over 500 feet, while the stars and stripes will wave from a staff on top 50 feet higher. The obsorvatory will Ire a novelty in its way, and as the first ever erected of its kind, will form one of the greatest curiosities of the great exhibi bition. Its inventor is Mr. L. B. Saw yer, a well-known resident of Charles town District. The observatory will bo wholly of iron, tubular in form, and is to be built in sections which are firmly attached to each other. It will be eight feet in di ameter at the base and somewhat small er at the top. The column will be also strengthened on four sides by truss work, which extends from the base to the lop, and eight large guys of wire rope, each of which is capable of sus taining a weight of thirty tons, will also aid in keeping the tower in place. The most remarkable feature of the observatory is the fact that the elevator car will ascend upon the outside cf the shaft. An annulur car-, about twenty feet in diameter, elegantly upholstered, and capable of accommodating twenty live or thirty persons, will be raiesd like an elevator upon the truss work or guides. The car will be raised by eight wire ropes, each of which will he capa ble of sustaining eight tons with safety, the combined strength being more than ten timeB as great than is necessary to sustain the car freighted to its utmost capaeity with passengers. in addition to all other means of guarding against the possibility of acci dents, there will bo eight safety ma chines attached to the car or elevator, either one of which would hold, even in case all the ropes should chance to givs way, which is an impossibility. The lifting power will be supplied by a dou ble cylinder upright engine of 40 horse power, located in a building at the base. The gallery and look-ont at the top will be covered and enclosed by wire net work, and are intended to accommodate about 125 persons. — Plata. St..r. fa of & a be re French Eggs. The enouuuurt exportation of French eggs to England led recently to an offi cial investigation with (he following re sult as reported by the Pall Mall (Janette: "An impression prevails in some quar ters that by dipping a hen in a pail ot water and then chasing her around the poultry yard with a stick, she'will be induced on emergencies to lay two eggs a day. Consul Hotham, on the other hand, in his commercial report on the Calais for last year, expressed his opin ion that the whole secret of the liberali ty of egg-laying displayed by the French hen lips in the quality of soil of those districts in which hens are renowned for their laying qualities. Attempts have, he says, been not unfrequently made to introduce French poultry into England, under the impression that with proper care and management these fowls muy become a fair source of prolit— so far, at least, as eggs are concerned. A French hen, however, removed from her native soil, does not, as a rule, behave herself with that productive alacrity which dis tinguishes her in many, though not in all parts of France. At Amiens, again, the same quali ty of soil is found, and the poultry from that district are remarkable for their laying qualities; they are, indeed, per haps the most celebrated layers in that country. Several letters have, of late, appear ed in tlio public prints, purporting to give the history of that interesting re gion of Cecil county, whicli bears the name of "Bohemia Manor." In these letters arc two or three inaccuracies, both of figures aud of frets, to correct which, and to present me statements relative to the subject, that have never before appeared in the newspapers, is the object of this communication. The territory of Maryland was gran ted in 1632, by King Charles the First, of England, to Sir George Calvert (whose title was Lord Baltimore); but before the charter was completed he died. Cecil Calvert, his eldest son,and heir to his estate and title, obtained the grant intended for Ids father, and ap pointed his brother Leonard, Governor of this new province. It seems that Cecil Calvert (the sec ond Lord Baltimore) laid c laim not only to what is now the State of Maryland, but to all the Unit and water east of it as far as to the present State of New Jersey. This claim, so far as it referred to the Delaware, or South river, as it was theu called, was disputed by Governor Stuyvesaut, of New Amsterdam (now New York), who sent an agent to con fer with the Governor of Maryland in reference thereto. This agent was Augustine Herman, or Heermans, an office holder, land owner aud man of influence in New Amsterdam. He was a Bohemian by birth, and a surveyor or draughtman by profession. It is said that he pre pared a map of the country for the Governor of Maryland in consideration of which he received in 1660 a patent fora tractof landembracing nominally four thousand acres, but in fact nearly four times that much. This tract is bounded on tbe east by the old Choptank road, from the head of Back creek to the north branch of Bohemiariver;lhence down said branch to Bohemia river, and with Bohemia river to its confluence with Elk river, then up the same to the mouth of Back creek to the Choptank road before mentioned; at least so says the report prepared by Stephen Hyland, Tobias Iiuilolpb, Isaac Grathem and Robert Armstrong—commissioners appointed about the year 1802 to divide this property among Herman's descend ants. Augustine Herman named his new possessions after li is native land—Bo hemia, or B.hemia Manor—but he did not occupy them until about the year 1604, at which time he left New Am sterdam, as some suppose, because the Dutch were compelled to surrender it to the English. But a traveler who visited Herman fifteen years after the above date, writss in his journal: "For some reason, I know not what, Her man disagreeing with Governor Stuy vesanl, repaired to this place." Concerning "this place''- Bohemia Manor—its early inhabitants, ancient la-tLaarks, and other objects of Inter est, I shall have more to fay in subse quent letters. Charles P. Mali.kry.
