A select party was held at the resi dence of Mr. Gipson, in honor of Bert and Ruth Gipson, last Saturday even ing. A pleasant evening was enjoyed by the following voung people: Messrs. Woodie Maxey, Thomas Paynter, Ralph Sebree and the Misses Florence and Babe Egleston, Hattie Stiles and Ella Horn. Nampa is troubled with a gang of toughs who have committed several thefts of late. A gentleman from Nampa in speaking about them said t^at if something wasn't done to get rid of them, someone was liable to be killed as they are a tough gang who wouldn't refuse to shoot anyone held up by tbem if any resistance was shown. Mr. and Mrs. Pefley narrowly es caped serious injury while enroute to Boise City last week. The mail team ran away and coming up behind crashed into the buggy occupied by the lady and gentleman. Their team was terribly frightened and ran some dis tance bringing up square on the river bank within a few feet of the water. Mrs, Pefley was bruised considerably but not seriously hurt; Mr. Pefley suffered some, especially in his ward robe; one wheel of the buggy was broken to pieces. It was a narrow but fortunate escape. Everybody is glad that it was no worse. Mrs. McFadyen and son arrived in Caldwell on a special from Huntington last Friday eveing. She was called from her home in California to be at the bedside of her husband, shot by Franks, and said to be dying. Mrs. McFadyen was obliged to travel on a hand car several miles, also in a wa gon, no trains running, until arriving at La Grande, when for the first time since leaving Califomi i she was able to ride in the cars. After all the hard ship she has gone through since leaving California, showing wonderful nerve and pluck, at last arrived at DeLamar and is now with her beloved husband who is improving. The Goodhue ranch, near Parma, was the scene of a lively row last Sat urday night between the ranch hands and Mr. Ward, the manager. It seems that the ranch hands have had consid erable trouble in getting wages due them. One Mr. Shaw levied attach ments on some of the farming imple ments, also a cow, and with others went to take possession, when they en countered a negress who is employed as cook. The negress not having a razor took the next best weapon, a pitchfork, and started in to help Mr Ward by jabbing Mr. Shaw in the side and another man in the arm with it. Mr. Shaw became very sick, it being necessary to send to Caldwell for Dr. Ed. E. Maxey, who on arriving there examined their wounds and found them not serious. Mr. Ward and the negress will be arrested.

SOMETHING SUBSTANTIAL. TI m Marth and Iraton Ranch to ba Converted In a Gold Field—Bonded for $50,000—A Scow Building—100,000 Feet Contracted—Caldwell the Shipping Point. The McKinley Brothers, of Duluth, Minnesota, is a new firm commencing extensive placer mining operations in this section. Mr. McKinley, the chief personal representative of the firm has been here for some weeks. He is a near relative of the celebrated "McKin ley Bill" (vice versa) and is backed by immense capital. The Marsh and Ire tou ranch, on the Payette has been bonded for $50,000 and instead of rais ing cattle and horses on it as was the custom of former owners, the ground will be worked for yellow metal. The whole ranch is known to be rich in placer deposits. At present the new firm is engaged in the construction of an im mense scow, which will ply up and down the Payette river, carrying placer mining machinery. The river will be dredged and the ground along the banks worked. Everything to be done by powerful machinery. Upwards of 150,000 feet of lumber will be used in the construction of the barge. The Central Lumber Co., of this city, has the furnishing contract. In a short time the machinery will be shipped from the east and will be transferred from Caldwell to the Payette river-by team After looking the country over, Mr. McKinley determined that Cald well was by far the best shipping point It is hoped this enterprising firm will make this city headquarters. The first machinery shipment will amount to be tween 100,000 and 200,000 pounds. It will be taken up the Willow creek val ley, and the roads are receiving atten tion preparatory, as some of the boilers are very heavy. Mayor Gwinn had a long talk with Mr. McKinley and was most favorably impressed. It may be depended on that the eloquent mayor left none of Caldwell's good points in the shadow and that any apparent drawbacks were shown to be actual ad vantages slightly disguised. However,

Mr. McKinley was well impressed and after looking the country all over con cluded that Caldwell is the natural apex of a vast commercial and indus trial dome. Mr. McKinley will be out again in a few weeks and will proba bly bring his family out on a visit. NORMAL NOTES. The gentlemen were in a still smaller minority this morning. Miss Ruth Peterson is again in school after a visit to Emmett. On Thursday Miss Edna Horn lis tened to the morning recitation. J. B. Martin is in school again after an extended celebration at Emmett. Misses Anna Hartley and Nellie Gil bert have been on the sick |list this week. Miss Jennie Kelleher's bright face was missed from the Normal Thursday and Friday. It is the private opinion of the Nor malités that the'school is doing very finely and that Prof. Broxon is deserv ing of great credit for that fact. Rev. I. S. Hieks visited the Normal Friday afternoon and gave the school an interesting talk and highly com mended the members and instructor on the work done. In anticipation of celebrating the Fourth of July, Monday's geography class discussed the appropriate topics of storms, cyclones, tornadoes, aurora borealis and thunder, and lightening. In regard to three days vacation, equal right of suffrage was entended to the Normalités which resulted in a tie necessitating Prof. Broxon to cast the deciding vote which lie did in favor of the negative. Tuesday's work was broken in upon by the photograph man wuo presented himself for the purpose of "taking" the Normal School. The Normalités im mediately repaired to the lawn, ar ranged themselves in.a graceful group, and allowed themselves to be "shot at" after the usual fashion. That the weather was several degrees warmer than the 4th of January.—Prof. Broxon. That a certain Normal girl can eat any quan tity of ice cream.—O. Martin. Nearly all of the Middleton precinct people celebrated the Fourth at Cald well. We hope the Caldwell people will return the compliment when Mid dleton becomes the county seat and gives a celebration. The question of a new bridge across the Boise river has been the means of creating as much comment here as the senatorial question did some few weeks ago. If there ever was a time when such questions should be avoided it is now. It is done by placing a large spring seat in the shade of the fence, place your shovel against the fence, lie down upon the seat and there you are. Presto change. Bricktop.

CALL FOR CANYON COUNTY REPUBLICAN CONVENTIONS. Notice is hereby given that the Canyon county Republican convention, for nominating delegates to the Republican State Convention, which meets in Boise August 8, 1894, will be held at Payette, on Saturday, July 28, at 2 o'clock p. m. The convention for nominating county officers will be held at Nampa, on Saturday, September 29, at 10 a. m. Canyon county will be entitled to eight dele fates In the State Convention. The business to e transacted by said State Convention as set forth in the call of the State Central Committee is as follows. Candidates for the following offices will be nominated : 1 'Member of Congress, Justice of the Supreme Court, Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secre tary of State, Attorney General, State Treasurer, Auditor, Superintendent of Public Instruction, five district judges, five district attorneys, and all joint members of the legislature. All candi dates for judicial and joint legis ative offices will be nominated by the delegates representing the various counties comprising the several judicial antl legislative districts. A state central com mittee will also be elected. ' 'The convention will be called upon to vote up on the proposition of nominating a Republican candidate for United States* Senator, to succeed Senator Shoup; and in the event of affirmative action thereon, will nominate a candidate for that position. In order that tills proposition may be considered by the people, the various county committees are requested to embrace this information in the call for their respective county coi ivention. ' ' The precincts of Canyon County will he entitled to the following representation in both County Convention, namely: Caldwell 14 Emmett 8 Kuna 1 Lower Boise 4 Middleton 4 Nampa 9 Payette 10 Stuart 3 Total 53 The above named precincts are requested to hold their primaries for the purpose or electing delegates to first named county convention, on Saturday, July 21, and to the other on Saturday, September 22, 1891. By order of Republican County Committee. A. E. G ipson, Attest: Chairman. W. A. T raver , Secretary.

Maple syrup from corn-cobs is the •latest. By this discovery the cobs are worth more than the corn. Frank Shafer, of Lacon, III, boils clean cobs in water untill soft. The Denver News publishes the following suggestion offered by « druggist of that city in regard to freez ingice cream without ice:" Any body can freeze his own ice cream in five minutes, at the cost of only a few cents. If the preparation designed to be frozen is placed in a tin bucket or other re ceptacle it can be readily congealed by putting it in a pail containing a weak dilution of sulphric acid and water. Into this throw a handful of common Glauber salts, and the resulting cold is so great that a bottle of wine immersed in the mixture will be frozen solid in a few minutes, and ice cream and ices may be quickly prepared. THE NEW LIGHT. Edison announces that he has com pletely succeeded in producing a new light, which he calls the "fluorescent light." It is simpler than the incan descent and in every way preferable. The same style of globe is used, but the whole globe is aglow with a bril liant white light of wonderful illumin ating power, instead of the carbon fila ment. Crystals of tungstate are weld ed to the inside of the globe, a partial vacuum is created aud the light is pro duced by molecules of air iu rapid vibration striking against the tung3tate crystals. A low current of electricity is employed, and whereas in the incan descent light only 5 per cent is utilized as light, there is no perceptible heat from the new light. Its power is greater, at a much lower cost, than any light ever before produced. We have only just begun to get used to the In candescent lights through their general introduction and use, and now comes a substitute, which is likely to supplant them as rapidly as they,were orignally introduced, from the same inventor. FEEDING ALFALFA. a An experiment, carefully conducted at the Utah agricultural station in feeding alfalfa cut at different stages of its growth, has shown that steers fed on that which was cut just before coming iuto bloom made a gain of three fourths of a pound a day. A second lot fed when the grass had been cut in the early bloom made a gain of only half a pound, while a third lot fed on late cut hay, after it was out of bloom, made an average gain of only one-fourth of a pound per day. There is a lesson worth heeding in this. If you neglsct your haying when the grass is just fit to cut, you are letting the dollars run away from you. 'Some of our readers may not know that this means that Sister Poulton was inspired by the holy sspirit to utter great, prophetic »truths in an unknown language :and Bro. Isaac Lee was similarly iinspired to interpret what Sister ÎPoulton said. The writer on rseveral occasions has witnessed ithe so-called speaking in tongues ;and it is a profoundly impressive '.proceeding. We very clearly re imember one occasion when an •did gentleman was suddenly seiz tefi by "the spirit." For a mo ment, he sat as one petrified; then great drops of sweat broke out on his face and he began to ■tremble violently. The agitation 'increased; his lips began to quiv «er and his jaws moved rapidly for iperhaps half a minute before an iaudible sound escaped him, then Hie burst forth in "original Greek," «ontinuing for at least ten min utes. We will not vouch for the purtop of the "original Greek," becausc the tongue-talker was a a very j>ronounced old Welsh man with a broad brogue ; but it was Greek to all his audience ex cept another Welshman, who im mediately, after going through similar preliminary exercises, pro ceeded to translate the Greek prophecy into somewhat dam aged Welsh. We béfieve Wales, with Denmark a close second, has produced the most celebrated tongue-talkers of modern times. »Whether it is because ^the W elsh language is conducive of a great er amount of flexibility of tongue kthan any other, or because Welshmen, on account of their theater piety, are more freely en dowed with the "gifts," we are not prepared to say, but that they are exceptionably proficient is un questioned. Instances are recit ed where totally illiterate Welsh men have discoursed in fifteen or "twenty foreign languages without much as a grammatical slip, while other Welshmen with equal facility and accuracy have trans lated all of them into faultless "Vernacular. INCREASE POPULATION. Boise-Caldwell Interurban Should Do Same for Boise Valley as Electric Lines l)o in Iowa—Have Proved Great Help There. Now that the Caldwell-Boise Elec trie Railway will soon be in opera tion, it is interesting to note the effects in population in other places. It is ascertained that in every section of the country, the electric line en ables many more people to gain sus tenance than before the advent of the line. The tendency is to cut down the size of the farm, thus encourag ing more intensive farming. In speaking of conditions in Iowa, the Chicago Record-Herald says: "Officials of interurban trolley lines In Iowa have been doing some figur ing, with the result that the interur ban line appears in a flattering light as a population pusher. "In those townships in the state where interurban lines have been op erating the population has increased considerably in the last few years, whereas the population of the state in general has decreased. "This was shown by the census of 1905 when the total figures indicated that the state had lost about 30,000 people since 1900. During the same period the population in the towns through which the interurban lines run has increased in almost every in stance from 25 to 50 per cent.

Sales Day. Monday was sales day In Caldwell and as usual there was a large crowd in town, and the sales were very sat isfactory. While the amount of stock ws not near so large as at the April sales, yet what was offered was a much better quality and all brought good prices. People are beginning to realize that it pays to bring good stock; old broken down horses are not wanted at any price, while good ones sell readily at good prices, and it is the same with all other articles. If you have a wagon or buggy to sell it pays to have it clean, it often hap pens that a coat of paint will make a vehicle sell for more than enough to pay for the extra expense. The difficulties which have confronted the managers at. previous sales are now about overcome. At this last sale everything moved like clockwork, from the offering of the first bedstead to the sale of the last horse. There were 94 entries consisting of thirty-four horses, five cows, two wagons, five buggies, seven Bets of harness, twelve separate lots of chickens, ten pigs, five implements, besides numerous household articles. The next sales day will be on June 1st. All those who have anything to sell can have it listed by addressing H. W. Dorman, Caldwell.

Hannah brought a curiosity to the Tribune office that beats any thing of the kind ever seen by the agricultural editor of this paper It is a stalk of Stowcll's Evergreen corn that has two well developed ears of corn, both of which grow from one joint. A most instructive and delightful meeting was that of the eighth an nual convention of the Second District Federation of Women's Clubs held at Payette October 19th to 20th. N. C. in colors. Mrs. John Mc Glinchy welcomed the visitors warmly to the homes and the hearts of the Payette people. The presi dent's annual address was full of recommendations for the coming year among some of them were the fol lowing: That the club women work for stricter enforcement of the cur few law, that public sentiment be kept alive to necessity of supporting all measures looking to the betterment of the condition and control of dependent, crippled and delinquent children, that there be close co-operation with the state historical socety, that a travel ing art exhibit be sent to every school and library. There was no opposition except that Mr. Frank H Bowen was placed on an independent ticket for councilman. On election day the Socialists got out a circular asking the people of Caldwell to sup port the Socialist ticket headed by Mr C. W. Cooper. This ticket was not on the official ballot. Shorb, clerk; Ed Hedden, engineer; John Steunen berg and J. L. Bardsley, H. J. Zeh and C. Q. Adams, Thomas E. Walker and Ed H. Adam, councilmen. The new administration assumes charge of municipal affairs the first Monday in May. The administration is pledged to municipal ownership of tl>e electric lighting plant, interna! improvements consistent with reason able taxes, economy in administration, cleanliness and interest on daily bal ances of city funds in the banks. The Tribune is convinced that this administration will give Caldwell a good, capable service in city affairs The officers just elected stand high in the estimation of the people of Cald well.

CANYON COUNTY TO HAVE BIGGER AND BETTER FAIR
Big Broncho Busting Contest Will Enliven Things Fine Cash Prises.

Wild Mule Races to be a new Feature of Great Intereat—Dance will be Held each Evening on Street in Front of O. S. L. Station—Come for the Time of Your Life. A list of the special events, to be held at the Canyon County Fair, open ing October 1 and closing October 5, which has been issued by the fair management amply bears out their statement that the exposition this year will be bigger and better from every standpoint, than any of its pre decessors. The iair directors have authorized the expenditure of a large sum of money, in addition to the reg ular budget, to provide feature enter tainments, to be staged during the racing intermissions, assuring visitors continual round of amusements, and entirely eliminating the long tiresome waits between races. Before the building of electric and steam railways and the coming of water to reclaim what was then con sidered an unproductive desert, Can yon and Owyhee counties was one vsst range where countless thousands of cattle were fed In those days the cowbdy was king and reigned su preme. The coming of "the man with the hoe" deposed the monarch and he lives today only as a legend in the minds of the new settlers and the younger generation. To pay fitting tribute to the old west and to recall to the sturdy pioneers thrilling scenes from the days gone by, the fair direct ors have made arrangmentt for the reproduction of many events from tbe range days. During the first four days of the fair there will be bronco busting, roping, wild mule races, pony races an<\ other events showing the cowboy at work and at play. Skillful and daring acts of horsemanship participated in by the most noted and daring cowboys from the Wyoming rang^ who* will stop at Caldwejl enroute to the Pend leton Round.-Up, will be shown daily. The prizes offered by the fair board are large and will prove an added in centive for hard riding on the part of those participating. For bronco bust ing $150, divided into two purses $106 to first, and $50 to second is offered $25 will be awarded to the owner of the horse that is the hardest to ride.

A • wild mule race is scheduled for each of the first four days, with combined purse of $200.. Fifty dollars will be awarded each day, $35, to first and $15 to second. The fair manage ment furnishes the mules for this event and already have agents scour ing the state for the wildest specimens obtainable, regardless of the expense involved. This feature it is said, will prove to be one of the most exciting snd amusing of the special events. The ingenuity and skill of the most daring of the riders present will be taxed to tbe utmost to get results from the re fractory animals. Many laughable and exciting situations are certain to de velop«. Among other special «vente arrang ed for is a 5-mtle rclsy race with $100 to first, $75 to second, and $25 to the third. The race is ov*r a five mile course with a change of horses every half mile. A gentelmen's driving rscc, free for all, a ladies' driving race, with four wheel vehicle, motor cycle races, saddle hCrse race, shetland pony race, two horse wagon race, and a pony race are also on the list The harness events and the horse races will be filled over night. Many of the fastest horses in the northwest will be entered and the racing card this year will be of high order. Plans for handling the crowd dur ing the week are well advanced and visitors will experience no difficulty in te curing hotel sccomodstions at. reasonable rate.

CANYON COUNTY FARM LANDS INCREASED BY STATE BOARD OFFICERS ARE EQUALIZING ASSESSMENTS THROUGH OUT STATE—TIMBERMEN WANT REDUCTION. Ten Per Cent Raise on Sheep—Ad ditional Shortage Alleged to Have Been Discovered in Treasurer's Of fice— State Will Sue Bonding Com pany for Shortage. (.Special to Caldwell Tribune.) Boise, August 18.—The state board of equalization is still labor ing with the difficult problems that confronts them. But little has been given out as a result of their de liberations. The Assessors were heard Monday and Tuesday, the representa tives of the timber interests put in their plea for reductions. It has been intimated that Canyon county was in for a raise of 10 per cent upon agri cultural lands and that Bannock u uld be touched up for IS per cent raise in a like classification. Bonner county is scheduled for a reduction on agricultural lands. The timber interests are putting up a strong pica for a reduction which is supported by the usual lobby. The lumber business is at a low ebb beyond any question but the impression pre vails that they have always received very fair consideration in the past and that they do not have much coming at this time. This remark does not apply to Boise and Adams counties, where there was an extreme raise. The board early in their delibera tions decided to raise the valuations upon sheep and a ten per cent raise has been agreed upon. It is not believed that any radical changes will be made in the valuations returned by the assessors. The board has given out no intima tion as to what its attitude will be with regard to the valuations that will be placcd upon railroads and power companies. The total valuation of the state as reported by the assessors for 1915 is $299,615,914, as compared with $296, 705,015 for 1914. This does not include the railroads, and other utilities, as sessed directly by the state board. Canyon Gets 10 Per Cent Increase. The state board of equilzation made no changes in the assessed valuations of Canyon county, except irrigated farm lands which were raised 10 per cent. The ascsessment was complete except for railroads, telephone and telegraph lines. Additional Shortage. An^additional shortage, aounting to $11,171.50, has been discovered in the defalcation of ex-Treasurer O. V. Allen, according to a late report sub mitted to Governor Alexander and Attorney General Peterson. The re port is made by James S. Bogart, who was employed by the Governor and the Attorney General to expert the State Treasurer's books to secure the necessary evidence upon whicih tio base a suit to recover from the bond ing company the amount of Allen's defalcation. In the course of his in vestigation, Mr. Bogart discovered live different items, amounting to the sum above mentioned that had not previously been reported. These five items are amounts sent to the state of Idaho by the LTnited States Govern ment during the years 1912-13-14-15, the first being sent on May 16, 1912. The additioival amount of defalcation was found by Mr. Bogart by corres ponding with the treasury department at Washington. There was no record in any othen department of the state of these transactions, the money evi dently having come direct to the state treasurer who applied it to his own use without any record being made of it. As soon as the case can be put in shape, demand will be made upon the bonding company for the entire amount of the defalcation. Delay in commencing suit was at the sugges tion of Attorney General Peterson, who desired to have the matter upon a solid footing when he went into court, and the result of the Bogart disclosure entirely justifies his judg ment. Davis, a probable candidate for the Republican nomina tion for governor, was a Caldwell visi tor Monday. Captain Davis recently returned from the southeast. He states that there is every indication that the southeast will roll up its regular Re publican majority at the next elec tion. The word comes in from all sections of Idaho that the state will go Republican from president down. Captain Davis is a graduate of West Point, an ex-member of the state leg islature, ex-secretary of the Repub lican state central committee, ex private secretary of the governor of Idaho and ex-assistant attorney gen eral. He was born in Idaho. When asked as to his candidacy Captain Davis stated that it was a little early to talk for publication. He assured us that he would be a candi date and felt certain of landing the nomination. He has received pledges of support in his candidacy from all sections of the state. Not Solicited By Friends. Captain Davis has issued a state ment in which he states that his can didacy does not come from the insis tance of friends. After briefly review ing his education, training and exper ience Captain Davis says: "As to my character and reputation I hope I need say but little. I have spent nearly 20 years in more or less active public life, I have filled many positions of trust and responsibility and if either my honesty or integrity has been questioned, this has never been brought to my attention. Even my political opponents, so far as I know, have never questioned my hon esty or my loyalty to principle and conviction. "I was trained and educated in the greatest school for moral discipline in the world. I was tutored under such men as Goethals, the builder of the Panama canal, and I formed my ideals of public duty in a branch of the ser vice where even an official statement which varies from the truth is an offense. "My training, and I believe, my na tural talents, should make me specially lualified for the administrative work which pertains to the governor's of fice: If I am elected I hope to intro duce system and honesty, efficiency and dispatch into the transaction of the public business, to insure the hon est performance of duty on the part of every subordinate official; and I shall hope further to be able to lead in the work of unmasking sham and bun combe and hollow pretense and lack of candor in public affairs and in the work of driving from the public life of Idaho every individual whose per sonal honesty and whose ideals of proper public service are not above re proach. "I expect if I finallv become a can didate to make an active and aggres sive but withal the cleanest campaign ever made in the state. I shall do nothing to gain office which could pos sibly bring a thought of shame or re gret to anyone who may support me. If elected I shall enter office wholly untramnieled and unpledged, and shall endeavor to perforin my duties in such manner as to merit the approval of every honest man and woman in the state." CAMPBELL CARNIVAL SECURED FOR THE STATE FAIR IS MANAGEMENT SECURES THE BIGGEST AND BEST AT TRACTIONS IN WHOLE NORTHWEST. Counties ot State Take Interest by Pledging Support and Making Ap propriations—Biggest and Best Fair -in History of Idaho is now Assured. The Idaho State Fair, to be held at Caldwell September 28, 29, 30, October 1 and 2, promises to be the biggest tiling of the kind ever held in this sec tion of the country. Wild West Show. The management has secured the big Irwin Bros. Cheyenne Frontire Days Wild West Show for August 30 and 31. This stampede and round up is the biggest attraction of the kind in the world. There will be de picted all the glories of the good old days when the cowboy was king and every man who wished for any consid eration from his fellows "pounded the leather." While the big show comes a month before the fair, it was only possible to secure this big attraction at this time and the fair management wanted to give the people a chance to enjoy the spectacle. Messrs. J. B. Gowen and J. E. Rid dle are giving their whole time to the business of getting pledges of ex hibits that will eclipse the fair of any previous year. These gentlemen, to gether with J. S. Hurlburt, on a trip the first of the week secured the pro mise of a fine exhibit of horses, cattle, sheep and hogs from the ranch of Geo. Layton, near Boise. There will two milking contests, one for grade cows and small breeders and one for the larger breeders. Immense Carnival Company. Contract was signed this week with the Campbell Carnival Co., one of the largest amusement companies in the country. Some idea may be gained of the magnitude of this at traction when it is known that it tajkes 20 cars to bring the outfit. There will be several shows at the fair grounds given by the Campbell company, but the Big Time will be down town, in the evening. At the Carnival Grounds, running nearly 500 feet, will be found nil the shows, games and amusements that make for the' One Time of the Year. Appropriations by Several Counties. Several counties hav.e already made appropriations for premiums for the people of their counties. Others will do so, and the spacious State Fair Grounds will be packed and jammed with the finest exhibits that Idaho can boast—and that beats the world. The Canyon County Commissioners will make no appropriation, direct to the fair, at any rate. It is probable that they will appropriate small sums for school exhibits, boys' and girls' clubs, etc., and the state may do the same for clubs of like character. Messrs. J. B. Gowen, J. E. Riddle and M. H. Gibbons left Tuesday for a trip around the western end of the county, up through Washington coun ty, and stops in Boise and Ada in the interests of the fair. They will return the latter part of the week. SUDDEN DEATH OF MRS. PEPPARD SUNDAY NIGHT Mrs. James Peppard died suddenly Sunday night of gallstones. Hayes, Mrs. McMullan of Niagara, N. Y., and an eight-year-old girl that lived with her here. MAMMOTH CROP YIELDS IN BOISE VALLEY THIS YEAR CORN, WHEAT. BARLEY AND OATS PRODUCED IN REC ORD BREAKING QUAN TITIES BY FARMERS Corn Runs to 130 Bushels to Acre; Wheat Makes 68 Bushels; Barley 92; Oats 109; Clover Seed 9; Alfalfa Reaches Nine Tons to the Acre— Excellent Showing Made by All. The gentleman from Southern In diana was frankly skeptical of big yields of corn in Idaho. He had the same simple character and trustful ness of the gentleman from Missouri and was willing to be shown. The first field met with was declar ed good. It was new ground and he was assured he would see better. At the^next stop, a few miles ^south of | r " u " "* 1 .. .. Caldwell, lie entered the field with all the superior manner of the man from the Middle Western corn belt—and came back in half an hour in the same half-dazed manner of a groom after his first encounter with an Idaho bride. He declared that he had never seen —had never dreamed that such corn could be grown anywhere. The field he estimated would run between 125 and 130 bushels to the acre. And that is substantially the story of all the crops in and around Cald well this year. Corn, wheat, oats, barley, alfalfa, potatoes—all the my riad crops that gladden the heart of the farmer—all are of record propor tion; and that means a little better than anywhere else in the world. Field after field of corn will run better than 100 bushels to the acre. J. H. Trout, at Roswell, registered 110 bushels of corn last year; he declares that his yield this year will be very much better. Roy Johnson garnered 108 bushels of corn to the acre last year; this year it will be nearer 125 bushels. W. A. McKague has a good field, as has Harry Wahl. R. S. Brown of Wilder made 100 bushels last year; this year he will have a very much heavier crop. B. F. Leavell's corn crop will run between 75 and 80 bu shels; but then Mr. Leavell is unusual ly conservative. J. H. Forbes has a field that will run over 100 bushels, C. ~ Oellien has a fine looking field. For a state that only a couple of years ago was declared totally unfit for corn raising, this year's crop will prove decidedly enlightening. Good Wheat Yields. Threshing of the wheat crop is at ts height, but the crop yields are of an encouraging character, being heavy and of first class quality. The best single yield that has come to our attention is that of V. D. Han nah. Mr. Hannah averaged 68 bu shels of wheat to the acre. Among the yields of wheat that are reported are the following: Harrv Clemens, Kingsbury, 60 bu shels; Fred Chaney, 55 bushels: W. R. Bell, 52; Sam Vassar, 50; Smith Bros. 59; Gakey & Goble, 49; Waldo Weeks, 60; Will Osborn, Wilder, 65: Jess Mattingly, turkey red, 51; C. C. Green field, Huston, 55; C. F. Oellien, 51; Bent Altizer, 49; Louis Griffith, 37; Frank Weeks. 40; W. A. Adams 41; Neal Hibbs, 60; Henry Iverson, 64. Irvin Lee, in the Gem District, has a 140-acrc field of wheat that averages 60 bushels. All of the yields are good and only a small portion are reported. Barley and Oats Yield. The barley and oat crops will euual any previous yield—and the quality fully as good. J. S. Hurlburt had a yield of 92 bushels of barley; Lawrence Wamstad of the upper Roswell country, had a yield of 90 bushels of barley: T. O. Wheeler has 65 bushels; and several others run between. Oats are of good quality and run f ully un to the average. Fred Cheney has 110 bushels; C. F. Smith, 105: W. S. Rogers. 92; V. D. Hannah, 109 bu. Record Alfalfa Crop. Alfalfa will run to the banner crop this year. From all accounts the aver age will run near 9 tons to the acre, with four cuttings. Tbe first cutting was perhaps a little under the aver age, the second, a little better than the average, the third the greatest ever enjoyed, as well as the earliest; and the fourth cutting is now on its way •nerrily. On a number of farms the first two cuttings brought five tons, and the outlook is good for at le-st four tons from the next two cuttings Clover Seed. There is every prospect for a verv good clover seed crop. A. F. Tal bot reports nearly 7 bushels red clover *o the acre, and a Mr. Wagner, son-in. law of J. G. Whittig 10 bushels of Alsike. There are three field« of clover in the Gem District that are the equal of anv in the country. Thev are on the W. A. McKague place, the A. W Griggs place and that of C. T. How ard. J. L. Maxwell and E. B. Snell of the Gem District report that their alfalfa will go over 9 tons this year. W. A. McKa<rue reports about the same. C. V. Peckham of Greenleaf reports •in unusually heavy crop in nearly all tines around the Greenleaf community. \lfalfa was never heavier, and the corn promises well. Wheat, oats and hirley are of record dimensions and the promise of the harvest is indeed golden.

Miss Ruth Harris lies unconscious in the X'ampa General hospital, with a fracture at the base of the skull, which may yet mean death for lier, as the result of being thrown from a horse she was riding. The accident hap pened in front of the tire station, be tween 9 and 9:30 o'clock Tuesday eve ning. Miss Harris had been riding down First street south in company with Misses Selma and Agues Alexander at lively canter and they started to [turn into Ninth avenue. Just at this point the pavement ends and in pass onto the dirt street the voting lady's steed stumbled, tossing lier vio lently to the ground. It seems that she landed against the cement curb on the hack of her head. Remains Unconscious. Chief Mayhew and one or two of the firemen were quickly summoned to the side of the injured girl. She was carried into the fire statiom while physicians were being located. Hem orrhages from the ears and nose indi cated the seriousness of the injuries. On orders from the physicians Miss Harris was removed to the hospital where she lay all dav Wednesday with little sign of returning conscious ness. In addition to the supposed fracture at the base of the brain there is a three-inch gash across the bac' of her head. Carefful examination did not reveal a fracture at this point. Science Healers Take Charge. Some comment was occasioned when it was learned that relatives dis charged the attending physicians Wednesday morning and entrusted the patient to the care of Christian Sci ence leaders. Miss Harris, who is not quite 17 years old is a daughter of C. H. Har ris, a rancher living west of town. She and her companions had ridden in from the country and were about to start home when the accident oc curred. (Special to Caldwell Tribune.) Boise, Aug. 18.—Political interest which has been at a low ebb in Idaho for several weeks experienced a re vival this week in the formal an nouncement of Capt. Ii. G. Davis that he would be a candidate for the Re publican nomination for governor. The Captain's formal entry into the race was not unexpected but it served to stimulate public interest in the contest which is still nearly a year off and a number of more or less prominent individuals are being dis cussed in connection with the honor. It is conceded that Canyon's favorite son, Col. E. H. Dewey of Nampa, would be a strong contender for the nomination if he would enter the race, but the belief is that the Colonel will not solicit the nomination if he has to ■ ight for it. Yet it is a fighter that the party wants for a leader, and Col. Dewey will either have to declare him self or be counted out. Former Sena tor Davis of American Falls has an ambition to be Governor and it is de clared that he will have the Brady in fluence behind him. The American Falls aspirant has a considerable fol lowing of his own, and his candidacy is to be taken seriously. Lieutenant Governor Taylor has announced that "at the proper time" he will announce his candidacy. Just what is under stood to be the "proper time," or open season, for candidates for Governor nas never been officially declared, but former Governor John M. Haines is sure that it is not until sometime next spring. The former Governor feels that he would have defeated Moses Alexander just as easily as he won iiis renomination had it not been for the Allen scandal and asks for a vin dication, the most rigid investigation having failed to implicate him in any way. The name of Charles L. Heit man is receiving frequent mention, but the former Chairman does not seem to be greatly interested himself. The only sure thing about the con test for the Republican nomination for governor is that there has as yet been little concentration of sentiment in favor of any candidate. Republicans will be especially interested in select ing a man who can beat Mose Alex ander and are not inclined to take any chances. There will be a new candidate to select for Attorney General. General Peterson is serving his second term and will not be a candidate for re nomination. There are a number of aspirants for the position. Among them are: W. G. Bissell of Gooding; C. D. Smith of Pocatello; C. H. Potts of Coeur d'Alene; John Becker of Orofino; also Asisstant Attorney Gen eral Wing. If T. C. Coffin, also As sistant Attorney General, were a couple of years older, he might have strong influence in his favor. Coffin s but 28 years of age and is making great progress in his profession. He is not politically ambitious and an nounces that he intends to resign his position in a short time to enter into private practice. He will open an office in Pocatello. It is extremely probable that John Becker of Orofino will be appointed to a position as As sistant Attorney General. Judge Sullivan will be a candidate to succeed himself. The Judge has served upon the Supreme bench of Idaho for more than a quarter of a century. He is a man of strong con victions, clean in character, and has a long and honorable record to com mend him. If the people of Idaho follow the precedent of other states in retaining their Supreme Court Jus tices during good behavior, accom panied by able and honorable service, Judge Sullivan may continue in his present high position for many years to come.

Increases Cost But Not of Long Distance Service. Quality

Washington, D. C.—Nothing the present administration has attempted to "put over" has aroused such wide spread resentment and called forth such general and vigorous protests as Postmaster General Burleson's re vision upward of long-distance tele phone charges, effective January 21, 1919. Since the administration, under the pretext of its being a war measure, seized the telephone service of the country and placed it under Post master General Burleson, there has been growing dissatisfaction with the service. The limit of public patience, however, seems to have been reached when the now schedule of rates for long distance was announced. Not withstanding the announcement was accompanied by the carefully conveyed impression that th e new rates would be a public benefit, the facts are pret ty definitely summed up in the state ment of Chairman Hill, of the New York Public Service Commission, made in connection with the Commis sion's instituting legal proceedings in the federal courts to restrain the New York Telephone Company from putting into operation the new rates ordered by Postmaster General Burle son. Mr. Hill said:

"The new rates were promulgat ed by the Postmaster General with the statement that they brought about a decrease in charges, but analysis by the New York Public Service Commission gives the same results as analysis made by the public service commissions in Illinois, Ohio, Nebraska, New Jersey, Indiana, Missouri and other states; that is, that the rates are increased from 20 to 100 per cent. The effect of the order of the Postmaster General is to in crease charges for telephone service covering the bulk of trafic and making charges for certain service which heretofore were free." Burleson's Power Challenged. The New York Public Service Com mission .is not alone in resorting to litigation to test the right of Post master General Burelson to man handle the telephone rates of the coun try. At least nine other state com missions have instituted legal pro ceedings to prevent the enforcement of these new rates. These states are: Illinois, Nebraska, West Virginia, Ohio, New Jersey, Minnesota, Michi gan, Wisconsin and Alabama. In commenting upon its action in chal lenging Postmaster General Burleson's program, the Nebraska State Com mission issued a statement in which it says: "The Postmaster General has en tered into compensation contracts with telephone companies without making any audit of their books or survey of their properties. The Postmaster General has Increased the existing charges and has made new charges for service heretofore free without substantial investigation of their necessity and practicability The Postmaster General has con ducted the business without affording the public an opportunity to be heard " The state officials of practically all the states have registered their dis approval of the action in messages to various congressmen, and particularly to the members of the House Com mittee on Postoffice and Post Roads. The public protests against the new rates take on the air of indignation because of the attempt on the part of the Postmaster General to make it ap pear that the new rates are a drrease. To illustrate what are the real facts it is only neccssary to compare the new rates in action with the old. How New Rates Work. Under the old order, if John Brown wished to talk to William Smith, he might put in a call for William Smith: that is, he might ask the operator not <>nly to get the telephone number at which William Smith might b c called, but to call William Smith himself to the phone. Or John Brown might want to talk to William Smith at a certain hour and he could make an appointment to have William Smith put on the phone at that hour, Or lie might want William Smith to call him at a certain hour and have Wil liam Smith call him, with the dmrgc« reversed. Any one or all of these things, John Brown might have done under the old schedule without any extra charges over the published rates for a three-minute talk. Now it is different. Under Post master General Burleson's new sched ule, John Brown cannot talk to Wil linin Smith unless he puts in what is now designated a "person to person" call. The rate for such a call is 25 per cent greater than the minimum rate for three minutes' conversation. The only service John Brown can now net for the minimum rate is what is known as a "station to station" call. This merely entitles him to call a telephone number and talk to whom ever answer the phone. As only an infinitely small percentage of long distance calls are for "anyone there" at the number called, the number of cases where Mr. Burleson's new mini mum rate will apply, will be practical ly negligible. Not only must John Brown pa tra in order to have William Smith ex

himself put on the phone, but if he wishes to have Mr. Smith put on the phone at a particular time then an other additional rate i s charged, known under Mr. Burleson's new schedule as an "appointment rate." Moreover, if John Brown calls for William Smith and the operator re ports that he is not there, and Mr. Brown has the operator ascertain when he will be there, Mr. Brown is charged an extra fee for this service which is known as a "report charge." Rate Actually Doubled. All of these various services have been rendered by the tedephone com panies without extra charge and as the majority of long distance calls in cludes at least one, and maybe all of these services, the actual increase in rates under Mr. Burleson's new tele phone order approximates nearly 100 per cent. Another point upon which an effort was made to mislead the public was in the statement that the night rates are so much lower than formerly. This is true only on "station to sta tion" calls. That is to say, where John Brown simply asks for a tele phone number without asking for anyone in particular or making any appointment. On all long distance calls at night, regardless of the time of night, where the party calling asks for some party in particular or asks information regarding some party or seeks to make an appointment with some party there is no reduction from the day rate. The new rates mean an increase of thousands of dollars annually in tele phone bills of large corporations and a price to the individual so high as to be almost prohibitive. Under Post master General Burelison's administra tion of the postal department the mails have become so irregular and so undependable that the large business, banking and manufacturing concerns have been resorting more and more to the telephone. Now they fear that this service is going to be crippled even as the mail service has been crippled and at the same time (as with the mail service) the rates advanced The Larger Issue. In a larger sense, there is the men ace of an autocracy established under the pretense that it is necessary to make the world safe for democracy That is the issue which the various state commissions are bringing into the federal courts. No one believes the administration's seizure of the tele phone systems of the country was a war necessity, but having used the war as a camouflage to get control of this vast public utility it remains to bc decided whether that autocratic power can be indefinitely extended into the era of peace and used to suit the personal caprice of one man or advance the political fortunes of clique, at an added cost to the public of millions of dollars and, at the same time, a lessened quality of public ser vice, and in defiance of all state laws and regulations.

William E. Hawkes of Caldwell sailed Saturday from New York on the S. S. Pensacola with a large party of relief workers under the dir-etio of the American committee for relief in the near cast. In company with a number of other relief workers, many of them ex-armv men, Mr. Hawkes is going to Constan tinople, the headquarters of the com mittee in the great work of recon struction. Accompanying Mr. Hawkes are re tired army officers and enlisted men The work in which Mr. Hawkes and his associates are due to take an ac tive part in is being financed by con tributions from all parts of the coun try. Mr. Hawkes was educated at the College of Idaho, the Lewistön State Normal, and the Hartford Theologi cal seminary. He has had wide experi ence in executive and educational work, and has had charge of Y. M. C. A. work in the army. Shortly before he sailed Mr. Hawkes said that he was looking forward to permanent missionary work in Turkey, but that the relief program now being executed by the American committee for relief called for immediate atten tion. and he felt it his dutv to respond. The committee is sending to Con stantinople and other ports in Asia Minor a number of automobiles, am bulances and motor trucks, which will be used in transporting the vast stores of foodstuffs, clothintr and medical supplies sent abroad for the relief of suffering people in Armenia, Syria, Persia and Palestine.

E Geo. Dewey Announces Determination to Re main on Job* Renounc ing Intention to Stay. George Dewey, county agent, who announced some time ago that he would discontinue county agent work the first of the year to enter private business, has reconsidered and will re main in this work for. the time being at least, according to a statement made Thursday movning. Reorganization of the farm bureau through its affili ation with the national organization and enlargement of its scope of ac tivities to include work in marketing through co-operative effort which promises a greatly enlarged field of activity during the coming year, prompted .Mr. Dewey to reconsider his determination to leave the work. Pressure was also brought to bear through the membership of the coun ty farm bureau to induce him to re main. Mr. Dewey has been active head of the Canyon county farm bureau for almost two years, having taken up the work following the resignation of R. H. Musser, who became associated with the state staff of farm bureau leaders. In carrying out the enlarged farm bureau plans for 1921, all-day meet ings will be held shortly in every 'school district in the county. These meetings will be featured by the in auguration of practical methods to insure more favorable marketing con . ditions for southern Idaho crops. It is proposed to make state-wide mar keting associations for producers of all important crops and to handle the disposal of such crops in somewhat the same manner that has led to the unqualified success attending the or ganization of similar selling methods in California. New Year's day, the customary all day meeting at Lone Star will be held and a big oyster dinner will be served. This is a regular annual com munity event but this year further ance of the farm bureau's enlarged program will be given consideration.

PART OF NEAR EAST COMPARATIVELY QUIET While many of the former mission ary stations now occupied by the Near F.ast Relief forces have been much disturbed, some nearly broken up and some being in the "war zone" be tween the French and Nationalists Turks have been under fire, there have been no casualties of the relief forces for many months and the Sivas station has so far been undisturbed. Mr. Hawkes says their Turkish gov ernor has been friendly under date of October 12. He tells of "60 camel loads of supplies" arriving, an evi dence of the uncertain transportation and showing a touch of picturesque ( ness. Mr. Hawkes hopes to get home for next college commencement, al though he may later return to Asia Minor to continue the work.

BUSIN ATP ESS ST OLDS FF CE FIGURES REVEIL This Year Promises to Better 1919 Record; Holiday Trade Marked by Final Rush. Business slumps have nothing to do with the post office receipts according to James Ford local postmaster. De spite the loss of two rural routes, those at Huston which formerly went out of this office and the fact that a re duction has been made in the postal rate, the 1920 business through the lo cal office will probably exceed that of last year, according to a statement made by Mr. Ford Thursday. Last year which far exceeded any single fiscal year in the volume of business transacted, postal receipts showed a total of more than $S6,000. Seventeen per cent of this gross amount was de ducted. however, because of its nature as a revenue stamps and because of a proportionate reduction resulting from the war measure, three cent postage rate then in vogue. In spite of this re duction, the total postal receipts for 1919 aggregated $29,707, just $30 short of the amount required before an office can be admitted into the first class. This year, in spite of the business depression and the loss of the two routes now centralized, at Huston, pos tal receipts will probably exceed the 1919 business through the local office, according to Mr. Ford. Only in one month has the total fallen below the 1919 standard. December is, of course, as yet undetermined hut Mr. Ford be lieves that the volume of Christmas business will equal, if not exceed that of last year. Last December, Cald well people spent $3600 during the month with the post office. Final'Scramble. One of the remarkable features of this year's holiday rush was the fact that the greater share of business was done during tile two days immediately preceeding Christmas. Mr. Ford ex pressed the belief that many persons who had fully decided not to send Christmas presents this year, changed their minds at the last moment. At any rate, most of the packages which rent through the local office were mailed so late fhat there was no pos sibility for them to reach their destina tion before Christmas Day. .In general, however, the Christmas trade was handled more expeditiously than it was in the past by the post office department, not only Caldwell, but over the nation generally. Most packages were so mailed and eared for that, even when the destination was remote, a single package was never handled more than three times. Five years ago when Mr. Ford be came postmaster at the local office, the annual business ran in the neigh borhood of $20,000. This year prom ises to exceed $30,000, which means a net increase of 100 per cent in five years. These figures are taken as be ing fairly indicative of the rspid deve lopment of Caldwell and the tributary territory.

The January organ recital to have been given at the Methodist church next Sunday, has been postponed un til Sunday, January 9, according to an announcement made Thursday by Prof. F. F. Beale. This step was taken to give students at the College of Idaho an opportunity to attend. Class work will not be resumed at the college until after the day on which the concert was to have been given and many students will not have returned by that time. This change is for January only, according to Mr. Beale, the February concert will be given the first Sunday in that month.

S POOL MILLIONS OF WOOL CROP Two Years Experience Heightens Respect for •mall Flock Owner; emoves Barrier. Boise—Idaho Farmers, for the most part ownera of small flocks of sheep, pooled 2,131,000 pounds of wool in 1919 and 1920, says a biennial state ment issued by the university extens ion division, based on reports from E. F. Rinehart, field animal husband man, and R. B. Millin, sheep special ist. This pooling, says the extension division, "was a long step toward so lution of the problem of the farm flock owner, who has found difficulty in getting his clip on the market in less than carload lots. It has been only a few years since Idaho farmers were convinced that they could not keep sheep on the farms, in competi tion with range sheepmen. "In 1919, 609,000 pounds of wool were marketed co-operatively, at a gain of $48,720 over what the farmers would have received, had they gone into the market individually. In 1920, more than 1,522,000 pounds were pool ed, more than half of it through the farm bureaus, or in organizations con nected with them. Sixteen counties had wool pools. "J"he extension spe cialist participated in the formation of a tri-county association that pool ed 149,000 pounds and in formation of other pools, with 340,700, as well as rendering assistance to pools pre viously organized, that pooled 266,900 pounds. -»-"The most of the wool pooled in 1920 was consigned to reliable com mission ^firms, that do business on commission only. A small quantity of wool in the northern part of the 1 state is still in the farmers' hands and , 255,500 pounds have remained in the warehouses in the Boise valley await ing a market. A few pools have re ceived advances ranging as high as 25 cents a pound. Pooled woo! has faced, of course, the same general market stagnation that has confront ed the wool trade as a whole. Wool was pooled in the several counties in 1920 as follows: Boise valley, (Ada, Gem, Can yon, Payette) 255,000 Bingham ..123,409 Elmore 25,000 Fremont-Madison (9|% range wool) 741,173 Gooding (estimated) ' 60,000 Idaho 80,000 Jefferson 70,700 Jerome 66,000 Latah 16,000 Lewis 11,809 Lincoln 18,000 Minidoka 65,000 Twin Falls and Washington coun ties made no reports.

Popular Teacher Dies of Pneumonia secrated life," always cherry, always Widely Known and Competent In structor Answers Roll Call Christmas Evening. Miss Millie E. Howard, who has lived in the Einmett country for 20 years and who has been a Canyon county teacher for the last three years, passed to the Great Beyond at her recent home in Greenleaf Christmas evening. She taught at Lake Lowell two ytars and was teaching the in termediate grade of the public school at Greenleaf the present term. She was taken ill Thursday eve ning, December 16 and made a brave fight -against an insidious attack of pneumonia, but owing to complica tions, the battle for life was lost. The school, church, community and family have suffered an irreparable loss in the passing away of this con helpful and kind, devoted to her church and school—how we shall miss her! The teaching force of Can yon county has lost one of its most conscientious and successful teachers in the passing away of Miss Howard. To the bereaved family we offer our sympathy and prayers. We also feel keenly the loss of a true friend. The funeral services were held at the Greenleaf church, conducted by Rev. Wells. Sunday at 2 o'clock, after which the body was taken to Emmett where it was intered Monday.

POPULAR YOUNG COUPLE ARE MARRIED TUESDAY Miia Margaret King and James Boone United in Mkrriage at Nampa. 1 Decision was reached at a meeting , of the local Red Cross chapter held James Boone, a local attorney and son of Dr. and Mrs. W. J. Boone, and Miss Margaret King, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Howard King of Nampa, were united in marriage at the home of the bride's parents Tues day evening. Dr. Boone conducted the services. The marriage came as a climax to a romance that began in the halls of the College of Idaho where both were students and from which both are graduates. Mr, Boone is also a grad uate of the Yale law school. At pres ent he is associated with Attorney General Roy Black as an assistant in that department. He is a native son of Caldwell. During the war he served as a first lieutenant in the arm ed forces of the United States and at the close of the war opened a law office in Caldwell with Clarence Hill, both of whom are now employed by the state. Miss King is one of the popular members of Nampa's younger set. Her father was for a number of years postmaster at that place. Mr. and Mrs. Boone will make their home in Boise for the time being. Nampa Prepares for Big Seed Show Unusual Interest and Splendid Ex hibit* Anticipated at Junc tion City. (Special Correspondence.) Nampa.—Elaborate preparations are being made here for the entertain ment of from 1000 to 1200 visitors who are expected to attend the state seed show which will open early in Janu ary. Thursday, committees were se lected by the Chamber of Commerce to canvass the town in an effort to provide rooming accommodations for visitors. Indications point to this year's ex hibits far exceeding in quantity and quality anything that has heretofore been shown at an Idaho seed show Already the warehouse of the Idaho Equity is comfortably filled with things that will be shown at the Moonbeam. C. B. Ahlson, state seed commissioner in looking over the field here Wednesday and making final preparations for the show, asserted that approximately three times is many exhibits will be listed this year as were shown at Pocatello a year ago. One hundred and fifty local Odd Fellows answered roll cal Wednesday evening when that event was staged by the local organization. The eve ning was largely taken up with the consideration of informal reports made by members of the building committee preparatory to arriving at some defin ite conclusion relative to the construc tion of a Caldwell 1. O. O. F. build ing.

.ED LOOK TON Try Now for Lower Rates to New Markets; Preparations Made to Begin Baling Shortly. Considerable criticism has arisen in this county relative to the attitude taken by Leonard Way, rate expert with the public utilities commission, who is quoted as being opposed to any effort to obtain a reduction in the $11 per ton freight rate now in vogue be tween southwestern Idaho and a north ern Idaho market. Mr. Way pointed out in a letter addressed to the Sand point Chamber of Commerce that on the basis of present quotations in northern Idaho of $27.50 per ton for hay, it was possible for growers in this section to market their hay in that part of the state despite the high freight rate. Local hay producers point out, how ever, that Mr. Way was wrong in as suming that northern Idaho offers a $27.50 market, that this price is pro hibitive and that dairymen in eastern Washington and northern Idaho, who are the leading consumers, are selling their stock rather than pay that price. It is also pointed outh that an $8 per ton quotation locally for hay simply means that it will be turned and not that there is profit in selling the hay at that price by growers here. Asks Lower Rate. Efforts are now being made to ef fect a reduction in this rate to north ern Idaho. In the face of a $10 rate to middle western points, local men interested in the hay situation express the belief that the $11 rate to north ern Idaho is altogether too high. Thus far, no large amount of hay has been sent out. One car, destined for northern Idaho, was to have left Wilder Thursday. Baleing will prob ably be undertaken shortly, however, as several operators are ^preparing to put their machines in the field. At a meeting to be held in Wilder Monday evening, the situation will be thoroughly reviewed and what further action is to be taken will be decided upon. Thus far. Jim Smeed, who was to have beensent east to represent shippers here, has not gone awaiting a definite settlement of market condi tions. A slight slump in Kansas City quotations following closely on the heels on the reduction in the freight rate practically eliminated that market for the present. •

THINKS CONGRESS WILL SOLVE WOOL PROBLEM. (Special Dispatch.) NAMPA— W. S. McClurc, for many years prominently identified with the National Wool Growers' association, has- returned from Washington where he spent some time recently in the in terests of the wool growers and sheep men of the United States. He express ed confidence that congress would en act some legislation shortly designed to aid the wool grower and relieve the present situation. He said that a temporary embargo on all wool im ports to be followed by a truly pro tective tariff, might reasonably be ex pected. A series of experiments have recently been made by Dr. Follok, an oculist of this oity, to test the truth of nn article published some time since by a celebrated physician in Eng land, which alleged that the last scene view ed by a dying man would remain impressed upon the retina as does the impression upon • daguerreotype plate, in each experiment that Dr. P. has made he has found that an examination of the retina of an eye with a mi croscope reveals a wonderful as well as a beautiful eight, and that in almost every instance there was a clear, distinct and marked impression. We put these facts upon record in the hope of awakening an interest in the subject that others may be induced to enter upon these interesting ex periments, and the cause of science advanc ed. The recent examination of the eye of J. II. Beardsley, who was murdered in Au burn, conducted by Dr. Sanford, corres fionds with those made elsewhere. The fol owing is the published account of the ex amination :

••Ai nrsi we suggested me saturation or the eye in a weak solution of atrophine, which evidently produced un enlarged state of the pupil. On observing this we touched the end ot the optic nerve with the extract, when the eye instantly became protuberant. Douglas and Democracy. - I Mr. Dodglas deserves the thanks of the nation. IIo has just rendered service to the country which settles conclusively his claim to a position among the venerated patriots and philanthropists of the land, lie has given us something new to talk about. The Indian Mutiny has become wearisome since the fall of Delhi; the Mormon trouble has not yet burst through the crust of uncer tainty and become the frightful red flower of rebellion, which some predict, and many fear it Will be 5 the panic has become panic- , stricken, and fled. In fact, all the old sen sation events have become threadbare, and we are beginning to find ourselves hunger ing for a fresh novelty, when the physical ly dwarfish, but intellectually gigantic Son- ' ator from the Sucker State roagnanimious- j ly interposed to rescuo us from the listless j apathy into which we were relapsing for j want of something to interest us. There are few spectacles more absorbingly inter- , esting than a conflict of great forces, and when the Senator from Illinois stood up in the Senate Chamber to demur to certain sentiments in the President’s Message, the eye of the nation instinctively turned to the spot to witness an exertion of all that won derful strength the Supposed possession of which has earned for him the title of the •‘Giant.” Democracy is a mighty force.— 1 Douglas is a mighty force. The conflict of , two such forces, therefore, was a spectacle which had something of the fearful sublim ity which attached to one of those gladia torial death combats, in the Coliseum wherewith the eld Romans were wont tore gale themselves.

The Illinoisan is putting forth all his I powers. Never before did his physical vig- 1 or, his undaunted courage and his won drous controversial abilities shine forth j more brilliantly than in this mighty strug-! gle. With admirable adroitness he forti- j ties his position by quoting the words of the President himself, thus forcing those who shot at him to shoot through the per- 1 son of poor Mr. Buchnnau. The Rector's Daughter. In the quaint ol»! village of Thyndon, England , dwells its good old rector, a widower, with one unmarried daughter. The other lives at Merton’s End—as $ happy and adorned wife. We have something to tell of that fair dame—-a deed so courageous that the village has been two or three degrees prouder of it self ever since it happened. The squire had fallen in love with the fair Adelaide, and the wedding day was to he on the morrow of that on which our adventure happened. Grand prepara tions were made for the wedding; and the rector’s fine old plate, and the costly ■gifts of the bride, were discussed with pride and pleasure at the Hare and Hounds in the presence of some strangers who came down to a prize fight which had taken place in the neigbor hood.

1 hat night Adelaide, who occupied a separate room from her sister, sat up late—long after the household had re tired to rest. She had had a long inter viow with her father, and had been -reading a chapter to which he had di rected her attention, and since, had pack ed up her jewels', &c. She was conse «iuently still dressed when the church ■eloclv lolled midnight. As it ceased, she ■fancied she heard a low noise like that •of a file ; she listened but could dis tinguish nothing clearly. It might have been made by some of her servants still about, or perhaps it was only the creak ing of some of the old trees. She heard nothing but the sighing of the winter wind for many minutes afterwards.— House-breakers were mere myths in primitive Thyndon, and the bride elect, without a thought of fear, resumed her occupation. She was gazing on a glit tering s»*t of diamonds, destined to be worn at the wedding, when her bed room door softly opened. She turned, looked up, and beheld a man with a black mask, holding a pistol in his hand, standing before her. She did not scream, for her first thought was for her father, who slept in the next room, and to whom any sud den alarm might be death, for he was old. feeble, and suffering from heart complaint. She confronted the robber boldly, and addressed him in a whisper: *• You are come,” she said, “ to rob us. Spare your soul the guilt of murder.— iUy father sleeps next to my room—and o be startled from bis sleep would kill mu. Make no noise, I beg of you.” The fellow was astonished and cowed. • We won’t make no noise,” he replied ullenly. “ if you give us everything lui.uly.”

Adelaide drew back and let him take ier jewels—not vviihout a pang, fur they »ere precious love gifts, remarking at lie same time that two more masked u ilia ns stood at the half opened door. Vs he took the jewel-case and watch on) the table, and demanded her purse, ic asked him if he intended to go into or father’s room. She received a sur* affirmative: “lie wasn’t agoin to m a risk, and leave half the tin be i mdl” She proposed instantly that she ouId go herself, saying : “ I will bring l hi whatever you wish, and you may lard me thither, and kill me if I play Ise to you.” The fellow consulted his mrades, and after a short parley, they ;reed to the proposal ; and with a pis poitiled at her head, the dauntless rl crossed the passage, and entered the 1 rector’s room. Very gently she , >le across the chamber, and removing I > purse, watch, keys and desk, gave i mi uj) to the robbers, who stood at the | jr. The old man slept peacefully and I inly, thus guarded by bis child, who ■ tly shut the door, and demanded if ■ y were yet satisfied. I The leader replied that they should

\mhmi tney got the snow ot plate cad out below, but that they couldn’t her out of sight, and that she must with them. In compliance with this ndate, she followed them down stairs he dining-room, where a splendid a k fast had been laid, to save trouble hurry on the morrow. To her sur e, the fellows—eight in number ;n assembled—seated themselves, prepared to make a good meal.— •y ordered her to get them out wine, cut her own wedding cake for them ; then, seated at the head of the table, was compelled to preside at this ex rdinary revel. hey ate, drank, laughed, and joked ; Adelaide quick of an eye and ear, thus lime to study in her quiet way, igures and voices of the whole set. hen the repast was ended, and the • transferred to a sack, they prepared .epart, whispering together, and ] ring at the young lady. For the time, Adelaide's courage gave way, die trembled : but it was not a con

! sultation against her, as it proved. The leader, approaching her, told her they did not wish to harm her—that she was “ a jolly wench, reg'lar game,” and that they wouldn’t hurt her, but that she must swear not »o give an alarm till nine or ♦en the next day, when they should be off all safe. To this she was of course obliged to assent, and then they all in sisted on shaking hands with her. She noticed during this parting ceremony, j that one of the ruffians had only three fingers on his left hand. Alone in the despoiled room, Adelaide faint and exhausted, awaited the first gleam of daylight; then, as the robbers did not return, she stole up to her room, undressed, and fell into a disturbed slum ber. The consternation of the family the next morning may be imagined; and Adelaide’s story was still more astound ing than the fact of the robbery itself.— Police were sent for from London, and they guided b°y Adelaide’s lucid descrip tion of her midnight guests, actually suc ceeded in capturing every one of the gang, whom the young lady had no dif ficulty in identifying and swearing to— the “ three fingered Jack ” being the clue to the discovery. The stolen prop erty was nearly all recovered, and the old rector always declared—and with truth—that he owed his life to the self possession and judgment of his eldest daughter. The only ill-effect of the great trial to her nerves, was a disposition on 'he the part of the young heroine to listen to midnight sounds, and start uneasily from troubled dreams; but tune and change of residence soon effected its cure.

Balloon Fatalities. The recent unfortunate and probably fatal balloon ascension of Mr. Thurston, which has created such a painful inter est throughout the country, has also brought out, through the columns of tne newspaper press, many scraps of histo ry connected with balloon traveling.— The Providence Journal has compiled quite a list of fatalities, and adds that it does not know of one distinguished aero naut that has not met with a violent death by means of a balloon. Amongst the first who commenced these voyages were M. Pilatre and M. Remain, of France. They made an as cension from Bologne. June 1*3, 178-3, with a Montgolfier balloon, a fire being kindled underneath, and the balloon as cending by means of rarefied air. At an amazing height, the balloon took fire, burned the chords by which the car was suspended, and the unhappy occupants were precipitated to the earth, dashing them to pieces in a manner too shock ing to mention. M. Zambecari, accompanied by a friend, made an ascent from the same place, September :2,1812. On descent, the balloon became entangled in the branches of a high tree, and before it could be disengaged it caught fire. The aeronauts jumped out. Zambeeari was killed on the spot, and Bonoga survived but a short time. About the same time a mechanician, named Biztorf, ascended from Man heim. At a considerable height, he per ceived that his vehicle was damaged,— Me opened the valve, descended with great velocity, and was dashed ?u pieces «gainst a iutiv.

Madame Blanchard ascended from Trivoli, July 8th, 1819, during the prog ress of a fete there. At the height of two hundred feet, the balloon took fire. She was precipitated on the pavement, and instantly killed. Mr. Harris, a very experienced a»ro naut, was killed May 24, 1824. He went from City Road, London. At the height of two miles, he commenced to descend very rapidly, was precipitated to the earth, and dashed to pieces. A Mr. Green ascended from CardilT, July l lih, ISIS. His body was found some time alter, on the Flat House Shoals, in the centre of Bristol Chan nel. A Mr. Arban, a celebrated French a*ronaut, ascended from Barcelona in September, 1818. Nothing was heard of him till the middle of November, when his body was found near llosas. Lieutenant Gale ascended from the Hippodrome of Vinceniles, on Saturday, September 8th, 18-50. Some days sub sequently the body was found in a clump of ferns, his limbs broken and mutilated, the face completely eaten away by dogs and other wild animals. He had previ ously met with narrow escapes. Janies Goulston made an ascent in the evening, from the Bellevue Gardens, June 2d, 18-52. The balloon was a new one, forty feet high, thirty-eight feet in diameter, holding twenty-three thousand cubic feet of gas. It being cloudy at the time, the car was lost to view in two minutes. He fell from his vehicle in attempting to descend at the town of Lees. A considerable quantity of blood and brains marked the spot where he struck the earth. Mr. Knight ascended from Bombay, December 14, 18-52. in the presence of a large concourse of natives, amongst whom was the Rajah or Dar, who prom ised the teronaut two hundred rupees, if he went up and came down again, of which the Rajah entertained great doubts. The balloon travelled straight out to sea, and Mr. Knight has not since been heard from. In September, 1851, Mr. Merle and a companion were carried off in a bal loon that broke from its moorings; they ascended to such a height that Merle was frozen to death, and the other de scended in the greatest peril.

One long summer afternoon there came to Mr. Davidson’s the most curi ous specimen of an old bachelor the world ever heard of. He was old, gray, wrinkled and odd. He hated women, especially old maids, and wasn’t afraid to say so. He and aunt Patty had it hot and heavy, whenever chance threw them together; yet still he came, and it was noticed that aunt Patty took unusual pains with her dress whenever he was expected. One day the contest waged unusually strcng. Aunt Patty left him in disgust, and went out in the garden. “The Bear !” she muttered to herself, as she stooped to gather a blossom which attracted her attention.

“What did you run away for ?" said a gruff voice close to her side. “To get rid of you.” “You didn't do it, did you ?” “No, you are worse than a burdock bur.” “You won’t get rid of me neither.” “I won’t eh?” “Only in one way." “And what?” “Marry me1" “What, us two fools get married?
