Great a the abuses then 9eemed to be, it may be confi dently said that not the most extravagant des cription of the most violent Republican parti san, in the last canvass, ever approached th reality as it ha9 since been exposed to th public eye. ‘Nobody imagined that Ireaso was nestling in the very highest pinnacle o the Capitol; that corruption was spreading it poisonous influence through the subordinat places; and that violence was gravely medi tated against the very organization of th Government. Some of your own servant appear new, by their deliberate •dtoiMiom

to have been laboring to betray you into the hands of your enemies. A delay of four years more would probably have left you bound hand and loot foreyer in the hands of a mili tary oligarchy. You were clearly right, therefore, in the stand you took in favor of general reform.— And that portion of our fellow-citizens which permitted its political strength for so long a time to be used in upholding a policy which proves to have been so treacherous, must by this time have become convinced that no se curity was left but in a change of rulers.— And all must see, that even the evils which we are likely to be called to encounter, are not comparable in their magnitude with those which must have ensued from a continued and systematic demoralization under the old system. Mr. Cobb, Mr. Thompson and Mr. Floyd are but types of a general policy which had for its object to subvert the Government as established in 1789, and conducted by Washington and Jefferson in its true spirit, and to substitute in its place another, which would have attempted the subjugation of your liberty and your will to the narrow and selfish purposes of slave extension on the continent of America. The love of liberty as an ab stract principle of general application, is evi dently dead among this class of men. The spirit of our ancient struggle has evaporated, and in its place has come the determination to be masters, honestly, if possible, but if not, at any rate to be masters. With such a temper, demonstrated as it has been in all the acts of violence and fraud which have since been made patent to the world, it is very plain that no safety could be hoped from any further toleration of it within the departments of the Government. Whatever else they may lose, the people of thepe States will at least congratulate them selyea that they have saved the right to Lave rulers of their own choosing, yet under their control, and ready faithfully to reflect their will. This consideration alone ought to com pensate in their minds for all the difficulties of the present times. 'If we have any regard for the memory of our fathers, if we have any respect for the safety of our children, we must see to it to keep our political independ ence sure. That there can be no doubt of the correct ness of this view, I think can be seen in the dir-rtioti which has been thus far given to the insurrection in the slaveholding States. The basis upon which their attempt at reconstruc tion rests is the right of one man to rule over another’s will by force. With this exception, very little change haB beer# attempted in the frame of our Government. The forms have been generally preserved with great care.— The difference is mainly in the spirit in which it is to be adtoinistered. Could we have con sented to tontinue that spirit at Washington, there would have been no rebellion, and we should have had a Federal Government justi fying the sway of force and fraud. We re fused to be slaves, and the consequence is, that the experiment has been transferred to Montgomery in Alabama. It ought not then to be overlooked bv you, that the only public question immediately be fore you for your consideration, turns upon this point. The revolted States desire to es tablish a reconstructed Government upon their new basiB. They hope to be able to persuade some of their ancient associates among us to join then in such a union. The only difference is to be in the expunction of the Declaration of Independence. That such is the true state of the tacts, I need only to appeal to the late speech of Mr. Alexander H. Stephens, the Vice President of the new system, to prove. Mr. Stephens was not himself originally an advocate of the separation whicli lias tuken place. He seem9 to have embraced it at last, rather from necessity than choice. Hi9 sen timents are not, then, to be regarded a9 those of an extreme revolutionist, but rather as com ing from the moderate class. Yet, in this re spect, it will be seen from the following ex tract, which I quote 89 I find it in a newspa per, that they go quite the length which I have described: “The prevailing ideas entertained by Jeffer son and inoPt of the leading statesmen at the time of the formation of the old Constitution, were that the enslavement of the African was in violation of the laws of nature; that it was wrong jit principle, socially, morally and po litically. It was an evil they knew no* well how to deal with; but the genera! opinion of the men of that day was that somehow or oth er in the order of Providence, the institution would be evanescent and pass away. “Our new Government is founded upon ex actly the opposite ideas. Its foundations are laid, its corner-stone rests upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery, subordination to the supe rior race is his natural and moral condition This, our new Government, is tbe first in the history of the world, based upon this great physical, philosophical aod moral truth.” It comes to this, then—the Vice President of the so called Confederacy founds his new Government upon a single idea, and that is force. And he has the boldness to pretend that this is the first example in the history of the world, of a government of the kind, when boys in the schools might have told him that his’ory has been made up of instances of the kind, from the days of Pharoah and Xerxes, of Alaric and Attilla, of Genseric and Maho met, down to the present Sultan at Constanti nople. It wa9, on the other hand, the pecu liar characteristic of Jefferson and his com peers, that they boldly cut loose from this old doctrine, and advanced a new one which marked the great political advance of the Ia9t age. They assumed that man had natural rights of bis own, which hi9 stronger neigh bors were bound to respect, and that when he did no wrong, lie ought to have no wrong done to him. The people of Europe, as well as the people of America, regarded this as the distinguishing feature of the new nation that had succeeded in establishing its own rights against the laws of force. And the ef fect of this action has been gradually to mod ify the theories even of the most absolute des potisms of the world. Hence it is that at this moment, when some of the people of the slave holding States have made up their minds to renounce-and disavow the new faith, they can be only regarded as person* who have turned their backs on modern truth, and returned to antiquated error. They are, in fact, creating the bulwarks of a military despotism. The very rule, thp application of which they con fine to a subjugated class may be presently extended by a few of their own number, over themselves. Nay, more, it ought to be re membered that those who make themselves the exclusive arbiters of the rights of their neighbors, can find no fault whenever those neighbors succeed in any effort to turn the tables upon them 1 It must be obvious that the assumption of such a theory as a rule of action in govern ment, implies so much latitude in the abuse of power, however acquired, as to render any political association with persons entertaining it, far from safe. The great mass ot the American people would nol tolerate the no tion that any possible state of things, except downright subjugation, could compel them to adopt it. They still continue to believe in the doctrines of the fathers, so openly repudiated. They still maintain the great principles upon which the Government is admitted by Mr. Stephens to have been founded. They yet propose to preserve the spirit in which it was originally administered. In their eyes, the ' change proposed, so far from being an im provement, would be discreditable to the po litical intelligence of the nineteenth century. If j| be the pleasure of the revolted States to stand before the world as as the exponent of such ideas, let them stand alone. Even the autocratic monarch of all the Russias is at . this moment proving by his action, how very i little sympathy he has with these exploded i notions. The whole world is moving forward [ excepting the people ruled by King Cotton F It remains y et to be seen whether even hit l throne will be safe from the consequences o! j such an experiment. If l am right, then, in my views, the con » elusion inevitably must be that the politica 9 revolution of the last year marks a great eri in American iuitory, aecood only to that o

our independence. It saved us from the im pending domination of a slaveholding absolu lism. 1 did hope that it might have been ef fected without a convulsion. I did believe i might have been followed by a policy which while it wronged no one, would in the en< save even the slaveholding States from th< perils of their situation. In these expecta lions, it would seem,from present appearances that I was much too sanguine. The deeper ate agitators have precipitated the more mod prate and patriotic portion of their fellow citizens into a revolution. They have stakec their all upon the maintenance of their politi cal supremacy as a slaveholding oligarchy.— We cannot refuse the issue tendered to us, ii we would. Their whole action since the 6tl of November has been aggressive, insulting treacherous and violent, a very natural corol lary from the principles on which their or ganization is now based. We have no choici but to sacrifice our independence, if we con sent to their demands. The question is be tween our cherished law of 1770, resting upon the rights of man, and the old notion of Ala , ric, the Goth, revived in i860, that force may be preceded by fraud, and that might make* right. We are now the champions of law and Republican liberty. Retreat is impossible, even if it were to be desired. We must stand firmly by the old faith, or be disgraced for ever. Deeply as I regret the causes which have conspired to give the impending struggle unnecessary elements of bitterness, I cannot, on looking back, discover how it could have been avoided, excepting by the utter emascu lation of a free people. I must repeal, that it is with great regret 1 leave you in this emergency, for another field of duty. I do so only under the belief that 1 may be of more service there than here.— Whether that be so or not, however, will after all depend much more upon the people of the United States than upon their agents abroad. Foreign nations will very naturally look with more attention to the action of the principals than to that of their representatives. If they see union in counsel and energy in action, if they find wisdom in deliberation and heroism in the field, above all, if they discover a calm determination to carry the Government firmly through all its trials, in steady consistency with the purposes and policy of its founders, then will follow, a9 the day follows the night, their brightening sympathy, their admiration, their confidence, and perhaps even their co operation. So it was in 1778. Soil will be ever when honest men courageously uphold the right. Permit me now most earnestly to bid each and every one of you, my fellow-citizens, an affectionate farewell. Contributor to the Shoe and Leather Re porter gives some valuable hints in regard to the preservation of leather. The extreme heat to which most men and wouicu expose boots and shoes during winter, deprives leather of its vitality, rendering it liable to break and crack. Patent leather, particu larly, is often destroyed in this manner.— When leather becomes so warm as to give off the smell of leather, it is singed. Next to the singeing'caused by tire heat, is the heat and dampness caused by the covering of rubber. Close rubber shoes destroy the life of leather. The practice of washing harness in warm water and with soap, is very damaging. If a coat of oil is put on immediately afier washing, the damage is repaired. No har ness is ever so soiled that a damp sponge will not remove the dirt; but, even when the sponge is applied, it is always useful to add a slight coat of oil by the use of another ^AU varnishes and all blacking containing the properties of varuish should be avoided. Ignorant and indolent hostlers are apt o use such substances on their harness as will give the most immediate effect, and these, as a general thing, are roost destructive to the leather. When harness loses its lustre and turns brown, which almost any leather will do af ter long exposure to the air, the harness should be given a new coat of graiu black. Before using ibis grain black, the grain sur face should be thoroughly washed with potash wateruntil all the grease is killed,and after the application of the grain black, oil and tal low should be applied to the surface. This will not only “hasten the color.” but make the leather flexible. Harness which is grained can be cleaned with kerosene or spirits of turpentine, and no harm will result if the parts atWHed are washed and oiled immediately afterwards. Shoe leather is generally abused. Per sons kuow nothing or care less about the kind of material used than they do about the pol ish produced. Vitriol blacking is used un til every particle of the oil in the leather is destroyed. To remedy this abuse the leath er should be washed once a month with warm water, and when about half dry, a rvil nml tullnur vhmilil he nnnlied.niid

the hoots set aside for a day or two. This will renew the elasticity and life in the leather, and when thus used upper leather will seldom crock or break. Hand leather is not generally properly used. When oil is applied to belting dry, it does not spread uniformly, and does not in corporate itself with the fibres as when par tially dampened with water. The best way to oil a belt is to take it from the pullies and immerse it in a solution of tallow and oil. After allowing it to remain a few mo ments. the belt should be immersed in wa'er heated to one hundred degrees, and instant ly removed. Rancid Bitter.—To a pint of water add thirty drops—about half a teaspoonful—of liquor of chloride of lime. Wash in this two and a half pounds of rancid butter. When every particle of the butter has come in con tact with the water, let it stand «tu hour or two; theu wash the butter well in pure wa ter. The butter is then left without any odor, and has the sweetness of Iresb butter. These preparations of lime have nothing in jurious in them. The Wiggins Ferry Company, of ! East St. Louis propose to run a fer ry boat for the accommodation of foot passengers exclusively. The Rockford, Rock Island & St Louis R. R. is completed within eight miles of White Hall, and the same distance south of Win Chester. The new wings of the Chicago Court IIou3e approach completion. The inereased office accommodation is of the most elaborate description. Sixty-eight new cells have been constructed in the county wing, aDd they connect with those tinder the old building. The new edifice eon ! tains six fire proof vaults, and the | whole building is thoroughly venti lated. Oa Thursday last the new atmos pheric brake was tested, with the greatest success, on the Chicago and Northwestern railroad. The result of tho experiment may be gathered from the following facts: On the first trial, while the train was progressing at the rate of thirty miles an hour, the track being wet and slippery, the locomotive and train of six ears were brought to a halt nineteen seconds after tho brake was applied, and within a space of eighty feet greater than the length of the train. On the second trial the track was sanded, liut the speed was about forty miles an hour. The train was brought to a standstill in eighteen seconds. The invention is calculated to render railroad travel much safer than it has been, and doubtless the new brake will ,so«n be in general use. A boy named James Gobbins was run over and killed, on Thursday fast, ou the Illinois Central Railroad, in the suburbs of Chicago. A few evenings ago, while the Davenport Brothers were giving one of their seances at Library Hall, Chicago, and making things vanish most mysteriously, some sly thief made one of the performers’ violins “vanish” in an equally mysterious manner. The instrument has not been recovered. The Chicago Tribune of the 27th says: “While Mr. Richardson is lying at the point of death in New York for having agreed to marry a lady already separated from her husband upon her obtaining divorce Mr. R. II. Leonard is shot in Cin cinnati by the devoted and affection ate Horace Phillips for‘accompany ing Mary Cummings, a young widow from the theatre.’ We cau dimly comprehend how there might be danger in waiting upon the move ments of a semi detatched wife, es pecially in a lawless community like New York, where no courts of jus tice have been bold for several years. But why the death penalty should he awarded to one who accompa nies a young widow from the thea tre, in a city which has advanced be yond the need of Bibles in' its schools, seems not so clear.

The Bay City “Journal” relates a melancholy case of poisoning. A German girl by mistake swallowed a quantity of arsenic, and instead of calling in medical assistance she iook a dose of cathartic pills, under the supposition that they would act as an emetic. The pills had, of course, a directly contrary effect, and the girl died. A few days ago a girl entered a shoe store in Saginaw and called for a pair of number two shoes. On -a pair being supplied she found them too small, and asked for a pair of “larger twos.” This process went on for some time, the shop man, for “twos,” supplying threes, foars, fives and sixes. At last a pair of large “sevens” fitted the girl, and she went her way rejoicing, be lieving that she had on a pair of number “twos.” The girl, whose vanity made her believe that she possessed a Cinderella foot, tho shopman nngallantly says has a pedal extremity as large as an or dinary sized shovel.

On Monday I left Albany about 12 o’clock, intending to take 2 o’clock train North for Manchester, but 1 found I could not go until 5 o’clock. As it rained, I spent the time in the depot reading. At 5 o’clock I start ed, and when just beyond Lansing burgk we came in collision with a freight train from the North. In the general derangement of the trains, by reason of the high water, there was some misunderstanding, and a collision took place. It was an awful affair. The locomotives were dashed to pieces. The bag gage car went over the locomotive, and the freight car mounted on top of the baggage car. Many were ve ry seriously injured—none killed outright. The car in which I was, brought to a stand still on a narrow embankment about fifty feet high on | one side, and twenty-five on the other. It is marvel that we were not thrown off. About 8 o’clock in the evening, after walking quite a distance, we took some cars which had in the mean time come down from the North. As it was a single trace we had to go ahead backwards and at a very slow rate. Just be fore reaching Hooeic junction, we learned that the bridge over the riv er bad become unsafe, so we all got out and, following a lantern, walked over the bridge which was a pokor ish piece of business, but we had to do it or stay in the cars all night. As we could not make the connec tion to enable me to go on to Man chester, I conluded to go to Iloosic Falls where there is a good hotel. There were about a dozen of us who walked over the bridge, most of them who lived at Hoosic Falls. On crossing the river we found nothing but a locomotive and tender, no cars. As they assured us there was no danger, and as Hoosic Falls was only dbout a mile and a half distant, j we all got on ; I stood next to the boiler; two ladies were next to me j and the others were either in the ca | boose of the locomotive, or on the tender. We started about ten o’clock. It was very dark and rain ing. We had to go backwards. The track was on the bank of the river, j The river was fearfully high, and roared like the Niagara. We moved along very slowly, and as we reached a point about half way, we came to j a very dangerous point A high wall had been built up to protect the track from the river. It appears that between dark and. the time we arrived, the water had undermined this wall, and swept away all the foundation upon which the track j rested. The track whs thirty five feet above the water. When the | locomotive came upon the rails, thus | left without any support, it of course ! went down instantly. There was but one scream. I caught hold of something to which I held until tha locomotive struck, and then 1 found myself in the water, lying on my back, with my left foot caught in some of the iron work. Immedi ately I went under the water, or rather the water came boiling over me. American Children. They seem to have an odd idea over in Eng land of the treatment of children in this coun try. The London Suwlty 77,/cxof May Oth says: “The American children—boys and girls—go to school together. They are said to be very dibicult to manage, and both boys and girls are whipped if they do not behave themselves, and they altogether have a some what rough time ..f it. Hut surely they arc better off for magazines than any children in the world. The present number of St. Nich olas proves this. How excellent it is! The little Americans need not mind being whipped if they have every month such an amusing magazine to comfort them.” Windy. Mr. Ernest Ingersoll, in his interesting ar ticle on “The Metropolis of the Kooky Moun tains,” Scribner for July, says that “in con gratulating herself that Cheyenne has from one thousand live hundred to two thousand more miles of wind a month than she, Denver asserts no strong claim to being a calm local - ity. * * * A good motherly woman,hating frivolity, and camping to please her children in the mouth of a canon, is what thisdare-devi 1 wind loves above all things to meet with. It holds still till she has made everything ready, and is just reaching out to set her frying-pan upon the nicely glowing coals; then—piff! and the embers are going over the top of the hill, and the whole camp devotes itself for the rest of the evening to collecting scattered ar ticles. There i* a yarn about a miner who, being swift of foot, chased bis vagrant tire and held his skillet oyer it as it traveled . When his bacon was done he found himself fifteen miles from camp!”

“Enlisted/* Our city readers are again reminded of the entertainment at the Opera House to-night and to-morrow night, the proceeds of which will be devoted to the benefit of the Grand Army Post. The play “Enlisted for the War; or. The Home Guard,” iB a pleasing one, and we are assured by the management that the various characters have been assumed by those competent to do them justice, and that the rehearsals indicate the actors are well up in their parts. The first scene opens at the beginning of the late war; the farm and home of the Widow Trueworth,—whose son and only sup port had a short time previous enlisted, and I whose father had died in the meantime,—is ■ put up at morgage sale, and is bid in by Wilder Rowell, the guardian of Gaylie Gi f ford, an heiress, who had always made he r home with the Widow Trueworth, but at t his

11 III U la UIJM 111 HI 6CUUU1. ivuuiu iiuunuiui is in love with Gaylio Gifford; this coming to the knowledge of Wilder Rowell, causes that worthy, who desires to win the heiress in or der to secure her fortune, to offer Robert True worth the farm he has just purehasd if he will leave and not interfere with Howell in his love-making. This offer Robert rejects with scorn, and is warned by Rowell that he will be made to repent his refusal. Gaylie Gifford arrives from boarding school and learns for the first time that the “old home” has been sold to Wilder, and thinks that he bought it in for her with her money, in order that her old friends might not be turned out of a home. Wilder explains that he bought it. for his own use, and intimates that lie would like to make Gavlic his wife. Gaylio ' happens in and hears hot words passing be- j tween Robert and Rowell, and learns that | both of them are in love with her. Rowell gets a commission as colonel of the regiment 1 to which Robert belongs, and peremptorily ' orders Robert to his quarters This is resented by Gaylie who delios her guardian for his con temptible exercise of the power he has bought, and declares herself the “Home Guard, the Arm friend, enlisted for the for the war.” The next scene is laid two years later, at the headquarters of Col. (Wilder) Rowell, in Virginia. Gaylie has been writing to Rob ert Trucwortli, the private soldier who has often been recommended for promotion for brayery, but who who has been kept down by Rowell; Rowell has intercepted her letters; she thinking this is the case, lias sent an old and trusted servant, “Crimp,” with a letter direct to Robert; Crimp passes the lines, and gels into Rowell's headquarters and conceals himself. Gen. Grant calls at the headquar - 1 tors, which is presided over by one of Row-, ell’s aids who dislikes smoking; Grant is recognized by the sentinel, Robert Trueworth, but is ordered to halt and give the counter sign ; upon his arrival in the tent, after being requested by the aid to throw away his cigar, Gen. Grant inquires who the faithful sentinel is, and about his record for bravery,- etc.; Rowell appears, after the General’s withdraw al, and examines the mail that has been i brought in for his command. He intercepts a letter from Gaylie Gitlord to Robert True- ! worth, and is detected by Crimp, who is con cealed. Robert is relieved and appears in the tent to claim his mail; accuses Rowell of in tercepting his letters, and a quarrel cus ues; Robert is taken to the guard house on Row ell’s orders; on the way he meets Gen. Grant, who tells him he “may want a friend,” and to call upon him (Grant.) The next scene is two years later, at the close of the war; Robert Trueworth has been promoted to the colonelcy which Wilder Rowell held, and arrives home, to he greeted by a rousing reception in his honor—Gaylie Gillord is there to meet him, and the troubles, trials and tribulations here end with Rowell’s discomllture and,Robert’s success. There are two comic characters in the drama, Crimp, the negro, and Hiram Jcnks, the auctioneer’s son, who is in love with Mattie Trueworth, Robert’s sister. The above imperfect outline will give the reader an idea of the “plot.” There is no#“blood and thunder,” but several pleasing..tableaux dur ing the play. ‘ Mr. Yates, who has charge of the enter tainment for the Rost, will be ably assisted by a large number of ladies and gentlemen and Joe Hooker Post. All should turn out and give the “boys” a routing benefit.

With His Little Pistol. Every day, almo t, the readers of daily pa pers are shocked by reading of how a boy has accidentally Shot and killed his sister, brother, cousin, playmate, mother or some other inno cent person, by the careless handling of tire arms, and so common are such occurrences that unless an accident of the kind occurs iu our very midst it is read and forgotten in a day. Last Friday morning this community was “hocked by the announcement that at 10 o’clock the night before, IIoward Hardest}’, perhaps better known as Lukcy, a lad of 15 years, had accidentally killed himself while playing with a pistol. A Rrgistkh reporter hastened to the scene of the tragedy, and from the lips of the dead boy’s mother learned the following facts:

Howard, in company with two or three of his companions, went with the excursion to Peoria, Monday week, and while there they visited the 00 cent store and each of them pur chased a 00-cent revolver, a cheap, cast-iron seven-chambered death-dealer, carrying 22 calibre cartridges. Parties on the train will remember there was considerable shooting going on while a part of the excursion was side-tracked at Kuwait station on their return home, and the wonder is that somebody was not killed or maimed that night, Thursday night, Howard went to his home, in the south-east part of the city, and tired his pistol oir, despite the protests of his mother, who cautioned him he would hurt himself or somebody else, lie promised her he “would l>e careful,” and commenced load ing the pistol again, and he was engaged In this when his mother left him to go to her room upstairs. Hardly had she reached her room when she heard a pistol shot, followed by a scream. She hastened down stairs, and while going down heard a heavy body fall in the kitchen. The poor mother knew then that her worst fears were about to be realized; knew that her boy was shot, though she did not realize that before she could reach him lie would be dead. The door that opens into the kitchen is at the foot of the stairs. Arrived here, she called to her boy but received no answer, and attempted to open the kitchen door, ,md in doing so had to push the dead body of her boy, who had fallen against it, be fore she could get to him. The alarm was immediately raised, and Dr. Harris summoned, but the boy was dead be fore any assistance reached him. The bullet penetrated the second rib on the right side of the breast, and cut one of the large arteries, killing hiiu instantly. The smoking pistol, with six chambers still loaded, lay by the out side kitchen door, where he was standing when the accident occurred, after which he had strength enough to stagger across the small room, as though attempting to reach his mother, when ho fell dead. The boy’s parents never allowed him to own a pistol, and he intended trading this one off the next day. He worked in Curtis’ cigar factory, and was considered a steady boy. IIis remains were buried Friday afternoon. There ought to be a stringent law against selling fire arms of any kind to boys and youths, and parents cannot be too careful in watching their boys, to keep them from hand ling such dangerous weapons. "With this request I comply with the trnkt nleasure. In this existing crisis of onr country's fate every indication of a'natioHel, patriotic spirit, is hailed with joy by every loyal heart. And when, as in this instance, it is exhibited by those whose thoughts are in stinctively pure, haying no partisan mo tives to influence them, bo patriotic prej udices to gratify, no petty ambition to subserve, no interest other than ia their country's prosperity and good name, we rejoice at it even the more from a convic tion that it most tend to strengthen the resolves of the loyal, eneanrasre the hopes of the desponding, arja bring to si pause trw nlnttinira n( tha mKli:. w r o . -...liiuua, Before doing the mere act I am delegat- ed to perform, I hope yon will 'consider
the occasion as justifying a few thoughts

as to the duty and interest of onr State in tne present emergency. In the origin al causes which have produced it, she, thank God, has' had no share. Amongst the foremost and bravest in winning onr independence-; amongst th truest and wisest in forming our government, and among6t.the first in adopting it, her sons have uniformly given it a faithful , and zealous support. No treasonable thought, as far as we know, ever entered the mind of one of them ; certainly no threat of treason was ever whispered by them. They ever felt the immense advantage of the Union ; they saw evidenced by every thing 'around them the blessings it con ferred npon Marylsnd and npon all. Prosperity unexampled, a national power increasing every year with a rapidity, and to a degree never before witnessed in a nation's history, and 'winning for us a name challenging the respect and admira tion of the world. They saw in the ex tent of the country, and the differences of climate and habits, elements of strength rather than.of weakness, and apprehend ed therefore no parricidal efforts in any quarter to destroy the government. If occasionally murmurs of dissatisfac tion were heard elsewhere, they were attributed to the whining disposition of some ami the disappofnted"ambition of others. They were ridiculed, subjected to no other punishment but left to stand as " monuments of the safety with which error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it." No "whiskey insurrection" ever occur ed within our borders. No ordinance of nullification was ever threatened by us ; and, if we continue true to patriotic duty, no ordinance of secession, direct or indi rect, open or covert, will ever be adopted by those in authority, or if madly adopt ed, be tolerated by the,peopIe. To this steadfast attachment to the Union we are not only bound by gratitude to the noble ancestry by whose patriotic wisdom it was bequeathed to us, an 1 by the unappreciable blessings tho bequest has conferred upon us, but by the assurance, which the most stolid intellect can hardly fail to feel, that its destruction would not only and at once, deprive us of all these, but precipitate n& hita irreparable ruin. In this ruin all would more or less participate, but our geographical position would make it to us immediate and total. A peaceable disseverance the good and gicat men who have heretofore guided our public councils ever predicted to be ira nossible. The nroclumations now trum peted through the land, tho marshalling of hosts by thousands ond tens of thous ands, the whitening of onr waters with and immense naval marine, the blockade of ports, the prostration of commerce, the destruction of almost all civil employ ment, the heated tone of the public press of all sections, belching forth tho most bitter enmity, all, all testify to the truth of this prediction. THE DEBT OF THE STATE. From the Now Orleans Bee.] It is pretended that although the State Constitution, by a late amend ment, limits thile debt of the State to twenty-five millions of dollars, yet that the Legislature may lawfully endorse bonds or other obligations to an unlim ited amount, provided these bonds and obligations are not those of the State or for which the State is primarily bound. The absurdity of this proposition is apparent to every reasonable mind. What was the object of the people of Louisiana when they voted upon the amendment to their fundamental law limiting the debt to twenty-five millions of dollars ? Was it not to secure them solves against incurring obligations of any kind in excess of that amount ? Was it not to prevent their lahw-makers from creating debt or obligation in any shape beyond the amount named?- What matters it whether it be bonds of the State or bonds of corporations for which the people are responsible? The only difference between the two classes of obligation is, that for the bonds of the State, the State only is responsible, while for bonds not issued by the State but only endorsed by the State, she is only responsible if the principal maker of the bonds should fail to pay. It is a law maxim familiar to every body that an act which cannot be done in a direct manner cannot be done in an indirect manner. The Legislature is the mere agent or attorney of the peo ple. It cannot lawfully go beyond the special power granted to it by the Con stitution, any more than an individual holding a special power of attorney can lawfully exceed his authority. The mistake which our law-makers make is that they construe their power to be general and not special. But what else can be expected from the men who assemble at the Meehan ics' Institute than continual stretches of authority. They go not there to pass wise laws for tile benefit of the people but to sell their votes for any scheme, however monstrous. The word lEPUr DIATION is no favorite word of ours, neither would we advise that the threat should be uttered, but assuredly unless a stop shall be put at once to the reck less extravagance now daily practiced by those whom we are forced to recog nize as our law-makers, repudiation will not be for us a question of choice but of necessity. There is such a pro ceeding as revolution by statute. There is also such a proceeding as robbery by statute. Purchasers of State bonds are bound to enquire into the lawfulness of their issue,'precisely as the capitalist or bank er who discounts a promissory note signed by one who acts as attorney for another, is bound to enquire into the power of the attorney to bind hli prin cipal. Those who deal with agents cannot plead ignorance of the extent of the powers of such agent. The debt of the State at the present time, according to the figures in the re port of Auditor Graham to the Legis lature now in session, amounts to twen ty-eight millions of dollars, which is an increase of eighteen millions in four years. In a comparison of expendi tures in previous years, we find they have increased from two millions andt a half in 1866, to seven millions in 1870. This is an indirect method ofvio lating the Constitutional prohibition touching the debt and excessive taxa tion is another. The situation of tmhe State finances is truly alarming, and it is our duty to warn capitalists in'States i against unlawful issues of bonds by this State and unlawful endorsements by the State of bonds issucal by corpo rations legalized by our Legislature for mlerely speculative purpos*es. The Subjugation of France. [From the Cinhinnati Gazetto.] It is reported that the money indem nity denmanded of France by Prussia is 10,000 million francs, or 2,000 million dollars. The conditions which this will create are serious enough to interest every European power, for they will make a much greater change in the bal ance of power in Europe than will be made by the seizure of Alsace and Lor raine, or by the subjection of Germany to the supremacy of Prussia. The an nual interest on this sum at 5 per cent -which is as low as either France or Prussia can borrow-is 100 million dol lars, a sum more than three times as great as the annual military expenses of Prussia. HI ow her military power will be increarid by such a tribute may be inlagined. Such a tribute is incompatible with 1 the indlependence of France. Even if it be possible for her to pay it, it will make her incapable of maintaining any military establishmoat of her own, or 1 of any effort in her defence. It is equal to the entire interest bearing debt of the United States, to pay the interest on which we had to tax at an enormous rate everything we could see, hear, or have a notion of, including a tax aver aging 419 per cent. on imported goods. But France had a debt before of about 2,000 million dollars, and now has her war expenses in addition, and all the claims ot her citizens for property doe stroyed. Her financiers could not col- 1 lect a revenue equal to her expenses before. Iow shall they, when the debt I is quadrupled or more ? This demand 1 is simply that France shall be made tributary to Prussia forever. And this I tribute would be an aggrandizement of 1 Prussia, and an addition to her already I threatening military preponderance, which deeply concerns the safety of every country in Europe. It may be 1 questionable whether France, rather 4 than bind herself to subjugation by this tribute, should not let Prussia under take the task of collecting it. Democrat.] The proclamation of the Governor con - veuing the Legislature in extra session will n6t be' received at first by the peo pie with flvor, lint we believe the Ex eoutive bhas qcted with great wisdom in taking this step. The sixty days of the reg;qlar session expired at 12 o'clock last might, with lit tie of the needed ie$sslation acnbmplish ed. Indeed, were the Legislature to dissolve now the gravest consequences would befall the State apd the Democrat ic party. We should' be left with nione of that real reform legislation which the public interests so much dematld,, and this would ber considering the situation, a great calamity to the State. For the meagre results of so many professions atal so many pledges ; for the disApoint ment of so many hopelt, and almost the absolute failure of so long and heroic a struggle on the pant of the people, the Democratic party would be held respon sible; this would be a heavier load than we could well carry, and if required to shoulder it we might well, anticipate a great and dangerous disaffection in our ranks in the approachmin canvass. We ate gratified, therefore, at the ac tion of the Governor in calling an extra session. But it is not true that the ulholo or the greater part of the res possibility rests upon the Democrats. There has been unfortunately a woeful lack of, unanimity and agrossiveness amongst them. WASHINGTON, March 2.-While Judge Leonard was still smarting under the desertion of Packard by Hayes, he told the following story: Just before the count in that State, and while the visiting statesmen were there, he was in a room in a New Or leans hotel with John Sherman. Wells and Anderson were there or.at least oile of them. While there, and in the prts ence of Leonard, Sherman said that everything rested with the Returning Board, and the Returning Board must do what was right. Then re impressed on them the calamity which must fall upon the negroes, the Southern Repub licans, and the country if the Tilden electors should be returned. As he warmoed to the subject, tears streamed from Sherman's eyes. He said emphbati cally that it all rested with them, and if they needed any protection, they could have not only the United States army, but fifty thousand militiamen from Iowa and Illinois. Afterward, about the time it was de te.unined by the friends of Hayes to de sert Packard, Judge Leonard went to Washington. To John Sherman he ex pressed surprise at the dosertion. Sher man remarked that the times were changed and that it was no longer expe dient or possible to uphold the bouthern Republicans with the United States troops. In reply, Leonard reminded Sherman of what he had said in New Or leans in regard to the possible employ ment of the United States troops and State militiamen to sustain a Republi can-aatsional Administration, for the safety of the negroes and the Southern Republicans. In the course of the con versation Leonard said : "Mr. Sherman, you are an old man and I am a young mI.u, and I may be mistaken; but either what you said in New Orleans was wrong, or what you say now is wrong."-New' York Telegram. TILE EXPENSIVE SENATE. "Vhy Uncle Snan Groans--LeRnons and sugar. [Brooklyn Eagle.] The Secretary of the Senate has made his annual report to that body. A careful examination of the items of ex penditure contained therein shows that the spirit of economy practiced by the House has not yet prevaded the north wing of the Capitol. Among a few of the miscellaneous articles for which the Government has to pay are pocket books worth from $1 to $8.70 a piece, pocket-knives costing $21.79 per dozen, rubber corkscrews at $4.50 per dozen, visiting cards printed from plate, au tograph albums worth from eighty-five cents to $1.25 a piece, Mark Twain scrap-books, mourning cards, six brass castors for chairs in the Senate cham ber cost $18, gum camphor costing 830 has been purchased, dozens of gallons of bay rum and cologne, bottles of castor oil, French blacking, combs, brushest ice, etc., are frequent Items in the list. Shaving materials, Pinaud's soap, toilet bottles, Brown's ginger, olive oil, and, in fact, an assortment of articles sufficient to thoroughly equip a fancy store, have been bought by the Secretary for the use of the Senate. One dozen of Martinique snuff cost $10. The Senate generously allowed $100 compensation to T. A. Jones, an em. ployee, for injuries received while re pairing the Senate elevator. Mr. Jones was incommoded for nearly a week by his injuries. Eight lunches for the Committee on Appropriations cost $120, and six boxes of lemons and 120 pounds of sugar were required to mix the drinks. The cost of investigating the frivo lous charges against Senator Grover, of Oregon, and his alleged participation in electoral vote for Tilden, cost $10,217 34. James Redpath received $1,548 for services as clerk to the sub-commit tee. Redpath's chief business was to arrange the reports into a sensational manner, placing small cap head lines over those portions of the testimony taken which showed that the Demo. crats had terrorized the negroes. Sena tor Chrlstiancy informed the Eagle correspondent last winter that he re fused to sign the report simply because of the presence of Redpath's obnoxious head lines. Murphy, the Senate steno grapher, received $1,200 for compiling for publication the proceedings of the Electoral Commission. J. A. Burbaud, the confidential private secretary of the late Senator Morton, was. paid $12 a day for services as special clerk to the Committee on Privileges and Elections during the political investigations of 1876. George E. Bullock was paid $10 per day for forty-three days " for extra ser vices rendered Committee on Privileges and Elections while acting under Sen ate resolution of December 5, 1876, to investigate elections held in certain States, in examining, assorting, etc., certain telegraphic dispatches furnished said committee by the Western Union Telegraph Company, from January 21, to March 4, 1877, inclusive." There is a flavor of cipher telegranms in this item of expense. TIIE COLD WAVE. Causes, Extent and Efect of the Veatnther TVe've Bleen Hlavitg. [Philadeiphia Times.] The cold wave which reached the West and Northwest on the winter solstice, December 21, accompanied by a large fall of snow, was modified in this city and vicinity by warm winds from the south, which made it a day of snow, rain, fog, ice, sluch and storms. Since then the wind has been princi pally from the northwest, and, being deprived of a large portion of its heat by passing over vast areas of snow, the weather, to the great joy of dealers in ice and the venders of poultry and other articles likely to be injured by a mild temperature, has grown colder. On Monday morning the thermometer indicated 20 degrees above zero in some parts of this city, and on yesterday morning, in like exposure, 18 degrees. In Europe, and especially in England, the fall of snow has been unusually heavy, and in Canada and some parts of New York and the New England States the depth is three feet. The fall of so great a quantity of snow imme diately after a mild weather which preceded it is not common, and is due to climatic influences which might be traced across the Atlantic. If the cold weather which is now prcyailing should continue even to a late period in the spring the winter must be far shorter than the many which have preceded it. In thle winter of 183.5-36 the ground was covered with snow from the 25th of November till late in April, and on the 10th of that month a team loaded with two tons of iron crossed the West Branch of the Susquehanna on thle ice, and in 1874-756 the ground continued frozen from Thanksgiving Day to the last of MaItrch. Although severely cold weather is a cause of much suffering to t~e poor and increases the demands on the charitable by the diminution which it onuses of out-door labor, yet it is not without its sources of enjoyment and its benefits. Setting aside the pleasure and healthful exercise of skating, which the ice-covered streams afford to the young and those of larger growth, the ground Iby lt.in'g ulIsiy tfro,,,n is mnore

open when spring arrives for the per meation of moisture, and is more rea dily penetrated by the roots of plants. As the temperature is generally higher when snow is falling than after it has been deposited, and, being a poor con ductor of heat, it protects the roots of plants from the injury which the ex pansion incident of freezing and thaw ing would produce. It is well known by every owner of a laundry that extreme cold produces evaporation almost as readily as ex treme heat, and vegetation unprotected by snow where exposed to a high degree of cold is deprived of moisture and per ishes. The almost eatire failure of the wheat crop in Pennsylvania in 1875 was due to this source. The cold was severe and long continued, but the fall of snow comparatively small. As a consequence the grain and grass be came dry and Itfeless, so much so that a field of winter grain set on fire by the sparks of a locomotive burnt with the rapidity of stubble. The severe cold of winter also aids in destroying the larvae of insects, and thus helps to keep in check one of the great sources of disappointment and loss to the husbandman. DISSECTING AN ELEPHANT. Sun, 28th ult.] Professors and students of the Colum bia Veterinary College, on Thursday morning, dragged the carcass of the baby elephant that died the day before in Central Park into their court yard. Then they prepared to hoist it to their dissecting room. The great weight of the animal alarmed them for the safety of their pullies and hoisting ropes, but reflection overcame this ditfficulty. At nightfall they had fitted up an incline plane, placed the animal upon it, and adjourned for the morrow's work. There gathered yesterday about the body, Prof. Spitzka, Dr. Finlay and a score of students. Before fixing the ropes and tackling, they stripped the monster of its skin, thereby saving the hoisting of a hundred pounds. Sling ing the body upon the table, the stu-. dents prepared for the autopsy. Two seniors, G. II. Borns and C. A. Meoyer, with a junior, went with sharpened knives at the abdomen, while Profs. Dr. Choppin, President of the New Orleans Board of Health, submitted as the re suits of his observations during the late elpidemic in that city, the fol lowing : 1. Yellow fever is a ipecifie disease, not indigenous to or originating spon taneously in the United States, and its appearance in this country Is always due to a specific cause. 2. That the germ hypothesis of the infection of yellow fever is the only theory which explain satisfactorily to my mind the phenomena and spread of yellow fever, and the only one which leaves us a hope of relief from its future visitations. 3. The habitat or cradle of yellow fever is in the West Indies, in the At lantle and Gulf coasts of South America and of Mexico, and in South Africa. 4. That all the great epidemics of yellow fever In the United States, from the time of its first Introduction into Boston in 1093 to the present time, can be directly or remotely traced to a for eign country or to a foreign germ. 0. That it cannot be indigenous to any place where a freezing temperature is annually experienced. 0. That marsh miasm, city filth, or garbage have no agency in the creation of yellow fever; if the special matter or germ of yellow fever be not present, a corrupt atmosphere, however obnox ious otherwise, will not produce the pestilence. 7. If the germs of yellow fever be present, defective drains, cesspools, de composition of animal and vegetable matter, heat and moisture may become the potent distributors of the germs, and of epidemic disease and death. S. The infection of yellow fever once established in the body, this evil form of life must run Its course. 9. Conditional quarantines cannot and will not be effective so long as cu pidity is an attribute to human nature. 13. Le lieutenant Hobson, lois de son récent passage à New- ; York a raconté en détail son aventureuse expédition sur le j « Merrimae.» qu'il a coulé, on s'en souvient, dans le chenal de i Santiago. Apres avoir abandonné le «Merrimae,» Hobson et ses hommes se sont cachés entre les poutrelles d’un radeau ; ils y sont restés pendant toute une nuit. A l'aube, une embarcation à vapeur contenant des officiers espagnols, s’est approchée, et le lieutenaut Hobson a décidé de se rendre comme prisonnier : de guerre. Voici ce qu’il raconte :

< J'ai nage vers la chaloupe à vapeur et à ce moment elle t'est dirigée vers moi. J'ai crié en espagnol : « Y a-t-il un ofïi cier à bord ? » Un officier a répondu d'une façon affirmative, et j'ai cric de nouveau en espagnol : t J'ai sept hommes qui veulent se rendre.» Puis j'ai continué à nager, et lorsque je suis arrivé à côté de la chaloupe, j'ai été saisi et retiré de l'eau. « En regardant autour de moi dans la chaloupe, après que l’on m'eût retiré de l'eau, j'ai constaté que c'était l'amiral Ga vera lui-même qui m'avait sauvé. 1 out dabord.il a paru eton-j né et indécis en me voyant, parce que j’étais couvert de suie, d'huile et de poussière de charbon, ce qui rendait mon apparence peu avantageuse. C’est dans la chambre des machines du < Merrimac » où j’avais dû travailler pendant quelque temps que j'avais sali mes vêtements. « Avant de coukr le « Merrimac,» j'avais passé autour de moi mon ceinturon d officier, afin qu il fut possible d établir mon identité si je périssais, et lorsque, après avoir été retiré (le l’eau, j'ai montré ce ceinturon à l’amiral, il a compris et a parti satisfait. Les premiers mots que l’amiral Ccrvcra m'a d.t.s, lorsqu’il a su qui j étais, ont été ceux-ci : « Bienvenudo se a usted.» Ce qui veut dire : « Soyez le bienvenu.» « Mes hommes et moi. nous avons été traités avec cour toisie tout le temps que nous sommes restés prisonniers. Je leur ai dit te que je prouvais leur dire sur l'exécution du projet que j’avais été chargé d’accomplir, et ils n’ont pas cherché à en savoir davantage. •• Mes hommes ont été retirés du radeau et nous avons avons tous été conduits dans une cellule du fort Morro. Gai demandé la permission d écrire une lettre à l’amiral Sampson, mais lorsque l’amiral a été informé de ma demande, il est ve nu auprès de moi et m a dit que le général Linares ne permettrait pas que j envoie ma missive. L’amiral semblait très contrarié mais ce n'est qu'un jour ou deux après que j’ai appris ce qui le préoccupait.

« Le meme jour, i amiral a air qu il enverrait un canot v ers le navire-amiral américain, afin d'obtenir pour nous des vête ments et informer l'amiral Sampson que nous étions sains et saufs. Plus tard, j'ai appris que le général Linares voulait lions j maltraiter et que, pour cette raison, l'Amiral Cervera désirait i informer aussitôt que possible notre flotte que nous étions en ; sûreté- L'amiral espagnol savait que lorsque le général Linares ! apprendrait que la flotte américaine était informée de rutrej situation, il n'oserait pas nous faire déniai « Lorsque nous sommes arrivés au fort Morro, les solides j portes de> cellules dans lesquelles on nous avait mis ont été ] tenues fermées une heure ou deux, mais lorsque j'ai protesté auprès de l'amiral contre cette réclusion, ce dernier a ordonné de laisser nos portes toutes grandes ouvertes. Nous avons pu j alors voir la rade de Santiago, la ville et l'escadre espagnole. Tous les officiers de l'armée et dr l'escadre sont venus nous J voir ce jour-là et leur conduite 5 notre égard a été des plus] courtoise-, « Le général Linares n'est pas veau, mais fl a fait dire que j

puisque tous tes autres officiers étaient venus nous voir, il croyait inutile de faire comme eus. Je ne sais pas ce qu il vou lait dire, mais je sûr que ce n'est pas â lui que nous devons d'avoir été sauvés et si bien traités.» Le lieutenant Hobson croit que c’est grâce â l’amiral Ger cera que lui et ses hommes ont été échangés contre des prison niers espagnols.

CONDITIONS OF TRADE. Review of the New York MarketsStocks and Bonds. 2tw Yokjc, March 25. There are too many uncertainties this week to permit any aggressive movement on the part of the bulls. The silver ques tion, the Bebring Sea difficulty, the legality of the Heading deal, the break in Northern Pacific, andHho approach of April settlements all contributed to restrict operations. Investors, too, were somewhat discouraged by the fancy prices at which some of the good dividend payers are held. On Friday there was an upward spurt on the strength of the anti-silver develope ments at Washington; but the silver advocates are not beaten by any means, and they may be expected to renew the battle at the earliest opportunity. Nevertheless, Wall Street is not ser iously alarmed in this respect, having full confidence in the presidential veto. The undertone cf the market is un questionably strong; and slocks, being in strong hands, would no doubt read ily respond to favorable conditions. The industrials have exhibited consid erable activity, but this I can hardly deem a satisfactory feature in selecting them as leaders in view of their hereto fore eratie character. The monopoly issues have introduced an element of uncertainty into the stock market which calls for special caution on the part ot investors and speculators, if not for specific caution on the part of the exchange itself in admitting indis criminately so-called securities to its list Many of them are already illegal, and the others are destined to become so. When that result comes, the profits they are now making out of an ex clusive control of prices will disappear. f. The stock issued by these orgsnizations have been "watered" to the extent of many times over the true value of their assets; what then will .be their market valuation when the law has deprived the organizations of the power to arti , facially inflate prices? It requires lit tle foresight to discover that these issues constitute a most formidable danger in the future cf the stock market. Any day, a new law or a decision of the supreme court of the United States may withm twenty-four hoars wipe out tens of millions of the market value of this illegitimate scrip, with consequences of the most far reaching character. The action of the Standard Oil in dissolving its trust ar iingements is a significant warning, frpile of its enormous wealth and solidity and ;ts unquestioned power of resistance, its sagacious managers deem it imprudent to face the omnipot ence of the coming assert on of the public will, and the trust is forearm log itself by putting its great interests under some more normal form of man agement. In striking contrast to this prudence, the sugar monopoly, with no choice between early failure and a more complete grasp upon the entire industry! is making another enormous lasoe of stock at an enormously ex aggerated inflation of its true value. The flooding of the stock market with such vast issues of scrip that has no true and permanent baa;s of value can not be regarded at anything short of a standing grave menace to Wall street interests. Operators and investors should be warned that the chief aim of the promoters of these schemes is to transfer their scrip into other hands at the highest poible prices and then maybe leave the disorganized concerns to their fate. WASHINGTON, Dec. 31—Boies Penrose, senior senator from Penn sylvania, died suddenly at his hotel apartment here tonight from pul monary thrombosis- He had been ill since Tuesday, first with a severe cold., which rallied quickly to treat ment, but on Thursday his condition became more serious. He made little

progress toward recovery from that time. It was not until late today, how ever, that his physician, Dr. Roy D. Adams, realized that his condition was desperate. Heroic efforts jwere made to save him. and while it was realized that he was gravely ill his death was described as sudden. Worn out by a long illness a year or more ago, which kept him long! from the senate, Senator Penrose came back early in the year and for the last few months was working in his old time legislative form on the tax bill, which takes effect tomor row. With this out of the way, he took up the tariff, attending daily meetings of the committee, often over-taxing his strength. Except for his nurses and physi dan, the Pennsylvania senator, long a power in politics and in the senate, was alone in his large apartment on the top floor of a hotel overlooking the city when he passed away at 11:30 o'clock tonight. Up to within five minutes of his death his condi tion dad been described as "quite comfortable." Then he lapsed into unconsdousness and died peacefully. The senate will reconvene Tuesday at noon and immediately adjourn out of respect. U. S. Senator Boies Penrose of Pennsylvania was one of the most

interesting personalities in the upper house, which he entered in 1879 as the successor to the late Senator Donald Cameron, one of the wealthiest bachelors in the senate. HIGH COURT OK'S GAS TAX STATUTE Decision Unanimous — Involves Total of $237,353, plus Pen alties—Validates No, 31 HELENA—Montana supreme court Wednesday upheld the constitutional ity of the 1925 gasoline tax law which provides that refiners and dis tributors shall pay a tax of two cents a gallon. The unanimous opinion of the court involves a total of $237,366.60, plus penalties, in unpaid gasoline tax es. This fund is to go into the state treasury. The opinion also validates Initia tive Measure No. 31, the "Good Roads" bill passed by a majority of more than 72,000 at the last general elec tion. That measure provides for a three-cent tax on gasoline, the entire fund raised to go to the state high way commission for the construction in conjunction with federal aid, of permanent highways. During the last two years the state supreme court has held uncon stitutional the 1921 and 1923 gaso line tax measures passed by two previous legislatures. The 1925 law, which has been held constitutional, was drafted by Albert H. Angstman, assistant attorney general, and the legal battles conducted by the state have been handled from district court

to the supreme court of the United States by Mr. Angstman, Attack on the 1925 law was made by the Silver Bow Refining company j of Butte on the ground that it at tempted to amend a statute which , , . , had been declared unconstitutional | It was an amendment of the 1923 { law. To this the court replies that the 1925 legislature had the power, before 1921 and 1923 acts were de clared unconstitutional, to remedy by amendment the constitutional defects and therefore the 1925 act is valid as against the objection that an uncon stitutional law can not be amended. STORES CLOSING FOR THREE DATS; Business To Suspend Sunday. Monday and Tuesday For Celebration Of Fourth Laurel business, except for must services, will suspend for a period of three days at the beginning of next week for celebration of the Fourth. Placards to that effect were posted this week in stores and markets, announcing the three-day holiday for Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, July 2, 3 and 4. The closing duplicates the one for observance of Memorial day at the end of May. The two three-day hitches will constitute the only va cations many store operators and employees will have this year, and customers are urged to stock up with provisions to carry them from

Saturday to Wednesday morning. Recognizing the situation, Gov ernor Sam C. Ford has proclaimed Monday a holiday in Montana, for use in connection with Tuesday, the Fourth. Banks and postoffices, in most instances, will not be open for business Monday, and none Tues day. This service was conducted by mission at the request of the Flat head Indians. They, in 1831, sent four of their courageous tribesmen to St, Louis to consult with Gen. El fn!H } 1 1 I Unusual Prices, Heavy Yields, Greater Acreage Contribute i 21 Per Cent Increase I Total. value of crops harvested in | Montana during 1947 reached the ■ all time peak of approximately $288 | million, which was $66.5 million j more than in 1946 and nearly three j times the average value for the j preceding 10 years. All wheat, with a value of $166 million, accounted for three-fourths of the gain over 1946 in the total crop value. Other grains and flaxseed were responsible for 21 per cent of the increased value, the Montana federal agricul tural statisticial service at Helena said this week. Unusually high prices were large ly responsible for placing the total crop value at such an unprecedented level. Record season average prices were established for corn, wheat, rye, flax and dry peas in 1947. The price of oats was the same for 1919 and barley was only 3 cents per bushel below the 1919 average. Compared with 1946, prices received by growers were appreciably higher for all commodities except alfalfa seed, apples and cherries. Increased output on any principal crops also contributed to the high production value. Quantities of corn, spring wheat, barley, rye, flaxseed, dry beans, sugar beets, all hay, apples and cherries exceeded the 1946 harvest. These larger crops more than offset the reduced produc tion of winter wheat, oats, potatoes, seed peas, alfalfa seed, sweet clover seed, mustard seed and sorghums. Montana's crops came through with better than average production despite heavy winter kill of winter wheat, late May freeze damage to grains and hays and deficient

Montana farmers brought more new land under cultivation during 1947, which helped to increase the total acreage of crops harvested by some 380,000 acres above the area har vested in 1946. The nation's all-crop production in 1947 was only a little below the average of the five best years in history. Only in 1942, 1944 and 1946 was the all-crop figure larger than in 1947. f FUNERAL IS HELD FOR Funeral services were held at Smith's chapel in Billings Wednes day for Mrs. Florence Beatrice Smith, 39, a native of Laurel who had resided in Fromberg and Bil lings since her early childhood. MI* SEEDS MORE ACRES WIRIER WHEAI Winter wheat seeding in Mon tana this fall covered 1,593,006 acres, 8 per cent more than the 1,475,000 acres seeded in '49. It is also slightly above the average for the period 1939 to 1948, but is well below the all-time high of 1,949,000 acres planted in the fall of 1946. Montana farmers had a good ap portunity this fall to drill their winter wheat without delay because of the weather in September and October. Nearly all of the acreage is in the established winter wheat belt with but little on the fringes where risk of winter kill is high. The crop got off to a favorable start, and with thick stands and barring unusually severe conditions during the winter the survival is expected to be good. Condition of the wheat Dec. 1 was 92 per cent of normal, cam pared with 85 per cent a year ago and 69 per cent of the correspond ing period two years ago. The 1951 crop as indicated Dec. 1 is 30,267,000 bushels, or 5,055,000 bushels more than this year's crop

average from 1939 to 1948.
