Bill to Enable Dakota, Montana, Washington and New Mexico to be Admitted Into the Union.
The Introduction of the Bill the Out Come of a Conference by the Democrats of the House.

WASHINGTON, D. C., Dec. 22. The following is the text of the Springer bill for the admission of Dakota and other territories. The introduction of this bill is the outcome of a conference by the dem­ ocrats of the house, and the bill is likely, therefore, to pass that body within a short time. It will then go to the senate, where it will be amended and returned to the house to die—if the amendments prove ob­ noxious to the controlling spirits of that body: A bill to enable the

Montana, Washington to form constitutions and state govern­ ments, and to be admitted into the union on an equal footing with the original states: Be it enacted by the senate and house of representatives of the United States of America in congress assembled: [SEC. 1 defines the boundaries of the pro­ posed states.]

SEC. 2. That all persons residing within the limits of said proposed states, qualified by the laws of said territories to vote for representatives to the legislative assem­ blies thereof, are hereby authorized to vote for and choose delegates to form a conven­ tion in each territory and the qaulifica tions for delegates to such conventions shall be such as by the laws of said territo­ ries respectively persons are required to possess to be eligible to the legislative as­ semblies thereof and the afore­ said delegates to form said conven­ tions shall be apportioned among the several counties within the limits of the proposed states, in such dis­ tricts as are hereinafter provided, in pro­ portion to the population in each of said counties and districts, as near as may be, to be ascertained at the time of making said apportionments by the persons here­ inafter authorized to make the same from the best information obtainable tn^t said apportionments shall be made by the gov­ ernor, the chief justice and the United States attorney of each of said territories, ar any two of them and the governor of each territory shall, by proclamation, order an election of the delegates aforesaid to be held on the Tuesday next after the first Monday in November, 1887, whicli procla­ mation shall be issued at least ninety days prior to the time of said elections and such elections shall be conducted, the returns made, the result ascertained,and the certifi­ cates to persons elected to such conventions issued in the same manner as is prescribed by the laws of the said territory regulating elections therein for delegates to congress. The number of delegates to said conven­ tions respectively shall be ninety-nine and all persons resident in said proposed states who are qualified voters of said territories under the laws thereof shall be entitled to vote upon the election of delegates, and upon the ratification or rejection of the constitutions, under such rules and regula­ tions as said conventions may prescribe.

SEC. 3. That the persons hereinbefore authorized shall divide said proposed states into thirty-three election districts, in each of which districts three delegates to the said constitutional convention shall be elected. In voting for such delegates each qualified voter may vote for not exceeding two persons, and the candidates highest in •otes shall be declared elected.

SEC. 4. That the districts in which dele­ gates to the constitutional conventions are to be elected shall be formed of contiguous and compact territory, bounded by county lines, and contain as nearly as practicable an equal number of inhabitants, according to the census of 1885, or the latest enumer­ ation of the inhabitants thereof but no dis­ trict shall coutain less than four-fifths of the ratio required for three delegates. Coun­ ties containing not less than the ratio and three-fourths may be divided into separate districts, and into as many districts as the population may require.

SEC. 5. That the delegates to the con­ ventions thus elected shall meet at the seat of government of each of said territories on the second Tuesday of January, 1888, and after organization shall declare, on be­ half of the people of said proposed states, that they adopt the constitution of the United States whereupon the said conven­ tions shall be and are hereby autborized to form constitutions and state governments for said proposed states respectively: Pro­ vided, That the constitutions shall be re­ publican in form, and make no distinction civil or political rights on account of race or color, except as to Indians not taxed, and not be repugnant to the consti­ tution of the United States and the princi­ ples of the Declaration of Independence: And provided further, That said conven­ tions shay provide, by ordinances irrevoc­ able without the consent of the United States and the people of said states, first that perfect toleration of religious senti­ ment shall be secured, and that no inhabi­ tant of said states shall ever be molested in person or property on account of his or her mode of religious worship secondly, that the people inhabiting said proposed states do agree and declare that they forever dis­ claim all right and title to the unappropri­ ated public lands lying within the bounda­ ries thereof, and to all lands lying within said limits owned or held by any Indian or Indian tribes and that until the title there­ to shall have been extinguished by the United States, the same shall be and re­ main subject to the disposition of the United States, and said Indian lands shall remain under the absolute jurisdiction and control of the congress of the United States that the lands belonging to citizens of the United States residing without the said states shall never be taxed at a higher rate than the lands belonging to residents thereof that no taxes shall be imposed by

the states on lands- or property therein be­ longing to or which may hereafter be pit chased by the United States or reserved for its use: Provided, however, That nothing herein, or in the ordinances herein pro­ vided for, shall preclude the said states

from taxing as other lands are taxed any lands owned or held by any Indian who has severed his tribal relations, and has ob­ tained from the United States or from any person a title thereto by patent or other grant, save and except such lands as have been or may be granted to any Indian or Indians under any act of congress contain­ ing a provision exempting the lands thus granted from taxation but said ordinances shall provide that all such lands sball be exempt from taxation by said state so long and to such extent as such act of congress may prescribe thirdly, that the oonded debt of said territories incurred for the erection of the public buildings of the ter­ ritories shall be assumed and paid by the said states respectively.

SEC. 6. That in case constitutions and state governments shall be formed in com­ pliance with the provisions of this act, said conventions forming the same shall pro­ vide by ordinances fot submitting said con­ stitutions to the people of said states for their ratification or rejection, at an election to be neld in each of said territories on the first Tuesday after the first Monday of No­ vember, 1888. at which election the quali­ fied voters of said proposed states shall vote directly for or against the proposed consti­ tutions, and for or against any provisions separately submitted. The returns of said elections shall be made to the secretary of each ot said territories, who. with the gov­ ernor and chief justice thereof, or any two of them, shall canvass the same and if a majority of the legal votes cast shall be for the constitution, the governor shall certify the result to the president of the United States, together with a statement of the votes cast upon separate propositions, and a copy of said declaration^ constitution and ordinances.

SEC. 7. That until the next general cen­ sus, or until otherwise provided by law, said states shall be entitled to one representa­ tive in the house of representatives of the United States, except Dakota, which shall be entitled to two, which representatives, together with the governors and other offi­ cers provided for in said constitutions, shall be elected on the same day of the election for the adoption of the constitutions: and until said state officers are elected and qualified under the provisions of each con­ stitution respectively, and the states re­ spectively are admitted into the union, the territorial officers shall continue to dis­ charge the duties of their respective offices in said territory.

SEC. 8. That the counties of Grant, Rob­ erts, Day, Brown, Edmunds, Walworth, Boreman, Hettinger, Bowman and all that part of the proposed state of Dakota north thereof, shall constitute the first congres­ sional district, and that portion of the pro posed state of Dakota lying south of said counties shall constitute the second con­ gressional district of said state and in each of said districts in Dakota, and in each of the states of Montana, Washington and New Mexico, one representative in con­ gress shall be elected until otherwise pro­ vided by law after the next decennial cen­ sus of the United States, and at the time prescribed by general law for such elec­ tions in other states.

SEC. 9. That sections numbered 16 and 36 in every township of said proposed stat'i of Dakota, Montana, Washington and New Mexico, and where such sections, or any subdivision thereof, have been sold or oth­ erwise disposed of by or under the author­ ity of any act of congress, other lands equivalent thereto, in legal subdivisions of not less than one quarter section, and as contiguous as may be to the section in lieu of wnich the same is taken, are hereby granted to said states for the support of common schools.

It is stated that of the 100 persons on board at the time ot the disaster only fourteen are known to have been saved. The "John H. Hanna" was built in Madison, Indiana, in 1876 and hailed from Louisville, Ky. She was of 877 tonnage and was owned by the Ouachita river consolidated line. Several of the passengers were seated in the cabin hav­ ing a merry time and with no thought of the impending catastrophe* Many of the crew and passengers were asleep when the fire broke out and spread with quick rapid­ ity. As soon as the fire was discovered Engineer Merriam set the steam pump working and tried to battle with the flames but the fire swept through the boat like ablaze on the prairie and the ^engine room was soon in flames. Then to add further to tjie consternation a steam pipe burst and filled the place with scald­ ing steam. Dec. 23.—The ruffianly conduct of Jem Smith'sj freinds at the ring side, has disgusted every lover of fair play in the kingdom, and the unjust and cowardly decision of the referee in declaring the fight a draw, instead of giving stakes to Slavin, who had his man whipped from the start, has added to the exasperation of the sporting men. All accounts of the mill agree that Smith was not in it, and this fact, together with the actions of the thugs who were at the Ting side in his behalf to prevent bis being whipped, will render it impossible for him to ever again obtain reputaole backing, while every pugilist of reputation will be abundantly justified in treating his at­ tempts to arrange a fight with contempt. Preparations are being made by the Booth Company to start their oyster business here. As. was told in the News some time ago, this concern is one of the largest dealers in oysters in the country. The building at the foot of Smith street, formerly occu pied by Mr. Boyle, has been leased and improvements are being made. Within a few weeks, it is expected, they will be ready to start business. The Booth company has houses in all the oyster centers. They began business at Baltimore. Headquarters are now in Chicago where most of the oysters bought in the east, are shipped and from there distributed throughout the western states. In conversation with the superintendent, who is to have charge of the local house, it was learned thaf they will be in shape here to handle 60,000 oysters daily. These, it is expected, will be supplied by the oystermen in these waters. This will make a market not only for Perth Amboy, but for Totteuville, South Amboy and Koyport oystermen as well. A force of men will be kept busy opening tne bivalves and already a carload of tubs have been brought here in which to pack the oysters for shipment direct to Chicago. At tne central house in that city they are capable of handling :500,000 oysters daily. A sailor from a barge moored be tween the Barber Asphalt works and the dock of the American SmeltiDg and Refining company’s plant, was held up near Maurer at 3 o’clock this morning by three highwaymen,accord ing to reports from the vicinity. The sailor was badly beaten, but made a desperate struggle and got away, be-' fore they could relieve him of any valuables. This is the second time this week that men have been held up on this lonely road. The police are now working on the case of A. F. Stuobs, the Philadelphia paint agent, who claims that be was robbed of a sum of money. The police think that the robberies are being committed by a gang of local, well-known toughs. Stubbs came to town this morning and at 10.30 o’clock was at police head \ quarters where he was seen by a News reporter. youner men got on. At the plant of the American J Smelting and Refining Company it was said they had been told of a holduD there last night and that the victim>-as a boat man, bnt they did not known the name of the man, but understood he belonged on a boat in that vicinity. Burglars visited several places in the business district last night, but, as far as can be ascertained, all they took was a small axe and a screw driver from one place, which were found in another place, and some clothing, which was found in the yard, in the rear of the store from which it was taken. The tools were taken from the surveying and engineering offices of Mason & Smith, over the Weinberg store, at 102 Smith street, and the clothing was taken from the Wein berg store. The nearest thing to any clue is the fact that three men were seen running from the yard back of the

southeast corner of Fayette street, where the burglars paid their first known visit of the night shortly af ter midnight. They tried to enter at the rear of the millinery store of Harry Levinslon, at 342 State street, thinking, It is believed, that they were at the windows of Aaron Kauf man’s jewelry store, at No. 344, next door. People living on Payette street in the rear of these stores heard their dogs barking and, look ing out, they discovered three forms in the darkness making stealthily away. Among those who saw them were members of the Munroe house hold and also some Italians. Coniil Not Gain Entrance. They were unable to gain entrance to Levinston’s store because of the iron bars over the windows. There is a low roof near the windows and this aided them in reaching to the windows. About an hour later they went to the store of Weinberg & Company, on Smith street. They went around to the rear, through the alley be tween that building and that of Frank Neer, on the east, and tried to enter the Weinberg store through the iron-barred windows. The iron bars hindered them, but they broke the glass and reached in and drag ged out some suits of young peo ple’s clothing. But these maurau ders cared not for such articles, cash evidently being their object, and they left the clothing in the yard where it was found this morn ing. The burglars next crossed over to the ward in the rear of Sickles’ Brothers dry goods store, at 104 and 100, and got a ladder. SAYS BLUFFING COINGON Mr. Bloomfield Says the Freeholders Are Not Bound by Any Contract— The Instrument Signed by the For mer Board Was Violated and Bro ken, Which Vitiated It—Bloomfield Claims Contractors Are Overpaid. Charles A. Bloomfield Is not among those who think that the new Amboy bridge can not be opened as a result of his writ of certiorari. He holds that the board of freeholders can open the bridge if It desires. Mr. Bloomfield is evidently of the opin ion that there is some bluffing going on. He is always a busy man, and has been especially so, of late, which probably accounts fqr not being heard from on the subject. Not Bound by Contract. According to Mr. Bloomfield’s view, the board of freeholders Is not bound by any contract. Such an instru ment was signed by the former board of freeholders and the Sandford & Harris company, but laws were vio lated and the contract broken in the work of constructing the bridge, which vitiated the contract. Today, ' if Mr. Bloomfield’s position is right

ly understood, the present board is bound only to the actual value of material and labor, and the investi gation brought about by Mr. Bloom field tended to show that the contrac tor has already been overpaid about ISO,000 to 140,000 for these. Mr. Bloomfield still thinks that it is the county wjtich is owed, not owing. Need Not Accept Bridge. Under the circumstances as he sees. them, there is no necessity of formally accepting the bridge. The county has more than paid for it al ready. It is simply a question now of opening it. If a contract were to pave a street, and vitiate the contract in the course of its performance, could he, as a result of the city re fusing to pay more than the value of material and labor used, close the "street to the public and in a sense as sume the ownership of it in conse 'quence of the dispute? Somewhat like that Mr. Bloomfield looks at the mat ter. The bridge, he holds, is a pub lic highway of the county, and hav ing been more than paid for, can be opened and used, leaving to the law the adjustment of the dispute over the original contract. Only ii Short Time Before the City Will Be CrnmiiiHl for Room for Educating the Children and an $80,000 Building Above the Hos pital Is Contemplated—Money Is Scarce, Improvements Taking All. If the plans of the present Board of Estimate are carried out It Is ex pected that next year work will be started on a new school house on the property recently purchased from the Hanson Realty Company west of the city hospital. The new building is to have between twenty-four and thirty rooms and the estimated cost is about $80,000. If possible an addition may also be built to the high school. The Board of Estimate held a meeting last Friday night and the matter of having more school room in this city was taken up. It was the intention of the Board of Education last year to build two new schools, but they were not allowed enough money and this year only Improve ments are to be made to two schools. May Have Thirty Rooms. The idea of erecting a school, hav-^ ing between twenty-four and thirty rooms, it is said, is favored by every

To build a school of this sort would mean a great outlay of money at one time, but the estimate board argues that it is necessary to have more ac commodations. The city is growing at a greater rate than ever and it will be only a short time before the build ing will again be crowded and the cry for more room for pupils will be heard. When the high school was built a few years ago it was thought 'that it would be large enough to last for some years to come, but already it has been found that it is entirely too small and it is expected that next year, if possible an addition of four more rooms will be built. This is needed, but a new school' is to come first. Only Repairs This Year. This year the Board of Education was allowed $49,000 with which to purchase land, repair buildings and do numerous other things. They pur chased ground near the hospital, a new addition of eight rooms is to be added to school No. 5. making six teen rooms in all in that building. The estimated cost of this will be about $30,000. At No. 2 school, a court is to be put in, the front en trance changed and new floors laid. The estimated cost is about $9,000. This year the board will not have much money left. Some time this year, it Is said, plans for the new school will be drawn and submitted to the present estimate board and if things go well, the Board of Education will ask for the amount required, about $80,000, add if it is forthcoming, the work will be started. MR. PARKER AGAINST NEW BRIDGE OVER BAY Favors Making Double-Decker of Present Structure Across Newark Bay. BAYONNE, Aug. 10.—A hearing under tfie auspices of the special committee appointed by tlie Hudson county board of freeholders in regard to building a bridge across Newark bay, from Bayonne to Elizabeth, took place in Bayonne Thursday night. The general sentiment seemed to be i in favor of the bridge. Among the speakers was Congress I man K. Wa.vne Parker, of Newark. |He said in part: ; "I expected to meet others from Union who would tell us what they think, and that we should perhaps have estimates as to the cost of con struction and maintenance, and what travel would be likely. I know so lit tle about the construction and main tenance of a bridge that I will not say anything on that subject. You will have to consider it. “I begin with what will be my last word. Since I have considered this subject I have always insisted that there are too many bridges built where one would suffice. I thoroughly believe if any wagon road is to go across Newark Bay that it would be cheaper and better to make arrange ments with the railroad, which must rebuild the bridge, for the construc tion of a double decked bridge upon piers, so as not to obstruct naviga tion, and in order that wagons may go under or over the railroad tracks, and that the cost of tills communica tion may lie mostly paid by the rail road instead of being wholly put up on the counties. “We all know that tills is done on many railroad bridges, and 1 think it should lie perhaps a provision of gen eral law that no bridge should cross a waterway without providing for the accommodation and use of all roads. We have a provision in many United States laws that the bridge author ized to be built across a navigable waterway shall be a highway which can be used by any railroad upon proper terms, and thus telegraph lines and trolleys can be put across. That is, I believe that a bridge, which always does interfere with navlglion more or less, should be so arranged as to be used by as many people as j possible and the cost shared between I as many possible.” i ■ i ■ i -

VICfRAIDS AND POLICE TRANSFERS New York Is Having Trouble Of Her Own Along With Hottest Polical Campaign on Record. NEW YORK, Oct. 2G:—While Po lice Commissioner Bingham was an nouncing the changes in the police force, making one of the greatest shakeups the department has ever had, Dr. Parkhurst and officials of

me society lor tne prevention ot - Crime wore raiding alleged illegal resorts in the Tenderloin. At an early hour Robert McClIn tock, superintendent of the soo.iety, accompanied by twelve men from a private detective agency, invaded the Tenderloin and made five raids over the head of Police Captain Schlott ffltin. After the second raid was made the detective attached to the precinct "got busy” and four other raids were made by them. One of the society's raids was on the same house that ten minutes before had been entered by police detectives. More than one hundred prisoners were taken to the Tenderloin police station, mostly women. Professional bondsmen reaped ante-election bar vests such as have not been known in years. More than three-quarters of the prisoners were bailed out by “Bob” Nelson or his lieutenants. According to McClintock all the houses entered in the raids have been known to him for more than four months. The shakeup consists of the trans fer of S5 police captains, including every one in the greater city with the exception of Herman \V. Sehlottman. the present, czar of the tenderloin. Captains who have commanded precincts where the white lights blaze were sent to the rural sections of the Bronx, Queens county and Staten Island, while captains who had for gotten what, a street car looked like were brought back to the city. Bing ham’s order followed a two hours’ conference with Mayor McClellan. Politics in a way are responsible for the shuffling of the captains. In past years police captains have been transferred just before election, but never on such a scale as today’s re arrangement. One noticeable fea ture was the fact that the half dozen captains known to bo close friends of Timothy D. Sullivan and who were given good posts several months ago when the mayor and "Big Tim” were pulling together, drew the dullest kind of residential precincts in the new assignments. Captain Sehlottman, who stays at the tenderloin station, is a hard working, reliable policeman. He has I not done wonders in keeping the sec

lion orderly, but under his command the tenderloin police have been dili gent, and the district has furnished no police scandals. -- TO ORGANIZE YOUNG MEN’S CLUBS TONIGHT. Several days ago an unsteady man was noticed walking along the street in Texarkana. A man simply unsteady would not have been noticed particu larly, for Texarkana, like Little Kock, is the scene of a great many unsteady men. But the man looked sick, and when he reached a street corner lie lay motionless. A crowd of people gath ered around, and when a physician arrived and examined the man he re

marked: “(ientlemen, the poor fellow is dead.” The man waa placed upon a bench, oml the Coroner, who had been noti fied, summoned a jury ami held an in quest. “Well, gentlemen,” said the Coroner, after the consult*on, “what is your opinion as to the cause of death ? ’ Just then the corpse aniee, thrust his hands into his pockets and exclaimed: “I don't know what your opinion is, hut I’d like all-fired well to know who’s got my pocket l»ook.” The man started off, hut was stopped by the Coroner, who informed him that he would have to ]»ay the excuses. “The deuce you *ay. ^ oil talk like an undertaker who has conducted a funeral!” ‘T have held an inquest over your body, sir, and ns you have behaved ridiculously, the county won t allow me anything, and of course you 11 have to pay me. “I didn’t send yor yon. I didn’t tell you to hold an inquest. I was getting along first rate.” “Neither does any dead man send for me.” “But I wasn't dead.” “It. wasn’t my fault.” “Nor mine, either.” “You are a hypocrite, sir; you are deceitful You should not lie recog nized in this community; ami 1 want you to understand this w hen you die, don’t send for n»e, for I wouldn’t hold an inquest over you to save your life." —Littk Rock Ouzette.

ISH HAS FAITH IN THE FUTURE OF THIS CAMP Will. C. Isli, one of the best known mining operators in the west, who is heavily interested in the Yerington dis trict, spent Sunday last here on import ant business by which much was done to his entire satisfaction. Mr. Isli secured an extension of time for his payments to be made on the Gal lagher mine and other properties here. Shortly after his arrival he was seen by a Times representative concerning his views on the financial situation. He stated as his opinion that money would loosen up before a great while and that Nevada would come out of the scrim mage with flying colors. “Yes, we were pinched,” replied he to a question concerning the effect of the stringency upon him, “but by no means are we down and out. “Our deposits represent large sums, yet we, in common with hundreds of others, are at the mercy of the bank situation. However, we have every con fidence that all will end well and so far as we are personally concerned are not giving the matter much worry. “Those with whom we have been do ing business in Yerington have treated us most kindly.

‘‘I still cling to my belief that Yer ington is to be one of the best camps in the west. As soon as it is possible we will begin the development of our var ious holdings, which we believe are among the best in this section.” Mr. Ish and his associates have al ready spent enormous sums in Yering ton and vicinity. The district is to be complimented that they are so con scientiously among its strongest admir ers and staunchest supporters. GREAT FAITH IN RAWHIDE x Attorney E. H. Evans, formerly of this place but who recently cast his lot with the promising new camp of Raw hide, spent this week in Yerington, and of this latest addition to Nevada’s list of fortune-making camps, has the following to say: “I believe, beyond the shadow of a d>ubt, Rawhide will prove one of Neva da’s greatest bonanza camps. There are seven or eight leasers taking out rock which sparkles with gold, and almost any piece of it would be prized as ‘speci men ore.’ You may stand on Main street and in several different places see them sacking the high-grade right from the grass roots—rock that will run from 110 to $20 to the pound.

‘You would be surprised to see the number of people in this camp at the present time and the substantial frame buildings that are erected and in the course of construction. The population now numbers, I believe I am safe in say ing, over 2000, while each of the six or eight stages and autos that connect the camp with the outside world, are loaded to their utmost capacity each day with capitalists and business men looking for investments. “The recent financial flurry, it is true, lias injured the camp to a great extent, and but for this one thing I am sure Rawhide would now be a camp of from 4000 to 5000 souls, with several deals running up into the hundreds of thous ands to its credit. As soon as money matters become easier you will see a boom at Rawhide that will have seldom been equalled in Nevada.” Mr. Evans is enjoying a good practice in Rawhide and will return the first of nest week. Several Yerington people, he says, are interested in this new camp and all are enthusiastic over their pros pects. ‘‘KIDNAPER?1 The celebrated trick horse and Califor nia be.'iuty, will appear at the Owl hall on December 13th, in his wonderful per formances. New York City capital is in the field with a proposition to erect a custom smelter in the Yerington district for the treatment of the product from the var ious mines. Through the efforts of Sam Davis, chairman of the state publicity commis sion, the attention of the Harlemites was called to the opportunities for smelt ing operations here. They, in turn, in quired into the proposition and stand ready to back the enterprise with their experience. Some of the parties inter ested are men well known in the copper industry, among whom might be men tioned Jack Wilcoxen, a millionaire op erator of Butte, formerly of Virginia City, Nevada. L. C. D. Kakins of 17 Battery Place, New \ork City, is the man who is at the head of the scheme to erect a cus tom smelter here. Local Capitalists Secure Bond On Good Property A deal of vast importance to Rawhide ■was consummated this w’eek in Yering ton. The bond held by Ira Wagoner of this city on the Mascot group of claims was transferred to E. H. Whitacre and associates. While the amount involved was not made public it is known to rep resent a large sum. The Mascot group consists of six claims, being among the first locations in the Rawhide district, located by Messrs. McLeod and Wadge. It takes in nearly all of Mascot hill in the very heart of the Rawhide pay belt. Mr. Whitacre and those associated with him will at once inaugurate an ac tive and thorough campaign of develop ment. Their advent into the Rawhide district at this time means much for the new’ camp. They have plenty of cash to thoroughly open up the estate, which will prove the existence of ore at depth and the continuity of the rich vein sys tem which show so remarkably well on the surface. The gentlemen who have taken over the bond are confident that the Mascot will prove a winner. The surface show' ing is good and the location unexcelled in that section. Rawhide is to be con gratulated upon the gentlemen having become identified with its development.

Yeringtou, Nevada, November, 30, 1907. Mr. K. H. Harriman, 23 Wall st., New York City. Dear Ed: My attention has been called to an article appearing in the Yer ington Times of even date wherein it is stated that you have instructed your agents to run the “stub” train from Fort Churchill to Wabuska whenever there is any human live-stock consigned to the latter place. I understand that you took this action to relieve your pas sengers of the heart-burn which natur ally follows a few hours’ residence in that part of God’s domain given over to you, “Dago” red and a poor, unfortu nate dispatcher that some day must have committed a terrible crime to be so pun ished. Now, dear Ed, I have every confidence in the Yerington Times. I appreciate the fact that it is regarded as the George Washington of Nevada papers. How ever, on the very day before reading the unstinted praise you et al. received at the hands of the Times editor, I was compelled to cover the distance from Churchill! to Wabuska by the tie route. For your enlightenment, I wish to in form you that there are exactly 100,756, 631 wooden cross-liars under your main line rails between the two points. Keep the change. Let me say here, Ed, that I do not lay the blame at either your doors or those of vour employes. It was all my own fanlt Withal, I am very sore; sore from the soles of my feet to the crown of my head. I wish, as a friend of mine, you would use your good offices to in duce the proprietor of the “Poca a Poca” at Churchill to change his brand. The made-while-you-wait stuff that he dishes out in his liquid-refreshment par

lor is, indeed, very poor, manufactured, I understand, from a compound of red ants and young tulles, which thrive in the neighborhood in abundance. Another thing, Ed, which occurs to me: If you are actually sincere in your desire to afford your passengers every comfort, I for one would like to see you improve your roadbed between Churchill and Wabuska. There are, at present, tons upon tons of loose cobbles between the rails, which make walking exceed ingly painful. If you really want your ticket purchasers to enjoy your hospit able treatment, why not- make a boule vard for that twelve miles. Again, you would be doing your patrons a service by providing life rafts where you have filled in the swamp lands. It is very humiliating, I assure you, to be com pelled to stand in the water up to your waist because you happen to meet a train at such a place one, too, that is going in the opposite direction to the one you are traveling. These art- simply sug gestions, Ed, which are called to your attention for the common good of a 1 which, I realize, you are very painstak ing about. When I left Churchill I had a grip and an overcoat, both of which weighed in the neighborhood of 30 pounds. Before arriving at Wabuska they weighed at least 175 pounds, avoirdupois. Enclosed please find check for an amount to cover excess baggage. Trusting you are well and that our mutual friend, “Teddy Bear,” is still on your trail, permit me to be as ever, Your friend, K. I,km.ih Smaii.i,. P. S.—I have heard it whispered around of late that Theodore is still doing a fine business. K- E. S.

A resume of the mining operations at Silver City during the month of Decem ber shows that all the mills and cyan ide plants were run to capacity and that the ore taken from the several proper ties now being worked gave very satis factory net proceeds. At the Succor mine Messrs. Rllis, Rckley and Cassidy are making a good showing on their lease and are now shipping ore. John Rarsen is also leasing with some success on the northern part of this claim. At the present time Joe Hardy and associates, lessees on the Hartford, are extracting a good grade of ore, which is being shipped to the mill of the Nevada Min ing, Reduction & Power Co. The Hart ford has had a very successful season. The Midas, owned by Paul Rennet, is now under lease to Moore & Dinan, who are taking out ore. They hope to have a milling liefore Christmas. The les sees on the Silver Hill mine have just completed a long run that is said to have paid very well—Jerry Donovan, F. Windish and Dennis Nolan having the lease. Three different leases are now runningon the Buckeye, one by Jack In dertnuhl, Tom Mayne and George Wil son, and Hardwith & Homines, and a milling has just been made from there At the Hayward mine, owned by the Nevada Mining, Reduction & Power Co., the cables and wires for the tramway from the mine to the mill at Dayton have already been stretched, and most of the surface work at the mine has been completed. Between 30 and 40 men are to lie steadily employed and all the en

ergies of the company are being directed toward opening up the Hayward, al though it owns several other good prop erties in this camp. At the Under ground, Ninnis Bros, have just finished a milling at the McTigue mill, ami have also just made a shipment of bullion and concentrates. Fred Ninnis, by the way, recently married one of Reno's fair daughters, and is now living at Silver, having the best wishes of many friends here. The Emigrant mine, owned by the Keating estate, is now being oper ated under the direction of Jack Keat ing. The Woodbury, Donovan and Phillips cyanide plant has had a very busy and and profitable season, and is now being given all the tailings it can handle. Many improvements have been made in the past few months to the Phillips plant, which have decreased the cost of operation and increased the capacity and percentage of extraction. Three new 50-ton leaching tanks have been added, and also a standard derrick with clam shell bucket to dredge the tailings from the reservoirs The boom has a sweep of SO feet ami the mast is 90 feet high. Two large reservoirs are beingconstruct ed near the derrick that will have a ca pacity of 2,500 tons. The derrick was lmilt by the American Hoist & Derrick Co., of Minneapolis, and is operated by tlicir standard electric hoist with 15 horse power motor. By the use of this der rick the tailings can be taken from the reservoirs, either wet or dry, and in winter or summer.

(From Flitted State- Investor.) Among the new copper properties that are destined to play an important part in the production of that metal is the Mason Valley Copper mines at Mason valley, in the Yerington district. Al ready under skillful management and scientific development, more than a mill ion tons of ore, running from 4 to 5 per cent copper, have been blocked out in these properties, and an SoO-ton smelter is in process of construction near by. The Mason Valley properties are in | charge of Jules baburthe, well know n as a successful copper mine manager of wide experience. For more than three years development operations have been : progressing, until finally they have now reached the point where the company: lias proven the value of the property and ' feels confident of the outcome. During the past year this group of copper mines ; has shown remarkable results from de t velopment work. Developments below j the 170-foot level are very encouraging, while on the upper levels big slopes of ore have added considerable value to this property. An important feature market ! w ise of the Mason Valley stock is its small share capitalization, there being | only 254,000 shares outstanding, which , allows for the conversion of the convert ible bonds. The Mason Valley properties are fort unate in having railroad transportation, as a line has been completed from the j

smelter site at Wabuska, Nev., (a sta tion on the Southern Pacific railway) to the mines, a distance of 16 miles, and the Mason Valley Mines Company has entered into a contract for the transpor tation of its ore from the mine to the smelter. This railroad is owned and op erated by the Nevada Douglas Copper Company, and will be completed to the mines of the latter company within the next few months. The management anticipates handling 300 tons of ore per day from the Mason Valley mines alone as soon as the smelt er plant is ready for operation. There are a number of mines within a radius of 50 miles of this smelter, which have small tonnages in sight and can be op erated at a profit when the smelter is completed. Some of these properties, not being able to operate at a profit in the past on account of excessive freight charges, were compelled to send their ore to Salt bake or San Francisco smelt ers at a freight charge of >6 per ton or more. The Mason Valley smelter has already entered into a contract with the Nevada Douglas Copper Company for the reduc tion of 250,000 tons of ore, 10,(XX> tons of which are to l>e delivered each month, month, and several other companies are endeavoring to contract with this smelt er. Consequently it is anticipated that the smelter will be able to run at full ca pacity almost from the start.

Tile town of Day ton has been very quiet—I am speaking now in regard to i the native population—they have been ! gone for a long time, but by and by they will loom up with plenty of monev—to buy booze. 1 think the law in regard to selling whisky to Indians is a travesty on justice as it stands. Last Saturday a party of gentle men, leaded by, I. H. Kent, the l'allon merchant, arrived in Yerington for the purpose of talking of the matter of raising sugar beets \^ith the farm ers of .Mason Valley. After having individual talks with some of the local busirlcss men, it was arranged that ;, I public meeting be held at Eagles' I Hall in the evening. The meeting was not very largely ; ttended, but was very interesting. Mi^ Kent, while by no means an orator, is a very flu ent and convincing talker, and he ex plained the sugar beet business in a plain, busines man’s way, talking from the standpoint of dollars, and how they can be accumulated. Messrs Brambwell and Burney, of the sugai com, any, also did some o ftlie talking Among the facts brought out, were the following: Sugar beets should yield not le -s than twelve tons to the acre on re i sonably good ground. This is the minimum figure, with good cultivi tion. In the Fallon district a? high as 25 tons has been gathered from 'a large tract. The selling price of the crop, delivered on the ears, is $7 per ton, the company paying freight U: the mill. This will give a minimum i yield of $84 per acre.

A great deal of hand labor is neces sary in the cultivation of the crop The company offers to sec that the necessary labor is found, and will advance the neces-ary money to pay for tlie help, taking its pay when the crop is delivered. The cost of thin ning, weeding, hoeing and gatherin ; is $21 per acre, for the first 12 ton^ Each additional ton ctsts 60 cents Trie labor cost puts the beets on the wagon, ready to haul to the depot. The company furnishes the seed the machine for planting- and doe: the planting, for $2.75 per acre. The farther must furnish the horses, wag ons, and all necessary team work To sum it up, the farmer must furnish the land- do till the team work ai d haul the produce to. the cars. The company practically does the rest For this, the land owner gets $7 for every ton of beets delivered at the cars, less the cost of production, whch lie knows ebfore he plant sa seed In the beet business there is no -orting of the product—no culls. A beet is a beet, small or large, and goes to help with thetonnage. In addition to the above offtrs of tre beet company, part of the price of the b ets is advanced t othe grow er during the months of May, June and July. After introducing' Mcsrs. Brant well, Burney, and Hansen, and a Jap anese named Xishiyama, who is the the head of a Japanese contracting firm to furnish labor, Mr. Kent left for Fallon, and the other gentlemei have been busy during the week, mak ing a canvass of the farmers, to, ar range for the planting of beets. The potato crop having paid so well thi< year, many of the farmers have dis played reluctance to changing their crops, but a small acreage has been promised, sufficient to give the new departure a trial. This is what the beet men want, for the present—to get the cultivation of the big roots staited in the valley, so that in fu ture they may have a big. supply for their mill. They -ay they do not hope to make any money next ycat from the beets shipped from Mason Valley, but that when they have shown the agriculturists of this tl trict how profitable it is to raise beets, they expect to see a large acre age, and then they will get theii profits.

I it is saw oy mose laminar win tlu^ culture of beets that it is very beneficial to tired soil. A crop oi two of beets raised on a piece of tir f land will give it the element- it needs the most, and for years afterwards ii will yield greater grain crops than ever before. This is caused bv tin deeper cultivation necessary for the beet crop, and by the action of tin sun, and the fact that beets absorb from the atmosphere elements whiel the wheat or oilier crops have takei from the soil. A committee of citizens has beer busy, assisting the beet men to meet the farmers, and they have become si entrusiastic in the mater that a smal company is being formed for the pur pose of putting in a tract as an ex periment. The idea is that it wil • how up the posihilities of the valley and encourage diversity of crops which is the thing necessary in devcl oping the country. Messrs Bramwe'l, Hansen, and Bur

ney, after spending several days vis iting the local laml» owners, went ti Fallon, and in a short time wdl return an dagain talk over the beet * ituatior Tvitr the local land owners. MR. BRYAN JELLS ALL ABOUT SILVER The subjoined article, written es pecially for the Reno Gazette by "the Great Commoner,'’ YV. J. Bryant is reproduced li^erc because the subject is one of supreme importance to Ne vada. and the author the foremost ad vocate of free silver in the world. The fight waged for twenty years prior to 1896 for the remonitization of silver was forced upon the world by falling prices. Three international conferences . were held during that period to devise some way of escape from the bankruptcy that threatened the debtors of all lands, and, through them, business in general. Even in 1896 the Republican party pledged itself to international bi metallism and one of the first official acts of Fresient McKinley was the appointment of a commission to so licit the co-operation of the leading nations of Europe to open the mints to the white metal. Blamed Failure on Gold Talk.

Former Vice-President Stevenson and Senator Wolcott of Colorado, were members of this commission, and the latter, speaking in the United States senate, charged that the failure if the commission was due to the fact dial Secretary Gage of the treasury lepartment, was making speeches in favor of the gold standard, while the -ommission was appealing to Europe or aid in the re-establishment of the luoble standard. The general objection raised by the .financiers to /bi-metallism, whether in lependent or international was that it is difficult to.maintain an exact parity between the two metals, but this argu ment was conclusively answered by in ternational l'i-metallists who contend ’d that fe joint agreement between na tions would reduce fluctuations to a fraction so small as to create no dis urbance to business, and they pointed out that a continual rise in the value of the dollar was mote injurious to the world than any slight variation in the "dative vaJue of the metal under in ternational bi-metallism could possi bly be. Britian Threw Her Influence. Tha theoretical objections to the louble standard, however, had but ittle influence compared with the (radical objection raised by ’Great ilritian's opposition. Being the great reditors nation of the world. Great llritian threw her influence on the ide of a rising dollar, her financiers being short-sighted enough to imagine hat she could permanently prosper y a policy that did injustice to other nations and it was injustice to com pel debtors to pay in a dollar that constantly appreciated because of legislation that gave to gold a mo nopoly of the privilege of mintage. Conditions are now entirely changed An abundant currency has been se cured from other sources, but, while Che debtor class is no longer suffering from a rising dollar and falling prices, as it was prior to 1896, the chief argu ment against silver coinage has dis appeared and new arguments bring a demand for bi-metallism from the very classes that opposed it.

Now that the bullion m a silver dol lar is worth more on the market than the bullion in a gold dollar (a situa tion produced, not by legislation, but in spite of it) we hear no more of the ‘dumping ground" bugbear or of the “melting pot test.” Silver Dollar No Longer Cheap The silver dollar is no longer a “cheap dollar,” is it the gold dollar that is cheap, if we may borrow the phraseology employed by the finan ciers twenty-five years ago. And, just as the objections to silver are being silenced by the unprecedent ed demand for that metal, the world awakens to a need for basic money so great that gold will not supply it, and the situation in Europe is made still more acute by the fact that we have absorbed* much more than our per capita share of the gold coin of the world. During and since the war the vol ume of paper money has been swollen to fabulous amounts and no resump tion of specie payments can be thought of without a very large in crease in the quantity of standard money. Gold is a fair weather friend. To use a faminiar phrase often ap plied to individuals, it is “invincible

Better Than Charity Loyal to the Labor! . . . (A nagy Mogulok most is elvezik magas fizetesiiket, s ugvanakkor szazaval veszitik el kenyeriiket meg a varos nal is a szegenv munkasok. Jo lesz elolvastatni veliik e sorokat, talari eszre ternek, mig nem lesz keso! Szerk.) Tf you must cut salaries, cut at the top of your list and not at the bottom. By that we mean cut the high salaried men and not the day laborers. Cut off of the five and ten and fifteen thousand dollar a year man and all of those above before you touch the little fellow. In the first place the laboring man is the man who is the father of large family, the hi gh salaried man generally has only one or two children if he has any at all. So we hurt the little ones when we take five or ten dollars from the man who is making only thirty or forty dollars a week. We are taking the food out of their hungry mouths, we are taking clothing off of their backs. We are depriving them of that new pair of shoes that they will need to go back to school this winter. In the case of the high salaried man we are doing nothing more than depriving his wife of a trip down to New York to take in the shows or a little jaunt over to Paris and the Riviera. Or maybe we are keeping her from getting a new car this winter, or a new fur coat. At any rate she won't starve and many a laboring man's home will have the dark shadow of starvation over it if we cut his wages. So at least, this winter, why not practice the golden rule, why not be fair to labor that has so gallantly stood by America and American institutions. Why not give them a square deal this winter (and that's better than charity) and if any cutting is to be done on the salary list to do it at the top. Once cut at the top is equivalent to twenty or thirty at the bottom. Be loyal to the labor!.... THE BIRMINGHAM SPORTLIGHT Bv JACK KATONA, Editor of Sports.

Az Egyesült Államok Igazság ügyminisztérium figyelmeztető leg Jelenti, hogy a regisztrálási Időszakot nem fogják sem elha lasztani, sem kitólni. A regisztrá lás utolsó napja december hó 26.-lka. Earl O. Hamson, az Igazság Ugyminisztérium Idegen Regisz trálás osztálya igazgatója, hatá rozottan kijelentette, hogy de cember havában sem az egész hónap alatt, sem részben — nem fogják a posták zsúfoltsága miatt és a karácsonyi vásár mi att a regisztrálást elhalasztani és ahogy egyesek képzelték: ja nuárban folytatni. “Tény, hogy ez a kérdés tár gyalás alá került”, mondotta Mr. Harrlson. “Gondoltunk arra, hogy a postahivatalok munkája enyhítése érdekében néhány hét re felfüggesztenők a regisztrá lást. Bebizonyult azonban, hogy az 1940-es Idegen Regisztrálási törvény erre nem ad felhatal mazást. Ugyanakkor a Posta osztály vezetősége biztosított bennünket, hogy a posta készen áll a regisztrálást és a karácso nyi forgalmat egyidőbén lebo nyolítani. “Oly idegeneket, akik augusz tus hó 27.-e előtt már az ország ban tartózkodtak, a regisztrálás utolsó napja, tehát csütörtök, december 26. után nem regisz trálnak. Mindazok, akik eddigeié abban a hitben éltek, hogy a regisztrálás Idejét esetleg kitól ják, igyekezzenek minél előbb regisztrálni és ilymódon a tör vény kívánalmainak eleget ten ni. El akarjuk kerülni, hogy az utolsó percekben rohanják meg az emberek a postahivatalokat.” Ismét figyelmezteti Mr. Harri son azon idegeneket, akik már regisztráltak, hogy el ne mulasz szák az Immigration and Natu ralization Service-t értesíteni, mihelyt állandó lakhelyüket megváltoztatják.

“A nem-polgárok, ha bár mennyire Is a legjobbat igyekez nek tenni, nem tettek eleget kö telességüknek, ha regisztrálás és ujjlenyomatozás után elköltöz nek, anélkül, hogy erről 5 napon belül értesítenék a Washington, D. C.-ben székelő Immigation and Naturalization Service-t. A mint ezt már többször jelentet tük, az elköltözés bejelentésére szolgáló lapokat bármely posta hivatalban be lehet szerezni ' díjtalanul. Mi jól tudjuk, hogy sokan elmulasztják ezt a fontos kötelességet, mert igen sokan, akik már regisztráltak nem kap ták meg a regisztrálásról szóló kártyát, mert az az illetők elköl tözése miatt visszajött hozzánk. A törvény 100 dollárig terjedő pénzbírságra, x vagy 30 napi bőr- ! tönbüntetésre, vagy mindkét rendbeli büntetésre Ítélheti azt, aki a törvény e rendelkezését nem veszi figyelembe.” Mr. Harrison azokhoz is szólt, akik abban a hiszemben halo gatják a regisztrálást, hogy eset leg december 26.-a előtt polgár jogokat nyerhetnek. A regisztrá lás utolsó időszaka itt van és veszélyes dolog a regisztrálást túlságosan halogatni. Sokan azt remélik ,hogy még a regisztrálás befejezése előtt behívják őket a polgárosodási vizsgára, vagy állampolgári ügyük addigra valamiként tisz tázódik és igy esetleg addig-addig halogatják a regisztrálást, míg késő lesz. A regisztrálás semmi összefüggésben sincs a polgáro sodással, Illetve a honosodással. Ezzel szemben hátrányos a ké sőbbi polgárosodásra és amellett, mint mondottuk a regisztrálás elmulasztását súlyosan büntetik.

“Mindenki vegye azt is figye lémbe,” folytatta Mr. Harrlson, / “hogy a postahivatalok, ahol idegeneket regisztrálnak nagyon el lesznek foglalva a karácsonyi forgalom miatt, különöskép a Jövő hónapban. Éppen ezért, a kik az utolsó napokra vagy órák ra halasztják a regisztrálást csak sok üggyel-bajjal lesznek képe sek a törvénynek eleget tenni.” VAz Idegenek Regisztrálási Osz tálya igazgatója ezután a szülők és gyámok figyelmét hívja fel arra, hogy 14 éven aluli gyer mekek (menekült gyermekek is) regisztrálása érdekében a szülő nek, vagy gyámnak kelfemegje - lénnle a regisztrálási hivatalok ban december 26. előtt és a kér désekre ott válaszolnak kell.

Hozzáfűzte még, hogy amint a gyermek 14. évét elérte, harminc napon belül személyesen kell je lentkeznie a postahivatalban re gisztrálás és ujjlenyomat felvétel érdekében. “örömmel jelentem,” mondot ta Mr. Harrison, “hogy a becslés szerinti 3,600,000 az Egyesült Államokban lakó idegen közül eddigelé már 2,800,000 idegen regisztrált. SWIM The party-line lads certainly took a leaf out of the employers' union-bust ing book when they went into court recently in an effort to halt hearings on Communist-domination charges against 10 CIO unions. In the first place, they entered court * under the Taft-Hartley Act, which they profess to hate more than any body else does. They used the old employers’ trick of charging conspiracy. They attempted to use the legal weapons which unionists learned years ago to abhor. Furthermore, their entire action was directly contrary to the old trade un ion “rule” that you try to settle inter-family quarrels out of court. The party-liners certainly knew these things and how unionists gen erally feel about them, but they took legal action anyhow.

The “great conspiracy” in which CIO leaders are engaged is about as conspiratorial as a drink of plain water. They took their case before the CIO convention last year. They discussed it openly from the speakers’ platform. Philip Murray and his colleagues said 'bluntly that the CIO should rid itself of Communist influences. Constitutional changes which would - permit the CIO to deal with the Com munist problem were presented * to the delegates—and a majority of delegates approved the changes. One of the moatf amusing accusa r , tions made by the lefties is that the CIO “has set everything up so it can kick out lb unions.’’ The manner in which they make the “charge” indicates they’re talking about some great secret. The hearing committees offer the second opportunity—snd the Executive Board ' offers the third. HOW ABOUT IT? By RUTH TAYLOR Seems to me lately as though I’ve done nothing but talk about public relations—and how to improve them. And here I am again, right back at the old stand. The trouble with most people is that they hear only what people want to tell them. That is, from their friends they hear how good they are, and from their enemies how bad, but they never really know what kind of an impression they make on the people they meet every day. You have to be mighty interested—one way or the other —in a man before you’ll bother to talk to him about yourself. You know how it is. You know how you will dislike a man for manner ism—or like him for it—but you wouldn’t think of telling him so until it affected a subject on which you felt strongly. But all the time you’re storing up little unconscious pictures of him, and your opinion of him is jelling without very much more than an impression to go on. That’s just what the other fellow, does about you! You can’t expect other people to make an effort to understand the reasons for your actions, and to give you a break—unless you, too, have made an effort to understand other people and to approach their problems with an unbiased mind. Unbiased does not mean that you must have no opinion of your own—but simply that you as sume that your opponent’s motives are as good as your own and try to find out what those motives are. You’ll never convert a. man by merely silencing him. You have to understand wliy he thinks what he thinks to get him to think differently. I collect stories about Andrew Fureseth—and one of the best was that Andy didn’t give a damn for your opinion but respected your reasons for these opinions. To my way of think ing that is one of the finest characteristics a man can have—be cause such a man will play fair with everyone—including himself. Why all this? Well, think it over. There is labor unrest. There is misunderstanding about labor. The public relations of labor, the merchandising of the labor movement, is the job of each and every individual trade unionist. You are the man by whom the public—those people whom you meet every day—will judge the whole organization. How do you stack up?

One of the main_arguments at the. Republican administration for the past two yean has been that busi ness Should be encouraged.. Union economists have long argued this is nonsense, that things just don’t work that way. Last week they had some powerful figures from offi cial sources to back up their argu ments. Business outlays fo» new plant and equipment in 1954 will drop to $26.7 billion, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the De partment of Commerce. TODAY IS YOUR LUCKY DAY! BF BOTH TAILOR How many people do you know who act as though today were unlucky? Who fritter away today and let all the important work pile up for tomorrow? Perhaps it is a good thing to feel that the i sun will shine on tomorrow and that good fortune will attend your every activity—but why not be free to enjoy the good when it comes? My grandmother always used to darn the largest hole first. She said it made the work go faster to feel that everything else she had to do was easier than what she was doing. And that can be applied to the work any of us have to do. If you have anything really difficult to tackle, why wait until the last moment, and let the thought of it spoil your today and tomorrow? Do it now. The quickest way to do many things is to do one thing at a time. The task just ahead may be hard and unpleasant—but there isn’t any difficult job that lasts forever— and once it is done with, tomorrow will be free for the things you really want to do. There is another thing to remember. “Tomorrow is often the busiest day of the year.” That came to me in a letter from Pat Gorman. Like Shakespeare’s Hamlet, he can always be de pended ypon for something quotable. I liked the line, stuck it up on my desk and watched. Sure enough—whenever I let things slide for tomorrow—that day something happened to upset my schedule and I slipped further behind. There is only one space of time that is completely ours—and that is today. Upon how we use it will depend what happens to us on the tomorrows. That has been said over and over, again by poets and philosophers, sages and scholars. It has been applied to every subject under the sun—from the child facing his lessons to the nation planning its security program. Today—and today only —belongs to us. . Look at today as twenty-four hours of opportunity, twenty four hours in which to put your thoughts into words, into action. The big job you’ve waited to tackle because you weren’t quite sure you could do it, the letter you meant to write, the chore you’ve left undone—do them now. Tomorrow may be too late. And—today is YOUR lucky day!

PRE-DIGESTED NEWS Hr BOTH TAYLOR Every time the Sunday supplements run short of special features, it seems to me they dig into the files and come out with some account of pre-digested food in capsule form—and how they will sustain life and do away with anything the writer happens to think of at the time—storage of foods, prepara tion, serving, etcetera. Somehow these pre-digested foods never did seem to take the public fancy. Cooking may be work, but it is lots of fun too —-and eating can be enjoyable to the eyes, and the nose as well as the palate. There is nothing appetizing about, a capsule! But with television, and radio and so much to do and so many interests, there is a definite tendency to take pre-digested news and then to pride ourselves on a wide knowledge of the facts. We take our news in capsule form, far too often. In our home, we have a game we play sometimes. We read' the news carefully—and in so far as possible, check back to the source material of that news. Then we read the columnists and listen to the commentators and see how many different slants we can find given to certain basic and fundamental facts. The result of this game is that if the time is short, we concentrate on reading the news and letting the comments thereon go by the board.

ON INDIVIDUALISM By RUTH TAYLOR According to the opponents of our way of life, we are doomed to eventual defeat because we put so much stress upon the indi vidual—upon individual liberties and individual rights. In fact, those who believe in a collective society, whether it be under the rule of the State or of a Dictator—not that I have ever been able to see any difference—condemn our individualism as archaic. We established our individualism long years ago, when the first pioneers came to these shores. A man stood or fell on his own ability. He helped his neighbors and his neighbors helped him. A few attempts were made at communal settlements, but they soon 'failed, because the drones wanted to live on those who tilled the soil—and those hard-working individualists soon got tired of being tajcen for suckers and stood on their individual rights, proclaiming that those who won’t work, won’t eat! It isn’t always easy to be an individualist. There are many times when it would be much simpler to accept the mental rule of State or Dictator, to be told' what to think, how to work, and to have our minds ruled for us. But that is not the American way. We have regard for the person and we believe in the sanctity of the individual. We respect and defend the State because it represents the composite convictions of its individual citizens. We believe in the credo that the individual has rights only in the same ratio as he has responsibilities. We also believe in the re sponsibility of the State toward its citizens and toward those States who are like minded. We fought a war to prove that point in our internal affairs. We joined in two wars to prove that point to the world. Communist propaganda—always aimed at disrupting and di viding a people—has cleverly played upon our ideals as individuals. They 'have talked peace in which we believe—'but at the same time they have crushed their satellites by force of arms. They have talked freedom for the downtrodden, in which we also believe— but instead of liberating their subject peoples they have bound them tighter. They have boasted of their great social benefits— but whom do they benefit? The poorest worker in ibis country has more than those in the “Paradise of the Workers”. There will always be some who will fall for what they want to believe, but I do not believe that an individual American who stops to think, will not see the fallacy in arguments that bear no relation to deeds. We have been too long trained to think and act as individuals, within the framework of the republic that was set up for us by men who believed in the individual, to be led astray in our thinking. Our individualism is our strength. Let us be proud of it and show to the world that individuals working together can not be defeated. .

So Labor May Know Pres.-elect Kennedy’s problem In re vitalizing the many federal regulatory agencies la strikingly revealed by a court case in which the Federal Power Com mission was rebuked in scathing terms for what the court intimated was a commission failure to protect the pub lic from extortionate gas prices. The case involved the Hope Natural Gas Oo. and a group of other companies, and the FPC awarded a permanent certificate for New York natural gas sales at prices above 23 cents per thousand cubic feet The Public Serv ice Commission of New York challenged the certificate, baaing its objection on curlier Supreme Court decisions In which the FPC had been reversed in similar cases. The U.S. Court of Appeals in Wash ington, D. C., with three judges speak ing unanimously, bluntly pointed to the most recent of these Supreme Court decisions—the so-called Catoo case. * * * In the 1959 Catco case, Judge George T. Washington wrote for the Circuit Court, the FTC had been specifically warned against issuing permanent cer tificates for gas at “suspiciously higher” * prices without having in its record a clear finding that the rate was "re quired by public convenience and neces sity." The Supreme Court had said in the Catco case, Washington continued, that' allowing initial sales of gas at a high price may lead to a “windfall for the natural gas company with a consequent j squall for the consumers.” The process of letting the gas company install the high prices, while the FPC investigates' later whether they are "just and rea sonable,” means that the review is sub ject to “inordinate delays” and is with out the protection to consumers that they can get refunds of money paid if the rates are finally held to be ex tortionate. . .^.The Supreme Court pointed, out that approval by the FPC of a hlgher-than usual rate may result In a “triggering of general price rises” in the area. It said that the FTC has a right to Issue a higher-price certificate but only under conditions so “that the consuming pub lic may be protected while the justness and reasonableness of the price ... Is ' being determined” under procedures that follow. Hie Supreme Court “expressly” stated again, Washington reminded the FPC, that it was "the intention of Congress that natural gas shall be sold ... at the lowest possible reasonable rate con sistent with the maintenance of ade quate service in the public interest.” • * *

At this moment in his opinion, Wash ington struck out on his own. He said the Circuit Court believed that the Catco decision was intended to tell the FPC that the phrase the “public interest” during a period of rising natural gas prices “demands a real administrative effort to hold back prices." There was nohlng in the record presented in the new Hope case, he declared, that “would Justify the conclusion that the commission has adequately performed this duty.” There could scarcely be a stranger Judicial rebuke to a regulatory agency. The court said that the FPC had been ordered previously not to allow rising gas prices without protecting the In terest of the consumers but once again had failed In Its duty. How did such a situation come about? Mr. Eisenhower repeatedly declined to reappoint FPC members who had shown in earlier decisions that they took the commission’s regulatory role seriously. Mr. Kennedy will find that this situa tion prevails, in greater or lesser de gree, in many regulatory agencies and agencies with quasi-judicial powers. Under Mr. Elsenhower their membership has changed, or attempted to change, the ground rules, and they have be come at least partly the creatures of interests they were intended to regulate. Some new legislation may be needed, a thorough congressional inquiry is cer tainly needed, and some new agency members are needed as the terms of present members expire. NEW YEAR THOUGHTS •, RUTH TAYLOR Just about now the preparation of New Year editions is under way. Statisticians are busily adding up long columns of figures and proving that while you can't get anything but four out of adding two and two—if you add six and six upside down, you won t get twelve! Commentators are picking what they con sider to be the high lights of the news of the past year, and determining the future in the light of the peaks alone. Don’t get me wrong. I am in awe and admiration of any one who can add a column of figures and come up with the answer twice. And the ability to dramatize day after day, as the commentators^ do, fascinates me. But somehow New Year’s Eve and New Year’s Day have a more personal application to me. It is a time to imi*™- m, one’s account with one’s self. To weigh the gains and losses in character in the past year* To determine what is our goal for the year to come and to chart a course toward that goaL I do not minimize the importance of the over-all picture. But as I have said so many times in the past—in a land where men are free, thexourse that country takes is but the summation of the desires of its citizens. Its righteousness is the righteous ness of the individual man and woman. Its strength is the strength of the individual. Because we are a people who do not take orders, we are of necessity bound to-keep the laws which we ourselves make. Because we are free to choose, we may not abili or cast the blame for failures on some one else. We have a personal re sponsibility which we cannot and must not shirk. Therefore, this New Year it behooves each one of us to draw up a balance sheet on our own lives, not glossing over the mis takes, nor yet playing down the successes. But candidly, cor rectly and courageously, that from this analysis we may main. our resolves for the New Year. And when we have done this, when we have set our sights for the coming year, let there be no repining, no looking back. Ahead of us we have three hundred and sixty five days to spend. Some will bring happiness—let us enjoy those days to the full Some will bring happiness—we are not children, we can endure the time of our testing. Whatever the New Year brings, let us face it gallantly. It is the way in which we live that counts. It is the spirit in which we live that marks our accomplishment. It is what we are that matters. There is a Resolve of Johnathan Edwards that I have quoted before. I do so again because I think it embodies all New Year Resolutions. RESOLVED: To live with all my might, while I do live! A Happy New Year to you all!
