Our mother is a woman ? wife, sister?, pretty cousins are women ; and the daughters will be if they live long enough. And then there is a love of women in general which we do not deny. A fine, magnifi cent specimen of the sex, full of life and health, a ripe red cheek, and flashing eye, is something that does one good to look at as she illuminates the humdrum sidewalks, and every day streets. A North River Steamer under full headway, with colors flying, is rather a pretty sight ? rather stirring and inspiring ; and we pull up our tiied nags to see her pass and admire the | swell she cuts. Comparatively, howcv- j er, the steamer sinks into insignificance, or some other very deep water, by the side oi a well kept, well dressed woman. } There is no rubbing it out ; women are j the ornament, charm, blessing, beauty and bliss of life ? men's life, of course. Any means that can be devised for preser ving them should be publicly made known. 1'hey are different from any other kind of fruit. You cannot pickle them ; you can not do them up in sugar and set them in a cold room, with a paper soaked in bran dy over their mouths. You cannot put1 them up in rans and seal them up air. tight, without injuring their form and fla vor. Now, as men are so dependent upon women for life's choicest blessings, s proper mode of preserving them becomes of great moment, and we are sure that the public will thank us for an infallible re ceipt. Have the feet well protected ; then pay the next attention to the chest. The chest is the repository of the vital or gans. There abide the heart and lungs. It is from the impressions made upon these organs through the skin, thai the shiver comes. It is nature's quake ? the alarm bell at the onset of danger. A wo man never shivers from the effect of cold upon hor limbs, or hands, or head ; but let the cold strike through her clothing on her chest, arui off go her teeth into a chat- 1 ter, and the whole organism is in a com motion. One sudden and severe impres sion of cold upon the chest, has slain its tens of thousands. Therefore, while the feet are well looked after, never forget the chest. These points attended to, the natural connections of the dress will sup-: ply the rest, and the woman is ready for the air. Now let her visit her neighbors, j go shopping, call upon the poor, and walk lor the good of it ? for the fun of it. TO RETAILERS. BY I>K. CHARLES JEWETT. Ye, who, regardless ot your country's good. Fill up your coffers with the price of blood, Who pour out poison with a liberal hand, And scatter crime and misery through the land, Though now rejoicing in the midst of health, In full possession of ill-gotten wealth ; I Yet a few days, at most, the hour must come, When ye shall know the poison -seller's doom, And shrink beneath it: for upon you all, The Indignation of God shall fall. In vain, ye strive, with hypocritic tongue, To make mankind beiieve ye do no wrong ? Ye know the fruits of this accursed trade; Ye see the awful havoc it hath made; Ye pour out men their death and end less woo, And then assort ? we wish it wore not so. But 'tis a truth, and that ye know full well ? That some will drink, as long as ve will sell. But should ye cease from selling, one and all, The fetters would at once from thous ands fall, And tho' they now are voluntary slaves. And rush with open eyes down to their graves, Twould grant a respite, give them time to think, And when they, shuddering, viewed the awfid brink, From which they'd just escaped, they'd take heed, Reform their lives, and bless you for the deed. But here the old excuse yet meets us I stin, "If I don't sell tho poison, others will." Then let them sell, and ye ll be ne'er the worse ; They'll have the profits, and they'll have the curse. If some slill do wrong, ye should re fuse ; The sins of others can not you excuse. 1 Is it, in fact, a pririlege to sell What kills the body, dooms the soul to i hell ? Bear this in mind : ye have at your command The power to bless, or power to curse the land. If ye will sell, intemperance still will roll, Iler wave of bitterness o'er many a soul. Still will the wife for her lost husband mourn, And sigh for days that never shall re turn. Still that unwclcome sight our eyes shall

greet, I Of beggared children roaming through the street ; And thousands whom our labors cannot save, Go trembling, tottering, reeling to their grave. Still loitering at your shop the livelong day, While scores of loungers pass their hours away ; And e'en the peaceful night, for rest or dained, Will with their noisy revels be ordained. The poisonous cup will pass, and mirth and glee Gild o'er the surface of their misery, Uproarous laughter fill each space be tween ? Harsh oaths, ungodly songs and jests obscene. And there ye ll stand amid that drunk en throng, Laugh at tho jests, and glory in the song. Hew oft ye see the children of the poor With unshod feet, unwilling, throng your door, And carry with them as they homeward j go, That which must work deep misery and woe ; That which will change the father to a beast ; That which will rob a mother of her rest ; ' And take from half-fed children needful bread, And give them curses, frowns, and blows instead ; j Which tears from drooping age its shel ter warm. All this ye see, and seeing still procure, To make you rich and all around you poor. Poor out your poison till some victim dies, Then go and at his funeral wipe your eyes. Join there that mourning throng with solemn face, And help to bear him to his burial place. There stands his wife, with weeping children round, While their fast falling tears bedew the ground. From many an eye the gem of pity starts, And many a sigh from sympathizing hearts, Comes laboring up and almost chokes the breath. While thus they gaze upon the work of death. The task conclude*, the relics of the dead Arc slowly settled to their damp, cold bed. | Come, now draw near, my money-mak ing friend ; | You see the starting, come and see the end. ; Whenyou first filled his glass, o*e would ^ suffice ; ? Next rwo were wanting, and now iieue he lies. Look now into that open grave,and say, Dost feel no sorrow.no remorse to^iay ? Does not your answering conscience load declare That tock cvescd avarice has laid him there ? Recall the virtues which he once pos sessed ? How justly honored, and how richly blest, With health uninjured, character un

stained ; While at his hearth domestic comfort reigned ! Go meet liini there ? a smiling wife you'd see. And prattling children climbing up his knee ; His heart was cheerful and his conscience clear, And thus he journeyed on from year to year. Till, oh, sad day ! when first he chanc ed to drop Within the confines of your slaughter shop, You tilled tor him the intoxicating glass. Loud cracked your jokes, and bade the bumper pass, And while he thoughtless poured the ruin down, You counted future crops from seed then sown ; And you have reaped even all his earth ly store ; But death has snatched him, and your harvests'* o'er. Now, since the earth has closed o'er his remains, Turn o'er your books and count your honest gains. How doth the account for his last week begin ? '?Monday the twenty-fourth, one quart of gin A like amount for each succeeding day Tells on the book, but wears his life away. Saturday's charge makes out th' account complete, "To cloth five yards, to make a wind ing sheet*" There, all stands fair, without mistake or Haw, How honest trade will thrive, cimiki.o nv LAW. The dome of the Capitol at Washington is the most ambitious structure in Amer ica. It is 108 feet higher than the Washington Monument in Baltimore. 68 feet higher than Bunker Hill and 23 feet higher than the Trinity Church tower at New York. It is the only considerable dome of iron in the world. It is avast hollow sphere of iron, weigh ing 8.000,000 pounds. How much is that Nearly 4,000 tons, or about the weight of 70,000 full grown people, or about equal to 1,000 laden ears, which, ' holding four tons each, would reach two miles and a half. Direclty over your head is a figure in bronze, "Ameri- ! ea," 14,985 pounds. The pressure ol the iron dome upon its piers ami pillars is 13,477 pounds to the square foot St Petersburg presses nearly 20,000 pouuda more to the square foot, and St. Gene vieve, at Paris, 66,000 pounds more. It would require to crush the supports of our dome a pressure of 557,270 pounds to the square foot The cost was about $1,000,000. The new wings cost 500,000. The architect has a plan for rebuilding the old central part of the Capitol and enlarging the park, which will cost about $3,200,000. Tho Knot oi* Hluc and Gray. Upon mv bosom lies A knot of blue and pray ; * You ask me why. Tears 1111 my eyes As low to you I say : I had two brothers once ? Warm-hearted, bold and gay ; They left my side ? one wore the blue The other wore the gray. One rode with Stonewall and his men, And joined his fate to Lee ; The other followed Sherman's march Triumphant to the sea. Both fought for what they deemed the right, And died with sword in hand ; One sleeps amid Virginia's bills, And one in Georgia's sand. The same sun shines upon their graves ? My love unchanged must stay; And so upon my bosom lies, The knot of blue and gray. Macaulays Mother.? Lord Macau lav, the great essayist and historian, wrote these words: -Children, look into those eyes, listen to that dear voice, notice the feeling of even a single touch that is bestowed upon you by that gen tle hand ! Make much of it win e- yet yon have that most precious of all gootl onifts ? a loving mother, head the un fathomable love of those eyes; the kind anxiety of that tone and look, liowe\ei slight your pain. In after life you may ? have friends ? fond, dear, kind friends; but never will you have again the inex pressible love and gentleness lavished | upon you which none but a mother be stows. Often do I sigh in my struggle with the hard, uncaring world, for the sweet, deep security I felt when of an evening, nestled in her bosom, 1 listen- I cd to some quite tale, suitable to my age read in her tender and untiring voice. Never can I forget her sweet ^lances cast upon me when I appeared asleep; never her kiss of peace at night. Years have passed away since we laid ( her beside my father in the old church- ; yard; yet still her voice whispers from , the grave, and her eye watches over me as I "visit spots long since hallowed to < the memory of my mother. j Bkigiiam Young's Ui.ii Agf..? What Three Women Said. ! The other day going back to Cleve 'laud, I sat behind tl.Tee women for an hour or two. They were all triendly to I each other, and they didn't mind my ! presence. "Did you hear abont Sarah Lamb 7 asked one. "Goodness ! No !" answered the other. "Well, Sarah's got her pay, I tell vou !" continued the first. "\ou know "she was a whole year trying to catch that rcd-hcadcd widower. \N ell, she finally married him; and what do you think f They say that he sueers at her ?actually uses oaths? when things go ; wrong, keeps her Ironi going to church ; is set'agaiiist company, and won't let : her use above two eggs in a sweet cake !" i "Mon-sterous !" exclaimed the others, i There was a moment ot silence, aud then one of the trio spoke up. . "Did you know that Mrs. Lancey l had a new empress cloth dress ? "You don't say!" exclaimed the others. . e "Yes, I do ! I know for a fact ? tor she wore it past our house the other day That dress never cost less than I seven dollars? the bare cloth; and there's the making and trimmings , thrown in. Just think of a woman iu her circumstances going to such an ex pense; why, if I hadu t seen it with uiy own eyes, I could ut believe it. "It is awful !' exclaimed the otheis. "And the worst of it is; she seems to , hold her head so high !" continued the first. "I've heard that her grandfather i had to go to the poor-house when he broke his leg, and yet she holds her head up with the best of us ! Of course I don't want to backbite any one it isn't mv nature to talk behind people s back-but I will say that, I shouldnt wonder if such extravagance brought that family to want tor bread betore spring comes!" Nothing was said for the next live minutes, and then one of the two ex claimed : "Land sakes ! but I'd almost forgot ten to tell you Lizzie Thorburn has a new hat !" ' What, another? "Yea, another! she wore it to chinch last Sunday! Think ot lhat a gi.l having three hats in one year ! % "Shameful !" they cried in a chorus. "I don't know what the world is com ins to," continued the first. "W hen 1 was a girl, one hat had to last me j seven years; while now a girl wants at least two a year, if not three. I tell you, when I sat in church last Sunday, and saw Lizzie come slipping in with thai new hat (must have cost Three dollars at least) I felt queer. The late of the sinful people Sodom and Gomor iah came to my mind in a second; and I shouldn't have been surprised if Liz zie had been stricken then right down! They pondered over it tor two 01 three minutes, and then one of them replied: . "So, Mary Jane Doolittle is dead is she?" . "Yes: poor thing, was the reply, "dead and buried a week ago. Han nah was at the funeral, and she says that Doolittle never shed a tear? never even blew his nose!,' "lie did'nt?" . "Xo, he didn't! Hannah watched him all through, and she says he has a heart like a stone. It' he should be arrested as her murderer, I shouldn't be the least surprised. Poor woman.! I met her only last August, and I could- see that she was killing herself. I didn t ask her right ?out about it, hut conld understand that Doolittle was a cold hearted wretch. lie didn't have much to say; but just one remark he made convinced me of his cold heartedness. He askd for soap to wash himself, and when she handed him a piece he looked at it, sneered like, and says he : \M?ry Jane, you mustn't buy any more yeller soap!" "Did he say that?'' "lie certainly did. Ill go before any court in the laud and swear to it? I had to get ott; the train then, and missed further information.

A Beautiful Incident. On a beautiful summer's day, a clergy man was called to preach in a town in Indiana to a youug Episcopalian con gregation. At the close of his dis course, he addressed his young hearers in such words as these: Learn that the present life is a pre paration lor. and has a tendency to eternity. The present is linked to the future throughout creation, in the veg etable, in the Animal, and in the mural | world. As is the ^eed, so is the fruit; I as is the egg, so is the fowl, as is the ? boy, so is the man; and as is the ration | al being in this world, so will he bo in j the next: Dives estranged from God I in the next: and Knoch walking with God here, is Knoch walking with God in a calm .and belter world. I beseech you, live, then, for a blessed eternity. | Go to the worm you tread upon, and I learn a lesson of wisdom. The very caterpiller seeks the food that fosters it for another and similar state, and, more wisely than man, builds its own sepul cLer, from whence, in time, by a kind of resurrection it comes forth in a new creature iu almost angelic ionn. An<J now that which crawled Hies, and that which fed on comparatively gross food, sips the dew that revels in the rich pas tures an emblem of that paradise where flows the river of lite, and grows the tree of life. Could the caterpiller have been diverted from its proper element and mode of life, it it had never attained the butterfly's splendid form and hue it had perished a worthless worm. Con sider her ways and be wise. Let it not be said that ye are more negligent than worms, and that your reason is less available than their instinct. As often as the butterfly flits across your path, remember that it whispers in its flight, "Live for the future." With this the preacher closed his dis course; but to deepen the impression, a butterfly, directed by the hand which guides alike the sun and an atom in its course, fluttered through the church, as if commissioned bv heaven to repeat the exhortation. There was neither speech nor language, but its voice was heard saying to the gazing audience, "Live for the future." Unwuittkx Sidk ok Great Mf.x. ? No doubt Moses snarled and got angry when he had a severe cold in his head, and if a fly bit his leg while he was in the dessert why should we suppose he did not jump and use violent language, and rub the sore place? And Ca-sar ? isn't it tolerably certain he used to be come furious when he went up stairs to ijet his slippers in the dark and found that Calphurnia had shoved them under the bed so that he had to sweep around them widely with a broom-handle. Be Independent, ? Don't hang round and wait for somebody else to go ahead. Break your own path. Do what you want done, yourself. Don't put off to day's work until to morrow iu the hope that it w ill be done for you. If you want to succeed, take off your gloved and collous your own hands on the plow handles. It you are a woman, and Bridget goes off in a huff, be independent, and wash your own dishes, and scrub your own floors, and laugh in her face when she orncs back, expecting to be received, with opeu arms. There is nothing liko showing fat*?, even if it be fate in the shape of an ill tempered Bridget, that you are inde pendent of it, and can get on without it. When people find you don't want any of their help they are always eager to help you. Things that you do not stand in need of will be offered you freely. When you see a duty before you, do it, and dont stand shivering on the blink, for fear somebody will say some thing about it. What matters if Mrs. A. says you are a fool, and Mrs. B. ex presses the opinion that there is some thing wrong in your upper story! What they say does not alter it. Don't a?k everybody's advice about everything. Have pluck enough to decide for yourself. If you want to buy a bnshel of corn don't spend a day run ning about asking X. Y. and Z. where you had better buy, or if you hadn't b.'tter wait until giain falls. Don't be a slave as to what anybody else is going to say abeut you. If you have enemies, and of course you have, unless you are a born idiot, let them fling out at yen. Show the world by your daily life tliat your enemies have lied. Live lying slanders down. Lift up your head and be independent of them. Have no confidants and go be tween. Mutual friends are disastrous failures anywhere outside of Charles Dickens' novels. In all matters of right and wrong judge for yourself; decide for yourself; stand for yourself. Be independent. Do not cast your burdens upon others. Greene, in which Andrews and Greene were killed almost instantly and Fitzgerald danger ously wounded. The difficulty origina ted about the Hibernian meeting on Monday night, at which Andrews was elected President. Fitzgerald claimed still t<5 be president of the Hibernian Society, and denounced the election of Audrews as a farce. Greene took ex ception to Fitzgerald's remarks, and threatened to draw a weapon, but Fitz gerald drew first and shot Greene through the heart. Andrews then shot Fitzgerald, acd Fitzgerald in turn shot. Andrews, the ball piercing Andrews' skull at the top of the forehead. The affair caused intense excitement, as all were well known citizens. Andrews was the head of the firm of Andrews tfc Brother, and was ptesident of the How- j aid Association, after Mr. Rock wood's death last summer. Mr. W. L. Greene was a clerk to Andrews' brother. Fitz gerald is a prominent lawyer, and was a Republican State District Attorney. Andrews #and Greene were natives of Vicksburg, and Fitzgerald of Jackson, Miss. [By request. ] THE LO.IG AGO. Ota ! a wonderful itrMm is the river Time, As It runs through the realms of tears. With a faultless rhythm and a musical rhyme And a broader sweep and a surge sublime. As It blends In the ocean of years ' How the winters are drifting like flakes of snow And the summers like buds between. And the years In the sheaf, how they come and they go On the river's breast with Its ebb and Its flow, As It glides In tbe shadow and sheen. There's a magical isle up the river Time, Where tbe softest of airs are playing. There's a cloudless sky and a tropical clime. And a song as sweet as a vesper chime. And the Junes with the roses are staying. And the name of this isle is the "Long Ago," And we bury our treasures there; There are brows of beauty and bosoms of snow. There are heaps of dust? oh! we loved them so? There are trinkets and tresses of hair. There are fragments of songs thit nobody sings. There are parts of an Infant's prayer. There's a lute unswept and a harp without strings, There are broken vows and pieces of rings. And the garments our loved used to wear. There are hands that are waved when the fairy shore By the Utful mirage Is lifted In air. And we sometimes hear through the turbulent roar Sweet voices we heard in the days gone befort, When the wind down the river was fair. Oh ! remembered for aye be that blessed Isle, All the day of our life until night ; And when evening glows with Its beautiful smite, And our eyes are closing In slumbers awhile. May the greenwood of soul be iu sight.

"You seem comfortably sure of her, Tom." "Well, why not, mv dear Jack, when I've only to ask, ami the little lady's mine? I'm immensely taken with her, but I've hung ofl' about ? " The dip of advancing oars d re .v tied ' the rest of the sentence, but Miss Daisy Campbell in her hammock behind the alders had heard enough to destroy her peace. Fearful of betraying her pres ence by thu movement of a linger, the girl lay rigid as marble, watching with ? strained eyes two fragrant blue wreaths I of smoke gliding past iter retreat, till ^ through an opening in the bushes fur- , ther lip the brook sho caught a fleeting l glimpse of a bircli canoe beneath the ! smoke, and of the smokers, two gay ' , sun burned youths with guns ami fish ing-rods. Tom Raymond sat in the stern, tall, handsome Tom, who had but now boasted of his easy conquest of herself. In that moment of wounded pride and fierce indignation Miss Daisy thought that she could have cheerfully seen him drown. " 'Oh, she's a daisy,' hummed Jack McKeen; and ns the mocking tenor smote Iter ear the quivering listener thought she could have seen J ack drown, too? the saucy, idle tell tale! Why need he proclaim to the birds of thu air and the fishes of the water that the lady in question, Tom's little lady to be had for i the asking, was no other than herself, Mrs. Blunt's city niece, little Daisy j Campbell ? How indelicate, outrageous I And yet the song hurt her far less than Tom's words. If Tom, Tom Ray mond, could sing so lightly of her, why might not Jack sing what lie pleased, and all Oakland listen? So that was the way Tom was iti the habit of talk ing about her I She had heard before that young men by themselves were ex cessively free in discussing their lady friends, and now she had proof of the fact. Unmannerly, detestable creatures, especially Tom ! "'I've only to ask, and the little lady's mlue,' those were his very words," moaned hapless little Daisy, hiding her hot face among the hammock cushions in an agony of humiliation. She had always felt that If Tom had a fault it was self-conceit, but she wouldn't have believed he could be so conceited as this. What had she said or done to warrant his boastful assertion? She would challenge Aunt Abby, she would challenge Tom's sister, to say that she had ever been silly with Ton, If there had been any silliness, it had been on his side, unless? truthful Daisy winced at the recollection? unless? well, perhaps she did let Tom hold her hand an instant longer than necessary the day he helped her over the fence, and she wished she had not clung to him in the thunder-storm. But at eigh teen what girl likes to be a prude? Though, for that matter, had she not more than once during their summer's acquaintance snubbed Tom for trying to make love to her? Still, he'd only to ask, and the little lady was his. That was his version of the story, and he had gloated over it to Jack. Daisy lifted her tousled brown head defiantly, and sat bolt-upright. "I won't be crushed? I will not !" she cried aloud, dashing her tears right and : left. "I'll go to Pinafore to-night just as if I'd heard nothing, and if hu chooses to ask for the little lady, why, j he may. She's sure of her own mind at last. She'll have her answer ready." Springing from the hammock, Miss Daisy walked with martial tread | through the garden into the kitchen to help Aunt Abby shell the peas for dinner. "You must have been lying in the sun, child," said that lady, glancing up from the pan in her lap. "It's bad for ! your eyes and bad for your complexion, j I don't believe that's a good place for ! the h.immeck." "It's a horrid placc," replied Daisy, falling savagely to work. "I'm going toaskAbrain to hang it where it was before." Abram was the Intermittent help of

the Blunt establishment, who carried on the farm and came night and morn ing to milk the cow. From the day she became a visitor in the household he had been Miss Daisy's willing slave, and now that Mr. Blunt was tempora rily absent, the honest servitor took It upon himself to look in at odd hours "to see if Miss Blunt and that posy-faced little niece of hern needed doing for." "Maybe fresh buttermilk will help that sun-burn," pursued Mrs. Blunt, still misinterpreting the cause of Miss Daisy's heightened color. "I'd try it. You'll hate to go to the falls a? red as a hollyhock." "1 hate to leave you alone so late in the evening, auntie," said Daisy, throwing a handful of empty pods at the chickens at the door stone. "I'm afraid you'll be nervous about the tramp that called this morning." "Xonsense, my dear; I'm not <me ot' the nervous sort. 1 always stay by my self nights when your uncle goes to his lodge meetings. It I get tired and sleepy, I lock the doors ami go to bed. When I lie on my good ear I can't hear a sound, you know, and your uncle can come in without waking me." "But how does he get inV" "Oh, he takes a key; we have two for the front door. There's the extra one over the clock. You'd l?etter have it to night; then, if I don't feel like sitting up for you, I won't. You won't be likely to get home before twelve." By twilight Miss Daisy's crimson had softened into sea-shell pink j Aunt Abby flattered herself that she had never seen the child handsomer than w hen, in filmy j draperies, sh? floated down the piazza steps to Tom Raymond's waiting phae ton. "The infatuated hoy looks as If he | was beholding an angel from heaven, ^ j muttered the pleased lady, who dearly loved Tom. But she said, prosaically : "Do drive carefully, Tom. Daisy, did you take the key?" "Yes, Auntie; it's in my pocket." "Pocket?? can they put pockets in i sea-foam?" laughed Tom, tucking the ( linen lap-robe about the young lady's billowy flounces. "I feel myself quite Inadequate to the care of this fluffy ele gance, Mrs. Blunt, 1 do assure you." "But it's his; lie has only to ask and It's all his," thought Miss Daisy, scorn fully, as she bade her aunt good-bye. In the whole region roundabout there was not a lovelier drive than this five miles between Oakland and Oakland Falls. Taking it by moonlight, on a perfeet July evening, with a fascinating young lady by his side, and h spirited horse obedient to his will, Tom Ray mond mentally acknowledged that the conditions were favorable for enjoy- ; uient. He had been planning this tete a-tete for days; indeed he had gone so far as ?o formulate certain momentous speeches to be delivered on this occa sion, but with the strongest desire to lead the conversation into sentimental channels, he was continually batfl.'d by nn intangible something In Miss Daisy's manner. He spoke of a lovely bird he was mounting especially for herself, and she discoursed of the swallows In Aunt Abby's chimney; he hinted at man's craving for afTection, and she de plored Abram's craving for drink; he i quoted Aurora Leigh, and she cited Mother Goose. She nang nasally like . Deacon Shed, mimicked 'Squire Eddy's late Fourtli-of-Jtily oration, and, In a word, was as captivating, frivolous and reckless as a heavy-hearted girl well could he. As she passed Grace Ray mond in the hall, that young lar'y whis pered to Jack McKeen that Dai?y Camp bell was the belle of the audience.

"With one exception, of course," amended gallant J ark. Proud, sensitive little Daisy! She pretended to listen to the mtnio; hut from Lord Admiral to Little Buttercup the entire company seemed to her to he chanting, "Pre only to ask, to ask, to ask? I've only to ask for the little lady." Her very fan kept time to this refrain. She was thankful when the opera end ed. For all that, on the homeward drive she wished herself back in the hall. It was so hard to meet Tom's lover-like gaze with indifierence, to school her warm, wayward heart against his tenderness, so precious but yester day ! At flnt she strove bravely to maintain her former vivacity, hut her liveliest sallies fell unheeded. The slo gan was In the air. Daisy knew Torn had something particular to say. Ah, well, for that matter, so had she. Clasp ing her cold little hands together reso lutely, she waited ih silence. "Daisy, I've been think! up ? " "Dangurous symptoms, my young friend; let the doctor prescribe." "I'm going hack to the medical school next week, Daisy." "So soon?"? in a tone of coo! regret. "And I want to ask you, Daisy ? " "I've only to ask, and the little lady's mine," prompted taunting memory, kindling in DaUy'seyesadangerousfire. Notwithstanding his vaunted assur ance, Tom hesitated over the vital ques tion, fidgeting with the reins till th? horse rebelled and started off at a can ter. Having soothed the animal's ruf fled feelings, Tom began afresh. "I)ai?y?" "Well, Mr. Raymond?" "Now, Daisy, you promised to call me Tom." "Did I ? It isn't half so pretty a name as Mr. Raymond. "I'm glad if you like my name, Daisy. I wish you'd lake it to keep." "You're too generous, Tom. I'm not a strong-minded woman. Shouldn't want to be called Mr. Raymond." "Don't tease, Daisy. You know what I mean. I'm just dying to make you Mrs. Raymond, my beloved little wife." "I should have to die if yon did, Tom. 'Beloved wives' are always under tomb stones." "Do be serious, Daisy. You must know I've been in love with yon from the first day I saw you." "Ah," thought Daisy, with curliog lip, "If I hadn't played eavesdropper,

what a happy little simpleton I might j be !" ''Serious, Torn ?" she said aloutf: ' "I am literal ly serious as the grave. You've made my stay at Oakland very pleasant; you've given nic glorious drives and sails and I'm no end obliged. But in tegard to this new favor you propose to eon fer upon me. no, no. Tom ; I must decline it, thank you." "Favor! Really. Daisy, I fail to see how I've provoked that sarcasm." "Let's not talk about It, Tom. Ah, we're nearly home." "But, Daisy, I must talk about it," pleaded Tom, seizing her hand. "Do von mean you never can care forme? Oh, Daisy, Daisy, don't say it!" His manner was eager, his tone peril* ous sweet, though now ?t the door, he made no movement to alight; it med as if he could not let Daisy go till she had promised to love him. "Don't be absurd, Tom,,' cried ?he, almost beside herself with the fear lest she might yield in spite of everything. "I'll never marry yon? never ! never! Why, Tom Raymond, I'd a* soon marry that hen-coop !" To do Daisy justice, she hardly knew what she said. Bent on convincing her overwise lover that she was not hi? to be had fur the asking, she h&d hurled the hen-coop into her sentence simply for emphasis. It wounded Tom beyond all expression. To ofler himself to a young lady a? a husband, only to be re jected by her as a hen-coop ? this he felt was too much for tinman nature to bear. Without further dallying he helped Daisy dismount, and drove away with a curt adieu. Wretched Miss Daisy gazed after him with lack-lustre eyes, feeling as spirit less as a glass of yesterday's soda water. How angry lie must have beeu to have left her to unlock the door for herself! And, oh, dear, what ailed the key! Would it never, never turn ? Oh, for strong tlngers! ? Tom's lingers! Pres ently It dawned upon Daisy that there must be some obstruction in the lock. By the aid of the moon she peeped in at the key-hole and saw the trouble. In locking the door on the inside Aunt Abby had forgotten to remove the key ! Daisy pulled the hell frantically till the pealed echoed through every room, pulled it till she broke the wire, but no sound of answering footstep! came. Far away in the north chamber Aunt Abby was lying on her good ear, sleeping the sleep of the innocent. "She never hears anything when she's on her left side," groaned Daisy, "and she may not turn over f<?r the nieht. Ob, what shall 1 do? What shall I do?"

Striving-. I started on a lonely road. A few companions with me went, Some fell behind, some onward strode, Bui all on one high purpose bent : T* live f?r Nature, finding truth In beauty and the shrines of art ; To consecrate our Joyous youth To alms outside the common mark. 1 turned aside and lingered long To pluck a rose, to hear a bird, To muse while listening to the song Of brooks through leafy coverts heard ; To live In thoughts that brought no fame Or guerdon from the thoughtless crowd To toil for ends that could not claim j The world's applauses coarse and loud. ( But still, though oft I bind my sheaf In fields my comrades have not known, j Though art is long and life is brief, And youth has now forever flown : . I would not lose the raptures sweet, Nor scorn the toil of earlier years; | Still would I climb with eagerfeet. Though towering height on height appears. A Night Watch in Algeria.

Only those who have experienced it can realize the excitement caused by witnessing a hand-to-hand conflict be tween two savage, untamed beasts. I have witnessed bull lights in Mexico and seen a python crush the life out of a ch I f in South America, but nevergazed on a more thrilling episode than on one hot Algerian nightat a water pool about 200 miles in the interior. Beside the pool were several trees of fair size, in the branches of one of which had been placed a small platform hidden among the clustered leaves, from which hiding place it was convenient to shoot any animal that might come to the pool to drink during the night. Thither re paired, one evening soon after sundown, Maecovoy and myself, accompanied by his Arab servant, a young fellow named Abilla, n ho bore our spare guns and acted as general factotum to us both on expeditions of this nature. It is difficult for me, in my cooler moments, to climb a tree, and the smooth straight stem prove J extremely troublesome to swarm. How ever, with the help of Mac and Asilla, I managed it and secured * comfortable perch. They followed with great facil ity, being both slight, active men, and at once made the guns ready. The moon rose gradually, and I had a good opportunity to study perfect si lence. Nothing can be more deeply si lent than a still night in the Desert. As therp is little or no vegetation on those vast oceans of laud there is no insect life, and for several hours after the moon rosti absolute silence reigned. We did not apeak. There was no wind. It seemed as if there was no living thing in that widespread expanse of country. I was beginning to feel sleepy and nod frequently, when a prolonged roar sounded close at han J. In an instant we were wide awake, and grasped our guns nervously. At the next instant the roar was answered from a location immediately beneath us. On looking down we saw a lioness lying on her belly, head between her paws, and her long tail waving luxuriously to and fro. She looked like a huge cat enjoying some pleasurable sensation. Almost in stantly a third "Woof! woof !" sounded atour backs. "Gad, Doc!" breathed Mac, "we are in for a bay to-night!" and a moment later two magnifll'int males stepped slowly and majestically into view. The female continued to purr and wave her tail gently. As soon as the two lions spied each other they prepared for action. Slowly ami carefully they neared each other, the lioness meanwhile watching them as a cat docs a mouse. Closer and closer they drew, while we, spellbound, reserved our fire to witness the terrible duel that was impending.

And now they crouch and with mu tual roars of rage sprint; at each other, and, meeting in mid-leap, fall, biting and tearing to the earth. We can hear their bones crush between their power ful jaws, like eggshells beneath a man's boot heel. The lioness, maintaining her tranquil attitude, watches '.ho conflict, as it seemed to my excited eyes, with a devilish smile on her face. Over and over they rolled while the sickening sound of champing bones filled the air, mingled with their frantic roaring and the movement of their bodies as they thrashed through the whirling sand. By this time my nerves were so wrought up that 1 could stand the terrific specta cle no longer, and, taking deliberate aim at (lie lioness, behind her shoulder blade, I let fly. Above the rumble of the smooth bore sounded the shriek of the lioness as the heavy ball crashed into her vitals. The two duelists at once ceased their encounter, and as one of them turned he received Maccovoy's rifie bullet in the head, the missile pierc ing the hollow over the eye, where the skull is weak, and entering the brain. Death was almost instantaneous. The other male, with a thundering "woof!" gave a mighty spring and landed half way up the tree trunk, nearly shaking us l'rom our perch, Asilla hastily dis i charged one of our spars guns slap-bang , into his face, but probably the charge oftlv grazed him, for, falling back, he disappeared into the darkness toward w here the moans and cries of the lioness grew fainter and fainter every moment. A visitor in t li** valley of the Yose niite in California says that one im portant fact to be observed there, but which is never mentioned in the guide hooks, uimI seldom in newspaper cor respondence, is that the women visi tors who explore the place to any ex tent do so on horseback and ride astride. The steeps are so abrupt that a woman who attempts them perched unnaturally on one side of a beast is sure to come to grief. and coming to grief on mountain trails where the precipices are a mile high is a matter of life and death. Women must eith er leave the glories of the Yosemite unseen or they must employ all the advantages which nature has given them. And really, when you come to think of it. why shouldn't women ride astride as well as men? Is there any reason against it except conventional custom? If there is any other reason, what is it? The materials used in the construction vary with the locality, hut he always selects a good, staple foundation. The lower parts of his den he makes of sticks, twig>. grasses, and so on. which he cements firmly with mud. He continues this until he reaches a point above high water mark, and then his work become more careful and of a much finer quality. The best twigs and the soft est grasses are used with great dex terity and success. If the colony is a large one there are various rooms in the den. and they Hrc invariably clean ami handsome. And the rat is a~ prudent a? he is fa>tidious. Not only is his den a central hall with side dormitories and extra rooms for extra occasions, but the outlets are iu four or five different directions, and are far away from the den proper, so that the inhabitants mav be protected against surprise and against the pre datory visits of th< ir hworn enemies, minks axul w ease la This muskrat engineering, while interesting in it self. is very injurious to the land* where it occurs. Sometimes immense burrows, forty or fifty feet long, are made, ami ajjain tunnels are dug through marsh hills, and frequently water rushing through these hole* en larges them until they assume danger ous proportions. Men have lost their live> by falling through them* under ground places, and only the experi enced trappers feel any security when venturing upon the marshes where the muskrals live. About ~?0,000 probably more musk rat hides will go from the Cam bridge, Md., region this year to New York. Formerly, when the fur was fashionable, the hides easily brought as much as '>0 cents each, but nowa days 10 or 15 is about all they are worth. "The average man will say that he would not eat a muskrat for flO, but the average man does not know what he is talking about. When handled well, the rat makes a thoroughly palatable dish, and this statement is made from experience. The cleanly habits and the pure, wholesome food of the muskrat makes him one of the most desirable of all wild animals for table use. An ordinary cook, how ever, will generally get nothing from a rodent except a failure and a bad odor. If the musk bag is cut and the scent is imparted to the meat it be comes worthless. The most success ful cook I ever knew is a colored woman whddoesn't know a letter in thealpha bet. but who has mastered every mystery of the kitchen, and she can get up a dish of muskrat that will turn the worst scoffer into an enthusi ast. I asked her how she did it. She skinned the animal very carefully, washed it well in fresh water; soaked it for several hours iu salt water, and then hung it where it would get the benefit of colli air. The longer it freezes the better It gets. After this she ' ither stews it, or, if she wants it fried, parboils It and friesit afterward. An old Maryland gentleman, who is somewhat of an epicure, says that between turkey and muskrat he will take muskrat all the time. The way the Indians cooked this animal was either to roast it on coals or boil it with corn.

A CHRISTMAS GREETING. A Merry Christmas ! May your cares in golden floods of joy be drowned ; Forget awhile your worldly wares. And send the brimming love-cups round. The feast is set. Come, young and old, And laugh awhile at changeless fate ; Secure within the Christmas fold. Where watchful Love maintains the gate. Strong Love, that lives in spite of care. And laughs at time. The load of years. Our bitter strife, and cold despair. Our vain regrets, and idle tears. Are lost amid Love's cloudless light All fare alike beneath Love's sway. And all are welcome? none may slight The wayward sheep that seek to stay. All faro alike? the old and young. The rich and poor, the mean and great. From every land, of every tongue, For careful Love niak)>8 wide the Kate : And led by Love's far-reaching liglit They come? a vast unnumbered throng, Whose hearts are tuned, this Christmas night. To sing the endless Christmas souk. A CHRISTMAS BLESSING. "Lionel." Thin lingers Mattered un easily about a frayed button on an equally frayed and worn overcoat, and a woman's anxious eyes looked deprecatingly into the husband's face. "What is it, Mary?" his tone was gentle, with an undercurrent of sad ness and despondency in it. "Christ mas comes to-morrow, Lionel." She did not look in his face now, but closely scrutinized the frayed button as if it were the absorbing object of her thoughts. "1 know it, Marv."' "Could ? could? you let me have a little money, Lionel? For the chil dren, you know, dear ? we have never let the day go past without something for them." "And we must not now," he said; "they will never be young but once, poor things." He took out u worn wallet from his pocket. "I have looked 'v. \U the old things in search of bits to make over into garments or fancy things for them," she continued apologetically, "but every thing is worn so close, Lionel. I try to be frugal and sav . ing." ller eyes were tilled with Wars now. "And you are, Mary. Where would we have been had it not been for your careful management? Will two dollars be enough. It is all 1 ha\e this morning. Heaven knows I wish I could make it twenty or a hun dred?there is no limit to the deserts of the good wife you've been to me, Mary. Don't cry, dear, it takes all my courage and strength to see you unhappy." The faded face was pressed against the frayed button now in a vain at- 1 tempt to hide the hot tears which would come, and his worn glove, much too thin for the season, smoothed the thin gray hair tender ly. "Then I must not cry," she answer ed, looking up with a forced smile. "Yes, it will be enough? more than I had expected, but I feel so wicked to ask you for money when I know you have so little to spare me " Yes, debt was the skeleton which danced, not only in the closet but all over the house, in this humble home, and Mary went back to her work, her face drawn up thoughtfully as she calculated just how many pennies could be spared for this or that, and balanced the difference between the strictly useful and more childlike but less material gifts. Two dollars after all was such a little drop in the bucket of necessities, to say nothing of the ornamental or the beautiful. It was not a debt of carelessness or of ex travagance, she could scarcely have born the self-reproach and the shame j of it if it had been, but was the nat ural result of long years of sickness and reverse. Lionel Webb in his younger days had just escaped with his life from an attack of spinal meningitis which ha.l resulted in a partial disability for life. He was very ambitious, and though obliged to accept work which had as little of manual labor in it as possible, still he did it often when stronger men would have been in bed with a physician in attendance, did it in such bodily tor ture that he hardly realized what he was doing. Mary had hershare of sickness, too; the anxiety and care atlendant on Lionel's disability wns enough to break a women of iron, which she was not, and in addition to it all, three darling children had sickened and died. Lionel had secured a new situation of late? he was growing better with years and could now take up a dif ferent cla.-s of work, and his present employer was a man of large wealth, employing many clerks in his gr>-at business. All this day Lionel worked in a maze of perplexity and regret. Mary's fac**, with the tears on it. was ever before him. To-night was Christmas eve. and all day long a procession of richly dressed mothers and fathers thronged the store buying, buying, from full purses, while Mary, his true, faithful wife, whose seventeen years of married life had been one long struggle with toil and care, had only a painful two dollars with which to do her Chrii>tmas shopping, and it grieved him .j the very heart's core. The rush was orer now, and in a half hour more the great establish ment would be closed, when an errand boy touched his arm. "Mr. Dale would like to see you in the private office, sir." he said respectfully. Lionel's h?-art sank in his bosom like lead. Could it be that in addition to his other misfortunes he was going to lose his situation? This engage ment had been provisionary, and his employer had made no sign as to whether his service was acceptable. He crawled rather than walked to the office in his nervous dread, for the past had been so persistently unkind to him that he was coming to dread : the future.

"Sit down. Sit down, sir," said Mr. Dale, carefully. Lionel took a sent near the pros perous business man. who noticed, as he did so, the look of care and de jection on his employe's thin face. "It has been my custom, sir. for some years to make my employes a little present on Christmas eve." he proceeded geniallv. a- he took a bill from his lesk drawer and laid it in Lionel's hand. "I presume you can find a use for it: or if you cannot, no doubt the good wife can, hey!" Lionel looked at the bill in dumb astonishment; if an angel had come in and clapped him on the shoulder he would not have been more sur prised. for it was a fifty-dollar bill. "But, sir," he stammered, "1 have beeTi witli you so short a time, 1 hare not merited such consideration." "That'* all right, sir. You'll have ample opportunity to make it up in your future years of service, for 1 do not intend to part witli so faithful an assistant." There was more in tiie manner than the kind deed itself, and Lionel's heart bounded with gratitude. He thought of Mary and of the many, many uses the money could be put to, warm blankets, the winter cloak Mary had needed for years, and? but his face fell. There was a dunning letter in his pocket at the moment which lie had concealed from Slary ? from the holder of a note against him fur fifty dollars and peremptorily de manding payment. No, no, it would be wrong to ap propriate one dollar of the gift for personal needs. Mr. I>ale wai a shrewd reader of faces, and Lionel's thin, anxious face had appealed to his sympathies strongly since he had entered the office, and he noted the change of expression. "What is it. Webb ?" he said, kind ly. "You look depressed and troub led."' As Lionel heard the kind voice and looked into the kind face an impulse came to him to tell this man his troubles. It was so hard to bear it alone and to wear a smiling face over a heart so filled with anxious care, 1 ami hardly knowing what he said, he poured out his story of the past, of Mary and of her pitiful shopping to day. "It hurts me so, Mr. Dale,'' he said, in conclusion, "that I cannot use even a dollar of your generous gift for her." "How much now would cover this entire indebtedness?" asked Mr. Dale. He was drumming thoughtfully on his desk and looking keenly at Lio nel, not in blame or in doubt of the truth of his story, but in making an effort to put himself in another's place "Fifteen hundred dollars would pay every dollar." Mr. Dale reflected? in the light of his millions the sum seemed a very trifle; yet here was a man whose strength and happiness were being wasted for the lack of it. "What would you say, then, if I should loan you this money and let you work it out gradually as you can afford it?" "Say, sir ! I should work on wings, it would make my heart so light." "Then put on your wings," returned Mr. Dale, smiling, "for we'll have the matter arranged at an early date. And now go home and spend this money for Mary and thechildren with a ch ar conscience." ! i Mother Lode Copper Mines - . >mpany is planning to develop its property on an extensive scale next year, according to information given the Dally Times by Superintendent W. Bertram Hancock, who is spend ing the holidays in Cordova with his family. At present fifty-seven men are em ployed at this copper mine, develop ing on four different levels below the mouth of the tunnel and stoping out the high grade ore. Recently about 100 tons of this metal was transport ed over the trail to the Copper River & Northwestern railway to the Ta coma smelter. This ore runs from 57 to 60 per cent copper. Will Instal New Mill. Arrangements have been made to instal a mill on the property next spring, with a capacity of 100 tons per day; a hydro-electric plant of 200 horse power for the mill. and also a compressor. An eighty foot dam will also be built, and a wagon road con

structed from the mine to McCarthy for the hauling of the ore during the summer months, a distance of four teen miles. Owing to the high water in McCarthy creek in the summer. caused by the melting snows and gla ciers at its head, the partly con can structed trail down the creek only be used by pack train and saddle horses for about eight months of the year, but after the freeze-up heavy freight sleds become available. $3,600,000 Worth Ore Blocked Out. The whole of the mining operations so far carried on in the Mother Lode mine are practically confined to the Marvellous, Godfrey and Hero claims, and consists of 5,415 feet of tunnels, crosscuts. drifts. etc. Since the erec tion of a tramway the work of explor ation and development has been car ried on expeditiously. The ore body follows the dip of the bedding planes in the limestone, and the main body varies from six inches to 29 1-2 feet, likewise the composition of the ore.

which in places may be all copper glance and in others a mixture of covellite, azurite and malachite, with considerable exide of iron. It is es timated that there is $3,600,000 worth of ore blocked out. and tonnage broken in stopes and on the dump. Where the Work Has Been Done. The property consists of seventy lode and placer claims. located in 1907, and subsequent years by Oscar Haglund. Oscar Sall and John Smith, and embraces an area of about 1,300 acres of ground in the Chitina mining district. These locations are for the most part in Marvellous and Indepen dence gulches, western tributaries to McCarthy creek, thirteen to fourteen miles above its mouth, where it flows into the Kennecott river. The Mar vellous, Godfrey and Hero claims, upon which most of the mining has been done, are all at the head of Mar vellous gulch, at an elevation of from 5,820 to 6,734 feet above sea level. The Marvellous claim is 3,191 feet due

east from the Bonanza mme, and one and a quarter miles southeast from the Jumbo mine, both properties of the Kennecott Copper Corporation. Occurrence of Copper Ore. The ore bodies occur as replace ments of green or of limestone, or as filling in cavities developed along fis sures, fault places, sheer zones and joints. or bedding planes m green stone or limestone. Aggregates of copper minerals are far more com mon in the greenstone than the lime stone. but the largest deposits that have been discovered up to the pres ent are in the limestone. The deposits of the Bonanza and Jumbo mines oc cur in the limestone within 90 feet of its contact with the greenstone, whereas the Mother Lode deposit is at least 900 feet above the contact which seems to indicate that copper occurs in nearly all parts of the for mation and that the formation of ore bodies is dependent only on favorable conditions of supply and deposition.

From the period from August 1. 1915, to Sept. 1, this year, there was a total of 428 arrests and 307 convic tions. BEHIND THE SOMME FRONT, Sept. 29. — There never was a time when so little was known of the kai ser's movements as at present. When he decides upon a trip to some point on the front, it is kept as secret as possible, and if ever reported in the German press is delayed until the royal visitor is far away — perhaps on the other side of the empire. It is believed Emperor William visits the [ front more frequently 'than any other ruler. Recently correspondents visiting the southern section of the Somme front did not learn until well past midnight that the emperor at 9 a’clock on the morning of the day just breaking would review as many of the troops as could be assembled at a point a few miles back from the fighting line, but still’within sound of the guns. ' The correspondents - were on hand before the appointed time — and had a chance to see some manoeuvring that would have done credit to first line troops in peace time. On the dot of nine the companies drew up in parade formation on a broad level ground that yard of an was formerly a back ancient chateau. They formed three sides of a square, at one end of which was a military band and in the center the officers. Half an- hour after the appointed time the kaiser arrived in a lean, gray automobile. He sprang from the car with the vigor of a young man. He wore the helmet Of a general of in fantry, but the tall boots, coming in front high above the knee, of a cuir raster. He cast from his shoulders the long cape with a fur collar in which he is shown in his favorite pic tures, and with a stride of long steps, lifting each foot high from the ground, his majesty walked toward that end of the formation where the band stood. His standard bearers, who always walk behind with his flag, had their

work cut out for them as he strode ahead. At first he paused just a mo ment, greeted the general in command, bowed and saluted to the other offi cers, and then turned down the line. He walked as one attempting to go through a dewy pasture and still keep one's feet reasonably dry, with great high steps. After making the rounds of three sides of the square the emperor then turned and strode to the center to chat with the various high officers gathered there, and then began to pin orders and medals on the breasts of the chosen few. It was only at the conclusion of this ceremony that correspondents stand ing at a little distance had a chance to see his majesty at close range, and to get a good look at his seamed and lined but strong, healthy, vigorous face. After the decorating the kaiser walk ed to the roadway that leads by the chateau, then faced about and pared to review the troops. pre Most of them were new troops, probably few had ever marched by their em peror before, and it was possible to detect some nervousness. But they paraded in the goosestep as bravely i and as stiffly as ever did a like set | of men on the Tempelhofer Feld. The commander made the custom ary address, in which he pledged loy alty to his majesty, and a firm deter mination to fight on. His voice rose and fell with emotion, and what he said obviously affected the emperor. The kaiser answered in a voice that from a distance was hard to under- j stand, though it was silver clear and more highly pitched than that of his general. The soldiers, however, could hear it, and their faces glowed as ' their emperor thanked them. ' The parade ended as abruptly as it i began. The emperor, hastily donning ' his fur collared cape, sprang back I ; into his gray limousine and was off

WASHINGTON, Feb. 14 (by Associ ated Press).—A statement issued by the state department yesterday an & non need that Secretary of State Robert Lansing had tendered his resignation to the President, and that the latter had accepted it, effective yesterday. It is learned that Mr. Lansing re signed after President Wilson had ac cused him of usurping the powers of President by calling a cabinet meet ing during President Wilson’s illness. Mr. Lansing denied that he intended to usurp power, and added that he be lieved the conferences were for the best interests of the nation, and were, proper and necessary because of the President’s condition. Mr Lansing stated that he would have been derelict, in his duty, if he had failed to act as he did. He there fore placed his resignation in the hands of the President, who accept ed. it. Quarrel Began at Peace Conference ' The state department has made pub lic a series of letters which passed be tween.the President and the secretary - of state. In one President Wilson said it had become known that the opinions of Secretary Lansing and himself dif fered dreadfully, and the administra tion had been embarrassed thereby. Mr. Lansing, in his final letter, said he was not unmindful that the con tinuance of the present relations '/as impossible, and said he had been con sidering the advisability of resigning since January of last year. The differences began at the peace conference, and had continued since. One of the chief causes of dissension was the government’s attitude toward Mexico. His last words here were that he was improving and his voice would not be impaired. Caruso’s repertoire in America in eluded the following: (Italian) “Aida,” “Rigoletto,” “La Boheme,” “L’Africaine,” Somnanbula,” “La Favorita,” “La Traviata,” “La “Les Huguenots,” “Fedora,” “Adrienne Le “Cavallieria Rusticana,” couvreur,’ "Pagliacci,” "L’Amore dei tre Re,” “Un Ballo in Maschera,’ ta” “Marta,” “L'Elisir "Lodolet d’Amore," “Manon Lescaut," "Madama Butter fly,” “La Fanciulla del West,” “Lu cia di Lammermoor,” “La Gioconda,” ',‘11 Travatore,” “Don Giovanni," “Germania," “Iris,” “Lucrezia Bor gia,” “Tosca,” “La Forza del Des tino.” (French) “Les Pecheurs de Perles,” “Armide,” “Faust,” “Julien,” “Le Prophete,” “Carmen,” “Samson et Delila," and “Manon.” The famous singer was the guest of honor at a silver jubilee celebra tion, on the 25th anniversary of his operatic debut in November 1919 at the Metropolitan at which prominent New Yorkers, including the mayor and other officials, spoke of his great artistic achievements. The appointment of fourth tea cher for Seldovia schools; the in clusion of Home Economics and Manual Training in study cours es; the acceptance of creden tials of Mrs. Mabel Shotter, res ide nt applicant for the position these were the outstanding an nouncements made by W. K. Kel ler, commissioner of education, as contained in his telegram re ceived by the local school board this morning. The appointment, effective at once, came as the result of repre sentations made by the local board, showing the need of the teacher. Decision was delayed due to the matter of funds. While the main office of the new appointee will be to relieve the work of the primary depart ment, the general work of the school is broadened to include home economics and manual training. Taking a moving picture of a belligerent bull moose at a dis tance of 20 feet, and shooting another with an antler spread of 70 inches, were two of the ex periences that gave James T. Swann of Tampa, Fla. added thrill-punches to his recent Alas ka hunt. Under the direction of Tony Martin, Seldovia guide, assisted by Zenas “Shorty Beach, Seldovia packer, Mr. Swann cov ered the west inlet district for Ko diaks, then recrossed the inlet for “Moose Val moose and sheep. ley,’’ a favorite district of Mr. Martin’s, was the scene of the latter hunt. While no bear trophy was ob tained, there were many excel lent chances for shooting game. But the hunter got more thrills from his moving pictures. Close range pictures were taken of the big brownies, one huge fellow proving himself rather an un comfortable close-up subject. Another fine length of film was devoted to two large black bears, cavorting about in bear-like fash ion. But the big thrill came when in answer to an imitative call from Guide Martin, a sturdy, average

sized moose came into the open and moved toward hunter and guide, with every indication of engaging in battle. The animal was not a sensational trophy, so Mr. Swann swung his camera into action and began to crank He continued to film un away. til the moose got within 20 feet, whereupon he hurried to cover. The 70-inch trophy was ob tained when a giant moose dashed into the open in answer to a chal lenge from a smaller adversary. But the took pretender one look at the newcomer and sped for the woods, leaving a clear field and a fair shot to the man from Florida. Besides excellent motion pic tures of mountain sheep, two fine specimens were obtained. Mr. Swann hunted out of Sel dovia in 1927 under the guid ance of Harry Lewis, with Martin as packer. A return hunt is planned, probably for next year. The big game hunter was an Anchorage-bound passenger on the M. S. Princess Pat Wednes day afternoon. He was on his way to Seward to catch a sailing of the Alaska S. S. Company for the outside.

RAILROAD ISSUES NEW TIME TABLE TO GOVERN FREIGHT TRAIN SCHEDULES Freight trains on the Alaska! Railroad are running according! to schedule effective May 16. I While this is not a new policy, for the railroad, it is an innova- j tion in that printed schedules have been issued for the guid a nee of government employees and every effort is being expend ed to follow them. Northbound freight trains are scheduled to leave Seward daily l at 30 p.m. except Sunday and southbound freights are due here i every day at 5:30 a.m. except Monday. In addition to these through trains there is a special termed “the Portage turn" pressed into service when there is sufficient freight here to warrant it. This Portage turn runs only as far as' Portage with its load which is then picked up by the regular train, as a much greater- ton nage can be carried on the com paratively level terrain from Por tage on in to Anchorage. As the period between April 1 and June 15 is the titawing per iod resulting in soft track con ditions as well as uneven and rough tracks, it is considered particularly important by rail road officials to keep the track in the best possible running con dition to insure safe operation of trains. Therefore three crews of men recruited from the Eklut na School were sent out last I week to repair ties on the rail- i road track. Four are working at the Eklutna tunnel, six at Divide and the remaining six are busy here in the Seward yard. Annual Stale Fair Meet Set for December 18

The annual membership meet ing of the Alaska State Fair, be held at 6 p.m. in Inc. will Grange hall tomorrow night. All members, and those interested in the development of the Alas ka State Fair who wish to become members, are urged to attend this important meeting. Sam Cotten, president, reminded valley resi dents that membership is but $1.00 per year and may be pur chased anytime right up to the meeting hour. Annual reports will be made by members of the board of di recors, including the annual audit which was recently completed. Several proposals will be made regarding changes in by-laws and policies of the corporation. In addition, directors will be named to fill vacancies on the board of directors and members are asked to consider persons for nomination, and if possible, to contact such persons prior to the meeting to determine whether or not they would accept an office if elected.

Paul Choquette of Hom er, chairman, Mrs. Gordon Lyon of Anchorage and Ben Fleenor of Ketchikan, members, represented the five-man commission at the hearing. Other members of the Commission are Henry Camerot, Fairbanks, and Robert Scott of Nome. Chamber Members Hear Borough System Explained Representative James Hurley spoke at the December 16 meet ing of the Mutanuska Valley Chamber of Commerce and an swered a number of questions pertaining to boroughs. He point ed out that during the past two weeks he has spoken on this subject to over 200 persons at six different meetings. It is hoped, Hurley stated, that various committees that have been named following some of the meetings, will come up with a unified proposal regarding borough boundaries in this area. These committees have been con tacting as many persons as pos sible and speaking to groups in an attempt to develop unified thinking regarding the borough.

'C. Ivan Branton of Palmer recently attended and partici pated in the 1961 winter meet ing of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers held in 12-15. December Chicago Branton is an agricultural en gineer with the Alaska Agri cultural Experiment Station. This is the first ASAE win ter meeting to include agricul tural engineering exposition, with the lates in farm equip ment and structure components on display. The winter meeting covered four major divisions; power and machinery, electric power and processing, farm structures, and soil and water conservation. More than 130 papers were read on agricultural engineer ing subjects.

The advantages of "systems engineering” for the modern farm was thoroughly covered at the meeting. Theme of the general session was "The Next 10 Years—Challenge and Re sponse," with _Newman A. Hall, chairman of the mechan ical engineering department at Yale University and Ross J. Martin, director of the engin eering experiment station at the University of Illinois, as principal speakers.

Student Council Conference Set For January 29-30 • 7 T The annual conference for high school student councils in Western Alaska will be held in Anchorage January 29 and 30. Meetings will be held in the West Anchorage high school building. All council members have been invited to partici pate. Members of each school council will participate in sep arate topic discussion groups. Specific problems of each school will lx? discussed by sep arate topic discussion groups, with each group representing one or more student from each school. Students will be permit ted to participate in their choice of topic discussions. The main points of each discussion will be summarized and presented to the general assembly. The purpose of the annual conference is to exchange ideas and policies of the Western Al aska schools.
